23 August
2371
Student Demonstration
TUESDAY, 23 AUGUST 1977
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
STUDENT DEMONSTRATION
Mr SPEAKER: This might be a convenient moment to refer to the incident of 3 August
in relation to a demonstration outside the House. Honourable members will recall that I
undertook to look into the circumstances that led to a member of the House being
prevented, or seeming to be prevented, by the police from addressing a group of demon-
strators in the grounds of these buildings on Wednesday, 3 August. Having received a
written statement both from the member and from the police inspector involved, I decided
that the most appropriate way to handle the incident would be to invite both to a discussion
in my office. First sickness, and then urgent public duty elsewhere, caused the date of the
meeting to be twice deferred, but we did get together on Friday last, 19 August.
I am happy to report that, as a result of the discussion, the member concerned, Mr T. J.
Young, graciously accepted Inspector Huggard's assurance that he had intended, but had
failed, to convey to Mr Young, not that he was requiring him to refrain from speaking, but
simply that he was limiting the number of speeches through loud hailers to the two that had
already been given. I shall be communicating these facts to the Minister of Police, and I
think the likelihood of a similar misunderstanding in future is remote.
I am aware of the extreme difficulty that sometimes arises in crowd control, and I do not
desire to comment adversely on the work of our police. But I should mention in passing that
the misunderstanding that arose in the present case would probably not have occurred if the
police officer concerned had not departed from my standing instructions that no sound
amplification equipment is to be used in Parliament grounds except on parliamentary
occasions or when the police, and only the police, have prior authority to use it for crowd
control.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): I thank you for the statement
and for the work you have undertaken to clear up this issue, but I think one matter is left
outstanding, and I should appreciate your comments on it. It relates to the right of members
of Parliament to address, with or without amplification, a body of people who have
assembled legitimately in the grounds of Parliament Buildings. There seems to be some
doubt on this matter. As it obviously comes under your area of control a clear statement of
your views on the matter should be given. That might preclude any difficulty.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I can certainly support the comment of
the Leader of the Opposition that we should be clear in this matter, but I want to raise a note
of caution. There have been occasions since I have been in the House when although a
member of Parliament might have an undoubted right to address a group of people
demonstrating outside Parliament Buildings it would be most unwise for him to do so. A
great deal of responsibility must rest with the individual member, and at times he should
probably forgo what could be seen to be political advantage in the interests of order. It is
very easy to exacerbate a situation of a type which the police may get outside the buildings,
and there are times when we would all agree that silence is the best way to deal with it.
Mr SPEAKER: As requested I will give this matter consideration. I shall not endeavour
to make a substantive statement today. I realise it is a difficult and sensitive matter, but I can
repeat that at no time have I given any instructions limiting the right of any member to speak
to a crowd assembled in the grounds. I think there are good reasons, which I shall perhaps
expand on slightly on a later occasion, why we should not encourage the gathering of crowds
here. We have had one or two unhappy incidents, particularly when a Governor-General
coming to open Parliament had to enter through a side door. However, I shall leave further
comment to a later occasion.

2372
23 August
Oral Answers to Questions
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Sales Tax on Vehicles
1. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Customs: What changes
are proposed in sales tax on vehicles, and in particular on buses?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): The proposed changes are as follows:
on 1 April 1978 sales tax on all vehicles other than motorcars and motor cycles will be
reduced from 40 percent to 30 percent; on 1 April 1979 sales tax on vehicles with a gross
vehicle weight exceeding 3.5 tonnes will be reduced from 30 percent to 20 percent, and this
will be further reduced to 10 percent on 1 April 1980; on 1 April 1980 the present decision
exempting the building and fitting of bodies to commercial vehicles will be withdrawn. The
body-building operation will attract the rate of tax applicable to the vehicle on which the
work is performed. Passenger service vehicles are already exempt from sales tax, and no
change is planned.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Livestock Incentive Scheme, Northland
2. Mr H. N. AUSTIN (Hobson), on behalf of Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei), asked the
Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation: How many Northland
farmers have taken advantage of the livestock incentive scheme instituted by the present
Government?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): I reply on behalf of the Minister in
Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation. The Rural Bank has received 425
applications under the livestock incentive scheme through its Whangarei office.
Mr Hunt: Does the Minister's reply mean that 425 applications have been approved?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I should have thought the honourable gentleman would know
that the word "received" means received. So far, 336 loans have been approved and 72
applications are at present being investigated. I should point out that the Whangarei office is
a sub-branch of the Auckland office and detailed statistics are not kept for that area.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Police Cars
3. Mr LANGE (Mangere) asked the Minister of Police: How many new police cars were
added to the force's fleet in the 3 years of the Labour Government, and how many have been
added since the present Government assumed office 21 months ago?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Police. In the 3-year term of a Labour Government the police vehicle fleet increased by 174.
This increase resulted from the vehicle programmes for 1973-74, 1974-75 and 1975-76. For
the financial years 1976-77 and 1977-78 when the vehicle programmes were approved by the
present Government the number of vehicles added to the fleet will be 52. However, approval
has been given by this Government to a 3-year motor vehicle programme which will provide
patrol cars in rural areas throughout New Zealand. The first 46 of these will be taken
possession of in September of this year, followed by 56 in 1978 and 32 in 1979. This new
policy has been warmly applauded by the New Zealand Police Association.
Mr Lange: Will the Minister confirm that since this Government took office no new
vehicles have been added to the police strength?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: In the 1976-77 year new vehicles have been added, and there is
approval for the 1977-78 year. For the year ending March 1978 a total of 794 vehicles will be
under police control, whereas under the previous Government there were only 742.
Mr Lithgow: Would the Minister agree that since December 1975 a better range and
style of car has been given to the police and that there is therefore a much better image than
there was in the previous 3 years under a Labour Government?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: That is a matter of opinion, but I would agree with the
questioner.
Mr Rogers: Will the Minister give the number of car replacements to coincide with the
same dates?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: I can give the total fleet. Under the previous Government it
was 742, and for the financial year ending 31 March 1978 the figure will be 794, or an


## p. 2373 (#11) ############################################

23 August
2373
Oral Answers to Questions
increase of 52 vehicles.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Is it not a fact that the replacement programme for cars under
this Government has fallen behind what it was under the Labour Government, and that this
will affect the operational efficiency of the police?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: I cannot agree with that. The total fleet number will be
increased and, in the light of economic circumstances I feel the Police Department is
receiving its fair share of new plant.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Crimes of Violence
4. Mr H. N. AUSTIN (Hobson), on behalf of Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei), asked the
Minister of Justice: How does the number of crimes of violence in Whangarei compare with
numbers in cities of a similar size?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Attorney-General): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Justice. Recent research shows that Whangarei is the third least violent urban area in New
Zealand, after Christchurch and Nelson. It has less violent offending than cities of a similar
size such as Wanganui and New Plymouth.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Nash Papers
5. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) asked the Minister in Charge of the Public Trust Office: Can
he confirm (a) that the agreement giving Professor Sinclair sole access to the Nash papers
expired on 16 November 1976; (b) that during this period Professor Sinclair did not refuse
access to the papers to any student; and (c) that the chief archivist has been given permission
to allow access to specific material with the concurrence of the Public Trustee; and, in view
of the importance of the papers to the study of New Zealand political history, will he ensure
that they will be made available for research whenever possible, and that a total ban will not
be placed on their use?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister in Charge of the Public Trust Office): I can confirm
that the agreement giving Professor Sinclair access to the Nash papers expired on 16
November 1976. Whether or not Professor Sinclair denied access to any student is not known
to the Public Trustee. Access was, however, given to a number of persons on the
recommendation of Professor Sinclair. The agreement between the Public Trustee and the
chief archivist for the transfer of the papers to the national archives prohibited access to
these papers for 10 years from 16 October 1970, or for such longer period, up to a maximum
of 20 years, as might be necessary. Exceptions were made for Professor Sinclair under the
agreement referred to and for some other persons, principally research students. However,
late last year, at the request of the chief archivist, it was agreed with the Public Trustee that
further access would not be permitted before 16 October 1980 to facilitate the sorting and
cataloging of the papers. The availability of access for research purposes after 1980 will
depend on the extent of the completion of this essential work.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Pensioner Housing, Whangarei
6. Mr H. N. AUSTIN (Hobson), on behalf of Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei), asked the
Minister of Housing: How much has been lent by the Government for pensioner housing in
Whangarei since the change of Government in 1975?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): Since December 1975 the Housing
Corporation has approved of loans totalling $263,000 for pensioner housing in Whangarei.
In addition, a Government subsidy of $179,942 was provided, making a total Government
involvement of $442,942. This assistance was to the Whangarei City Council for the
construction of 18 flats in Kamo Road, and to the Methodist Central Mission for 12 tenant-
contribution flats at Kamo.
Mr Hunt: Were any of the amounts mentioned by the Minister approved between
December 1975 and the end of March 1976?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I cannot give that information, but if the honourable member
wants to ask another question I will get it for him.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

23 August
Oral Answers to Questions
Police Smear Campaign
7. Mr LANGE (Mangere) asked the Minister of Police: In view of his reported statement
in the Dominion of 17 August, in which he said that a "smear campaign" appeared to be
under way against the police, could he be more specific and state who is responsible and
what steps are being taken to remedy the situation?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Police. His answer is as follows: "What I said was one could be excused for concluding that
some form of 'smear campaign' is under way. I was referring in particular to three specific
'Dateline' programmes on TV1. The first on 4 July 1977 when the whole programme was
devoted to unsubstantiated allegations against how Auckland detectives gained evidence.
The second was on 1 August 1977 when ‘Dateline' implied that the police had broken the law
to expose a computer employee who was suspected of leaking information. 'Dateline'
subsequently publicly made a correction. On the same programme there were two other
unfavourable inaccuracies that would have been obvious to anyone who had read the Chief
Ombudsmans report. Again last Monday night the 'Dateline' interviewer dropped the names
of Gerald O'Brien and Colin Moyle when addressing David Exel the Labour Party's
communications director. In the course of his reply, Mr Exel said it was not just a
coincidence that two senior vice-presidents and a former Cabinet Minister of the Labour
Party had been brought in to disrepute for allegations of homosexual activities. Referring
now to the second part of the question, about what steps have been taken to remedy the
situation, the commissioner has commenced what is hoped will be fruitful discussions with
the Director-General of TV1, Mr Allan Morris."
Mr Lange: Would the Minister not agree that the greatest adversity that befell the police
last year was that surrounding their efforts at Labour weekend, which the Police Association
itself condemned, and that these instances of media activity are but drops in the ocean?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: This is really seeking an opinion, but if the member cares to
ask a specific question I am sure an answer will be given.
Hon. M. Rata: In view of the Minister's statement that the "smear campaign" has
originated principally from three television programmes, can he indicate whether TV1 has
offered the Police Department the opportunity to answer the allegations made?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: To my knowledge no such opportunity has been given. The
commissioner is having discussions with the Director-General of TV1, and “Dateline” has
screened a correction.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Wairakei Hotel
8. Mr BELL (Gisborne) asked the Minister of Tourism: What plans has the Tourist
Hotel Corporation to add to the Wairakei Hotel?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): As part of the continuing programme of
development at the Wairakei Hotel a contract has been let for the construction of a new
swimming pool, patio, and barbeque area adjacent to the main bedroom block and
conference centre. This work should be completed by October this year, and the estimated
cost for the project is $50,000. A contract will also shortly be let for stage I of the total
upgrading of the public bar block. This development will include not only the redevelopment
of the present bars, but ultimately the provision of a family bar/restaurant to cater for the
growing visitor market to the Taupo region. Stage I should be completed by early 1978 at a
cost of $110,000, and the total scheme should be completed at an overall cost of $350,000.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Recreational Hunting Area for Thar
9. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) asked the Minister of Lands: Has his department
consulted with recreational hunting organisations whilst investigating the Lands and Agricul-
ture Committee's rider to the thar petition concerning a recreational hunting area?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): The Lands and Agriculture Committee's rider
states "that the relevant departments investigate the possibility of setting aside a recreation


## p. 2375 (#13) ############################################

23 August
2375
Oral Answers to Questions
area for the hunting of thar." The views and opinions of recreational hunting organisations
were submitted to the Lands and Agriculture Committee and these views were taken into
consideration by the departments. The investigation was carried out by the Forest Service,
Internal Affairs, the Treasury, Tourist and Publicity, and the Lands and Survey Depart-
ments. The matter was considered from the varying standpoints related to the respon-
sibilities of the departments concerned, Recreational hunting organisations were not again
consulted during the investigation by the Department of Lands and Survey, nor, I under-
stand, by any other department, as their views were known.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: How can the Minister claim that the matter was fully investigated
when the report from the South Canterbury Catchment Board relating to thar in the
Lawrence River catchment requested by the Forest Service had not been forwarded to that
department 8 days after the Minister had said the matter had been fully investigated?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I am not aware of the significance of that report. The member was
a member of the Lands and Agriculture Committee and he knows that the various
catchments that were looked at were on the western side of the alps rather than on the east.
The committee investigated the Whaturoa-Wanganui and the Landsborough catchments. In
both cases the catchments are adjacent to national parks. The thar is an animal with herding
instincts and lives at high altitudes. Taking those factors into account it was not possible to
find a suitable area where the thar could be controlled by recreational hunting alone.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: Does the Minister recall telling the Deerstalkers Association
conference that since 1972, 90 percent of thar in New Zealand had been shot, and with that
dramatic reduction in animal numbers does he still consider it not appropriate to designate
an area for recreational hunting?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I recall telling the annual conference of the Deerstalkers Associa-
tion that the numbers had been estimated to be reduced to about 10 percent, but I also
informed the association of the Government's decision, that it had not been able to find a
suitable area for the control of thar by recreational means alone.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Unemployment Statistics
10. Mr COOPER (Otago Central) asked the Minister of Labour: What are the latest
unemployment figures for Australia, the United Kingdom, Canada, the United States, and
West Germany, compared with New Zealand?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The latest available unemployment figures
for the countries mentioned are as follows: Australia had 332 793 registered as unemployed
with the Commonwealth Employment Service at the end of June; this represented 5.4
percent of the estimated work force. At the same time the United Kingdom had 1 400 000
registered as unemployed, a rate of 6 percent. The Canadian level of unemployment was
878 000 in July 1977, a rate of 7.9 percent. In May of this year the United States had
6 800 000 unemployed, a rate of 6.9 percent. In West Germany the unemployment rate in
April was 4.4 percent, or 1 000 000 unemployed. In New Zealand 6590 persons were
registered as unemployed in July, a rate of 0.6 percent. These statistics are collected by
different methods, thus making inter-country comparisons of limited value. Australia has
two different statistical series of unemployment, one of those registering with the Common-
wealth Employment Service for employment. The other is taken from a quarterly survey
conducted by the Australian Bureau of Statistics. The United Kingdom also counts as
unemployed the numbers who register with the employment service for placement. In
Canada and United States unemployment figures are estimated from a sample household
survey.
Mr Prebble: Would the Minister confirm from his survey of unemployment around the
world that the New Zealand criteria for registering as being unemployed are some of the
toughest in the world, and that is confirmed by the New Zealand census figures that revealed
that a large number of New Zealanders who do not have employment want employment,
and are not able to obtain registration; for example, housewives?
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I may have misheard the honourable member, but my impres-
sion was that he asked a question and then gave a little speech at the end. That is not in
accordance with our proceedings.
Hon. J. B. GORDON: No, I cannot confirm what the member said. The analysis would
be exactly the same between New Zealand and Australia. Any male or female who is

Tetramine Poison
17. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Minister of Forests: Would he advise what
research has been done on the systemic poison tetramine, and whether his department plans


## p. 2379 (#17) ############################################

23 August
2379
Oral Answers to Questions
to use the poison for controlling introduced animals?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): Between 1961 and 1965 the Forest Research
Institute made a study of all overseas literature related to the systemic poison tetramine to
assess its possible potential for the control of red deer. As a result, no tetramine was
imported and the poison has not been used in New Zealand. The Forest Service has no plans
to undertake any applied research on tetramine or any other systemic poison, and there are
no plans for using systemic poisons for the control of introduced animals.

Livestock Incentive Scheme, Otago
18. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North) asked the Minister in Charge of the Rural
Banking and Finance Corporation: How many applications were made by farmers in Otago
for the livestock incentive scheme in the year ended 31 March 1977, what was the nature of
those granted, and what are the figures to date for the current year?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): I reply on behalf of the Minister in
Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation. For the period from the inception of
the scheme to 31 March 1977 the Rural Bank's Dunedin office received 67 applications for
suspensory loans and 9 applications for assessable income deduction certificates. All of these
applications related to sheep, beef, or deer farms. There were no dairy applications. As at 31
March 1977, 42 suspensory loans and 6 tax option cases were approved. From 1 April 1977 to
16 August 1977 the details are: suspensory loans for sheep, beef, and deer farms, 147
applications received, 111 approvals issued; dairy, one application received, none issued;
total under that category, 148 applications received, and 111 approvals issued. Tax options
for sheep, beef, and deer farms, 24 applications received, 26 approvals issued; dairy, nil in
both cases. Totals for financial year to 16 August 1977, 172 applications received, and 137
approvals issued.
Richard Walls: Does the Minister agree that this is an excellent example of resource-
based regional development?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: Yes, I do.

which has given an extra amount of more than $100 million a year.

HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSION BILL
Interrupted debate on the question, That this Bill be now read a second time.
Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill): As you have said, Mr Speaker, I have 15 minutes left
in which to speak, which will leave me about 10 minutes after the dinner break. That will be
the third occasion on which I have attempted to say what I want to on this Bill.
Mr N. P. H. Jones: This will be the entree.
Hon. A. J. FAULKNER: Yes, as my good friend the member for Invercargill has said,
this should be regarded as the entree. The dinner break will give members the opportunity to
consider Part VI, particularly clause 59, and at the same time to ponder on some of the
remarks made by a very moderate and experienced member of a State Service union, Mr
Reddish. Members opposite should read what he had to say, because it impinges on what is
contained here. It is a fact of life that if working people are to get some recognition of what
they are doing in the face of confrontation then they have to be more than moderate. Unless
one is a confronter or a counterpuncher there is no recognition, and one is regarded as weak.
That is what happens under this Government. Mr Reddish, who said that moderation is
regarded as weakness, has a great deal more experience in industrial relations than people in
this House. One reason is that at one time all legislation affecting the work force appeared in
one Act. Now we have industrial legislation in the Commerce Act and the Industrial
Relations Act, and now we have some in this Human Rights Commission Bill.
It is interesting to note that the previous clause deals with privacy. In our innocence we
are trying to legislate to teach people to mind their own business. If that happened the world
would be a happier place, yet in the following clause we are setting up a commission that will
act as a busybody in industrial relations. I appreciate the humour in it, but it is ridiculous.
This just will not work. It is window dressing, and it will not stop people from minding other
than their own business. I do not mean that it should not be in the legislation. I know that a
number of people respect that it could be illegal to mind other people's business, and I
suppose that is progress. After all, we have spent whole afternoons here correcting illegal

Having dispatched the member for Roskill I shall give a brief history of the Bill. The
United Nations Organisation announced it had decided to promote international economic
and social co-operation in three broad fields, one area being human rights and fundamental
freedom, as defined in article 55 of the charter. New Zealand was one of the countries
represented in San Francisco to set up the Economic and Social Council as the principal
organ of the United Nations. Under article 62 the council was authorised to make
recommendations for the purpose of promoting respect for and observance of human rights
and fundamental freedoms for all. The council was empowered to draft conventions on
human rights as well as on other economic and social matters. Article 68 specifically directed
the council to establish a human rights commission to assist in the performance of its
functions.
Since the charter came into force the competent United Nations organisations have
produced several standard-setting instruments in the field of human rights, including the
Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Next year will mark the thirtieth anniversary of the
adoption of that declaration. I shall read article 2 of the declaration, because it is relevant to
the Bill. "Everyone is entitled to all the rights and freedoms set forth in this declaration
without distinction of any kind, such as race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or
other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status." For the Opposi-
tion's benefit I shall read article 13 of the declaration: "Everyone has the right to freedom of
movement, and residence within the borders of each State. Everyone has the right to leave
any country including his own and to return to his country." It is sobering to think that in
1976 the United Nations received more than 50 000 communications concerning allegations
of violations of human rights. By the Bill before us we are showing that as a nation and a
Government we are prepared to do something in our own right.
Perhaps it is scarcely necessary for me to reaffirm New Zealand's unswerving adherence
to the principle of non-discrimination in the exercise of human rights. New Zealand's
commitment to this principle is one of the basic concepts on which our society is built-belief
in the individual, the liberty of the individual, and equal rights for all citizens regardless of
race, colour, creed, or political belief; the inalienable right to participate by means of free
and democratic processes in forming a society, rejecting racial prejudice, racial discrimina-
tion, and colonialism; a commitment to strive to overcome poverty, ignorance, and disease;
belief in international co-operation to remove the causes of war, to promote tolerance, and
to combat injustice; economic, social, and political progress. Perhaps the overlying principle
is respect for human dignity, a principle that we believe to be universal.
As an example of our pursuance of those obligations, and the elimination of racial
discrimination, New Zealand enacted the Race Relations Act in 1971. The Act provided for
the appointment of a race relations conciliator, whose task it is to settle questions of racial
discrimination and to eliminate potential causes of inter-racial tension before they develop.
This Bill constitutes a further major step towards the completion of a task. The aim of
the Bill is to outlaw and to provide remedies for those forms of discrimination and invasion
of human rights that have not yet been formally covered by our laws. The Bill makes
unlawful discrimination against any person on the grounds of sex, marital status, religious or
ethical belief; it broadens the prohibition against racial discrimination contained in the Race
Relations Act. The Bill will establish a new equal opportunities tribunal, before which the
commission may commence civil proceedings if conciliation fails. The tribunal may also
consider appeals against rulings of the commission. Time does not permit me to go into the
equal opportunities tribunal in depth, as I had hoped to do.

that the people in that country were not afraid to express their political opinion or to
acknowledge that they were members of one or other of the two major political parties. If
this were the case in New Zealand, there would be a great deal less difficulty in this area.
The Australian Commonwealth Human Rights Commission Bill 1977 was introduced
into the Federal Parliament on 1 June by an Australian conservative Government. The
legislation sets up human rights commission with responsibility for Commonwealth and
territorial legislation. The function of the commission is to ensure that Australian Common-
wealth and territorial laws conform with the international covenants on civil and political
rights. The chairman has to be a judge or person with legal qualifications, and the
commission will have between 6 and 10 members. The Australian Attorney-General said
that most of the states had indicated they did not propose to join the scheme at this stage.
Nevertheless, the proposal is one that deserves serious consideration.
Another human right which this Government does not seem to value is that of privacy.
Part V of the Bill, which deals with privacy, is weak window dressing at its worst. Let us look
at what the commission is empowered to do. Under clause 58(1) it can (a) inquire generally,
(b) report to the Prime Minister from time to time, (c) report to the Prime Minister on any
other matter relating to privacy that, in the commission's opinion, should be drawn to the
Prime Minister's attention, (d) make suggestions, (e) gather information, (f) receive and
invite representations, (g) make public statements, and, best of all, under subclause (2), and
I quote: "The Commission may report to the Prime Minister . . . on any matter relating to
privacy on which the Prime Minister has requested a report." Apart from the surprisingly
dominating role played by the Prime Minister in all of this-and that does not really surprise
me when I consider the present Prime Minister-the powers of the commission are virtually

The Human Rights Commission Bill is, in fact, a very broad and positive document in

TERRITORIAL SEA AND EXCLUSIVE ECONOMIC ZONE BILL
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. I regret that, as I was overseas at the time, I was not able to participate in
the detailed examination of the Bill when it was before a select committee, but honourable
members will recall that when I introduced the Bill into the House I pointed out that it was
designed to reflect the principles embodied in the draft texts developed at the Law of the Sea
Conference. I shall say more about the work of that conference in a few moments, but first I
want to recall the key provisions of the Bill.


## p. 2394 (#32) ############################################

2394
23 August
Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Bill
Clause 3 extends the territorial sea from 3 to 12 miles. The extension was provided for
in the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zone Act 1965, but clause 9 establishes an exclusive
economic zone of 188 nautical miles beyond the territorial sea. This gives New Zealand a
total maritime zone of 200 miles, within which it has sovereign rights over all the living and
mineral resources. Members will note that the long title of the Bill asserts sovereign rights
merely over the resources of the zone; it does not assert full territorial sovereignty. As I have
indicated, in drafting the Bill we have scrupulously ensured that the legal status of the zone is
consistent with the draft articles developed by the conference, but it is still important to
stress that our rights in the zone are limited to its resources. The former high seas rights of
freedom of navigation or of overflight are in no way restricted. Indeed, in the course of the
Law of the Sea Conference there has been considerable discussion and debate on that point.
I refer members to Part I of the Bill. I think—and I am sure members will agree with
me-that the law relating to the territorial sea has been well settled since it was codified by
the United Nations at a convention in 1958, and the principal outstanding matter for
resolution by the present conference has been the breadth of the territorial sea. That has
been fixed at 12 miles. In clause 3, the Bill again follows the provisions of the conference's
draft articles.
Clauses 11, 12, and 13 are, in fact, the heart of the Bill. They establish the machinery for
the exercise of New Zealand's sovereign rights to determine how much fish should be caught
in the zone and by whom-the sustainable yield. The principles upon which those clauses are
based are drawn directly from the draft articles of the Law of the Sea Conference. I stress
that the articles in the composite negotiating text dealing with the living resources of the
economic zone have in fact a very special character. They were negotiated at an early stage
in the conference; they have been challenged many times, but have in fact prevailed without
any substantial amendment throughout three successive sessions of the conference—that, I
think, is a pretty fair indication of the extent to which they have been adopted and endorsed.
We believe that these articles as a whole are now generally recognised as an internationally
accepted legal regime for fisheries within the 200-mile zones. The addition, at the last session
of the conference, of revised articles on the legal status of the zone and on scientific research
means that the concept of the economic zone as a whole is now very close to being generally
recognised as a binding legal regime.
This evening I thought I would set out the broad political framework within which the
Bill has been established. I believe it is common knowledge, certainly amongst those people
who have been interested in the development of the conference, that for the past several
years the United Nations has been engaged in a full-scale review of almost every aspect of
the law of the sea. The work to prepare for the Law of the Sea Conference commenced as
long ago as 1970, and the first session of the conference opened in New York at the end of
1973. It is not widely appreciated, however, that the conference is probably the biggest
intergovernmental meeting ever held. It is certainly the most important conference ever
convened by the United Nations, and it is important to understand why so much time,
money, and energy have been focused on this series of meetings.
If we look back into history, we are reminded that the seas were open to all countries
and to their nationals to use very much as they pleased. Sovereignty was restricted by
international law to a narrow belt of territorial sea, and the main emphasis of the law was on
the freedom of the seas; there was little or nothing about the seabed beneath the oceans.
Recent years have seen enormous changes in technology and consumption, which have
challenged the basic assumptions on which the previous law of the sea rested. At least 20
percent of the world's oil is now taken from under the sea, and this figure will increase
significantly in the future. Vast deposits of manganese nodules have been found on the floor
of the deep ocean. Fish resources have become even more vital to the nourishment of a
hungry world, and to the economies of coastal states. Equally, it has become clear that the
world's stocks of fish are not inexhaustible. In some parts of the world, stocks have been
fished to the point of extinction, and it is now clear that conservation must be a basic
principle of the future law governing fisheries.
The development of technology and heavy industry has brought to light new and
disturbing uses of the ocean. We have pollutants such as oil-and, heaven knows, we have
seen plenty of examples. Pesticides, chemicals, and radioactive waste have been deposited in
the ocean at a quite dangerous rate. Ships carrying highly toxic materials ply the seas. Here
again, the concept of absolute freedom on the high seas has become obsolete. All of these
factors have combined to make a change in the law of the sea inevitable.


## p. 2395 (#33) ############################################

23 August
2395
Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Bill
However, there is one further development of a political rather than a technological
kind-which promises to change radically the concept upon which the previous law of the sea
was based. In the past, the law really benefited only the coastal states—and then only to a
very limited extent—and the major maritime powers; the principal benefits were enjoyed by
a few powerful and already rich maritime countries. When the United Nations decided in
1970 to convene the Law of the Sea Conference it embarked on a radical new course. It
adopted a resolution that the deep seabed, beyond the limits of national jurisdiction, was the
common heritage of mankind and was to be exploited principally for the benefit of the
developing countries. This meant that the conference faced a formidable task in fashioning a
new order for the oceans. Much of the old order had already gone or was fast disappearing.
The conference is increasingly working in a race against time to develop new rules to govern
a wide range of international problems. These are: the strategic, military, and commercial
interests in ensuring freedom to navigate and fly over the world's oceans; the ownership of
and access to the vast resources of oil beneath the sea; access to other important minerals,
such as cobalt, nickel, and manganese, on the deep seabed; the conservation and control of
the world's fisheries, a topic with which this Bill generally deals; the control of pollution in
the oceans; and the control of modern scientific research.
What then has the conference to show after six sessions of lengthy negotiations? I think
it is necessary to stress that the fundamental importance of the issues under negotiation is
often overlooked. When one considers the diversity of political, economic, military, and
other interests at stake, it is surprising to learn-and certainly worth noting that the
conference has come very close indeed to final success. At the sixth session of the
conference, which concluded in New York last month, a draft convention was produced,
called the informal composite negotiating text. It is a massive document of about 200 pages,
comprising more than 300 articles and 7 lengthy annexes. Very many of the articles
contained in the negotiating text are now in a form which commands wide support in the
conference. Most-and I say "most" advisedly-have now been successfully negotiated; and
it is significant that this measure of agreement has so far been achieved without a single vote.
It has been achieved, instead, by a process of discussion, negotiation, conciliation, and
compromise. It has certainly not been achieved by marshalling majorities and overriding
minority positions by force of votes in the conference itself. It certainly marks a very
significant achievement and very significant progress in the negotiations.
I should like to point out in particular that, at the recently concluded session, a number
of important breakthroughs on the remaining issues outstanding was achieved. There was a
compromise on the status of the economic zone, and the exercise of high seas freedoms in
the zone was negotiated. The economic zone provided for the sovereign right of coastal
states over resources, but it preserved the freedom of transit to other countries. Important
understandings were reached on the question of transit through straits and archipelagoes.
Hon. W. W. Freer: And across countries, sometimes.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: The zones extend beyond to include archipelagoes, and sea
lanes are provided through economic zones. Also, the rights of coastal states to impose
controls on scientific research by foreign countries-a question which is touched on in the
Bill-were negotiated in broad principle; the basic right is there for the coastal state to
regulate. It certainly does not have absolute power to prevent research in the area.
In the light of this high degree of consensus, it is tempting to ask what then remains and
how important it will be to New Zealand once this Bill is passed and we have unilaterally
established a 200-mile economic zone. When one talks of unilaterally establishing the zone,
it should be borne in mind that between 30 and 40 countries have already taken this action.
The Government believes that New Zealand's interest in the conference goes far beyond the
fact that the 200-mile zone is now widely accepted in practice and in international law. As a
small country, we are vitally concerned to have the eventual protection that a widely ratified
multilateral agreement will confer. It is one thing to talk of unilaterally establishing such a
zone, but it is another to take this action in conformity with a widely agreed and ratified
international convention. New Zealand also has a traditional concern for the rule of law, and
the avoidance of a situation in which the oceans become a battleground for competing claims
and a focus for conflict over the exploitation of the resources of the deep sea bed.
Both our immediate national interest and a wider international interest in a suitable
regime for the oceans demand that we continue to work actively for the successful conclusion
of the conference. Such a conclusion to the conference would have a very real significance
for the north-south dialogue, and also for the future of Antarctica. Only one major area of


## p. 2396 (#34) ############################################

2396
23 August
Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Bill
disagreement is still to be resolved, and this is the regime to govern the exploitation of the
minerals of the deep sea bed. While it is true that this issue is of little direct and immediate
concern to New Zealand, its successful resolution is crucial to the success or failure of the
conference, and, as I have already indicated, New Zealand has a vested interested in its
success.
This issue has proved extremely difficult to resolve. The fifth session of the conference
in 1976 was virtually deadlocked in a largely ideological debate between the highly
industrialised countries, which have the capacity to mine and exploit the nodules on the
seabed, and the developing countries, which maintain that the common heritage of mankind
should not be exploited by a few already wealthy countries. On the one hand, the highly
industrialised countries want guaranteed and permanent access to seabed mining-after all,
they have the technology, the capacity, and the resources; on the other hand, the developing
countries believe that the exploitation of seabed resources-a radical new departure in
economic activity-should not perpetuate the previous exploitation systems on land, which
inevitably favour those who have the resources, the technology, and the power.
New Zealand has taken the view that a compromise solution between these two
positions can be found, and that this will involve a dual system of access. The overall control
of mining activities should be vested in an international seabed authority, to which all states
would belong. Mining would then be conducted by both private companies and an interna-
tional enterprise, which would operate principally on behalf of the developing countries and
which would undoubtedly have to buy the expertise. The recent session of the conference
devoted a major effort to working out a compromise along these lines, and very considerable
progress was made. However, it was not possible in the time available to negotiate the
details of such a regime. Regrettably also—and I cannot explain how this arose--the genuine
progress on this issue was partially obscured by some last-minute changes in what seemed to
be the most useful text to have emerged so far on the key elements in this difficult and
complex issue.
Despite the major progress made at the sixth session, it is clear that, in view of the
complexities surrounding the regime for the deep sea bed, a substantial period of negotia-
tions is still required before the draft treaty will be ready for adoption. What is essential is
that the momentum demonstrated throughout the last session of the conference is not lost.
In particular, all participants at the next session must approach the negotiations on the deep
sea bed issues with the sense of urgency and seriousness of purpose that is required if these
issues are to be resolved and the conference brought to a successful conclusion. Equally, it is
vital that the states or private corporations with the capacity to do so do not, in the
meantime, begin unilateral exploitation of the deep sea bed. In my view, this would be a very
considerable setback. Not only would it run directly counter to the fundamental principles
upon which the negotiations are based and upon which a great deal of progress has been
made, but also, if this action were taken, there is a very real chance that it would spark a
reaction from others that could well put at risk all that has been achieved so far.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Could they do that in an economic zone without a Government's
decision?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: I am talking about the deep sea bed now, which is outside
the economic zone.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Well, within the 200 miles?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: Exploitation of the deep sea bed is occurring now and is
causing much concern. It is in an area beyond the different economic zones.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: So it is really free, except by agreement?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: That is the point at issue. In view of the fact that so much of
the draft convention is essentially agreed and so little remains to be negotiated, such a result
would be nothing short of tragic. [Time extended.]
I want to say a few words about a problem that has not surfaced openly at the Law of the
Sea Conference, but which has some bearing on the law of the sea-and that is Antarctica.
The Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Bill does not apply an economic zone to
the Ross Dependency. It contains merely an enabling provision which reserves the right to
take this step in the future, if desired. It is, therefore, fully consistent with the Antarctic
Treaty, which provides that there should be no new claims and no extension of old claims.
But, if we had omitted any reference to the Dependency, that would have been interpreted
as not maintaining that the potential for such a claim was there. If we had sought to add that
territory to the zone, that would in fact have been an extension. The provision in the Bill is


## p. 2397 (#35) ############################################

2397
Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Bill
fully consistent with the Antarctic Treaty, but it also retains New Zealand's flexibility
consistent with its sovereign claim to react to any future development in the area.
The exploitation of the resources of the Antarctic is to be discussed by the Antarctic
Treaty powers at a consultative meeting in London next month. The Government believes
that it would not be desirable, in the light of these forthcoming discussions and the obvious
practical problems involved, to establish an economic zone in the Ross Dependency at
present. However, it believes it is a matter of considerable urgency to develop a regime to
govern the exploitation of living and mineral resources in the Antarctic. The possibility of
unregulated commercial activity in the Antarctic is quite unacceptable on environmental
grounds. New Zealand is playing a leading part in the negotiations to deal with this problem,
that are at present under way, and the Government would prefer to see solutions emerge
through those negotiations rather than have individual Antarctic Treaty members, or even
outsiders, staking out their own positions on a unilateral basis.
I have chosen, this evening, to try to give the background to the Bill, because it is

itself sets out the manner in which the economic zone, particularly as it applies to fishing, can
be applied in the interests of this country. The Bill has already been extensively considered
by the select committee, and what I have seen of the submissions that were made indicates
that the interest centred on what follows rather than the content of the Bill itself; so I think
there is fairly wide agreement on the content of the Bill.

conditions laid down by the Minister. I ask the Minister whether this follows the trend
developing under this Administration of government by regulation rather than government

gives the Minister much power.

One of the most interesting and comprehensive submissions made to the select
committee came from the Fishing Industry Board, which stated that the board and the
industry fully endorsed the principles embodied in the Bill, particularly those provisions
enabling New Zealand to exercise its sovereign rights over the exploitation, conservation,
and management of the fishing resources within the exclusive economic zone. The industry
has long been concerned about the depletion of fish stocks in New Zealand waters. I
congratulate the Minister and the Government on the positive way in which they are passing
one of the most important measures we have had for many years. As I have already said, the
Bill outlines visionary measures which will prove to be historic in the development of this
major resource. At present, New Zealand needs every possible peaceful weapon and
economic tool to develop its exports, and this legislation is among the most important tools
in helping to develop the export industry generally. It will aid New Zealand's international
negotiations to gain greater access for its agricultural products to some of the largest
industrial nations. New Zealand will have every international right to expect a quid pro quo
in all its trading negotiations.
I think it is fair to say that New Zealand would have preferred to establish a 200-mile
economic zone in accordance with a comprehensive law of the sea treaty. However, foreign
fishing fleets continue to put pressure on our fishing resources. The extension of New
Zealand's jurisdiction of the 200-mile zone has therefore become urgent to ensure proper
conservation and management of the fishing stocks. A number of important developments
for New Zealand have taken place in the past few months. During the last legislative session,
it was not possible to be confident that an assertion of the 200-mile jurisdiction would be
internationally accepted, especially by the major distant water-fishing states of Russia and
Japan. As the Minister of Foreign Affairs mentioned earlier, 200-mile economic zone
legislation of one kind or another has been adopted by about 40 countries, including Japan
and Russia. Therefore, the establishment of a 200-mile zone is well-founded in international
law and in the practice of these States.
As such a zone is important to New Zealand, the Bill closely reflects the well settled
provisions of the revised single negotiating text of the Law of the Sea Conference, which
deals with fishing, and puts New Zealand in a very strong position to police these new
provisions. If the provisions of the Bill are not adhered to, there will be a maximum penalty
of up to $100,000, plus the forfeiture of the vessel. The Minister has mentioned some of the
main clauses in the Bill, and I refer to them again-the determination of the total catch that
can be harvested by all New Zealand and foreign vessels in the zone, and the allocation of
the surplus, over and above what can be harvested by New Zealand boats, to foreign vessels.
The Bill also establishes conservation measures, including closed areas, closed seasons,
prohibited species, and fishing methods. The Minister will have strong powers, and the
fishing industry can be assured of consultations between the Minister, the Fishing Industry
Board, and other fishing interests.

chipping away at the Bill, trying to undermine this most important measure. If he would only

Zealand waters. The Bill will enable the New Zealand fishing industry to take up the catch of

licences from time to time, at reasonably frequent intervals.

$26 million. The improvement is continuing, and in the past year we have exported $38
million worth of fish products. That progress will continue even more rapidly after the Bill

TOWN AND COUNTRY PLANNING BILL
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): I move, That the Town and
Country Planning Bill be introduced. The Bill is the first full review and consolidation of the
Town and Country Planning Act since it was passed in 1953. It is based on the recommenda-
tion of the Town and Country Planning Review Committee, which reported in 1973, but it
also incorporates measures proposed in the National Party's manifesto as well as changes
that experience has shown to be necessary since the committee reported. After considering
wide-ranging submissions, the review committee concluded that the basic system of local
planning was sound and well suited to New Zealand conditions. It has proved flexible and
adaptable, and has been progressively amended to widen the rights of the public to
participate in planning. The Bill builds on these basic strengths.
The review committee nevertheless acknowledged that some important changes in the
legislation were long overdue. In particular, it considered that the Act needed simplifying
and arranging in a more logical sequence, that third party rights to participate in planning
should be extended still further, that environmental considerations should be brought
directly into the planning process, and that more effective links should be created between
planning at national, regional, and local levels. The Bill aims to achieve all these recommen-
dations.
Since the Act was passed in 1953 there have been 12 amending Acts, and this has led to
various amendments' being inserted into the principal Act in a rather piecemeal fashion,
with confusion and, in some cases, ambiguity as a result. The Bill attempts to set out the
various provisions in a logical order, and an attempt has also been made to simplify wherever
possible the procedures and the language used, many of the machinery and technical aspects
will be transferred to the regulations. The Bill promotes a closer relationship and communi-
cation between national, regional, and local planning. It also provides for full rights of
consultation among the various authorities and bodies concerned with planning, and
provides wide-ranging opportunities for the public to take part in the planning process. I am


## p. 2409 (#47) ############################################

24 August
2409
Town and Country Planning Bill
fully aware of the present concern for the protection of the environment, and the Bill gives
more emphasis to environmental considerations.
One of the recommendations of the review committee was incorporated into the Act in
1973. This was the provision that declared certain matters to be of national importance, such
as the preservation of the coastal environment and the margins of lakes and rivers, the
avoidance of the encroachment of urban development on good farm land, and the preven-
tion of sporadic urban development in rural areas. These principles are retained in the Bill,
and are strengthened by further measures for the protection of the environment and the
conservation and wise use of New Zealand's resources. The National Party's concern to limit
the size of cities is recognised by declaring the avoidance of the unnecessary expansion of
cities to be a matter of national importance. The special relationship between Maori culture
and institutions and their ancestral land is also declared to be a matter of national
importance. Furthermore, recognition is accorded the complementary water and soil legisla-
tion.
The Bill contains a new regional planning system, which is designed to co-ordinate
central and local government planning. It provides for the Government's approval of
regional planning schemes, but this carries with it the important commitment that the
Government will support approved regional plans. It has been generally agreed that the
present regional planning provisions have not proved adequate. Concern at the lack of
effective regional planning has been expressed by a number of bodies, including the
Municipal Association, which said: "The association sees planning as having three
levels-national, regional, and district. While national planning can only be carried out
through central government the Municipal Association has consistently supported the
strengthening of the processes for planning at the regional level. To this end, we welcome
the current proposals for the early establishment of regions over the whole of the country
and the setting up of regional bodies, most of which will comprise members nominated by
territorial authorities having regional planning as their principal functional responsibility."
The Holmes task force, in its report on economic and social planning, said: "Regional
planning bodies need to be built up to provide an effective link between local and national
planning."
""
The Bill, therefore, strengthens the regional planning provisions so that united and
regional councils will be able to undertake effective regional planning. It should be noted
that this is the first time that our planning system has provided any statutory links between
national, regional, and local interests. It also gives the regions, through united and regional
councils, the opportunity to communicate with and directly influence central government far
more effectively than in the past. There is the potential for each region to have far more say
in determining its own future development. The Bill thus represents a shift in emphasis from
central to local government, in accordance with the Government's policy.
The procedures set out for preparing, changing, or reviewing regional planning schemes
are designed to encourage the greatest amount of public participation. Before the scheme is
actually prepared, regional planning authorities are required to call for submissions from any
interested body or person. When a draft scheme has been prepared, the public is again
invited to comment. Finally, there is a further opportunity for public comment when the
scheme is submitted to the Minister. In all appropriate cases, the comments of interested
parties can be made the subject of an inquiry by the planning tribunal, and local authorities
have the right to insist on any matters being referred to the tribunal. Once regional schemes
have been approved by the Government, the Crown will be obliged to observe and support
them.
The opportunity the Bill provides for the appointment of regional land resource
advisory committees illustrates the Government's concern that land must be considered a
national resource, it fulfils the promise made in the National Party's manifesto that such
committees would be set up. These committees are expected to comprise experts in land use,
and will be able to offer valuable advice to the regional authorities.
As far as district planning is concerned, the present system is basically retained,
although changes have been made to reduce administrative costs and delays and to simplify
procedures. Greater opportunities are provided for public participation in both the prepara-
tion and the administration of district schemes. These include an extension of the rights of
property owners and interested bodies, such as progressive associations and environmental
groups, to be heard by councils and the Planning Tribunal. In response to demands by local
bodies and many others, councils are given the ability to exercise better control over the


## p. 2410 (#48) ############################################

2410
24 August
Town and Country Planning Bill
protection of trees and bush and other areas of amenity value, and over the design and
appearance of buildings. The procedures for dealing with applications for such matters as
conditional uses and specified departures have been simplified.
Councils will be provided with wider discretionary powers, and with more authority to
delegate to committees and council officers. This will enable the committees or the council
officers to exercise certain discretionary powers in appropriate instances. Provision is also
included for a council, if it so wishes, to appoint a commissioner, who may or may not be a
member of the council, to hear objections to applications and make recommendations to the
council. For a district scheme, while applications for a council's consent will normally be
advertised, provision is made to enable applications, where the subject matter is of minor
importance, to be dealt with without the advertising of the application being required. It is
hoped that the effect of these changes will enable applications to a council to be dealt with
more quickly and at less cost to both the applicant and the council. That will also reduce the
time councillors will have to spend in dealing with town planning matters.
Part V of the Bill provides for maritime planning. This is a new measure, and is intended
to apply only to those coastal areas where maritime planning is found to be necessary
because of serious conflicts in the use of water. It is intended that an existing public
authority, such as a regional planning authority or a harbour board, would be appointed the
maritime planning authority. Again, in keeping with the rest of the Bill, wide rights for
public involvement in maritime planning processes are provided. The maritime planning
authority and every public body and local authority will be required, where applicable, to
observe and enforce within a maritime planning area the provisions of a maritime planning
scheme.
As far as public works are concerned, the Crown is now bound for the first time to
follow the specific procedures set out in Part VI of the Bill, except in cases of emergency or
where an exemption is given by Order in Council. It is anticipated that this exemption will be
rarely invoked and only when the national interest clearly requires it. Generally speaking, all
Government public works are to be designated if they are not permitted uses in terms of the
district scheme. Wider rights for objection and appeal than exist at present are also
provided. A new feature is that the Minister may refer a proposed public work to the
Planning Tribunal for a wide-ranging inquiry instead of its being subject to appeals. This may
be appropriate where a major work of public interest, such as a major power scheme, is
proposed. The Bill includes new provisions that make it necessary for outline plans of public
works to be submitted for consideration by councils before construction commences. The
plans will cover such matters as the height and shape of buildings and parking provisions. If a
council is not satisfied with these details, it will have a right of appeal to the tribunal.
The present Town and Country Planning Appeal Board has filled a very important role
in both the planning and the judicial fields, and its decisions have generally won the respect
of both local authorities and the public. The Bill provides more status for the appeal board,
and extends its jurisdiction. The board has been re-named the Planning Tribunal, and it will
operate in three divisions, each of which is to be chaired by a magistrate.
I have indicated the major changes contained in the Bill, and it is hoped that they will
assist in the improvement of town planning in New Zealand. It should be borne in mind,
however, that in presenting its report in 1973 the review committee stated: "Neither the
present Act nor any new or amended Act can of itself guarantee good town planning or
provide well-founded solutions to the problems which arise from the physical development
of our country." The committee further stated: "So much depends upon the skill and
imagination of the technical officers responsible for the preparation and administration of
district planning schemes, the technical resources at their disposal, and the local government
structure within which they must work. So much also depends on the extent of the
commitment of the elected members of local government to the concept of seeking the best
environment for all sections of the community which they govern.'
For success in town and country planning, it is essential that plans and their methods of
implementation be broadly acceptable to those involved. This includes all people as well as
local and central government. We must not lose sight of the fact that elected local
government representatives rightly feel they are the voice of the people who have democrati-
cally elected them. We must also recognise that the people who are affected by plans and
planners consider that their rights must be respected. While the principles involved in the
Bill are generally known and have been discussed with many interested parties, I should not
like to leave the impression that there have been detailed consultations. The time scale, the

acres of that land; that is the problem this Bill appears to ignore completely. It does not
appear to grapple with this. At a cursory glance, I cannot see how this Bill may be hailed as a
means to placate the Maori petitioners or satisfy the criticisms that have been made. How
does the Bill deal with this vexing problem?

Domestic Purposes Benefit-De Facto Relationship
2. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: Is it true, as
stated in the New Zealand Listener of 20 August 1977, that Beth Furmage of Hamilton was
asked by the Department of Social Welfare to sign a statement to the effect that she would
not sleep with her man any more than once a fortnight or have meals with him more than
three times a week, and, if so, can the Minister indicate how many other people have been
asked to sign such a statement?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): No, it is not true.
Mr Marshall: I understand that Mrs Furmage has had her case before the tribunal since
May. Can the Minister indicate when a decision might be made?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: A decision was made and published about 2 weeks ago. This
particular person has appealed twice unsuccessfully to the Social Security Commission, and
also to the Social Security Appeal Authority. She has now indicated that she will appeal to
the Supreme Court.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Was the lady in question asked to sign any statement, and, if so,
what were its contents?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: If a benefit is cancelled, or is likely to be cancelled, because two
people are living in a de facto relationship, the department may ask the couple to make a
statutory declaration of their mode of living.
Mr Hunt: A couple, or one person?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: It may be one person, or it may be a couple. No directions are
ever given as to how many times a woman can sleep with her boyfriends, because that is of
no concern to the department. The department is concerned to establish whether two people
are living in a de facto relationship, and, if they are, they are not entitled to a benefit that
would place them in a better position than a legally married couple.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: Would the Minister table the terms and conditions under which a
benefit may be cancelled if people are living in a de facto relationship?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: People may be asked to make a statement about their mode of
living. I would be happy to discuss the matter with the honourable member.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Would the Minister be prepared to table the actual declaration
this lady was asked to sign with the answers deleted?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: No such declaration was submitted to the department.

Unemployment Comparison with OECD Countries
8. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) asked the Minister of Labour: How does New Zealand's
unemployment rate calculated on a total basis, Government work schemes included,
compare with the average OECD rate of unemployment and the worst and best countries in
the OECD?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): New Zealand's unemployment rate,
registered unemployed plus those on special Government works, stood at 1.2 percent at the
end of July 1977. Although differences in the methods by which OECD countries collect
unemployment statistics makes rigorous comparisons difficult, New Zealand's rate of
unemployment is widely accepted as being amongst the lowest in the OECD membership.
For example, while New Zealand's rate including special workers has averaged about 1
percent this year, Sweden experienced an unemployment rate of 1.8 percent in April 1977,
and Ireland a rate of 12.8 percent in February 1977. These countries represent the best and
worst of the remainder of the OECD countries for which recent figures are available. No
average rate of unemployment is calculated for OECD countries.
Mr Falloon: Has the Mmister seen a recent Economist article that mentions that
14 000 000 people are unemployed in the OECD countries, and would he say whether the
New Zealand figures are seasonally adjusted, as are the OECD figures, and that they
represent a peak at this time of the year?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: No, I have not seen the article. I have had a report that it is
something I should read when I get time. Unemployment figures are adjusted every
fortnight. They are not seasonally adjusted to the extent that because it is a peak period at
present the figures are automatically boosted. Indeed, I am told that we have not yet reached
the 20 000 figure that was predicted in one quarter.
Hon. M. Rata: What comfort, if any, can we take from the Minister's comparison of
unemployment figures in New Zealand with those of other countries, and what remedial
action does the Minister propose to take to reduce New Zealand's unemployment rate?
Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER: Those two questions are quite unrelated to the original
question. One was seeking an opinion, and is therefore not permitted, and the other is
outside the ambit of the original question.
Mr Malcolm: As the Minister has said that the New Zealand figures are well below the
figures for other comparable countries, can he say whether the low New Zealand figure is a
direct result of the New Zealand Government's policy of maintaining full employment as
part of its overall economic programme?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The steps taken last year with the special subsidy scheme to
private employers resulted in a large number of young girls in the Whangarei area being

Clothing Factory Closure and NAFTA
9. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: Is he
aware of the closure of the Line 7 clothing factory at Palmerston North, which the managing
director, Mr B. P. Wilson, blamed in the Manawatu Evening Standard of 11 August on cuts
by Australia under the NAFTA agreement as renegotiated in April, and can he state the
steps he is taking to assist the 29 women and 2 men affected by the closure and also to
prevent further factory closures from the same cause?
Mr ALLEN (Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Industry): I
reply on behalf of the Minister of Trade and Industry. His answer is as follows: "I have heard
of the closure of the factory, and am informed that all Line 7's former employees have found
other jobs. Only two of them registered with the Department of Labour, and they were re-
employed within an hour of doing so. I am told that, although Line 7 sells to several overseas
markets, a fair proportion of the production from its Palmerston North factory was sold in
Australia. I am not aware of why these sales could not continue in terms of the arrangement
negotiated in April, under which special New Zealand quotas have been issued to Australian
importers totalling the same volume of apparel that New Zealand sold last year, or of why
Line 7 has been unable to sell against global quotas as a number of New Zealand companies
have been doing. These provisions have safeguarded New Zealand's apparel market in
Australia overall, but it is not within my power to modify the impact of Australia's quota
system on individual companies, all of whom will have been affected in different ways,
depending on the way in which their trade with Australia had developed, and their
expectations of further expansion."
Mr MacDonell: In view of a report in the Manawatu Evening Standard of 11 August of a
statement made by the member for Palmerston North: “I am going to see if anything can be
done at Government level. I won't say I am hopeful, but certainly a broadening of thought
has not reached the Government from a personal member of parliament level”, will the
Under-Secretary take steps to ensure that no more clothing factories will close because of the
disastrous NAFTA agreement?
Mr ALLEN: I do not think there is any suggestion that the factory closed because of the
NAFTA agreement. The agreement has completely protected the apparel industry in New
Zealand. As Opposition members know, the decision to close the factory was made by the
management.
Mr Lithgow: Would the Under-Secretary agree that the articles manufactured by Line
7, such as motor cycle protective gear, yachting protective gear, and boating gear, had a high
degree of synthetic content, and are subject to Australian global quotas?
Mr ALLEN: That is correct. This factory could have continued to sell its manufactured
garments to Australia had the management chosen to take its opportunities under the New
Zealand quota or under the global quota.
Hon. W. W. Freer: When are the special New Zealand quotas to be issued?
Mr ALLEN: The former Minister is out of touch with the position, and I sympathise
with his problem. The fact of life is that the Australian Government has already issued all the

Tourists-New Zealand-Australia
10. Mr BELL (Gisborne) asked the Minister of Tourism: Can he give any indication of
the trend of visitor numbers from New Zealand to Australia and vice versa?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): During the year ended 31 May 1977
New Zealand visitors to Australia declined by 3 percent-from 116 288 to 112 808. Visitors
to New Zealand from Australia during the same year declined by 5.6 percent-from 231 358
to 218 496. Arrivals for the month of May 1977 have been affected by the air traffic
controllers' strike in Australia. Although actual figures for June are not yet published, there
are indications that there has been an improvement. This trend has to be considered in the
light of total departures from Australia, which in February last declined 12.7 percent over
February 1976. Thus the decline in Australian travel affects not only New Zealand but other
competitive destinations.
Mr Bell: How do these statistics compare with the forecasts made by the Tourist
Development Council?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: The figures compare more than favourably with the forecasts.
In 1973-74 the visitors' numbers were up 35 percent; in 1974-75 they were up 25.9 percent;
and in 1975-76 they were up 8.5 percent.
Mr Hunt: How far do the Minister and his department attribute the decline in numbers
travelling to Australia to the foreign travel tax imposed by the National Government?
Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER: That is seeking an opinion, as I am sure the honourable
member knows.
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: The travel tax was imposed as a disincentive to travel overseas.
It was imposed on travel to Australia and beyond, and has affected New Zealanders to the
extent of a decline of only 3 percent.

Ohai Coal
13. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Mines: What has been the
demand so far this year by consumers for coal mined at Ohai, and has there been any
difficulty in supplying the market from this coalfield?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I reply on behalf of the Minister
of Mines as follows. The demand for Ohai coal this year is 6 percent down on the demand of
1976. Some 1600 tonnes of Mataura lignite have been used to supplement supplies to some
customers using pea grade coal, but all other industrial customers' requirements have been
fully met. After a very low demand for domestic coal in the first 4 months of this year, the
demand climbed sharply in May, and for the following 2 months could not be met. From
early August, the demand for all grades of coal has been fully met.
Hon. F. M. Colman: What are the prospects of supplying next winter consumers who
express a preference for Ohai coal?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: The Mines Department has plans in hand to ask the dealers
to stock more coal during the summer months so as to be able to cope with the exceptional
demand during the winter months. If the dealers respond to that plan, it should be possible
to meet most of the demands.
Mr T. J. Young: By how much was the supply of coal short of the domestic demand in
Dunedin and Invercargill?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I regret I cannot give the figures for specific areas. The
demand, of course, is related mainly to industrial use, and fluctuates when one or two major
consumers change their demands. I gather that that has been one of the causes of the short
supply of coal this season.
