URGENT QUESTIONS
Mercury Levels in Fish
Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Health, as an urgent question, Is it correct
that some fish being sold in Auckland contain mercury in excess of the maximum level
permitted by the Food and Drug Regulations, and which may be harmful to human health,
and, if so, what action does the Minister propose´to take?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The Department of Health is aware that large
sharks, sometimes sold as lemon fish, contain mercury in excess of the maximum permitted
level of 0.5 parts per million. This maximum level in fish and fish products was established in


## p. 2427 (#65) ############################################

24 August
2427
Urgent Questions
February 1971. Since that date, the Department of Health, in conjunction with the
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, has monitored samples of fish offered for
sale to the public. Generally, the permitted levels of mercury have not been exceeded. The
level of mercury in the shark is related to age and size of the fish. The older and larger fish
generally contain elevated levels of mercury, and should not be consumed by humans.
Present sampling indicates that excessive levels of mercury are limited to Auckland. The
Auckland Medical Officer of Health has issued a warning to all fish wholesalers that the
Department of Health will prosecute anyone who is found to be selling for human
consumption shark (lemon fish) which contains mercury in excess of 0.5 parts per million.
Control at this stage is being concentrated at the wholesale level, as it is in this area that non-
conforming fish are being sold to the retailer. Should officers of the Department of Health
have reason to believe that fish containing mercury in excess of 0.5 parts per million is
offered for sale for human consumption, the fish will be seized to prevent sale to the public,
and prosecution will follow. All medical officers of health are investigating the possibility of
shark (lemon fish) which contains mercury in excess of the legal limit being sold in their
districts, and appropriate steps will be taken to protect the consumer.
Prison Outbreak-Addington
Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central), on behalf of Mr KIRK (Sydenham),
asked the Minister of Justice, as an urgent question, Due to the recent amount of public
concern over the violent outbreak of four prisoners from Addington Prison, what steps has
the Minister of Justice taken to: (1) make a full inquiry into the breakout; (2) satisfy the
public that the breakout was an isolated incident and is unlikely to be repeated in this or
other prisons; (3) reduce the number of prisoners being held in Addington to the 25 that it
was designed to take; (4) ensure in the future that prison officers will not be exposed to
excessive vulnerability, which occurred in the recent violent example at Addington Prison;
and, (5) ensure that a breakout of the type experienced at Addington Prison will be guarded
against in the future interest of public safety?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Acting Minister of Justice): In reply to the first part of the
question, an inspector visited Addington Prison within 24 hours of the escape. The
department awaits a full report from the superintendent. This has been delayed because
some of the injured officers could not be questioned at the time. Secondly, any comment on
the matters raised will have to await the report. Thirdly, all medium security prisons are
overcrowded. The muster at Addington Prison can be reduced only by increasing strains
elsewhere. However, it cannot be assumed at this stage that overcrowding caused the riot.
Fourthly, steps have been taken to reinforce the staff at Addington, but in most prisons here
and overseas the staff are vulnerable to concerted attack. Fifthly, all possible steps will be
taken to guard against a similar outbreak in the future.

Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Deputy Prime Minister): I move, That this Bill be now read a

Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I want to take the opportunity afforded by this
third reading of reporting to the House at least some of the proceedings in Committee; and I
undertake that my reporting will not be nearly as lengthy as those proceedings were. Some
important aspects should be recorded, because I believe that the proceedings in Committee
last night exhibited a stubborness on the part of the Government that I found distressing,
and also a willingness to be indifferent to the quality of legislation, which disappointed me.
In both the introduction and second reading of the Bill I drew attention to what I
thought were defects—or, at any rate, a particular defect-in the Bill. During the second
reading debate it seemed quite plain that the Government paid no attention to that and was
quite prepared to go on, regardless of the need to make some amendments that I thought
were necessary. Indeed, in the Committee stage information emerged which showed that
criticisms I had levelled during the first two stages of the Bill cut more deeply than the
circumstances had then suggested to me. I had believed that we were setting out to cure
some incidents that may have occurred—and I use the word “may”, because it is not
certain-within the last 2 or 3 years, but during the Committee stage the Acting Prime
Minister, who was in charge of the Bill, said that the practice went back to 1957; so it is not
just a matter of 2 or 3 years, but of some 20 years. The member for Franklin intervened in
the debate to say this was all a storm in a teacup, and undeniably the discussion wound
through a detailed course that might have wearied some members who are not as interested
as I am in constitutional questions. But I think it is much more than a storm in a teacup. The
member used that phrase because, in his judgment, no problem of any magnitude had
surfaced during the period; in any case what the Bill sought to achieve was of no great
importance, and the number of people affected is limited. In effect, I judged what he was
saying to be this: that what we have before us now is near enough and ought to do what is
required to be done.
Well, near enough is not good enough. As I said last night, it is unreasonable to expect
this Parliament or any Parliament to put through perfect legislation. There will always be
defects of one kind or another, simply because we do not have time to give to Bills the
minute inspection that is required of a judge when a section in an Act comes before him for

I shall summarise in very short compass what the Bill does-and it is a technical Bill.
Clause 2 provides that where the House resolves that any particular matter before it—a Bill,
for instance-is carried over to a succeeding session it shall not lapse on the prorogation or
dissolution or expiration by effluxion of time of the Parliament in being. That provision is
contained in subclause (1) of clause 2. Subclause (2) goes on to say that where any business
survives a dissolution of a Parliament the House may provide, by that resolution passed at
the time or by any subsequent resolution passed in the same session, for that business to be
continued while Parliament is not in session. A distinction must be made between the
prorogation of a Parliament to continue with the same Parliament next year, and the
dissolution of a Parliament to be followed by an election and the creation of a new
Parliament, because when Parliament is dissolved it ceases to exist, and for business to be
continued when Parliament is not in session after an election means that the business will be
continued while Parliament is in fact not in being. It is not in existence. It does not come into
being until Parliament is assembled and the elected members are sworn. The subclause goes
on to say that in those circumstances provision is made for the appointment of members to a
committee, and for varying the membership of that committee.
The next subclause states: "Every such committee shall have . . . the privileges,
immunities, and powers of a Select Committee of the House of Representatives, and shall be
deemed to be a committee of the House of Representatives". I am not wholly confident, but
I have little doubt that that will cure future defects. I do not believe, however, that it cures
defects that may have occurred in the past and, as I said, the past has been shown as going
back over 20 years. Members sitting on the committee unsworn will be protected from the
liability they may be under for a breach of the immunities that attach to them, and
particularly liability to a civil suit for damages for defamation. The provision also enables
them to enjoy the privileges and the protection of the Standing Orders. Subclause (4) goes
on to say that a member may sit or vote as a member of a committee notwithstanding that he
has not taken the oath. This is the matter to which I take exception. I believe it is desirable to
make that provision retrospective and to ensure that anything that may have been done over
that considerable period of years will be cured. I suggested a form of words that would
achieve that objective. They might be improved on; it may be that some different form of
words is desirable. At all events, I am sure some language is required to make sure not only
that we secure protection for the future but also that we secure protection for what may have
been done over a period going back several years. That disposes of that matter.
The next and only remaining clause is entitled "Validation", and it was on this clause
that the Acting Prime Minister relied as being an answer to my argument. I say, and I
continue to say, that that has nothing to do with it. It deals with a totally different point. That
clause simply says, "An Act resulting from the passing . . . of a Bill carried
forward"-notwithstanding that it may have been initiated in one session and perfected in
another-shall be exempt from criticism, because “anything done under any such Act,
whether before or after the commencement of this Act, shall be as valid and effective as if
the introduction and passing of the Bill, and all other proceedings... had taken place within
one session."
Rt. Hon. B. E. Talboys: All being part of the proceedings of the House of Representa-
tives and any committee in relation to it?
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY: Proceedings taken under the Act, not under the Bill; in
relation not to the Bill, but to the Act. This applies solely to an Act, not to a Bill, and says
that no exception can be taken to an Act of Parliament on the ground that its passage has
spanned two sessions of Parliament. It is a small point, I concede, and one could be charged
with making a mountain out of a mole hill; but I do not think that is right. It is our job to see
that legislation is as good as we can make it, and even if a defect is minor its preservation is a
criticism that can be levelled against us. Our job is to do the very best we can with legislation,
notwithstanding the fact that there may be defects in it that are examinable and open to
criticism by a court at a later stage. There is a legislative vacuum that needs to be filled. I
have suggested a way of filling it, and I am ready to consider whether an alternative may be
better than the words I have suggested. I have no doubt whatsoever that there is a vacuum,
and it is no great credit to us that we pass a Bill that should have remedial words included in
it.

The Bill will be found deficient in relation to the constitution and the statutes of the

Mr SPEAKER: I issue a word of admonition in this matter. It is one of the valued
practices and privileges of the House that, when a member feels his honour has been
impugned or something of very strong emotional significance has happened so that he feels a
great urge to correct it, or if he feels that he has done a wrong to somebody else by making a
mistaken statement and he wants to correct that, he seeks leave to make a personal
explanation, and the House almost invariably grants leave. I encourage the House in any
way I can to grant such leave. But if a member feels that in the course of debate someone
else has said something that he disagrees with, or even something that is incorrect, I think it
comes near to abusing the privilege merely to correct that statement, unless it is of such
strong emotional import as to impugn the honour of the member rather than something that
is mistakenly, or, he may suggest wilfully, put the wrong way. In the absence of feeling either
that their honour is impugned or that they have unwittingly been unfair to some other
person, I feel that members should be very slow to seek leave to make personal explana-
tions.

TERRITORIAL SEA AND EXCLUSIVE ECONOMIC ZONE BILL
Interrupted debate on the question, That this Bill be now read a second time.
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone): Last night I commenced my speech just before the
adjournment of the House. The member for South Canterbury, and the member for
Western Hutt, who preceded me, said that the Bill was an outstanding achievement for the
present Government. However, this could not be further from the truth. The Bill is the
result of many years of discussion at the Law of the Sea Conference, an agency of the United
Nations. Arising out of that world debate, many countries, including smaller ones such as
Fiji and Samoa, have taken the initiative in establishing an exclusive 200-mile economic zone
around their shores. There is, therefore, nothing special about the National Government's
action. I am sure the Minister in charge of the Bill would agree with me that there would
have been concern if the Government had not introduced this measure. The New Zealand
fishing industry has been urging the Government to declare such a zone, and to give the
legislation some urgency. If other urgent Government business had not prevented the
Minister from being present at the select committee hearings he would have known the
concern of the fishing interests.
The 17 submissions made to the committee expressed hope for the early implementation
of the legislation, and an indication was given that the Bill could become law about October.
The wealthy nations, which have the power to exploit the 200-mile economic zones, are
taking a very strong interest in the outcome of the Law of the Sea Conference. The
developing Third World countries need to have their interests protected, and are vitally
concerned with the final outcome of the deliberations. The committee was fortunate in
hearing from officers of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, especially those who had partici-
pated in the various sessions of the Law of the Sea Conference. Mr Mansfield's report was
very valuable. He told the committee that the Law of the Sea Conference is at present
deadlocked on one or two vital issues, especially minerals and manganese nodules. The
latter is of great interest to New Zealand, because there are considerable deposits of
manganese nodules in its economic zone. The legal status of economic zones is one of the
major issues to be resolved at the conference. A package deal is emerging from the
conference, which will resume again in March 1978. It is likely that two further concessions
will be necessary before the deal can be completed.
As the Minister indicated last night, the conference has been under way since 1970.
Major nations such as the United States of America have as many as 100 representatives at
the conference, and the 2000 other delegates represent 140 to 150 countries. Although New
Zealand's participation in the conference has been small, it has also been very effective. The
officers of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs are to be congratulated on their effective
outstanding representation of New Zealand, which has much to gain or lose from the
outcome, and from the carving up of the wealth of the oceans. The Foreign Affairs personnel
have won some important concessions for New Zealand. One matter that was successfuly
resolved in New Zealand's favour was the inclusion in the zone of the small off-shore islands
such as the Chatham Islands, Auckland Island, Campbell Island, and the Kermadec Islands.
New Zealand's economic zone is now the fourth largest in the world.
The future wealth derived from the zone could have a very significant bearing on the
country's future. Despite this, the Bill could be said to show unilateral action by New
Zealand, which perhaps should have awaited the final outcome of the Law of the Sea
Conference. However, it is unlikely that there will be any conflict between the final draft on

the economic zone, and this Bill. If there is a clash of interest, then no doubt Parliament will

Many States have made similar unilateral claims to a 200-mile economic zone, and more
are likely to follow. The New Zealand Bill closely follows the revised single negotiating text,
which has received substantial approval from 150 of the States participating in the Law of the
Sea Conference. With the 200-mile zone, New Zealand gains a new dimension. For the first
time in our history we now have a common border with Australia, where our economic zone
merges with the Australian zone, at about Norfolk and Macquarie Islands. In a single step,
New Zealand will jump from being one of the world's smallest nations to having control of
the fourth largest territorial sea region in the world. Our neighbours in the Pacific are
moving in a similar direction. Naturally, there is great interest from the super powers. A few
months ago the South Pacific Forum discussed the implications of these zones for the region.
The very heavy responsibility of managing New Zealand's economic zone rests with the
Government. We will control considerable wealth, and I hope that, as a country, we will not
be too selfish about that wealth.
It is significant that the committee had no submissions from the major powers which will
be greatly affected by the implementation of the Bill, and I think particularly of countries
like Japan-which has a major fishing interest off our coast-the United States, Korea, and
Russia, to mention a few that have apparently accepted New Zealand's right to extend its
economic zone in this way. Apparently, they are prepared to negotiate fishing and mineral

balance, with which the rest of the Bill deals.
Clause 13 is the first provision dealing with the balance, and is headed "Apportionment
of allowable catch for foreign craft". This is a good clause, and provides that the Minister
shall consider the past history of overseas fishing vessels and overseas fishing companies in
foreign countries. In other words, he will see whether they had been engaged habitually in
fishing within our exclusive economic zone. He will also consider whether they have co-
operated with New Zealand fisheries in research, and whether they have co-operated with
New Zealand in the conservation and management of our fishing resource. I emphasise that
I consider that a very good clause, in that it ensures that the Minister will look carefully at
the record of the Japanese and the Soviets, or whoever else might be interested, and check to
see that it is a good one, before he decides on how he will apportion the balance of the
fisheries resource. Logically, he will also consult the Minister of Foreign Affairs on the other
factors that come into international trading.
We then come to the actual licensing clauses. The conditions under which licences may
be granted are set out in clause 15. In particular I refer to the fact that the Minister may
attach to a licence conditions on many aspects, and certainly on all or any of the following
matters. He will lay down the areas within which fishing is authorised under the licence; the

age, and quantities of fish that may be taken; the methods by which fish may be taken; the

checked when they come in and checked again when they go out. He will also lay down
statistical and other information required, and rules about the conduct of foreign fishing
craft, and certainly about the display on board the foreign fishing craft of the licence issued
to it, the marking of the craft, and other means for its identification. That ties in closely with
the means of policing, control, and co-ordination, because the signs will have to be readable
from the sea and from the air. Further down in the list of details covering the licence, it is
provided that the Minister may order the installation on the foreign fishing craft and
maintenance in working order of a transponder or other equipment. Here again I refer to the
mechanics of carrying out control, and believe this will be a key piece of equipment enabling
the vessel to be checked by electronic means through the signal as it is flown over or passed.
A tremendous number of conditions are laid down in clause 15, but I believe they are all
sound and answer the requirements. Certainly they were backed by everyone who presented

which relates to licensing offences, but merely comment that it is adequate, and backs up the
law by providing for sensible penalties. Clause 20 provides for the extension and cancellation
of licences, and gives the power to control by suspension and also by confiscation. Further on
in the Bill there are a number of clauses that provide the teeth of arrest. I refer particularly
to the apprehension of offenders and the change made in clause 23 by the select committee.
The original subclause (7) was struck out and replaced by a new one, which provides that
"where any fish is detained under subsection (1) of this subclause, it will be held in the
custody of the Crown (either on board the foreign fishing craft from which it was seized or in
such other place as the Minister may direct)". Without the insertion of the words "held on
board the foreign fishing craft" the policing authorities would have had a very difficult task.

inclusion of those words was definitely needed. I consider that part of the Bill is now very
good indeed.

I should like to refer in passing to clause 27, on which there has been some comment.
Members opposite have been urging the Minister and the Government to get on with it, and
I am sure that most New Zealand fishermen want the Government to move fairly quickly.
The clause deals with the interim and transitional measures. They are very important,
particularly to most of the people who made submissions. Anyone who has viewed at night
from an aeroplane the floating cities out at sea will realise the effect on the local fishermen of
seeing that tonnage of fish, as mentioned by the member for Petone, being taken almost
under their eyes. Therefore, I welcome clause 27.
Before concluding, I should like to speak briefly about the administration and policing
of the area. Obviously I am not in a position to say what will happen, but all of us can make
assumptions. Certainly I have heard many silly assumptions made by people outside this
House. Some people seem to think that the only hope for our defence forces is to take part in
policing our fisheries, but that is nonsense. Our Navy is needed for much more than hunting
and checking on fishing vessels, and to suggest otherwise is an insult to the Navy. I am sorry
that the Minister of Fisheries is not here to deal with this subject, because many people
would like to know how control will be exercised. It is a very interesting topic, and we could
well ask what effect it will have on our defence forces; what extension will be needed in
fisheries protection; who will control it, and where it will be controlled from. All those
details will be given by the Minister, but I simply want to make some assumptions. First,
there will not be a lot of frigates or other naval vessels rushing here and there checking on
foreign fishing vessels. Secondly, very small fisheries protection craft will not be sent into
rough waters to do the same. The secret of control will be in the setting up of good control
centres, partly staffed, and certainly assisted by defence personnel, and probably controlled
by personnel from the fisheries division of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries. We can
also assume that, because of their expertise and background, our defence forces have been
slowly working on this subject to gather information. I would be surprised if they have not
mapped, plotted, and recorded data.
The next question is, how will control work? I believe it is fairly simple once a good
control centre has been set up. Air surveillance can be used as part of training for Air Force
personnel. This ties in with the provisions of clause 15(3) (m) dealing with the marking of
foreign fishing craft and with the use of other means of identification, such as transponders.
In other words, a licence having been issued, it will be possible at least to plot where the
fishing vessels should be, as long as the identification carried by them can be read from
aircraft. By such means we can check whether they are in the right place. Other fishing
vessels will provide reports, because with this type of cut-throat competition it will not be
difficult to obtain adverse reports from fishermen if a competitor is working outside his
licensed zone. To a certain extent reports can be made by the civil airlines, such as Safeair
during its flights to the Chatham Islands. There could be observers on ships in some
instances, as laid down in the Bill, particularly if a a licence is granted to transfer fish at sea.
We have to realise that at times it will be necessary for the Minister to grant licences to
permit the transfer of fish from a small ship to a mother ship in subzones well away from
port. There will have to be some permanent on-the-spot checks by teams of observers, and
observers will also be needed to check on net sizes and the different species being taken, and
on the conduct of ships at entrance and exit gates or at ports.
Finally, I should like to comment on the way in which punishments or penalties will
work, and again I can only make assumptions from my reading of the Bill. Clause 19, dealing
with licensing offences, is sound. The greatest punishment-and this came clearly through
from the submissions at the select committee-will not be the fine, but the loss of fish, and
we can do something about that provided we have storage on shore or authority to hold fish
on the vessel. I am sure that much of the policing can be done at Ministerial level or at
Ministry of Foreign Affairs level. We can deal straight with the foreign company concerned,
and I am sure that the threat of the loss of the fish, as mentioned in the Marlborough paper
from which I meant to quote, will be an important deterrent. It is quite obvious that the
Japanese particularly want to come back here, and nothing would be a greater punishment to
them than the loss of their licences.
The aim of the Bill is to make provision for the exploration and exploitation, conserva-
tion and management, of this 200-nautical-mile zone. This is one of the greatest leaps
forward for this country since Waitangi. The Bill charts a very sound course for our future in
the overseas trade for fish. It is a great thrill for fishermen to know that Parliament is doing
something about it. I thank the Opposition members for their co-operation on the select

Mr LANGE (Mangere): It is something of a distinction to follow in two successive
debates speakers who have referred to measures before the House as, first, being a great
leap forward for mankind, and second, the greatest leap forward for New Zealand since
Waitangi. I shall try to do justice to that type of entry into a debate.
The member for Marlborough asserted that the nautical mile varied according to the
part of the globe in which you were. He tended to run down the idea that it could actually be
measured in metric terms. However, the interpretation clause contains a definition of
nautical mile as meaning the international nautical mile of 1852 metres. I am sure that both
he and I have learnt something about metrication of previously specific nautical distances.
This Bill has an impact other than on fishing, which quite reasonably has been the major
subject of the debate thus far. Part I declares the territorial sea of New Zealand, and
observes simply the extent and influence of the sovereignty of New Zealand over an area
four times that which pertained before the Bill was introduced. That recalls to mind the time
when I was acting for a young man who wrecked a bar in a liner coming down the New
Zealand coast. During a day in court the liner's progress was plotted, and because it was 3.6
nautical miles off the coast at the time, and since the consent of the Attorney-General had
not been sought, no action could lie against that young man. By this Bill New Zealand is
extending its power to control New Zealand citizens without specific reference to the
Attorney-General.
The Ross Dependency in Antarctica will also come within the provisions of Part I
without qualification, and that is in breach of the spirit of the Antarctic Treaty enshrined in
the Antarctica Act 1960. Part I provides that where there is now territorial sea, the bed of
the territorial sea and the internal waters are vested in the Crown and deemed to have always
been so vested. However, the spirit of the Antarctic Treaty was that there would be no
extraterritorial claims by any party, but that such claims as were current at the time of the
treaty would be held in limbo, and each party agreed to honour certain arrangements about
the territorial sea. I suggest that Part I, extending as it does the territorial sea concept to
Antarctica, is in breach of that treaty.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: What dates?
Mr LANGE: If the member looks up the 1970 amendment to the Antarctica Act he will
find it in the first schedule. The member for Waitemata might do that instead of venturing
dates.
I turn now to the issue of the economic zone, and this is where there should be, and are,
some misgivings about the legislation. I do not disagree with New Zealand's falling in with
international arrangements and respecting the conventions that those conferences have now
reached, but I do suggest that the principle set out in the Bill is wrong in that we are relying
far too heavily on the power of a Minister to issue a regulation, and that Parliament is
surrendering its power to a Minister and allowing him to make our law by Order in Council. I
refer specifically to Part II, which is deemed to come into force at such time as the Governor-
General by Order in Council may declare. Until that is done, under the "Interim and
transitional measures" in clause 27 the Minister has unfettered power to make such
regulations as he thinks appropriate for the conservation and management of fisheries
resources beyond the territorial sea, and he also has the power to prescribe the penalities of
up to $100,000 for breaching the offences that he-not the House-has created. That is a bad
provision, because the House should determine the measure of control New Zealand should
exercise within its economic zone.
I suggest that one reason clause 27 is in the Bill is that Part II contains clauses 12 and 13,
which allow the Minister to apportion the available catch between domestic and foreign
fishing fleets, and within those fleets. I also suggest that Part II is not in operation because
the Minister will need all the mileage he can get by taking powers under clause 27, so he need
not have regard to the factors set out in clause 13. As I understand it, clause 13 reflects the
understandings reached at international conferences as to the duty of host countries to make
available unfished resources to fleets from countries that previously exploited those
resources. By bringing clause 13 into play, but relying on ministerial ordinance under clause
27, the House is authorising the Minister to fly in the face of international convention.
Under clause 13 the Minister must have regard to whether the fishing craft he is
proposing to licence has a history of fishing New Zealand waters. He does not have to take
that into account if he acts under clause 27. Under clause 13 the Minister must also have
regard to whether those countries have co-operated in fisheries research, the conservation

suggest that that is the way in which our fishing industry should be developed.

used Nimrod aircraft for surveillance. It seemed to me that our Orion aircraft, provided they

The Bill's provisions covering licensing offences, suspension and cancellation of

I turn first to clause 2, the interpretation clause, and the definition of the word “bay”,
which is integral to the coastal concept from which the zone is measured. The clause
describes a bay as being “an indentation of the coast such that its area is not less than that of
the semi-circle whose diameter is a line drawn across the mouth of the indentation". I
wonder if the Minister could tell us how big an indentation must be before it is considered to
be a bay. For instance, is Poverty Bay considered to be an indentation? Is New Plymouth to
Cape Reinga a bay, or is the small area within that indentation comprising Raglan and Port
Waikato a bay for the purposes of this measurement? The clause limits that with subclause
(a) by stating: "The area of an indentation shall be taken to be the area bounded by low-
water mark around the shore of the indentation and the straight line joining the low-water
marks of its natural entrance points". That seems to me to be a rather vague phrase that is
capable of a variety of interpretations, and just where you determine there is an indentation
that is a bay, or whether you decide it is part of a larger bight, which normally is a bay, I do
not know. I should like the Minister to tell me.
Appended to the Bill is a map that is of no legislative force whatsoever showing a series
of semi-circles drawn around the New Zealand coast. If one looks at that it seems as if the
natural entrance points are totally disregarded, and it is the larger bay area that is the
starting point from which the 200-mile area is measured. That point should be cleared up
before we dispose of the Bill so that we know just what it is that we are legislating for, and
what area of coast measured by which departure point.
The next point I want to take up with the Minister is clause 8(c), which enables
regulations to be made regulating the construction, operation, and use of artificial islands,

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Attorney-General): I do not propose to take up the fairly
esoteric issues raised by the honourable member for Henderson. I prefer to leave them to
the Minister. I do, however, as Attorney-General want to make one or two comments about
this historic Bill, a Bill that I feel very privileged to make a few comments on at this stage. In
another capacity I am giving material expression to my belief that this is historic legislation
by proposing, as Postmaster-General, that there be a special stamp issue to commemorate
the declaration of the 200-mile zone which will appear when the zone is an accomplished
fact.
I should like to talk briefly about the legality of what we are doing in passing this
legislation-not that this has been an issue, but for the sake of the record I feel that
something should be said. My mind goes back to a visit I made to Lima in Peru in 1972, when
foreign affairs officials there were very much involved in the law of the sea. Peru was one of
the first nations to declare a 200-mile zone. It did so to assert jurisdiction over the anchovy
shoals that inhabit an area of the eastern Pacific separated by the cold Humboldt current
from the South American coast. Peru was prepared to take the step of unilaterally declaring
a 200-mile zone off its coast, and in those days it was regarded as a rather extravagant step to
take. Now, between 35 and 40 maritime nations have done the same thing.
Times have changed, and they have changed very quickly. It is, however, an unusal step
for New Zealand to take such action ahead of the signing of an international convention—as
the member for Henderson would agree-particularly when we need the protection of that
international convention, not having the international muscle effectively to assert our rights
without the force of law behind us. International law is, of course, no more made up
exclusively of conventions than our own domestic law is made up of statutes alone. There is
also customary international law, which the member for Henderson referred to, that builds


## p. 2450 (#88) ############################################

2450
24 August
Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Bill
up over time, where there is sufficient acceptance within the international community for a
rule or a concept that may fall short of a fully consummated convention, but none the less
can be acted upon as accepted law.
The Law of the Sea Conference has dragged on and on, admittedly for good reasons, to
the point where the facts of life-and in particular the intensification of the exploitation of
fish-have led between 35 and 40 maritime nations to make unilateral declarations of fishing
and/or economic zones. To date most have declared only fishing zones. New Zealand and a
few others have gone a step further by declaring 200-mile economic zones as well. We do so
on the basis that an international custom has developed with respect to such declarations,
and-though there is not yet a convention in existence-we and a lot of other nations in
effect assert that it is not illegal to declare such a zone; we do so with the near certain
knowledge that there will be no challenge in any international court.
The international community's intent about the declaration of these zones is now clear,
and it is only the deep sea bed issue that holds up the consummation of the convention. We
are not alone. Australia is in the process of drafting such legislation. Canada, the United
States, and the United Kingdom have already declared such zones. More to the point and
most relevant to our own position, the USSR and Japan are not in a position to challenge the
legality of our action, having themselves already declared support for the 200-mile concept.
I should like to allude briefly to the specific problem of surveillance. Certainly the idea
of a small country with limited resources embarking on surveillance of the fourth largest
economic zone in the world does, at first sight, present possibly formidable problems. A
number of ideas have been put forward for the most effective surveillance of the zone. One
suggestion-and I am sure other people have heard it—was that perhaps the economic zone
could be divided into specified areas for the interested maritime powers. They could then
conduct their own surveillance in their own zones. While this may have some superficial
attraction, frankly it is not a realistic proposition. For a start, it is in derogation of the
sovereign rights that we have taken in this Bill, and we would not want these to be qualified
by in effect delegating to foreign maritime powers the task of surveillance, though we would
certainly expect them to police their own ships pursuant to agreements that will be reached.
Secondly, this idea cuts across one of the important provisions of the Bill, which is to
reserve for New Zealand the right to determine the total allowable catch and apportion it.
Thirdly, the fish are not evenly spread throughout the economic zone; they move from one
area to another, and no one has yet developed with real precision a method of predicting the
way in which even supposedly non-migratory fish travel from one area to another over large
areas of sea.
This then leaves a surveillance problem. None the less, I believe there is no need to be
defeatist about our ability to implement our surveillance role effectively in the future. We
know, for example, that satellite technology is being developed overseas to a very high
degree of sophistication. We know that with the aid of satellites it is possible to detect ships
as ships in a large area of ocean. With growing technology we may soon, with the aid of
satellites, be able to detect ships by type. With good communication with the maritime
powers that fish within our zone, and with their full co-operation about the location of their
vessels, there is no reason why a very effective system of surveillance cannot be evolved.
I want now to allude briefly to environmental matters, which to my way of thinking are
of considerable importance. During the past few years, with the worldwide surge in
environmental concern, attention has inevitably turned to the ocean. Some very alarming
facts have been uncovered. For example, it has been learnt that on average between
5 000 000 and 10 000 000 tonnes of oil pour, leak, or are spilled into the ocean every year.
The sea has become the repository for everything from atomic waste to mustard gas, from
used cars to non-biodegradable plastic that will never decay. We have had warnings from
such eminent scientists as Jacques Cousteau that without control there will very definitely be
a day of reckoning.
As the Minister for the Environment pointed out in a recent speech when opening
Conservation Week, although the conservation of the oceanic environment is everybody's
responsibility, it has, in the past, been nobody's responsibility. Now, with many maritime
States declaring economic management zones, sizable areas of ocean are at last under some
specific jurisdiction. Clause 25 gives New Zealand power to make regulations for the
protection and preservation of the marine environment of the zone. In my opinion, that
provision is potentially one of the most far reaching in the Bill.
Last night the member for Mt. Albert went on at great length about the need to secure

the maximum benefit for New Zealand, without acknowledging the very important provi-

As other members have said, this is historic legislation. Perhaps, when the history of
the 1970s is written, this Bill will rank as one of the most important. New Zealand is an island
country, and is isolated in the greatest expanse of sea in the world. It is dependent on
maritime transport for its well-being; is surrounded by waters relatively unpolluted, by world
standards, with resources the limits of which nobody can presume to predict—but there is
every indication that they are very great. Legislation of this sort is necessary not just for the
protection of our own interests; it is also in keeping with the actions of several other
maritime countries to start bringing to an end the chaotic state of affairs that has predomi-
nated for too long in jurisdictional matters affecting the sea and its exploitation.

COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES BILL
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. As honourable members will be well aware, this is a very short Bill of six
clauses and two schedules. It is very much of a routine nature. The Bill has two purposes.
The first is to enable the membership of the Commonwealth to be more easily ascertained
for the purposes of interpreting New Zealand legislation. There are, of course, a number of
New Zealand statutes containing provisions relating to Commonwealth countries. By way of
example I refer honourable members to the Visiting Forces Act 1939 and the Shipping and
Seamen Act 1952.
Experience has shown that it has been difficult in court cases to determine whether a
country was a member of the Commonwealth on a particular date. The first schedule to the
Bill sets out all the members of the Commonwealth, and power is given to the Governor-
General in Council to add to the first schedule the names of countries that subsequently
become members of the Commonwealth, and to delete the names of countries that leave. In
the past, when a country has become a member of the Commonwealth, but is a republic
recognising Her Majesty the Queen as Head of the Commonwealth but not accepting her as
Head of State, special legislation has been introduced to ensure that reference in New
Zealand legislation to the Commonwealth and to the countries of the Commonwealth
applies to that particular country. The Bill will accomplish this by simply adding to the
schedule, and the Commonwealth Countries Act will stand for them all.
The Bill also makes provision for a certificate to be issued by the Secretary of Foreign
Affairs when, in a specific instance before the court, the schedule is not accurate. This could
occur when a country has left the Commonwealth-Pakistan for example-but the proceed-
ings before the court relate to a time when the country was still a member.
The second purpose of the Bill is to streamline in one short measure a provision which in
the past has been made in separate Acts for virtually every Commonwealth country.
Previously it has been the practice for Parliament to pass separate Acts for each Common-


## p. 2454 (#92) ############################################

2454
24 August
Commonwealth Countries Bill
wealth country that becomes independent. This procedure has been necessary because in
various legislation-the Reciprocal Enforcement of Judgments Act and the Fugitive Offen-
ders Act are examples-Commonwealth countries are referred to as "Her Majesty's
Dominions". Honourable members will appreciate that in recent times most of the newly
independent countries have become republics. The Bill will enable us to bring into one Act
all the separate legislation, and in future all that will be necessary as Commonwealth
countries change their status is an amendment of the schedule by Order in Council. That is
really the beginning and the end of this legislation.
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert): The Opposition has examined this Bill and, as was
intimated when it was introduced, agrees with the principle. It is a tidying-up procedure, but
I must confess that I was a little concerned to hear the Minister say, "This is the beginning
and the end of this legislation." I hope that is not so, and that it will be used frequently. The
Labour Party holds very closely to the belief that the Commonwealth is and should remain a
very important section of the international scene. Since the end of the war there has been a
major change in the structure of the Commonwealth. Although the time span might seem
considerable to some, in a relatively short period in man's development major changes have
taken place within the Commonwealth as throughout the world. One has only to look at the
second schedule to the Bill to realise how frequently Parliament has been called upon to
clarify the status of a member of the Commonwealth.
From time to time, for reasons best known to themselves, countries have changed their
status, and over the years Parliament has been required to introduce legislation accepting
that changed status. As I have said, the Bill tidies that up. It gives the Governor-General the
authority to make adjustments by way of regulation as the circumstances require; but we on
this side of the House hope that in the foreseeable future there will be no requirement for the
Governor-General to amend the legislation so that nations are deleted. Our first considera-
tion must surely be to see that the Commonwealth remains as strong as it is today. It is the
responsibility of all in this House, and certainly the responsibility of governments of the
more affluent members of the Commonwealth, to see that those within the group who are
desperately in need of assistance are assisted. I have been pleased to notice that the Prime
Minister has recently made several speeches in which he has made it abundantly clear that he
believes there should be a greater effort on the part of the wealthier Commonwealth nations
to help those which are less fortunate.
I do not want to go into the whole matter of aid on this Bill, because I realise, Mr
Speaker, that you would quite properly draw my attention to the fact that it contains nothing
relating to aid; but the principle is very important in the Commonwealth's development.
Without arguing whether we give enough aid—and we on this side of the House do not think
the aid given to the Commonwealth is adequate—I can say that the Opposition believes that,
when the Bill is passed, the Government should do everything it can to strengthen the
Commonwealth bond. The basis for doing that is to increase the economic stability of the
less fortunate Commonwealth nations and to continue to expand the preferential import
licensing procedures and other trading opportunities for the nations that so desperately need
that help. We commend the Bill and endorse its principle, believing that it will be a much
tidier way of dealing with what is likely to be a constantly changing Commonwealth
situation.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): I thank the honourable
member for his comment, and I do not argue with what he said. Every New Zealander has a

BUILDING PERFORMANCE GUARANTEE CORPORATION BILL
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. In its 1975 election manifesto the National Party stated: "A building perform-
ance guarantee scheme will be introduced to protect the home buyer from false claims for
unsatisfactory workmanship, and to help promote and maintain the ethical and professional
standards of the building industry." This Bill gives effect to that promise. It was introduced
towards the end of the 1976 session and referred to the Commerce and Mining Committee
for recess study. Submissions were received from virtually all directly involved parties and
organisations; as a result, several amendments have been made. The Bill as it now appears
before the House is, I believe, a much improved document. I thank particularly those
members of the Government caucus housing committee who worked so hard over a long
period to put this scheme into legislative form-in particular, I thank my colleagues the
member for Birkenhead, the member for Kapiti, and the member for Rangiora. The
evidence given to the committee has also enabled us to present a Bill that will allow the
promise in our policy to be fully implemented.
The Bill is divided into six parts. I propose explaining each part and the considerations
that led to the acceptance of the approach finally adopted. In determining its philosophical
attitude, the Government had a choice: it could either build the scheme around the concept
of guaranteeing the performance of the builder, or it could give a warranty relating to the
home itself, which would apply within the time limits proposed regardless of whether the
owner was a party to the original building contract or not. In the event, we have been able to
achieve a fairly neat balance. At the same time, we have had to make sure that the legislation
does not unfairly tip the balance in favour of either the home owner or the home builder.
The conscientious builder who scrupulously observes his responsibilities is equally entitled to
protection against vexatious and frivolous claims as is the owner against defective or
negligent workmanship, or faulty materials.
Clause 2 contains the definitions. I draw attention particularly to the definitions of
"builder", "building contract", and "building contractor". As one of the purposes of the Bill
is to make sure that the terms of a building contract are complied with, or that if they are not
relief can be afforded, it is essential that the parties and the terms used are precisely defined.
So "builder" includes subcontractors and agents; a building contract must be written, and
must refer to a residential building; and the building contractor is the person who signs the
contract and who, in the first instance, is responsible in all respects. As long as the building
contractor is legally capable of carrying out that role, then all claims finish with him.
However, if he is no longer available within the 6-year term, then rights must be pursued
through to other parties, and for this reason the term "builder" is given the wider meaning.
Then we come to "residential building". It is important that we know the type of
building that can be covered by an indemnity granted under this Bill. Remembering that the
purpose of the Bill is to give protection to the home owner, the definition of residential
building makes sure that only buildings intended for use exclusively or principally as a
dwelling are covered. Thus, a doctor's surgery attached to a house would not preclude the
house from inclusion under the Bill. The definition embraces own-your-own flats and blocks
of flats, but would exclude hostels.
Part I of the Bill establishes the corporation. It is proposed that the corporation shall
consist of six members: the chairman to be appointed by the Minister, one member to be
appointed after consultation with the New Zealand Master Builders Federation, one
member to be appointed after consultation with the Consumers Institute, one member to be


## p. 2456 (#94) ############################################

2456
24 August
Building Performance Guarantee Corporation Bill
appointed after consultation with the New Zealand Manufacturers Association, and one
member to be appointed by the Minister, plus the Director-General of the Housing
Corporation. I am sure that a corporation so widely representative of those whom the Bill
affects will be able to administer the scheme with sympathy and impartiality. I emphasise
that the three members to be appointed after consultation will not be representatives of
those organisations, but will be members of the corporation, to provide an overall balance in
the corporation's composition.
I should at this stage comment on the two suggestions that were made and are relevant
in discussing Part I of the Bill. First, that the scheme might have been better if, instead of
establishing a new corporation, we had allowed the Master Builders Federation and the
Consumers Institute to operate it jointly. Overseas experience indicates that for such a
scheme to work, and to work in the impartial manner that is desirable, it should be
administered by an independent body.
In the original Bill it was proposed that the Building Performance Guarantee Corpora-
tion should consist of a chairman and between one and four members appointed by the
Minister, together with the Director-General of the Housing Corporation and the general
manager of the guarantee corporation if he was not an officer of the Housing Corporation.
Evidence was given to the select committee that a corporation with this constitution could be
interpreted as being too closely associated with the Housing Corporation, and that, as the
Housing Corporation could be an interested party as mortgagee, this would be undesirable. I
accepted this criticism, and for this reason we have changed the composition to that which I
outlined a few minutes ago. I am confident that such a corporation will give full effect to the
intentions of the scheme.
Part II of the Bill defines the functions and powers of the corporation. The functions are
simply those which are necessary to carry out the election promise of the Government. Part
III is an important part of the Bill. It sets out the details of the indemnities that the
corporation may issue, the terms of the indemnity, and describes the risks that are included,
as well as clearly listing those matters that are not covered. A person wishing to have a house
built will apply to the corporation, nominating his builder, and the corporation will, for a fee,
issue him with an indemnity which may be subject to such conditions as the corporation
deems fit. The corporation will have the discretion to refuse to issue an indemnity. As I have
already said, the purpose of the Bill is to provide protection to the home owner against a
builder who fails to perform satisfactorily.
Mr Hunt: It doesn't do it very effectively.
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: The fact that the member for New Lynn makes that sort of
comment does not impress me one little bit. I imagine that as the corporation builds up a
fund of experience it will be able to sort out those builders whose record indicates they are a
bad risk, and I can envisage that there will be some in respect of whom the corporation will
refuse to issue an indemnity. The builder of a "spec" house will himself apply for an
indemnity. He cannot, of course, indemnify himself against his own workmanship, but he
will be able to offer to a subsequent purchaser an indemnity that will give added confidence
and protection to his customer. Clause 21(4) provides that every indemnity and the
protection it affords attaches to and runs with the land or residential building to which it
applies. It is, therefore, fully transferable from owner to owner during its currency.
Clause 22 provides that an indemnity shall be for a period of 3 years for materials and 6
years for any other cause, generally workmanship or design faults. In the original Bill the
indemnity period for materials was 2 years. In addition, many materials will be covered by
warranties issued by the manufacturer. The change to 3 years was made for several reasons.
Clause 21(5) establishes that the indemnity period begins when it is executed by the
corporation. However, the proviso to clause 22 delays the commencement of the 3- or 6-year
period until the start of work by the builder if notice of this is given within 7 days.
Clause 24 deals with claims. Clearly there has to be a limit within which claims must be
made, and this has been set at 90 days after the damage or other subject-matter of the claim
became known to the owner, or which by reasonable diligence he ought to have known
about. Having regard to the fact that the residential building may have taken from 3 to 12
months or even longer to complete, and that the indemnity starts from the commencement
of building, I thought that 3 years 'was a more realistic indemnity period for materials. At the
same time, the Government was faced with the problem of deciding whether the 90 days in
which notice had to be given should extend beyond the actual indemnity period. If it did,
there was a real risk that as the period reached maturity there would be a rush to establish


## p. 2457 (#95) ############################################

24 August
2457
Building Performance Guarantee Corporation Bill
claims, and it would be very difficult to determine whether or not they qualified or occurred
within the indemnity period. It was thought better, therefore, to extend the 2-year period to
3 years, and require claims to be made inside the indemnity period. In the case of the 6-year
period, it was considered that no hardship would result if claims were required to be lodged
before it had expired.
Clause 23 deals with the risks that are covered, and those that are not. In broad terms,
the indemnity can be defined as covering three areas: first, any failure to carry out the terms
of the building contract; secondly, any failure to erect in accordance with the standards of a
competent and diligent builder; and, thirdly, any significant defect in the materials-in other
words, the contract, the standards of workmanship, and the materials. Paragraphs (a) to (1)
of subclause (2) set up clearly those aspects that are not covered. In essence, they amount to
factors over which the builder has no control. and include normal wear and tear; damage
caused by improper maintenance or lack of normal maintenance; any defect in design,
materials, or workmanship that has been agreed to or accepted by the owner; and any
designs, materials, or labour supplied by the owner other than with the prior consent of the
corporation. Finally, in this clause subclause (3) enables the corporation to modify the terms
of its indemnity by excluding specific matters, or by including any of those specifically
excluded by clause 23(2).
Part IV is the other important practical part of the Bill. It sets out the responsibilities of
both the owner and the corporation in making and dealing with claims. Clause 4 I have
already dealt with to the extent that it provides that claims must be made in writing within 90
days of the owner's becoming aware of the defects. The corporation must investigate the
claim and advise the owner whether or not the claim is accepted.
Debate interrupted.

Poison for Noxious Animals-Research
1. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Minister of Agriculture: Did he see the report
carried on TV1 on 14 June 1977 which referred to a new killer poison three to four times

necessary Agricultural Chemicals Board registration?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I reply on behalf of the Minister of Agricul-
ture: The chemical in question is a coded compound, two samples of which have been
imported into New Zealand and made available to the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries
research stations at Wallaceville and Invermay. It is an anticoagulant and it is being
evaluated as a possible poison for opossums and rabbits, with particular emphasis being
placed on tests to determine its toxicity to non-target species. The chemical's common name
and the chemical name are known only to the research workers and to the Agricultural
Chemicals Board. Registration is not required at present as it is being evaluated only at
Government research stations.
Mr Bruce Barclay: Is the Minister able to give any information about the residual effects
of this poison in the animals?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I cannot give any more information than I have given. The

Inflation-Comparative Statistics
12. Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth) asked the Minister of Statistics: Has he seen
the comment of the Labour member for Wanganui in the Wanganui Herald dated 10 August
1977, under the heading "57-year target", in which the Labour member claims "The
National Government's ambition of single-figure inflation would take 57 years to accomplish
at the present rate of improvement"; and, if so, is his claim correct, and how does the
present National Government's handling of the rate of inflation compare with the Labour
Government's record?
Mr Hunt: A point of order, Mr Speaker. I did not raise the matter the first time the
member did it, but the member added three words into the question printed in the Order
Paper. I suggest that this is clearly out of order under the Standing Orders.
Mr SPEAKER: When a question is to be asked there is a procedure to be followed.
Notice is given of the question, which is passed into the Clerk's office. Some doubtful
questions are referred—all too often, I am afraid—to myself. If the question then asked in
the House is different from the one that has been through the procedure, that clearly is out
of order, and we may as well not have the procedure. A member could put in one question
and ask a different one in the House. I did not notice that the question was different. The
difference could perhaps be mentioned, and then I can decide.
Mr Friedlander: I notice that the question that I lodged is slightly different from that
printed in the Order Paper, but the substance is the same. I would read it again as printed in
the Order Paper, if it would suit the House.
Mr SPEAKER: We are trying to get through 27 questions today, and I do not want to
waste time if we can avoid it. I suggest to honourable members that they be most careful not
to submit one question through the proper channels and then ask a different one in the
House, even if it is only mildly different. There may be good reason for it, but it is not good
enough. It must be asked as put in. Were the changes such that the honourable member
raising the point feels the re-reading of the question is warranted?
Mr Hunt: No.
Mr SPEAKER: Well, the point having been raised, would honourable members please
note in future to read the question as it has been submitted? Now we will have it answered,
in spite of the minor alterations.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics): I have seen the statement referred to,
and the honourable member for Wanganui has ignored the reductions in the rate of inflation
that the Government had achieved by the June quarter 1977, when the inflation curve had
declined to an annual rate of some 14 percent. Had he used this June quarter figure he would
have come up with a totally different answer, much closer to that of the 1977 OECD survey
report, which records a clear deceleration in the rate of inflation in 1976 and early 1977 in
New Zealand. Whereas the Government, in the 18 months since it took office, has made
significant reductions in the annual rate of inflation, the second Labour Government in its
first 18 months permitted the annual rate of inflation to treble, from some 1.9 percent to 5.8
percent, which is very close to the performance of the third Labour Government, when the
rate rose from 5.5 percent in December 1972 to 15.7 percent in December 1975.
Mr Hunt: Would the Minister not admit that the inflation rate for the second Labour
Government in the year 1960-61 was less than 1 percent for the whole year?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: Yes, I will admit that, but in terms of the performance of the
second Labour Government there was a very significant rise, a trebling, in the first 18
months, very similar to the record of the third Labour Government.

tion?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): Yes, I have seen the article referred
to. The Government's 1975 election manifesto and the associated publicity material dealing
with national superannuation made it quite clear that telephone and television concessions
will continue to be available to national superannuitants at the same rates and with the same
income tests as applied when National took office. This is exactly what the Government has
done. At the time the Government took office, the income limits for the concessions, under
the former age benefit scheme, were $88.20 a week for married couples and $60.80 a week
for unmarried persons. In accordance with our manifesto undertaking, these income limits
still apply. The only section of beneficiaries who no longer qualify for concessions are those
national superannuitants whose income exceeds the qualifying limit. All these people have
had substantial increases in their cash-in-hand payments under national superannuation. The
New Zealand Railways travel concession is still available to all former age beneficiaries now
receiving national superannuation, and will not be withdrawn until August 1978 when the
rate of national superannuation will be based on 80 percent of the average ordinary-time
weekly wage for a married couple. Several public statements have been made to this effect.
When national superannuation reaches 80 percent of the average ordinary-time weekly wage
for a married couple, the relationship between the benefit and the average ordinary-time
weekly wage will be such that further concessions will no longer be justified.
Mr Friedlander: In view of the statement made by the member for Wanganui, has that

Hon. H. J. WALKER: The Labour member for Wanganui is not the only member
opposite who has not been able to produce such a case. National superannuitants are all
substantially better off because of the introduction of the scheme.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Is it not a fact that contrary to what the Minister has said in his
reply the National Party's 1975 manifesto policy statement made no mention whatsoever
about telephone, television, and railway concessions being withdrawn? I have a copy of the

Hon. H. J. WALKER: There is no need for the member to show me. I have a copy of
the policy here, and I quote: "Telephone, television, and rate concessions will continue for
the same categories of beneficiaries, using the same means test and at the same rates as are
applicable when National assumes office." I understand copies of the 1975 National Party
manifesto are still available at $1 a copy, if members opposite would care to buy one.

Education-Kindergarten Teachers
21. Mr HUNT (New Lynn), on behalf of Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui), asked the
Minister of Education: Why do unemployed kindergarten teachers not have the same right to
apply for jobs as those in employment?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): Kindergarten teachers who are not
currently employed in the kindergarten service do have the same right to apply for
advertised vacancies as those who are in employment. However, there is still a large number
of bonded kindergarten teachers surplus to the establishment employed as supernumerary
teachers, and they, together with other teachers currently employed in the service, must be
given preference of appointment over those who are seeking to return, until all supernumer-
ary teachers have had the opportunity to win permanent positions. I hope it will be possible
to remove the preference position before the end of 1978.
Mr Hunt: As in the first part of his answer the Minister said that unemployed
kindergarten teachers have the same right to apply for jobs as those in employment but then
went on to say that those in employment received a preference, how can that possibly be
interpreted as being the same right to apply for jobs with the expectation of getting them?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: Of course they have the same right. Nobody is taking the right to
apply away from them. However, it is a question of whether or not they are appointed. The
member asked why they did not have the same right to apply for jobs as those in
employment. When an appointment is to be made to a senior position, particularly a head
teacher position, a supernumerary teacher does not have an automatic right to that
appointment. It is left to the employing authority to choose on merit.

Pills-Extra Cost of Strip Packaging
22. Mr COUCH (Wairarapa) asked the Minister of Health: In view of his department's
decision that six kinds of pills will be sold after October in individual strip tape packing, does
he know the likely extra cost of this procedure for 12 months for the country, and does his
department propose to extend the order to all other pills?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): As the regulations for the strip packaging of the
six groups of medicines do not apply to manufacturers until at least 1 September 1977, and to
retail pharmacies until at least 1 December 1977, it is not possible at present to indicate the
total extra cost. The Department of Trade and Industry estimates that the cost of strip
packaging will be less than 1c a tablet. Some medicines within the six groups had already
been strip packaged by certain manufacturers on their own initiative and independently of
the requirements of the regulations. At present there are no proposals to extend strip
packing to other drugs.
Mr Couch: What was the department's reason for strip tape packing?
Hon. T. F. GILL: The Government directed that strip packaging should be used for
these six drugs to avoid their overuse, particularly by young children under the age of five. In
1976, 1384 young children under the age of five were poisoned. Strip packaging will also
avoid the misuse of drugs-particularly barbiturates, tranquillisers, and certain
antidepressants-by elderly people who, perhaps in the middle of the night when they feel
they want a pill, are not always capable of selecting the right bottle and counting the right
number of pills to take.
Mr Couch: Does the Government expect this move to stop the poisoning of young
children?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Yes, it does. The many trials that have been carried out show that a
young child might open a bottle of pills, take a handful out, and eat a number. But the
difficulty of forcing his way into the strip packaging means that, at the most, he is likely to
get only one, and, having found that it was not very attractive in taste or in any other
gets bored with the proposition and does not take any more.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) said that the $1.15 million allocated last year had been
considerably underspent, by almost 30 percent. That had been surprising, because energy
resources played a very important role. The main reason for the underexpenditure had been
the Government's on-again, off-again policy on home insulation, and the fact that loans for
that purpose had been reduced from $150 to $85.
It was the last time the Commissioner of Energy Resources would be present for the
consideration of the Energy Resources estimate, as the department was to be disestablished.
The small department had been established by the previous National Government towards
the end of 1972, and had operated with a staff of 32 or 34. The commissioner and his staff
should be thanked for their contribution during a difficult period. No sooner had they put
their feet under the table than the energy crisis had hit the world—and had hit New Zealand
very hard early in 1973. The commissioner and his staff had been called upon to deal with a
crisis, and at one time the introduction of petrol rationing had had to be considered. As
Minister of Mines he had called upon the department to produce a white paper on the future
of the coal industry in New Zealand. A very valuable document signposting the road for coal
in the years ahead had been produced.
The Government's energy pricing policy was difficult to understand. Just when the
Government should have been encouraging the use of New Zealand's indigenous energy
resources it had introduced a pricing policy having the opposite effect. Why had the cost of
electricity been increased by 90 percent, natural gas by a similar amount, and coal by 82.9
percent, while industrial fuel oil had increased by only 17 percent?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources) said that the claims from the various
power authorities for handling the home insulation scheme had been available for only 9
months of the financial year, so the remaining 3 months would come to charge in the
following year. That accounted for the underexpenditure in the vote. It was appropriate that
the Committee should formally record a message of appreciation and a debt of gratitude to
the Commissioner of Energy Resources and his comparatively small staff for the work they
had undertaken, particularly at a time when the country's energy future had been
threatened.

Partly as a result of the Government's conservation programme and partly because of
the Government's development of alternative fuels, the country's previously high level of
dependency on imported energy had been reduced. In 1973 imported oil had accounted for
66 percent of total primary energy consumption. Because of increased production of natural
gas and condensate from Kapuni, conservation, and the use of coal, the percentage was
expected to fall to 45 in the current year. With the availability of Maui gas, increased coal
production, and further conservation, it was expected that the downward trend in depend-
ence on imported fuel would continue until at least 1985.
On a base of 100 for imported fuel oil, for industrial use coal worked out at 59, natural
gas at 75, and electricity at 153; so there was clearly a strong inducement to those requiring
energy for industry to use coal or natural gas as alternatives to imported fuel oil or
electricity, the last units of which were also produced by fuel oil.
