The Budget had presented comprehensive, wide-ranging, and imaginative energy
policies on conservation, exploration, research, the use of our natural resources, and pricing;
all of which had a bearing on what was a tremendously important problem. As Minister of
Science and Technology, he had been happy to assist the Minister of Energy Resources in
the development of those policies. An adequate energy pricing policy was one of the most
important ways of controlling energy consumption. Because electricity prices were now
based on cost, solar energy packages for homes were now very nearly economic. That had
not been the case previously.
The development of small hydro resources required adequate scientific back-up, not
only in the building of dams, but in the examination of soil structure and various botanical
and entomological features. The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research would be
setting up programmes to achieve that.
A $10 million on-shore exploration project had been announced in the Budget. It would
involve a great variety of scientific research and endeavour, in which the DSIR would play its
part. The enlargement of geothermal energy offered great possibilities, and DSIR staff
numbers were being increased to handle the research and development required. Provided
geothermal capability was used correctly and developed successfully, over the next 30 years
there could be a capacity of between 1750 and 2500 MW in our geothermal fields.
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources) said that the Government had seen fit
to do what the private sector had chosen not to do: set about the task of proving-and this
could be done only by drilling-whether there were deposits of oil or gas in several areas in
which the private sector had previously taken an interest, but had stepped away. Not only
must the Government try to find oil and gas, but if there was none it was important to
establish that as soon as possible, so that alternative energy policies could be developed. The
private sector no longer had an interest in five of the six oilfields it had been involved in.
As a partner in off-shore exploration, the Government received the information
available to the other partners; otherwise it had only such information as was on open file
and available to the public. No large oilfield had yet been found, but the Prime Minister had
made the point-as had been reported in the newspapers and was public knowledge—that
geological features in the Great South Basin had led the Government to believe it was worth
while investing a considerable sum of money, in partnership with the Hunt-Phillips consor-
tium, in prospecting in that area. Any find would have to be very large to be commercially
exploitable. The drilling was now at a depth of 2000 feet or more, and could be described as
"working at the rough edge of technology", which meant that the chances of finding a
commercially exploitable field were now that much less.
In the 6 months to July 1977 the coal levy had provided about $2 million and the gas levy
about $13 million, a total of $15 million. As had been stated in the Budget, the estimated
income from levies in the current financial year was $28 million, which compared with a very
much larger sum set aside by the Government for exploratory drilling and research.
Excluding exploratory drilling, provision for the expenditure of $3,714,000 had been made
for energy research and development in the 1977-78 financial year. Part of the amount would
be provided in the Scientific and Industrial Research vote, some would come through the
Energy Research and Development Committee, and some would be spread among Govern-
ment departments with an interest in energy.
A very useful contribution to New Zealand's energy future was also being made through
the exploratory drilling programme-coal, $2.06 million; geothermal, $4 million; off-shore
petroleum, $22.5 million; and on-shore petroleum, $10 million. The total cost of that
programme was $42,279,000, very much more than the $28 million expected to be raised
through energy levies.
The Commissioner of Energy Resources and his department had coped well with the
energy crisis and the development of sound energy policies. The Budget had placed very
strong emphasis on energy. Geothermal energy could make a considerable contribution to
New Zealand's future energy requirements.
The skills required for the oil programme would be bought in the first instance by
contract. Later, permanent staff would be engaged for the proposed new Government oil
company. In a letter to a New Zealand geologist who was abroad, a copy of which he was
prepared to table, he had outlined the skills required for senior positions. An operations
manager would be needed to supervise and control the operational and technical aspects of
the on-shore exploration drilling programme. He would need an appropriate degree and
extensive experience in the management of on-shore petroleum exploration. Also, a senior


## p. 2485 (#123) ###########################################

25 August
2485
Appropriation Bill-Estimates
petroleum drilling engineer, a senior petroleum geologist, and a senior petroleum geophysi-
cist as well as a drilling supervisor would be required. Contacts had been made with
consultants able to advise on the mix of skills required. The Government had been an active
partner in drilling and development operations for years, and a considerable body of skills
had been associated with the Government for some time. He did not belong to that group of
people, which unfortunately some Opposition members did, who were anxious to underplay
New Zealand skills and qualifications.
Progress reported.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
DG3 Dam at Clyde
1. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Mines: Has he seen the article
in the Dunedin Evening Star of 2 August 1977 by the newspaper's energy reporter stating
that "the proposed DG3 dam at Clyde could ruin a multi-million coal industry", and will he
state whether any investigation as to the possible coal and lignite deposits in the Cromwell
basin was undertaken and appraised before a final decision was made to proceed with the
scheme?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines): First I should like to thank the member for
agreeing to have this question transferred from an earlier day this week so that I could
answer it personally. I have seen the Dunedin Evening Star article of 2 August 1977
concerning hypothetical lignite deposits in the vicinity of the proposed DG3 dam. The
possible conflicts between the Clutha Valley hydro proposals and the development of the
mineral resources of the region have been taken into consideration since the early stages of
the proposals. The lignite deposits referred to were reported in 1971 to be of no economic
importance by the interdepartmental committee on the effects of the hydro-electric develop-


## p. 2488 (#126) ###########################################

2488
26 August
Oral Answers to Questions
ment proposals. As a result, detailed study of the lignite was not undertaken at the time.
There is, however, a proposal that there should be further studies, and we must remember
that we are dealing with hypothetical deposits, not proven deposits.
Hon. F. M. Colman: I am pleased to hear the Minister say that the deposits were
hypothetical. That is surely the basis of the question. If it is implied that the deposits are
hypothetical, and if they have been considered on that basis, would not the Minister agree
that it is almost essential if there is a considerable deposit of coal or lignite in the vicinity—a
deposit that could be recovered either by opencast or underground mining-that it should be
urgently appraised?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: It is important that the House and the member asking the question
should understand that there are numerous instances in Southland and Otago of lignite
deposits of one sort or another. Many of them are comparatively small. In fact, there is
reason to believe that there may be something of greater consequence in the Cromwell basin
itself. I remind the member too that whether the dams concerned in scheme H or scheme F
are involved, if there is a question of water covering the deposits this would still apply. I also
remind him that there are several examples where, in the course of developing hydro dams,
drills have discovered small coal deposits, and it therefore becomes a question of choosing
one type of energy development as against another. This was taken into full account when
the original proposals were considered and the schemes were originally designed. Opposi-
tion members will be aware of this, because at one stage the Labour Government approved
scheme' H, which covered very much the same area.

Coal Digging-Use of Mechanical Shovel
2. Mr BLANCHFIELD (West Coast) asked the Minister of Mines: Has he any plans to
use the mechanical shovel with a 10 cu yd (7.65 m³) bite, at present stored at Stockton and
Ngakawau, for its designed purpose of digging coal or removing overburden in the near
future?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines): The 10 cu yd shovel stored at Stockton was
procured for the removal of overburden overlying coal seams. The utilisation of the machine
is currently under review. It had been hoped that the shovel could be used in the mining of
coal for the West Coast thermal power station, but this station is now a number of years
away so consideration is being given to taking the shovel to Huntly, where it would be used
in opencasts associated with the supply of coal to the Huntly power station. The original
purchase, as the member will recall, was related to the earlier proposal to fire the New
Plymouth power station with either oil or coal. As a result of the Maui find the coal proposal
was removed and replaced with the gas alternative.
Mr Blanchfield: With the knowledge of the value of this indigenous fuel at Stockton, are
there no plans in the immediate future to extract the coal, and what is the purpose of sending
the shovel out of the district?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: It is believed that the large shovel can best be used in the Huntly
area, where there is a need to supply coal to the Huntly power station, which is due to be
completed in a matter of months, rather than waiting years as would apply to the West Coast
project.
Hon. F. M. Colman: If this piece of equipment is to be transferred to Huntly, does it
rule out the possibility of proceeding with the Buller thermal station; and if the Buller station
is to be proceeded with, would it not be appropriate to keep the equipment in the area?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: When I am able to table the power planning document for 1977 the

Mr Blanchfield: Would the Minister elucidate his statement that the thermal station at

Hon. G. F. GAIR: I am intrigued that the Leader of the Opposition could be so naive
about some of the physical problems with which the planners must cope. This machine was
ordered a number of years ago. It was a specially designed shovel for the New Zealand
situation, including New Zealand's wiring requirements. Between the time when the
machine was ordered and construction of it had commenced, and the time it could be
delivered, there was the important discovery of Maui. The Government of the day properly
chose to change the energy form for the New Plymouth power station from a coal or oil
alternative to an oil or gas alternative. An endeavour was made at the time to cancel the
order, but the construction had proceeded too far, and, because of the type of electrical
wiring that was designed specially for New Zealand circumstances and is not common in
other parts of the world, it was not possible for the machine to be resold as a new machine.

more today than it was at the time we bought it, and it is still in new condition.

present value should be estimated for 3 years, by which time some other use for the shovel
on an economic basis might be found. The calculation which derived the $200,000 payment
took account of storage and administration costs, and costs of deterioration and obsolesc-
ence, but the major component was the cost of financing the purchase at the Treasury-
nominated 8 percent rate of interest 3 years earlier than needed.” In other words, the Mines
Department was compensated by the New Zealand Electricity Department. I remind the
honourable member that, although this machine is stored in an unused condition in his part
of the world, I do not know of any efforts he made when his Government was in office for 3
years to do anything about solving this problem. We are now doing something.

Motorcar Models
6. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: What
positive action has been taken to stabilise or reduce the number of motorcar models
assembled in New Zealand?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): The honourable
member will be aware that the problem of model proliferation in the New Zealand
automotive industry is a complex and long-standing one, and I know that he has in the past
made statements about it. My view is that any satisfactory long-term solutions are unlikely
until a complete review of the industry and the policies that govern it is completed. Ideally,
this should take place in the course of the industry study programme, and I am hopeful all
sections of the industry will co-operate on such an exercise in the near future. As an interim
measure, I have already instructed my department to arrange a meeting with the motor
vehicle assemblers to discuss ways in which the number of models and model variants could
be at least stabilised, and possibly reduced. This meeting will take place next week, and
thereafter early consideration will be given to the lines of action which might be taken by the
industry and by the Government.
Hon. W. W. Freer: As the Minister is going to wait until there is an industry study, when
is the Industries Development Commission likely to commence such a study, and how long
will it take?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I cannot answer the first part of the question. I have
not discussed it with the commission. My view is that the meeting to be held next week by my
officers with the assembly industry should take place first. Replying to the second part of the
question, such a review would be comprehensive, and could take 18 months to 2 years to
complete. The important part of the situation is that we want the industry to agree to some
voluntary arrangement to see if we can reduce the variant aspect of the problem in the
interim.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Does the Minister intend to allow any new models or marques to be
introduced to the New Zealand market while this investigation or inquiry is proceeding?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: New models would be permitted, but only within
the tight criteria operating at the moment. A marque would have had to be deleted from the
New Zealand market, thereby making unused capacity available in the assembly plant. That
is the general rule. There could be exceptions for trade policy reasons outside of it, but I
hope we will not have to find such exceptions. If it is desirable for trade policy reasons to
have a new marque in New Zealand, I hope that the firms concerned will arrange an
agreement that will enable assembly to be undertaken in a plant where there has been a loss
of marque, and therefore room available.

Comalco-Clutha Power Usage
8. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Electricity: Has he seen the
report in the Dunedin Evening Star of 23 July saying that Comalco will use some of the
Clutha power, and can he state whether this is to be the case, and, if so, what effect will it
have on the present pricing agreement and on the amount of power available for other
purposes?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Electricity): I have seen the report to which I believe the
honourable member refers, where that statement was made. However, New Zealand has a
fully integrated power system, and alternative power developments are normally planned on
this basis. The concept of regional power allocations is a somewhat artificial view which is
not consistent with the way the power system is planned and operated. The allocation of
Manapouri power to Comalco, under the Act, is an exception arising from the historical
intention of developing and operating the Manapouri-Bluff smelter link in isolation from the
national grid. The present pricing agreement for supply to Comalco is in accordance with the
terms incorporated in the Manapouri and Te Anau Development Act. Discussions are at
present taking place regarding the pricing agreement with a view to revision taking into
account changed circumstances, and it is hoped that these discussions will produce a result
fair to both parties. Because these discussions are confidential, I am not in a position to give
any more detail.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Does Comalco have a contractual arrangement to have power
supplied from a source other than Manapouri, and, if so, under what terms and conditions,
and are those terms and conditions different from those that apply to Manapouri power?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I cannot answer that question off the cuff as it involves a more
intimate knowledge of the contract than I at present have. I remind the honourable member
that the Government and Comalco have been involved in very serious and earnest discus-
sions for some time. I think it will be some little while before those discussions are
completed. Quite frankly, to comment publicly or speculate on the outcome would be
unfortunate, and not in the best national interest.

Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I reply on behalf of

very important question and the member for Northern Maori may wish to submit a further
question for written answer to obtain more details. The Prime Minister's answer is as
follows: "To take the second part of the question first, a number of substantial developments
in the area of job training for young Maoris are either being studied or are being
implemented. For example: first, an inter-departmental committee is presently engaged in
examining programmes for raising the socio-economic status of the non-European popula-

training and promotion of various Maori activities. Secondly, the Vocational Training
Council is currently conducting research on the attitudes and behaviour of the multicultural
work force by initially studying five New Zealand companies.
"Thirdly, Cabinet has approved for 1978 pre-employment courses for young Maoris
from areas where no apprenticeship opportunities exist. The courses, which will be
concerned with introducing young rural Maoris to the urban life and urban employment,
have a target intake for 1978 of 90 boys and 125 girls. Trainees will be able to pass the first
qualifying test for the Trades Certification Board examination, which will become the main
attraction to an employer. Fourthly, the trade training schemes will be extended in 1978 with
the addition of four new courses, provision for 56 more trainees, and the establishment of
the scheme at the Taranaki Polytechnic, New Plymouth. This will mean that 16 different
courses will be offered to 370 trainees at 5 centres throughout New Zealand in 1978. Fifthly,
on 29 July 1977 the Minister of Labour announced the extension of the private sector
employment subsidy scheme, which is vitally concerned with arming young people with
skills, qualifications, and work qualifications needed to enable them to enter the labour
market. If these employment schemes and studies presently under way are successful, it is
my hope that there will be little need for the Government to provide any company with
further incentives to employ young Maoris."

BUILDING PERFORMANCE GUARANTEE CORPORATION BILL
Interrupted debate on the question, That this Bill be now read a second time.
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): When the debate was interrupted on
Wednesday evening I had started to discuss Part IV, which is one of the more practical parts
of the Bill. It sets out the responsibilities of both the owner and the corporation in making
and dealing with claims. Clause 24 I have already dealt with to the extent that it provides that
claims must be made in writing within 90 days of the owner becoming aware of the defect.
The corporation must investigate the claim and advise the owner whether the claim is
accepted.
In the case of a claim being accepted, the first duty of the owner will be to have it put
right by the builder. The corporation is not obliged or required to deal with the claim until
the claimant—that is, the owner-has taken all reasonable steps to have the matter dealt
with by the builder. Submissions were made to the select committee that this could be used
by the corporation to avoid its responsibilities. With this in mind I had a good look at these
provisions to see if it was possible to reduce this cause of concern. Consideration was given
to the insertion of the phrase "short of legal action". However, it is my view that this is
neither necessary nor desirable. After all, the corporation will be a quasi-Government body
and it would be extremely unlikely to want to defeat its raison d'être in this way. I believe
each case should be dealt with on merit, and that the corporation should be given the
greatest possible freedom to determine its own procedures and establish its own method of
operation.
I envisage that once the corporation has become involved it will act in a role rather like
that of a mediator. It will first endeavour to persuade the builder to correct the damage or
defect. Failing this, it will either reimburse the owner for the assessed cost of rectifying the
fault, or arrange for another builder to carry out the work needed. At this stage the
corporation assumes all the rights of the owner to the claim and may take such action,
including suing the builder, as is necessary to recover any satisfied claim. In order to
discourage vexatious or frivolous claims a franchise of $100 is imposed. The effect of this is
simply to require the owner to meet the first $100 of any damage or the costs of repairing any
defect. It will apply only once in each indemnity. In other words, after the $100 has been
deducted from a claim all other claims made in respect of the same dwelling will be met in
full.
Subclause (6) of clause 25 originally provided that there should be no appeal against a
ruling or decision of the corporation except on a point of law, or when the amount involved
was $100,000 or more. This aspect of the Bill was the subject of criticism from those who
appeared before the select committee. The original hope had been that the corporation
would be able to make a "once and for all" decision and that the parties would be required to
accept it without an endless series of delays and frustrations while appeals were heard. The
committee decided to remove altogether the references to appeals, so the corporation's
decision will be subject to the same processes of the law as any other individual or
organisation of a similar type.
Some consideration was given to imposing a ceiling of, say, $5,000 or $10,000 to make
only claims of real substance subject to appeal, but that was discarded on the grounds that
wherever a line was drawn anomalies would occur-some will be just inside, while others
would miss by only a few dollars. The committee was persuaded by the submissions that it
would be unfair, both to the owner and the builder, if the corporation was to be the final
point at which a decision could be made. There was, for example, the situation where the
corporation may turn down a claim to find that later the owner succeeded in a civil court
action for breach of contract against the builder for something that was covered by the
indemnity. The corporation is being established principally to protect the home owner and to
ensure that the building contract is complied with, and its activities should not be secret or
inviolate.
I should also like to draw attention to the fact that the scheme should and will be
voluntary rather than compulsory. It is expected that in the early stages about 50 to 60


## p. 2499 (#137) ###########################################

26 August
2499
Building Performance Guarantee Corporation Bill
percent of new houses could well be covered by the scheme, with this figure gradually rising
in a few years to between 80 and 85 percent of all new homes. In addition, the corporation
will be included among those within the jurisdiction of the Ombudsman.
Part V and Part VI are mostly administrative, and will be better dealt with, if necessary,
during the Committee stage when they can be scrutinised in detail. The corporation gives
effect to a National Party election promise. It will, I am sure, represent a shield and a
protection to the new-home buyer, and will do much to improve the standards and ethics of
the building industry. I envisage that the corporation will establish local committees in the
larger cities to deal with complaints in the first instance and who will in fact settle or dispose
of most claims with a minimum of fuss and formality. Members will notice that the definition
of building inspector has been removed. It is not desirable that the corporation should
engage in empire building. Local body inspectors, private building assessors, quantity
surveyors, and architects are well qualified to carry out this aspect of the corporation's work,
and will be engaged by the corporation as and when necessary. Since the Bill was reported
back to the House from the Commerce and Mining Committee, the president of the Master
Builders Federation has requested some comparatively minor amendments. These do not in
any way affect the general principles of the Bill, but they do cover a few matters of detail and
drafting which were worrying the federation. While I have not been able to agree to all the
requests, I shall move a number of small amendments during the Committee stage, and I
propose to circulate these well in advance by way of a Supplementary Order Paper. I believe
that the corporation established by the Bill, and the purpose for which it is being established,
will make a significant contribution to home building standards and to the ethics and
standards within the building industry.
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau): The Bill is an attempt to establish a
mechanism—the Building Performance Guarantee Corporation-to indemnify purchasers
of new houses against defective workmanship and the use of defective materials by builders
and developers. What evidence do we have that a problem exists? There appears to be an
established need for some form of indemnity and/or protection from defective workmanship.
The Consumer Council produced in evidence a pilot survey of new-house construction in
Porirua, which showed that 23 percent of new-home owners had grave cause for dissatisfac-
tion with the standard of construction of their homes, and that nearly 40 percent of the
owners had experienced difficulty in ensuring that builders honoured contractual agreements
to repair defects.
The Consumers Institute told the committee that its complaints advisory service had
received 1495 housing complaints during 1976. About half-768 complaints—had related to
new houses. Half of the complaints were about leaking roofs, windows, and doors,
inadequate foundations, insufficient support for beams, and other structural difficulties. It
was clear that if a broader definition of faults had been included—for example, walls out of
alignment and use of finishing materials of different quality or type-then perhaps 85 to 90
percent of the complaints received by the institute would have been major claims. As the
institute stated, the problems identified might well be the tip of the iceberg.
We must ask ourselves what form of redress already exists; or, why is this Bill
necessary? New-home owners have recourse at present to common law and contract law. In
practice, however, there are two main reasons why it is difficult for them to gain satisfaction.
The first is that individuals have frequently extended themselves financially in purchasing a
new home and are not able to afford the substantial legal costs and the time. Also, the risk of
failure may deter many from legal action. The builder may operate as an incorporated
enterprise, and after a brief speculative entry into the building market may wind up the
company, and the home owner will find himself with no legally existing person to sue for
remedy of defects.
If the present channels of redress are inadequate, we have to ask whether the Bill
improves matters. It attempts to indemnify against defects, but does very little, if anything,
to remedy the basic cause of the problem-the poor standard of building. That is the core of
the problem, and the Bill does nothing to remedy it. The most appropriate form of
protection is not to insure against defects, but to introduce methods that will force builders
to be more attentive to standards and to remedy defects. In my view, the Bill in no way helps
solve the problem. It does not cover alterations to existing houses, or speculative housing;
nor does it provide indemnities for people purchasing existing houses or near-new houses.
Additions and alterations to existing homes, the cost of which amounts to some $95 million,
are also not covered in the Bill.

## p. 2500 (#138) ###########################################

Building Performance Guarantee Corporation Bill
Clause 25 provides for the payment of a $100 fee, which is far too much for those on
modest incomes to pay. Clause 25(3) provides that the corporation shall not be required to
repair or make good defects unless the claimant has, in the opinion of the corporation, taken
"all reasonable steps and measures to induce or compel" the builder to make good the defect
or pay compensation. If the aggrieved owner is required first to sue the builder, with the
expense and risk involved, much of the practical virtue of the indemnity will be lost. The
Consumer Council suggested in its submission that an interpretation of "taking all reason-
able steps" should mean no more than notifying the builder in writing by registered mail, and
lodging a complaint with the corporation if, after 3 weeks, the builder had not rectified the
faults or made a substantial start. This will basically depend on the interpretation the
corporation adopts, and the steps it requires the aggrieved party to take.
To summarise, the Bill amounts to less than the building industry itself was prepared to
do in 1971. At that time the Master Builders Federation was prepared to introduce a quite
comprehensive new-home warranty scheme based on the British model. That scheme was
shelved at the last moment. Six years later this Government is unable to equal the protection
that would have been afforded by the 1971 proposal.
As the Consumer Council said in its submission to the Commerce and Mining Commit-
tee: "We are surprised to find that the Government plan amounts to far less than what the
industry itself was proposing to do in 1971. Then, the Master Builders Federation was
prepared to introduce a comprehensive new-home warranty scheme in conjunction with a
number of other organisations, including the Consumer Council, Standards Association,
Real Estate Institute, N.Z. Institute of Architects, N.Z. Institute of Valuers, N.Z. Building
Societies Association, and N.Z. Master Builders Federation. This scheme was to be based
on the British model. Unfortunately it was shelved at the last moment. The Consumer
Council is deeply disappointed that 6 years later the Government is unable to equal the

Building Performance Guarantee Corporation Bill
been informed by Government members of the committee that the Labour members refused

The building performance guarantee scheme will provide the owner of a new home with
a comprehensive warranty. The scheme is to be established by statute, and it will be
controlled by an independent corporation. That will achieve certainty, it will achieve
continuity, and it will achieve the independence of the scheme. I know that some concern
has been expressed, particularly by the Master Builders Federation, that the corporation
might become another arm of the Housing Corporation. That was one of the federation's
three objections to the Bill contained in a letter that the member for Manukau did not read
to the House, but which I shall refer to later.
I emphasise as strongly as I can that it was never the intention of the original
subcommittee that drafted the report on which the Bill was based that the corporation
should become an arm of the Housing Corporation. The Building Performance Guarantee
Corporation is to be attached to the Housing Corporation for pay and rations purposes only,
in a manner very similar to the housing commission's connection with the corporation. This
has been done to prevent the growth of a new bureaucracy, and members from this side of
the House, at least, found it very desirable indeed. Similarly, the Director-General of the
Housing Corporation is a member of the guarantee corporation only because the guarantee
corporation will use the Housing Corporation's reserve funds to back its guarantees. I am
sure that even the Opposition would agree that such an arrangement is entirely acceptable.
I note with some pleasure that the select committee decided to amend clause 3(1)(b) to
specify that three of the five members of the corporation, apart from the independent
chairman and the Director-General of the Housing Corporation, should be appointed by the
Minister after consultation with the New Zealand Master Builders Federation, the Consum-
ers Institute, and the New Zealand Manufacturers Federation; after all, these are the bodies
that represent the three major interest groups in any matter of housing guarantees.
The building performance guarantee scheme will provide a guarantee by the builder to
the owner that the home is erected in accordance with the building contract, constructed in
accordance with the standards to be expected of a competent and diligent builder, and is free
from significant inherent defects in any material. Liability will naturally not extend to those
materials or that workmanship that is supplied by the owner himself with the corporation's
written consent, or to other matters not normally connected with the responsibilities of a
builder.
For quite logical reasons the corporation will not provide indemnity in respect of fire
and earthquake-which are covered by other types of insurance-landslip, subsidence, or
erosion-except where subsidence results from something directly attributable to the
builder's work. It also excludes normal wear and tear, damage caused by improper
maintenance, or normal shrinking. The effect of the Bill is also to give protection in the
event of a builder's being adjudged bankrupt or going into liquidation, or for some other
reason not completing his obligation under the contract. It is envisaged that in certain
circumstances this could include the completion of the erection of a home in accordance with
the building contract.
The subcommittee's original report suggested that the period of warranty should be 2
years for materials and 6 years for all other matters, a total of 6 years in all. I am delighted to
learn that after considering the submissions the select committee has been able to extend the
period of protection in respect of materials from 2 years to 3 years; this can only enhance
what was already a very good guarantee scheme.
The primary responsibility for performance of the warranty obligation will rest on the
builder. In effect, the corporation will step in only when a builder fails to fulfil his
obligations. Although the builder will continue to be liable for any claim made under the
warranty, the corporation will meet only claims of more than $100. The intention is to reduce
the incidence of claims of little consequence being made to the corporation. The warranty
scheme will be backed by the Housing Corporation's reserve fund; that is why a Housing

Corporation representative will sit on the board of the guarantee corporation. The fund is at

During the course of the subcommittee's work on the Bill, and since then, questions

are talking about will be more detrimental than beneficial. I detected that sort of argument

purchase of a new first home is often described-in my opinion quite correctly—as the
largest and most important investment in a person's lifetime. The existing legal obligations of
a builder are quite extensive, but it is often very expensive for a new-home owner to pursue
his legal rights, as he has already-as the member for Manukau quite rightly pointed
out-stretched himself financially to the limit in purchasing or building his new home.
The Consumers Institute, in a press statement in April 1976, recorded the fact that from
June 1973 to December 1975 its complaints advisory service had received 3010 housing
complaints and that one-third of them related to new houses. That represents about 2.2
percent of all houses built during that period, to a total value of more than $2 million. The
remainder of the complaints referred to renovations and alterations, which I have already
mentioned. The Consumers Institute took the view that most of the complaints were
justified, and believed that they represented only the tip of the iceberg since many people
did not bother to complain to the institute. However, apart from the number, the institute
was very much concerned about the serious nature of the complaints, especially complaints
about new houses. Furthermore, the New Zealand Master Builders Federation, while
pointing out that most complaints are against builders who are not members of the
federation—and I agree entirely with that-has expressed the opinion that "legislation is
essential if all homes built in the future are to be subject to some sort of guarantee". Overall,
and quite apart from the Government's election manifesto undertaking, I am completely
satisfied that there is a proven need for a guarantee scheme and that it must be incorporated
in legislation.
The member for Manukau mentioned the scheme that the Master Builders Federation
proposed 6 years ago, and said that it went further than this scheme. I challenge that
statement, because I have studied the 1971 scheme with considerable care, but, even so,
whether or not it went further than the master builders were prepared to go in 1971 is of
academic interest as, for one reason or another, the master builders did not implement that
1971 scheme. The fact remains that it has been left, not to the Labour Government that was
in power between 1972 and 1975, but to the National Government to provide a building
guarantee scheme.
A possible objection to a guarantee scheme is that it might involve the registration of
builders or the registration of sub-trades; I am pleased that this scheme does not involve
registration. A further objection, which was made by a prominent Auckland builder at the
time the Bill was introduced, was that it could increase the cost of building by at least $500.
That builder said his company would not be prepared to venture into new materials because
of the possibility of a claim under a guarantee in respect of those materials. In my opinion
that argument is fallacious. It rests on the belief that the new-home owner must in some way
bear the cost of proving new materials.
I believe that the present scheme, which does little more than reinforce existing legal
obligations, will not be an expensive scheme, particularly by comparison with those

parts of the world. It will provide an effective and inexpensive means for both the owner and
the builder to resolve disputes arising from the construction of the home. Although the
primary purpose is to protect the home owner, it will also protect the builder because it will
enable him to recover more easily moneys that might be held against the completion of
certain maintenance work on the house. As one builder, a senior man in the Master Builders
Federation, remarked at the conclusion of one of his discussions with my subcommittee,

People have always been worried about defects—particularly when they concern the first

appear to be structural defects. The problem manifests itself in various places. The area
referred to in the Consumer article quoted by the member for Dunedin was in my electorate,

During 1973 and 1974, Labour held its own building boom, despite the fact that it was
earnestly requested and advised by the Building Industry Advisory Council not to continue
to pour funds on to the flames of demand, which were going far too high at that time. Labour
continued to build up the demand for housing, and poured on the number of houses, and
succeeded in doubling prices. It also succeeded in halving the quality, because it brought in
all sorts of fringe operators-people who have since left the industry, and who were never
members of it on any traditional basis. They came in as labourers and decided they were
builders; they came in as professional men-accountants and solicitors-and employed
labour-only gangs. Everybody who knew how to handle a hammer thought he was a builder,
and the industry grew and developed—
Mr T. J. Young: Was the member himself a builder?
Mr BRILL: The member himself was not a builder, but an amazing number of people
came into the building industry during that time, and were responsible in no small part for
the outcry that arose for some action to be taken on building standards and controls.
Individuals are quite well protected by the existing law. In every contract for a design-
and-build house, or the purchase of a "spec" house before completion, there are three
implied warranties. There is a lack of understanding of the stringent obligations imposed
upon builders by the present law. A Court of Appeal decision in Britain in 1966, which has
been affirmed in New Zealand on at least three occasions, held that three warranties were
implied in every such contract: first, that the builder would do his work in a good and
workmanlike manner; secondly, that he would supply good and proper materials; and,
thirdly, that the house would be reasonably fit for human habitation.
Those protections exist, but to invoke them leads to costly court actions and, frequently,
lengthy delays, usually when the owner-occupier of the house is already financially
strained-particularly if it is a first home, on which he is probably paying off first and second
mortgages, and developing the section, laying floor coverings, and the like. That is no time
for him to be involved in protracted and expensive litigation. Indeed, the builder himself
might ultimately prove to be insolvent by the time a court case proceeded; he may be out of
the industry and, indeed, out of the country.
A further defect is that there is no relief available to a subsequent owner. Under the
existing law, a person who buys a near-new house—perhaps less than 1 year old-will get no
relief unless he is, in fact, the person who entered into the contract with the builder. In the
case of a "spec" house which is completed before sale, there is no relief under the present
law, the situation being covered by the well known maxim, caveat emptor.
It was to relieve all those difficulties-not to extend the liabilities of builders—that the
guarantee scheme was conceived, and a few aspects of the scheme are worthy of note. First,
it is a voluntary scheme. It is not imposed on every builder or owner, but there is a strong
incentive to take up the scheme, because in the future only those buildings that are
guaranteed will qualify for finance from State organisations-in particular, from the Housing
Corporation, but also from the Government Life Insurance Office and other departments.
Even if the owner of a house obtains his finance from a private source and is not concerned
about that matter, he may in due course wish to sell the property, and the purchaser could
have access to State funds through one agency or another. If he does not have a guarantee,
he will cut himself out of that market, because nobody who is to be financed by the State can
buy that house. That being so, there is a strong incentive for every owner to insist upon a
guarantee, and I believe that the great majority will do so. It is not imposed as an absolute
obligation, but a steadily increasing number of people will seek guarantees.
It should also be made clear that a person who does not have a guarantee on a house
does not qualify for a Housing Corporation guarantee on a mortgage. This is a scheme that
will be taken up more and more. It is now possible for any mortgagee lending on a property
to obtain from the Housing Corporation a guarantee of the moneys lent, provided he lends
on the approved standard terms. That provision will be increasingly taken advantage of, and


## p. 2508 (#146) ###########################################

2508
26 August
Building Performance Guarantee Corporation Bill
only those people who have a guaranteed home will be able to take advantage of the
mortgage guarantee.
If the scheme is adopted, a relatively low premium will be payable-probably less than
$100 on any one house-because the scheme is being operated by the Housing Corporation,
an existing organisation, and the guarantee has the backing of the Housing Corporation
reserve fund, which already exists. The scheme will be similar to those of private insurance
companies. The actual procedure is yet to be laid down by regulation, but it will be not
unlike an insurance cover. There will be a standard form or proposal, which will be accepted
almost automatically. The cover will run for 3 years on materials and 6 years on work-
manship-the period of the limitation Act. Like an insurance policy, it has a franchise of
$100, to discourage petty claims and to provide an incentive to resolve problems between the
parties themselves. Also, like an insurance policy, the owner must take reasonable steps to
help himself. If he cannot resolve the problem himself, he hands it over to the guarantee
corporation, which then takes over all rights against the builder. That is the way the Bill will
really carry out its primary purpose.
The Bill will provide peace of mind for the owner, as he will know that, although he may
have some preliminary difficulties with the builder, once the problem escalates to the stage
of becoming a major worry it will be taken over by the corporation, the work will be put
right, and he can then proceed to take advantage of his new home without having all the
delays and costs involved in the present procedures. I should have thought that such a
scheme would be welcomed by the Labour Opposition; after all, the Opposition sets itself up
as a party that is concerned for the consumer. Now that Labour members are in Opposition,
they have put forward various suggestions for consumer protection. While in office they did
nothing whatsoever to assist the home owner or to protect him against faulty building
practices, but now they are in Opposition they oppose the positive efforts made by the
Government to implement a policy in its election manifesto. However, despite their
opposition, the Bill will go through the House, and I certainly shall welcome its implementa-
tion.

MINISTRY OF ENERGY BILL
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. This Government has been concerned at the difficulties facing New Zealand in
assessing the future needs for energy, and ensuring adequate and reliable supplies. Not only
is imported petroleum becoming increasingly expensive, but New Zealand's own resources
are in some cases inadequately explored and in others can be developed only at a cost to
other goals and to the social and physical environment. We are determined that long-term
planning for all forms of energy will be fully developed and properly co-ordinated. This
planning must consider the resources currently known and the need to locate additional
resources. The new ministry must also make certain that resources are properly developed
and used without waste, and ensure that the benefits of research into and development of
scientific and technological improvements are applied as widely and promptly as practicable.
The elimination of energy wastage and the wise and balanced use of each form of energy
must also be given full attention.
The new ministry will have an important place in government. Its actions and recom-
mendations will affect not only New Zealand's way of life in the 1970s and 1980s, but the way
of life of our children and their children for the rest of this century and beyond. The Bill
ensures that the Government will have firm control over the formation of energy policies and
their implementation. Those responsibilities already discharged by Government depart-
ments are brought together. The Government's operations in petroleum and natural gas are
also to be amalgamated. A close link will be kept between the Ministry of Energy and the
Government's petroleum and gas operations. This arrangement will allow a more flexible
relationship in the petroleum and gas agencies owned by the Government, while ensuring
that they retain all the advantages of commercial relationships with their customers and
competitors. The Bill does not seek to define the internal structure of the new ministry. It
seems at this stage that the electricity and mines organisations will continue in their present
form while the ministry is being developed. However, there are possible forms of organisa-
tion, particularly in the head office of the ministry, which deserve careful evaluation, and
which the new Secretary of Energy may consider it useful to recommend at some future
stage.
The production of coal, electricity, and other forms of energy has always been
undertaken by organisations responsible for each particular type of energy, and this is likely
to continue. Mine workers and operators, and electricians and power station technicians,
have skills and undertake tasks that are quite different from each other. The evaluation of
the strengths and weaknesses of existing and proposed policies must be given the highest
priority in the new ministry. The staff undertaking these evaluations will be involved in some
of the most important decisions concerning New Zealand's future that have to be made in
the next few years. A group will be formed, including people with practical experience and


## p. 2513 (#151) ###########################################

26 August
2513
Ministry of Energy Bill
professional expertise in all aspects of energy production, economic and financial evaluation,
and the assessment of social, commercial, and industrial energy needs. There are, of course,
some staff in the Ministry of Energy Resources with the requisite experience and skill, but
much more is needed than has been achieved. Having said this, I should like to commend the
Commissioner of Energy Resources and his staff for their achievements in recent years. It
will be apparent to members that this Bill will enable the Minister of Energy to appoint
committees to advise or assist the Minister or the Secretary of Energy. Many people outside
the ministry and the Government sector have experience and expertise which could be of
immense value to New Zealand. It is my intention to involve them in the development of
New Zealand's energy operations and policies wherever appropriate. The work of the New
Zealand Energy Research and Development Committee, led by Dr Maiden, shows the
extent to which such committees can stimulate action and spread involvement in energy
considerations widely throughout New Zealand.
The functions of the new ministry include those of the Ministry of Energy Resources,
but are defined to give clearer directions to the Minister and the Secretary of Energy. The
formation of a new ministry in which policy development and production are linked enables
the Government to function as a more effective catalyst. The formulation of balanced
policies between different forms of energy is no longer left to co-ordination and co-operation
among several different departments of State. This is to be the responsibility of the Ministry
of Energy and, as such, is a clear expression of the Government's own policies.
In particular, the ministry is to be responsible for forecasting levels of demand for all
forms of energy, and for influencing energy demands so that they do not exceed the
reasonable capacities of our resources. One of the most effective ways in which the ministry
can stimulate the supply of energy sources, or the development of new resources, or control
increasing demands, is by adjusting energy prices to ensure that all costs are recovered. The
Electricity Department has been the Government's agent in electricity pricing, while the
Department of Trade and Industry has been responsible for petroleum prices and margins.
The Government has decided that responsibility for all energy prices should be vested in the
Ministry of Energy. The prices of various forms of energy are controlled under different
legislation, most of which is not related to the Commerce Act. The methods of controlling
these prices will not be changed immediately, although the machinery used will be reviewed
at an appropriate time by the Government.
It is not easy to ensure that energy rises relate reasonably well to the costs of production
and to the most appropriate use and conservation of energy sources. Continuing to control
and adjust these prices through different Acts or regulations, each with its own criteria and
procedures, makes the introduction of a coherent pricing structure unnecessarily compli-
cated. More importantly, it makes it difficult for consumers to understand what the
Government is actually doing, and it is essential that everyone should know exactly what is
being done and why particular action is needed.
At present energy prices are controlled by a number of legislative measures; for
instance, the Commerce Act 1975 controls liquefied petroleum gas, natural gas, and
manufactured gas. The Motor Spirits Regulation of Prices Act 1933 controls petrol prices.
The Economic Stabilisation Prices of Automotive Diesel Oil and Fuel Oil Regulations 1975
control diesel and fuel oils. The Electricity Price Stabilisation Regulations 1972 control
electricity prices. The Stabilisation of Prices Regulations 1974 control coal, some other
petroleum products, petro-chemicals, and services including refinery services. The
Commerce Act allows appeals to the Commerce Commission and describes particular
criteria to be taken into account when prices are determined. The other measures do not
provide appeal rights and do not describe as fully the criteria to be considered. Furthermore,
the Commerce Act requires the Secretary of Trade and Industry, and in future the
Secretary of Energy, to consider particular applications impartially and free from Govern-
ment direction. Prices controlled under the various regulations are obviously determined
directly by the Government, particularly the retail price of electricity, which cannot be
increased without the approval of the Minister of Finance.
The Government does not intend to reduce the rights or increase the obligations of
energy suppliers and consumers as related to the prices of the various forms of energy.
However, the Government will be asking the Secretary of Energy to review the various price
controlled systems now in use, because price is such an important means of controlling or
stimulating the use of different forms of energy, and therefore a key aspect of the formation
of sound energy policies. The Department of Trade and Industry will still be responsible for


## p. 2514 (#152) ###########################################

2514
26 August
Ministry of Energy Bill
energy price inspections and for negotiating retail petrol margins. It will retain the first
responsibility because it already has a staff of price inspectors. The department is being
asked to continue its participation in petrol retail margin negotiations because petrol profits
represent only one source of income for service stations. Petrol retail margins need to be
considered in conjunction with the profitability of the other goods and services they provide.
Other matters relating to petroleum also need early attention. We need to know more
about the real extent of our coal reserves, and about the amount of gas and oil within and
around New Zealand. Not only are appropriate policies required, but also new initiatives.
The Government is determined that the future of New Zealand will not be restricted because
of a need to get answers to these questions. Similarly, the amount of energy that could be
obtained from our geothermal sources is known only in general terms. More use could be
made of sources that are reasonably well known, and a fuller investigation is needed of other
areas that could be useful. The Ministry of Works and Development has maintained a group
of staff with experience and expertise in geothermal exploration and development and in the
management of geothermal fields. The new Ministry of Energy will assume responsibility for
licensing geothermal developments and the general administration of the Geothermal
Energy Act. The Ministry of Works and Development will act for the Ministry of Energy in
many practical matters, because it will continue to undertake the Government's own
geothermal developments and operations, and will therefore be employing qualified and
experienced staff.
The Bill also refers explicitly to the functions of the Ministry of Energy in relation to
minerals. The Government is concerned at the relatively low level of development of New
Zealand's mineral resources, and will make sure that the new ministry devotes attention to
developing appropriate policies and plans for stimulating action in this area. The authority
provided under present legislation for the Minister of Mines or the Minister of Energy
Resources to set up or participate in commercial organisations is brought together in the Bill
and framed to cover all forms of energy. Any processing to be undertaken by a commercial
organisation in which the Minister participates may include processing energy into other
products. The Bill also provides the Minister with power to trade in energy. Similar authority
is provided in relation to minerals. The Natural Gas Corporation is to be absorbed by a
wholly Government-owned petroleum company. The Offshore Mining Company Limited
appears to be suitable, but careful consideration is being given to the relationships between
the company and the corporation. The Government wishes to make it quite clear that the
existing rights of the corporation's contractors and suppliers will be fully protected, as will
the employment of the corporation's staff.
A large part of the Bill is devoted to consequential amendments. Most of the amend-
ments have been described in schedules, but clauses 16 to 20 describe some amendments in
detail. This is to ensure that the Bill describes clearly the intentions of the House,
particularly in areas where the Government has engaged in trading and development
operations. Contractual obligations in these areas must be protected. As Minister of Energy
Resources I have become concerned at the difficulties the Government faces in basing its
plans for energy development on reliable information. The electricity industry has developed
a comprehensive statistical base for its own projections, but historical and expected future
demand patterns for other forms of energy are not so well known. Generally most of the
growth expected in the future can be reasonably well inferred, but it has become clear that
both the bases on which our forecasts are founded and the forecasts themselves can be upset
by large increases sought by individual industries.
By and large, industries endeavour to ensure that their energy needs can be adequately
met by approaching suppliers. However, this is not always satisfactory, and the Government
foresees a need for an earlier involvement of central forecasting and planning expertise in
the assessment of the benefits of increases in energy demand for particular industries, and in
determining the most suitable source of energy needed. For this reason, power to make
regulations requiring information about future energy needs is provided in the Bill. The
Ministry of Energy will be required to produce a single annual report to Parliament. I expect
that particular attention will be given to matters relating to energy production and consump-
tion as a whole, but the report will also provide information about each sector.
In concluding, I wish to emphasise this Government's determination to improve the
quality of New Zealand's energy forecasting and planning, and the use and conservation of
energy. The decisions made in the next few years will have a major impact on the economic
prosperity of New Zealand, affecting our styles of life and social and physical environment to


## p. 2515 (#153) ###########################################

26 August
2515
Ministry of Energy Bill
an extent that is only now becoming broadly understood. A great deal must now be done to
determine the resources that are available or could usefully be developed, and the wisest use
of our non-renewable resources. Similarly, we must be sure that we are using the best
technologies for extracting, converting, distributing and using energy, with the least waste
possible. The formation of a Ministry of Energy will enable the Government to ensure that
planning, policy development, and operations are properly co-ordinated. Similarly, the
merging of the Government's petroleum agencies will facilitate co-ordination of operations
and provide the Government with an organisation that can operate with the advantages and
stimulation that commercial structures provide. The Government is determined to ensure
that New Zealand's energy needs are given the full attention they demand. The action now
being taken to improve the Government's administrative machinery will be followed by
improvements and initiatives in energy Policies and operations.

suspended until the new secretary is appointed, and the new department is set up and

This is a logical consequence of a measure of this nature. Who is to make these major

good deal of urgency about getting the new ministry established and functioning as quickly as
possible. It is one thing to have the statutory machinery to administer a public service; it is

This development is not new to New Zealand. In fact, most members would know of the
energy policy of President Carter, and the establishment in the United States of a major
department of energy. President Carter has said that the major objective of this new
department will be to reduce the United States' dependence on imported energy. Surely that
should be the major objective of the new ministry in New Zealand.
We are constantly reminded of the present tremendous cost and burden to this country
through imported energy. The Budget tells us that the cost to import energy this year will be
about $550 million. A sixth of our import bill will be devoted to energy this year, a very
heavy commitment on our overseas exchange earnings. The escalation in the cost to New
Zealand of imported energy has been very fast and very dramatic. In 1973 our total energy
import bill was about $76 million. Just over 10 years ago it was about $40 million. For one
single month of this year it will be more than $45 million, and for the total year it will be
about $550 million. If our living standards and life styles are to be protected and enhanced, it
is vital to reduce this burden of imported energy, and turn more to our indigenous resources.
If we apply ourselves to this task I am optimistic that we can make a major impact in that
direction. We have some time at our disposal if we approach the task with urgency. The
major public debate in New Zealand over the nuclear question and whether we should have
nuclear forms of generating energy has been of great service in informing the public about
some of the alternatives and options available; but there is certainly no time to waste, and
these options will be possible only if we grapple urgently with the task.
Hydro energy still has much potential. Coal, natural gas, and energy farming is a distinct
possibility for New Zealand. The biomass, or energy farming, should be receiving every
consideration. The new ministry should have far-reaching effects on the energy scene. There
is a need to rationalise and to co-ordinate our energy policy. It needs to be more than just a
public relations job. The options are available to us, and we should grasp them. More than
7000 employees will be affected one way or another with the merging of these three major

statement by Mr C. W. Campbell, president of the Canterbury Manufacturers Association,
in the Christchurch Star of 16 August advocating the "iron bridge" concept for inter-island
freight rates utilising the Cook Strait rail ferries, and, if so, will he undertake, after
consultation with the Minister of Regional Development, to investigate this concept with a
view to its implementation?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Defence): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Transport, who states: "Yes, I have read the statement referred to. The "iron bridge"
concept has been advocated on several occasions in the past, even during the term of the last
Labour Government, which adopted a limited alternative scheme, known as the unit rate
scheme, under which the North and South Island rail portions of the journey are treated as a
single journey for charging purposes and an additional charge is made for the transport
across Cook Strait. The Government is fully aware of the need to foster regional develop-
ment in the South Island, and this has been recognised in the 1977 Budget, which provides
for the introduction of a differential between north-bound and south-bound inter-island
freight charges in the next freight rate review. I understand from the Minister of Regional
Development that details of this proposal, which will be designed with the object of assisting
South Island industries supplying North Island markets, have not yet been finalised, but the
matter is currently being studied by the Department of Trade and Industry.”
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: Does the Government accept the fact that, until such time as
transport and related costs are reduced for South Island manufacturers, those manufacturers
are not likely to be able to compete with their North Island counterparts?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY: The answer will come out at the investigation.
Mr Latter: Is it true that people who criticise the present system are criticising a unit
rate system brought in by the previous Labour Government?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY: I think that is true.

impressed on harbour boards and terminal operators the need to be prepared, and the

necessity for completion of their planning and infrastructures. Some delays have been

Trade Union Trust Fund-Payments by Non-union Workers
15. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Labour: Is he aware that
the National Party's election manifesto states on page 6 of the industrial relations section
that for those who are allowed to opt out of compulsory unions the appropriate fees will in
future be paid into a trade union trust fund, and, if so, is it still the Government's policy that
those who vote against compulsory unions, and leave, will still have to pay the equivalent of
union fees to the trade union trust fund, and, if not why not?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The member is confusing two distinct areas
of policy. On the one hand, there is the question of ballots on the unqualified preference
provision. If the majority vote is against the unqualified preference provision, then there
would be no compulsion to belong to the union. Persons who subsequently leave the union
will not be required to pay the equivalent of the union subscription to any other authority or
fund. On the other hand, there is the question of persons who are bound by the unqualified
preference provision seeking exemption from union membership. As yet there has been no
change to the provisions of the Industrial Relations Act 1973 relating to exemption from
union membership on conscientious grounds. The trust fund has its constitution in draft
form, as I indicated in answer to question 13.
Mr Prebble: How does the Minister explain the statement on page 6 of the National
Party's manifesto, which, under the heading "Trust Fund", reads: "For those who are
allowed to opt out of compulsory unions, the appropriate fees will in future be paid into such
a fund."?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Answers to other questions on the same subject, including
question 13 today, have made it clear that in last year's amendment to the Industrial
Relations Act no provision relating to the trust fund authorised employees to opt out of
compulsory unionism-and I use the member's own words. The ballot will be on the
unqualified preference provision.
Mr Prebble: Surely it is a reasonable interpretation that somebody who votes for
voluntary unionism is in fact opting out of a compulsory union, and why should he not be
obliged to pay into the advocacy scheme, as others are?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The member is again totally confused. Nobody has mentioned
the advocacy scheme within the trust fund. The point of establishing the trust fund was to
educate union employees, run seminars, and so on. The member's allusion to an advocacy
scheme has nothing to do with the matter, and does not relate to the original question at all.

URGENT QUESTIONS
Fishing Vessels-Limitation of Size
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Fisheries, as an urgent question, Is the
Minister aware that over 40 Auckland fishermen sailing seine boats are concerned about
regulations due to come into force on 1 September 1977 which would allow unlimited length
trawlers into traditional seine boat areas, and, if so, in view of the fact that (a) for 53 years
seine boats have had traditional rights in these areas, (b) over 100 families will be directly
and indirectly affected, (c) some of these fishermen have mortgages from the Rural Banking
and Finance Corporation, and (d) if the regulations come into force the catch totals of these
fishermen could be cut in half, will the Minister consider delaying the bringing into effect of
these regulations until the fishermen concerned have had an opportunity to put their point of
view to him?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): The honourable member's question
appears to be based on the outlined proposals for the management of the Auckland snapper
fishery as published in the July issue of Catch 77. These proposals have been the subject of
much discussion with the fishermen involved, the Fishing Industry Board, and other
members of the industry at Auckland in July and November of 1976, and again in March of
this year. However, following the publication in Catch further submissions were received
from some fishermen. These were fully and sympathetically considered with the subsequent
further modification of the proposals. Unlimited length trawlers will no longer be permitted
to fish in the Hauraki Gulf. The so-called traditional seine boat area has always been
seasonally open to trawlers, and there has been no limit on the length of any trawlers fishing
in the area. However, as from 1 September, vessels of 19 metres registered length or over
will be completely prohibited from the inner gulf area.

Urgent Questions
TV2 Programme on Tradesman going to Canada
Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Minister of Immigration, as an urgent
question, Is the Minister aware that the toolmaker represented on the "Perspective"
programme on TV2 on Friday, 26 August 1977, as a tradesman going to Canada because of
better working conditions, is in fact an undischarged bankrupt, and that the first meeting of
his creditors is not due until 6 September 1977, and can the Minister ensure that the person
does not leave New Zealand at this time so that he can answer to his creditors?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): I am aware of these facts. They were drawn
to my attention immediately after the programme had been shown by creditors who were
concerned. The man portrayed as a toolmaker is married to a Canadian, and I am advised
that her parents have offered to put up the money for their trip to Canada. I have no powers
under the Immigration Act to stop New Zealanders going overseas. I am advised that it is an
offence under the Insolvency Act 1967 for an adjudged bankrupt to leave New Zealand, or
to prepare to leave New Zealand, within 3 years after his adjudication without first obtaining
the consent of the Official Assignee, and I propose to draw details of the matter to the
attention of the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Police so that any possible action to
protect the public may be taken. I am also advised that the TV2 team involved in filming was
given details of this case at the time. If this is so, then TV2 deserves little credit for a
programme which misrepresented the facts.

The initial output from the Huntly underground mines would come in 1978, and the
estimated capital cost for the first mechanised mine was about $80 million. The Huntly west
No. 1 mine had been developed primarily to supply coal to the Huntly thermal power
station, and it would be supplemented by the Waipuna coalfield near Rotowaro. The
Rotowaro underground mines would be phased out about 1983, and would be replaced by
the Huntly east mine, which would supply the industrial and domestic markets.
Many comments had been made about the Labour Government's expenditure on the
Huntly power project and mines development. The initial programming and planning had
been done in 1972 and approved by the National Government. Between 1973 and 1975 work
had been done with no regard for the environmental and social effects on Huntly. Because of
the resulting damage the National Government had allocated $50,000 for general roading
purposes in 1976-77, $100,000 in 1977-78, and $50,000 for 1978-79. A grant of $108,000 had
been made to the Raglan County Council for repairing and upgrading Waikokowhai Road to
the Huntly No. 1 site. Mines Department expenditure on both project and private roading
had been $448,000 for an opencast haul road, $2,950,000 on the Rotowaro to Huntly No. 1
mine road, and $80,000 on the Rotowaro bypass. The Government had recognised that it
had more responsibility than simply to extract coal.
The Waipuna opencast No. 2 mine would be developed to supply about 45 000 tonnes of
coal a year to the Huntly power station. Recoverable reserves had been estimated at
3 800 000 tonnes, which would be sufficient to supply the station for 9 years.

Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) said he complimented the department on its fiftieth
anniversary. To celebrate that anniversary, the Department of Scientific and Industrial
Research had mounted a travelling exhibition, which had been seen by an estimated 100 000
people during a 32-week tour of 22 centres-a very good and useful public relations exercise,
as he did not think the public fully understood the part played by the department in the

More than 30 000 000 sheep and lambs were slaughtered each year in New Zealand, and
everybody knew the problems that continued to beset the freezing industry. A trial unit for
the mechanical skinning of sheep had been designed and installed at a Christchurch freezing
works, with the department and the industry working in co-operation. If the prototype was
approved and accepted by the unions and the freezing companies, it should add to the
productivity of the industry as a whole. The staff of the department were to be congratulated
for the part they had played in the project.
Recently there had been public discussion on energy farming, and the department had
taken the sensible view that, although it might be some time before energy farming became a
practical economic proposition, there must be advance investigation and research. At
Aorangi work had been done on the annual feed requirement of beef cattle grazing on
pasture. Basic research had been carried out to identify the requirements of animals of
