Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) said that the enterprise, ingenuity, and creativity of
the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research was praiseworthy. The Minister of
Energy Resources and international economists had said that the world was heading for a
liquid fuel crisis, and that during the 1980s world demand for oil would exceed supply. The
price of oil had skyrocketed, and New Zealand's oil bill had increased from $70 million in
1973 to more than $500 million; by the 1980s the price could have quadrupled.
In report 575, published in June, the department had suggested the production of oil
from pinus radiata, which New Zealand grew better than any other country. The advocated
process involved the gasification of the wood, which was broken down by heat into a methyl
gas. Union Carbon had developed a purex system, which involved the use of gasified urban
waste in Chicago. Laboratory tests in New Zealand had indicated that the scheme would
work with pinus radiata. Tests had proved that from a forest area smaller than New
Zealand's exotic forests, all New Zealand's oil needs could be produced at approximately
double the cost of landed oil. With the possibility of the oil price quadrupling in the next
decade, the prospect was exciting. Union Carbon had offered to test the process in Chicago
at a cost of $100,000. If results were as promising as it appeared they would be, the second
project would be to build a test plant for $1 million.
What had the Minister done about the report? Nothing had been included in the
estimates for the tests. The Minister of Energy Resources had confused the scheme with
another process involving hydrolysis that was being tested by the Forest Service, and which
consisted of chemical fermentation of trees. Why was the Government so lacking in
imagination that it would not spend $100,000 to test the department's idea?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Science and Technology) said that the National
Research Advisory Council had examined the total science requirements, and had made
recommendations to the Government on the extra emphasis to be placed on the develop-
ment of manufacturing, agriculture, and energy, on which the whole economy of New
Zealand was based, and also on social sciences. In order to carry out the department's
determined policy on energy, it had been announced before the Budget that provision had
been made for an increase of 10 in the DSIR staff ceiling in the energy field. The Budget had
made further provision for an extra 18 in the geothermal accelerated programme and 10 for
petroleum exploration, and there had been forward projections for a further 14, a cumula-
tive number of 42 extra places next year, with a further 4 for the following year. Like other
departments, DSIR had been subject to the sinking-lid formula, which had enabled the
Government to redeploy sensibly throughout the Civil Service positions which had been
generated as surplus in the various departments; and that policy was paying off.
Considerable effort had been spent on energy farming, which covered any process that
could recover energy from plant material. Much work had been done in the department's
physics and engineering laboratory to develop a small pollution-free burner, which could be
stoked once a day and then left to burn, for glasshouses and timber-drying kilns where a
standard low-grade heat was required for a long time. Some New Zealand scientists had met
Dr Melvin Kelvin, a Nobel Prize winner from the United States, and discussed with him the
use of plants for the production of hydrocarbons for fuel processing. Work had been done on
the pyrolysis of plants in order to obtain energy.
The tremendous diversity of DSIR activities was worth noting. Anyone who was
prepared to study the department's report would see the tremendous number of activities
that had taken place all over the country. Some people had suggested that research should be
rationalised. There was nothing wrong with certain types of research being done in a variety
of institutions, because they provided a different approach. Sometimes there was duplica-
tion, which had accelerated a research programme. The suggestion that rationalisation had
meant unnecessary expenditure was being carefully examined. Research was being done not

only in the DSIR but also within other departments of State, universities, and private

The cattle pasture problem was very interesting, as it dealt with the dry matter
requirements of cattle beasts at varying times of the year. On page 18 of the department's
report it was stated that the organic matter required by a 150 kg animal at maintenance level
in June was 1.5 kg a day, whereas for a 250 kg animal that gained 1.8 kg a day, 5.5 kg was
required for maintenance, but at the time of the growth that could be achieved with a
relatively lesser quantity, depending on the constitution of the grass and the temperature.
Those factors, which had not been thoroughly explored, would have great relevance for the
cattle industry.
Trials had not been carried out on the production of liquid fuel from wood, of which
there were large supplies. All that had been done so far was to develop work on a bench
scale, or a very small pilot plant scale. It was not considered necessary to move to the next
stage of development and spend vast sums of money, when such work was already being
done in the United States with existing plant.
For too long New Zealand had failed to understand the impact of science in all its facets,
and a substantial step forward in the rationalisation of scientific work had taken place in 1972
with the establishment within the NRAC of committees whose particular job had been to co-
ordinate scientific activity. The real requirements for research work in the social scientific
field should not be forgotten. Without adequate information and adequate knowledge of
many subjects in the broad category of social science, New Zealand would not be able to
develop in conjunction with its economic policies a rational, sensible policy related to the
people. Last year the NRAC membership had been extended to include two more people,
and he would shortly be completing the appointments. A prominent social scientist had
already been appointed.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Last Tango in Paris-Censor's Restrictions
1. Mr COOPER (Otago Central) asked the Minister of Internal Affairs: Can he give any
assurance that audiences admitted to performances of Last Tango in Paris will be confined to
those over 19 years of age?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): My department will endeavour,
within the limits of its resources, to ensure compliance with the requirements of the Act.
Clearly, however, it cannot police every screening of this or any other restricted film. The
onus of complying with restrictions imposed by the censor rests on exhibitors, who generally
do their best. Parliament made its will clear last year when it passed the new Cinematograph
Films Act, which laid down greatly increased penalties for exhibitors who admit people other
than in accordance with the censor's restrictions. The new Act also provides, for the first
time, for penalties for persons who gain, or attempt to gain, admittance to a film they are not
entitled to see.
Mr Cooper: Has there been any occasion on which there has been a conviction under
the Act, and what are the penalties for such convictions?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: Before the introduction of the new Act last year, the penalty was
$200, but it has now been increased to $2,000. In the case of any person of the class and
description of persons to whom a film may not be exhibited gaining entry when he is aware of
that fact, there is a maximum fine of $200.
Mr Hunt: Will audiences in Otago Central be permitted to see the film The Dambusters?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: That question has no relevance.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

rates.

3. Mr LAMBERT (Western Hutt) asked the Minister of Broadcasting: What evidence is
there to support the contention by Stokes Valley residents that their TV2 reception is
interfered with by the installation of power lines, and, if this is so, what is being done to
remedy the situation?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): The Broadcasting Corporation
acknowledges that TV2 reception in Stokes Valley is unsatisfactory. This would be the case
whether or not the power lines existed. For this reason the corporation proposes to install a
TV2 translator at the same site as the existing TV1 translator. Provided there are no
unforeseen delays, the translator should be installed before the end of this year. However,
no firm commissioning date can be given.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Is this evidence of a policy solely for the area described, or is it part
of a policy to improve reception in all areas where it is at present difficult?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: It is entirely up to each member to ask about his own area,
and many members have done so by letter. There is a programme for the development of
additional TV2 translators in the Wellington and Hutt Valley areas. These are difficult
because of the configuration of the land.

resolving the problem. The party was set up before the article appeared in the newspaper.

hazards?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: I can only say to the honourable member that before I
answered his question I investigated the matter. As I said before, the signalmen get 2 days
off in 6 weeks. That is still not satisfactory, but I cannot pluck signalmen off trees.

Forest Service—Planting of Native Trees
7. Mr LAMBERT (Western Hutt) asked the Minister of Forests: To what extent is the
Forest Service planting native trees for either production or conservation purposes?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): The Forest Service has planted more than 600
hectares with indigenous species for conservation, amenity, preservation, and enrichment
purposes. It should be noted that many thousands of hectares have been restocked in native
trees by natural regeneration in production forests of beech, tawa, and podocarp species.
For the kauri forests, a policy of enrichment planting has been in practice since 1932, and
48 000 seedlings are being planted each year to cover some 130 hectares. In podocarp forest
areas of the Rotorua, Wellington, Nelson, Westland, and Southland conservancies some 200
hectares are being planted annually, mainly with rimu, with smaller areas of totara,
kahikatea, and matai. The total number of seedlings used is about 70000. In addition, the
Forest Research Institute is to plant some 20 hectares of podocarp species at Tihoi,
Horohoro, and Whirinaki this year, and will use some 8000 seedlings in a variety of research
trials in these areas. As a result of the indigenous forest policy, logged forests, in which
regeneration is more difficult, are being retained as native forests, rather than cleared for
pasture and plantation, and planting of native trees in such areas could increase. In addition,
the Forest Service provides indigenious species to a wide range of organisations for amenity,
ornamental, and conservation planting. These include other Government departments,
schools, environmental societies, and the Chatham Islands.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I remind the Minister of Standing Order 81, which states that
a Minister's reply should be concise.
Mr Wetere: What success has the Forest Research Institute had in Rotorua in the re-
establishment of native trees in the area?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The member is, of course, referring to the Tihoi, Horohoro, and
Whirinaki areas. I cannot answer that question specifically, but if he likes to ask another
question I will try to answer it in brief terms, as Mr Acting Speaker suggests.

Company Takeovers Legislation
10. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga), on behalf of Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) asked the
Minister of Justice: Does he intend to introduce legislation this session to prevent persons or
companies issuing a bid for the takeover of another company, with the creation of
uncertainties similar to those that developed in Borthwick's bid for the Gear Meat Co.,
made through newspaper statements where there has been no discussion with the director-
ship of the offeree company prior to the newspaper offer, and where there is much doubt as
to whether the bid will succeed?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Acting Minister of Justice): I note with interest and welcome
the publication of an exposure draft on takeovers by the Stock Exchange Association of New
Zealand. I agree with the honourable member that legislation in this field will be necessary,
but it will equally also be complex. The Minister of Justice intends it to form part of a
comprehensive Securities Exchange Bill, which, as he announced at the beginning of this
month, he intends should be brought in within 2 or 3 years. Meanwhile the matter referred to
by the honourable member, so far as publicly listed companies are concerned, appears to be
covered by paragraph 1.4 of the exposure draft, which reads: "A false or uninformed market
must not be allowed to develop by the offeror or offeree company in either's shares. In
normal circumstances, the publication of an intent to make an offer, without actually giving
notice of or making that offer, will be regarded as an attempt to create a false market in
either share." It remains to be seen how effective the takeover code will prove without
legislative sanctions.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: As there already appears to be a provision covering the situation,
what proposals does the Minister have in mind to ensure that the letter of the law is upheld?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: I should emphasise that for the short term the only reality at
the moment is the suggested draft of the Stock Exchange Association. Because of the
complexity of the provisions required we prefer to make legislation a long-term aim. But
should we have to move-for example, in the event of the stock exchange rules not being
followed-we would move. One direction in which we could do so is by adjusting the control
limit of 50 percent or more provided in the Companies Act. If it is proposed to buy shares in
a company to the extent of 50 percent or more of the shareholding, prior notice is required to
be given and there must be prior registration of the takeover. We could lower the figure from
50 percent to, say, 25 or 20 percent. However, we would not consider making that alteration
unless it becomes apparent that the stock exchanges rules are not being effectively observed.

Education Vote, Palmerston North
11. Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North) asked the Minister of Education: How much of
the Education vote went to Palmerston North through the medium of Massey University,


## p. 2555 (#193) ###########################################

31 August
2555
Oral Answers to Questions
Palmerston North Teachers Training College, and Palmerston North Technical Institute in
each of the years 1974, 1975, and 1976?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): In round figures, the expenditure from
the Education vote for the institutions mentioned was as follows: Massey University,
$10,990,000 in 1974, rising to $11.3 million in 1975-76, and to $13.5 million in 1976-77;
Palmerston North Teachers College, $3,770,000 in 1974, $5.1 million in 1975, and $5.6
million in 1976; Palmerston North Technical Institute, $400,000 in 1974, $550,000 in 1975,
and $660,000 in 1976. That represents an increase from $15.1 million in 1974 to $16.9 million
in 1975-76, and to $19.8 million in 1976-77.
Mr Lithgow: How much of the total amount of $19.8 million in 1976 was spent on
bursaries and student allowances?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: That is very wide of the question.
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: As near as I can give it, $6.5 million of the $19.8 million spent in
1976-77 would have been paid out to students, either by way of a standard tertiary bursary or
in student allowances at the teachers' college.
Mr Marshall: Does the increase from $15.1 million to $19.8 million in those 2 years
represent an increase in the proportion of the total Education vote, or was it simply an
increase arising out of inflation?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I should think it was a greater increase proportionately than the
increase in the vote, because it rose from $15.1 million to $16.9 million-by almost 12
percent and then by a further 22 percent in the current year. That is far greater than the
increase in the Education vote, and it is better than inflation.
Mr Lithgow: Can the Minister confirm that none of the $19.8 million was actually paid
to people such as gardeners, farm staff, and so on, who work at Massey University, and that
it was devoted only to lecturers and teachers at the various colleges?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: That would not be quite correct. The $19.8 million was the
amount of money allocated from the Education vote. The university would have received
some income from other sources-for example, the farm-and some of the farm staff would
obviously have been paid from that income. It would not be correct to say that the $19.8
million allocated represented the total receipts; nor would it be correct to say that it excluded
payments to people such as gardeners, because some of them would be involved in the
maintenance of buildings and grounds.

Local Authorities and Overseas Loans
16. Mr REWETI (Eastern Maori), on behalf of Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay), asked the
Minister of Finance: What were the reasons for refusing to allow local authorities to take up
an offer of overseas loans at low interest rates, as reported in the Dominion of 12 August?

made in Auckland and the Auckland local authorities sensibly sought the views of the
Government on financing capital works by overseas borrowing. The Government indicated
that it would be unable to agree to overseas borrowing for the following reasons: first, the
works proposed to be undertaken by the two authorities, the Auckland Regional Authority
and the Auckland City Council, were purely local in nature. Secondly, they contained little

generally available on the market.

WRITTEN QUESTIONS
Education-Bursaries for Part time Students
1. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) asked the Minister of Education: What progress has
been made by the Department of Education in the implementation of recommendation 9,
chapter 4, of the select committee report on women's rights?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: Part time students in universities
have for many years qualified for a fees bursary, and a time limit on the duration for which
this was available was removed with the introduction of the tertiary bursary in 1976. Women
who had a break in their studies for domestic reasons would have especially benefited from
this change. The Government stated in its 1975 policy that it would, as part of its process of
introducing a reformed bursary, consult with interested organisations on the possibility of
extending the bursary system to extramural and "some part time students". It also stated
that, in consultation with interested groups, it would work toward an educational entitle-
ment which would be in the form of a continuing education bursary, available to all New
Zealanders at least once during their lifetime, but it recognised that the latter development
would have to be introduced in stages as a long term development. Following the bursaries
conference which was called in December 1976 to begin the process of consultation toward a
reformed bursary, it was decided that the Department of Education would prepare a
discussion paper on further developments. This paper, "Financial Assistance for Post-school


## p. 2559 (#197) ###########################################

31 August
2559
Questions and Replies
Study", has just been released and is being distributed to the interested organisations. It
takes up proposals for support to part-time students and examines in detail some of the
priorities and the implications. Time will be given for comment before a further conference
later this year. As the paper indicates, there are many possibilities for developing the
existing bursary system and it will be essential to examine closely the relative priority which
these should have, especially because the tertiary bursary system has doubled the cost of
financial assistance to tertiary students since 1975. The cost for the 1977-78 financial year is
estimated at more than $28 million. Proposals for extending support further to part-time
students must be examined together with all other proposals for reform.

Education-Broadcasting
3. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) asked the Minister of Education: What progress has
been made by the Department of Education in the implementation of recommendation 13,
chapter 4, of the select committee report on women's rights?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: This matter has been under
discussion with the television authorities and other educational organisations, as part of a
range of proposals for educational broadcasting on television. It has been agreed in principle
that it would be appropriate for the National Council of Adult Education to act as the
responsible advisory body for continuing education broadcasting as it develops. In 1976 a
continuing education unit was established by Radio New Zealand. The unit has produced
educational programmes for parents of young children and of adolescents; for dairy farmers
on breeding; and on other subjects such as water safety and energy resources. Radio New
Zealand has established an advisory committee, and a close liaison exists with the Depart-
ment of Education on specific projects. The National Council of Adult Education, which has
just received approval for increased staffing in this year's Budget announcements, intends to
appoint a project officer for broadcasting with immediate responsibilities for liaison with
Radio New Zealand. The experience already gained of working with continuing education
radio (which is highly flexible and permits considerable local variation through community
stations) will be very useful in planning developments toward educational television. The
National Council of Adult Education last year also co-sponsored a visit to New Zealand by
Mr Neil Barnes, a senior educational broadcasting specialist with the BBC. Mr Barnes held
discussions with all the broadcasting and educational agencies and organisations, and his visit
stimulated ideas for development. It should be noted that the television channels already
provide a small number of educational broadcast series quite closely comparable to some of
those broadcast by the BBC; these include, for example, such series as those on cooking,
gardening, car maintenance, consumer education, home alterations and repairs.

Waihi-Goods Transport Services
6. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Minister of Railways: Has he seen the report in the
New Zealand Herald of 21 May 1977, in which the Mayor of Waihi, Mr A. J. Dean, said that
"nearly 700 people worked in industry at Waihi and it was important to the town that it
retain contact with the rest of the country at an economic rate"; and, if so, can he confirm
that following his discussions with Mr Dean last month the department will provide a lorry
service which will enable manufacturers to send goods out of Waihi at the same rates as they
I would have been sent with a rail service?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: I have seen the report and I
can confirm that the department has held discussions with the mayor, councillors, and
business interests in Waihi about the provision of further goods services in the town. The
proposals include the introduction of a new direct service between Waihi and Hamilton that
will provide a link with existing rail services, giving Waihi direct access to centres in both the
North and South Islands. In addition, it is proposed to increase the capacity of the present
lorry service between Waihi and Auckland. The applicable rates will be similar to those
charged for the haulage of goods by rail, any addition being because of the additional service
given in providing a door to door service rather than having the customer take goods to the
railway station. I would point out that the position at Waihi is unusual in that a departmental
road route service has existed in the area for many years, and it is therefore possible to
develop a railway lorry service more readily than if such a service had not existed previously.

and Economic Advancement Act 1945; (2) if they were, are these registrations still in force;
and (3) what Maori fishing rights exist today?

Papatoetoe Railway Station-Goods Traffic
9. Mr LANGE (Mangere) asked the Minister of Railways: Can he confirm that the
Papatoetoe Railway Station no longer accepts parcels or goods for dispatch; if so, is this the
result of the fire which destroyed the goods shed last year; and what is he doing about
rebuilding the shed?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: Yes, the Papatoetoe Railway
Station is closed to parcels and goods in small lots. The goods shed was destroyed by fire on
22 August 1976, and, because only a relatively low level of small lots traffic was handled, the
volume did not justify the substantial cost of building a new goods shed. The member for
Manukau was advised of the proposed closure in March of this year after discussion by
officials with the businessmen's associations for Papatoetoe, Otara, and Hunter's Corner.
Small lots traffic for the area is now handled through the Otahuhu Railway Station, but
Papatoetoe is still open for the acceptance and delivery of goods in wagon lots and for
passenger traffic.

South Pacific Forum-Membership
13. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: What criteria
are applied for membership of the South Pacific Forum, and are there provisions for any
type of informal association for countries or territories which are not eligible for member-
ship?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: The South Pacific Forum
is a grouping of independent or self-governing South Pacific countries, including Australia
and New Zealand. There is no provision for membership or observer status being granted to
any non self-governing territory or metropolitan government. The present membership of
the South Pacific Forum comprises Australia, Cook Islands, Fiji, Gilbert Islands, Nauru,
New Zealand, Niue, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Western
Samoa.

Technical Institutes—Applications for Courses Declined
14. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: For how many new
courses in 1977 was permission sought, unsuccessfully, by the various technical institutes and
the Hawke's Bay Community College?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: Twenty seven applications for
courses to begin in 1977 in technical institutes and the Hawke's Bay Community College
have been declined. The most usual reasons for declining applications are, in order of
importance: (1) the size of the demand permits the subject to be taught efficiently and
economically only at the national institutes, i.e., Central Institute of Technology and
Technical Correspondence Institute (2) the course is offered by another regional institute
and there is insufficient local demand to duplicate the course; (3) the decision requires a
change in policy; (4) priority cannot at present be given to the subject. Consideration is still
being given to another 14 applications with broader policy implications.

Wairarapa Opossum Eradication
16. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister of Agriculture:
Does his department intend to institute a continuing survey of farms involved in the opossum
eradication programme in the Wairarapa to ensure there is no reinfestation, and, if so, when
can this survey be expected to begin?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: Opossum control operations
carried out at the request of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries are regarded as
conpleted once post operation assessments indicate that a satisfactory kill has been
achieved. This is followed by repetitive testing of cattle in the area as frequently as
practicable. The cattle testing results are the prime indicator of the success of the opossum
control operation, and will pinpoint any localised area where Tb-infected opossums may
remain. Prompt action will be taken to eradicate these. However, the pest destruction board
in the area may, should it regard the opossum a threat to agricultural production, undertake
opossum control in the course of routine pest control work.

Ohai-Morley Mine Development
20. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Mines: To what extent has the
decision of the Labour Government in May 1975 to develop a new mine from the Morley
mine at Ohai been actioned, and is it proposed to equip this mine with a continuous miner
and one alpine miner and associated equipment as was decided at that time?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines) replied: The proposal to enter the lower Morley coal
seam from the present workings of the Morley mine has been superseded. It is now intended
to gain entry to this 8 000 000 tonne block of coal by developing from the nearby Wairaki
mine, which was sealed following a fire in 1971. The coal in the upper levels of the Wairaki
mine is to be won by opencast methods, and this will be followed by a resumption of
underground mining. The continued development to the dip of the existing Wairaki
workings will lead to the exploitation of the lower Morley seam. The underground phase of
this operation will be completely mechanised. This new scheme has the support of the
mining community of Ohai. Finance has been provided in this year's estimates for the initial
stripping contract.

23. Mr WETERE (Western Maori) asked the Minister of Forests: Can he supply a regional

Government since taking office?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: The location of the 8227 hectares of land
purchased for forestry since the National Government took office is as follows: Northland,
2377 hectares; Coromandel, 339 hectares; East Coast Poverty Bay, 2438 hectares; Northern
Bay of Plenty, 293 hectares; Wairarapa, 513 hectares; Nelson, 887 hectares; Marlborough,
482 hectares; Canterbury, 321 hectares; Otago, 62 hectares; Southland, 683 hectares; a total
of 8227 hectares. These purchases have been mainly in regions where the land bank for new
planting has been likely to fall below the amount required for 3 years' future planting. It has
long been the policy of successive Governments and the Forest Service to keep land banks in
each region at this level. The precise area required in each region is governed by the planting
targets set for it plus any additional planting achieved through the use of special employees.
Exceptions to this policy are those areas where land suitable for afforestation is no longer

Wanganui Regional Museum
25. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Internal Affairs: When will the
Wanganui Regional Museum be gazetted as an official depository for archives?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs) replied: Although I have never been
asked to approve the Wanganui Regional Museum as an official depository for public
archives, I am advised that the question has been raised with my department and with the
chief archivist. Her view, which she has conveyed to the museum and to the Wanganui City
Council, is that it would be preferable to defer a decision on this proposal until next year,
when it is expected that the Archives Act will be revised and new provisions about regional
repositories included. This revision will follow receipt and consideration of a report on
archives development in New Zealand to be prepared by Dr W. I. Smith, Dominion
Archivist of Canada. Dr Smith is to come here next February and is expected to visit
Wanganui. As far as I am aware, deferring a decision on this will have no detrimental effect
on the Wanganui Regional Museum. However, should there be any evidence that it will, I
am prepared to consider an application sooner.

Education-Early Reading Materials Review
29. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) asked the Minister of Education: What progress has
been made by the Department of Education in the implementation of recommendation 4,
chapter 4, of the report of the Select Committee on Women's Rights?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: The Department of Education has
completed a comprehensive review of the currently used early reading materials, consulting
widely with all interested groups. The review includes recommendations on the need to
avoid role stereotyping of any kind, and for children and adults to be shown in a wide range
of roles regardless of sex or ethnic origin. It is also recommended that new material be
provided to schools in future on a "rolling revision" basis so that social changes are reflected
in the materials as they occur. A new policy to provide for the implementation of the
recommendations is now being considered by the Government. Teachers college principals
have been asked to have the attention of student teachers drawn to the problems arising
from sex-role stereotyping. In addition, a pamphlet on this subject is shortly to be published
for all teachers.
(19/8/77)
Education-Free Entitlement for Women
30. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) asked the Minister of Education: What progress has
been made by the Department of Education in the implementation of recommendation 12,
chapter 4, of the report of the Select Committee on Women's Rights?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: There have been a number of
developments over the past few years which have affected the entitlement to free education.
Although none of these are specifically for women, it is clear that women are using the
increased opportunities. Free education has for many years been available in secondary
school evening programmes to those persons who had not exhausted their entitlement of 5
years' free secondary education under section 85 of the Education Act 1964. Section 93 (5)
now extends this entitlement to permit adults to return full time or part time to secondary
schools, in the daytime, as a free entitlement. The number of adults so doing is increasing
significantly. In all secondary schools the number was about 70 in 1974, but it rose to nearly
500 in 1975, to nearly 1000 in 1976, and to an estimated 1350 in 1977. Of these the great
majority are women. A survey undertaken in 1976 showed that most such students had clear
goals, particularly vocational goals, for returning to secondary school. The majority is
studying at School Certificate and University Entrance levels. There has been a rapid growth
also in the use of the correspondence school (again, particularly by women) to complete
qualifications at the School Certificate and University Entrance levels. During 1974, 6800
adults enrolled at the correspondence school (63 percent women) in 1976, 10 000 (68
percent women), and in 1977, 11 200 (72 percent women). This is a free entitlement. These
are total enrolment figures over each year. As at 1 July 1977 there were 6048 adults (4358
women) actually studying. Changes to the tertiary bursary system also create wider oppor-
tunities for women. One of particular significance, made with the introducton of the tertiary
bursary, was to extend fees bursaries for university study to any student for all the required
components of a recognised course of study. Previously a fees bursary was available only for
the normal duration within which a full time student would be expected to complete the
course. This had disadvantaged part-time students who, though passing all their courses,
would still have had sections to complete not covered by a fees bursary, at the end of the
normal period. It disadvantaged women who had a break in their studies for family reasons.
Under the new system, a part time student, or in particular an extramural student, in effect
receives a fees bursary without a time limit. Women students undoubtedly receive the
greater benefit from this equivalent of a free entitlement. Where (for example, with the
special course for women to train for radio and television servicing trades operated this year
at the Auckland Technical Institute) courses are full year the normal bursary provisions now
cover women students no matter of what age. There are some women in this course who
have returned to training after domestic responsibilities. However, it should be noted that
the New Zealand tertiary bursary (unlike those of many other countries) is available to
people of any age and contains no limitations constraining students to move directly from
secondary to tertiary study. A significant number of women do return to study at tertiary
institutions under this provision. At universities, there has been a marked increase in the
numbers of students over 25 years of age in recent years. In technical institutes women enter


## p. 2569 (#207) ###########################################

31 August
2569
Questions and Replies
courses for which bursary assistance is available without an age limit, and secretarial courses
particularly have always included some women returning to train in this manner. It is
understood that the 1978 nursing intake at Wellington Polytechnic, for example, may include
up to 25 percent married women returning to train. A discussion paper on financial
assistance for post school study has just been issued by the Department of Education. It
raises many general and specific questions about the existing and desirable future forms of
financial assistance. This is seen as part of the process toward the Government's policy of
introducing a reformed bursary, and a first step toward its longer range goal of a continuing
education entitlement. A conference is to be held later this year. Proposals for changes to
the existing systems of study assistance will undoubtedly take into account the special needs
of women.

Education-Vocational Guidance for Women
34. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) asked the Minister of Education: What progress has
been made by the Department of Education in the implementation of recommendation 14,
chapter 4, of the report of the Select Committee on Women's Rights?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: The field of vocational and
educational guidance is a complex one with both local and national patterns. Because there
are many organisations and agencies involved or potentially involved with advice to women,
the Committee on Women has now accepted a co-ordinating function for the preparation of
suitable resource material. The Department of Education's role has been altered by the
Government's decision in principle to combine the Vocational Guidance Service with the
Employment Service under the administration of the Department of Labour. Vocational
guidance will not, therefore, be a function of the Department of Education. However,
within their normal work, vocational guidance officers have always given such assistance as is
possible to adults, and, when combined with the employment service, are expected to do so
more closely. The Vocational Training Council has a special subcommittee on women and
employment which has a particular interest in the development of guidance services. By the
printing of calendars, prospectuses, and special brochures or pamphlets, both universities
and technical institutes disseminate information about their programmes quite widely. Some
courses are also advertised nationally, as is Massey University's extramural studies section.
Liaison officers for these institutions visit secondary schools in their areas regularly.
Recruitment for teachers colleges is by national campaign (including television), and by
visits to schools of recruitment officers. Local secondary schools are themselves responsible
for their extension or evening programmes and for adult admissions to day classes where
these are operating. Schools issue brochures in advance of their courses and advertise as
well. Some schools have promoted adult admissions with very active campaigns through
radio and other local publicity. Others have experimented with "educational shops" to give
guidance services to their local communities. Regular use of radio is also now made by the
new Nelson Community Education Service and the community education section of the
Southland Polytechnic, for example. Where such agencies take an active and well publicised
community education role, they are also extensively used as sources of information about
educational opportunities. The most important sources of information are provided at local
and regional levels where they are more cost effective, except in such cases as the
recruitment of teachers, where the numbers involved and the common starting date for
recruitment make a national campaign justified.

National Superannuitants—Rates Rebate
42. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Local Government: At
What weekly income level does the rates rebate concession for married couples receiving
national superannuation phase out, and is it proposed to increase the income level this year?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government) replied: The income level for a
married couple for a full rates rebate concession is $3,768 per annum plus $156 for each
dependant. Where the income exceeds this amount the rebate is reduced by $1 for each $8 of
income over the limit. It is not possible to quote a figure at which the concession will phase
out as this will depend on the amount of the rates involved, on the total income of the
ratepayer, and on the number of dependants. National superannuitants are treated on the
same basis as all other ratepayers and must fulfil the income requirements set out above. It is
not proposed further to review the income level for a full rates rebate, which has already
been determined for this rating year.

New Zealand and elsewhere, and the council has viewed a number of these to assess their
value in future educational and information programmes.

terms of that agreement?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade) replied: The tariff preferences

agreements concluded between the two countries in 1959 and 1966. These agreements were

mutual phasing out of the preferences that each country accorded the other in terms of these
agreements was completed on 1 July 1977. The one area where Britain still benefits from

Railway Line Upgrading, Otago
72. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) asked the Minister of Railways: Has he seen the
Christchurch Press of 5 July, in which it is reported that the recently released findings of the
investigation into the 1 July goods train derailment at Mihiwaka, 3 km north of Port
Chalmers, confirmed that the derailment was attributable to a cracked rail, and, if so, what is
he doing to ensure that this section of the track is upgraded as a matter of urgent priority?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: There was no such report in
the Christchurch Press of 5 July, but I have seen a report in the Christchurch Press of 5

vicinity, and to replace any considered suspect. No further action seems necessary at this
stage, although I have told the general management of Railways that I am concerned about
that particular section of the track, and I have discussed it with them. The broken rail had a
defect that is not uncommon but it can very occasionally lead to a break. Regular inspections
are carried out on this section, as on every other operating line in the country.

Eviction by Police of Families at Upper Hutt
76. Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori) asked the Minister
of Police: Would he supply a report on the reasons why the police in Upper Hutt chose to
evict families, including infants, from a house at the weekend in the manner in which,
according to news reports, they did?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police) replied: Those evicted from the Upper
Hutt property comprised in excess of 30 persons, none of whom had any authority from the
owner to be there. The police acted at the specific written request of the owner of the
premises, who had made a complaint that those on the property had broken the front door,
had smashed windows, and had pulled down a shed on the property and used it to start a
bonfire. The owner was genuinely concerned for his property, and for that reason requested
the police to remove them. This is not a case of a normal citizen in lawful occupation of a
dwelling. Those concerned were in part members of the Upper Hutt "black power" gang
then on remand for the criminal offence of unlawful assembly, and were apparently intent on
wrecking the property. Surely the member for Southern Maori will agree that property
owners also have some rights in these matters when their property is in danger. The actions
of the police were entirely within the law at all times, and were carried out in a humane
manner. It is to be regretted that these people acted in the manner in which they did, but the
responsibility for the events was entirely theirs. It is a pity that the adults conducted
themselves in such an irresponsible manner, thus involving small children in such a situation.
(11/8/77)

Railway Line Upgrading, Otago
86. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) asked the Minister of Railways: Has he seen the
Christchurch Press of 5 July, in which it is reported that yet another goods train derailment
has occurred at Seacliff, 25 km north of Dunedin, the fifth this year and the second in less
than a week on this section of track, and, if so, what is he doing to ensure that this section of
the track is improved to prevent more derailments?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: I have seen a report in the
Christchurch Press of 5 August, which presumably is the one to which the honourable
member refers. The section of the track between Seacliff and Dunedin has always been
known as difficult, and some sections have tended to give trouble, particularly in bad
weather conditions. In this instance, a soft spot developed at a site which had not previously
been suspect, and the rails moved sufficiently to contribute to the derailment of a four-
wheeled goods wagon. For some time now, work has been under way on embankment
stabilisation in this area. As I pointed out in my reply to a similar question, regular
inspections are carried out on this section, as they are on every other operating line in the
country. However, particular attention is given to known trouble spots.

School Textbooks Scrutiny
87. Squadron Leader DRAYTON (St. Albans) asked the Minister of Education: Is he
prepared to consider a system of school textbook scrutiny as practised in Texas, and
publicised by Mrs Norma Gabler on her recent visit?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: I am well aware of the issue raised
in the honourable member's question. It is one to which I have given a great deal of
consideration, even before the recent publicity given as a result of Mrs Gabler's visit. It
raises the very big question as to the extent to which the Department of Education—as an
agency of central government-should be given the responsibility for determining the actual
textbooks to be prescribed for use in State schools. It seems to me that a more likely and
effective way of providing a form of public scrutiny would be one that placed the responsibil-
ity on the principal and controlling authority of a school to have procedures for prior
consultation with parents where the selection of potentially contentious textbooks might be
an issue.

or to unforeseen increases in estimated expenditure, some local authorities find themselves
in overdraft beyond the legal limits at the end of the financial year—a situation that very
often rights itself over a short period. I should like to explore possibilities other than the
imposition of statutory penalties on either elected members or staff of local authorities in
breach of the Act in an endeavour to find a satisfactory way of overcoming the problem. In
my opinion, the issue raised by the Controller and Auditor-General could be resolved if
greater efforts were applied to the proper training and qualification of local government
staff, on whom rests the responsibility for guiding their councils in these matters."
(12/8/77)

particular tax exemptions, and any tax rebates he may be entitled to. I stress that all former
age beneficiaries on national superannuation are receiving significantly more cash in hand
payments than they would have been receiving if the age benefit had been retained.

Air Traffic Controllers, Auckland
94. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of State Services: Is it
correct, as reported in the Auckland Star of 29 June 1977, that 600 days' holiday were then
owing to air traffic controllers at Auckland International Airport, and that the only way of
remedying this was to transfer officers from secondary airports to Mangere, and, if so, what
action has been taken in the meantime?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services) replied: It is correct that a substantial
accumulation of leave has accrued to air traffic control staff at several airports. At Auckland
it is estimated that in excess of 600 days' leave will remain untaken at the end of November
1977. This situation is caused primarily because of a decision by the State Services Tribunal
in May 1976 on a claim by the Public Service Association, which gave an additional 8 days'
annual leave each year to all qualified air traffic controllers, and the introduction of a revised
shift cycle that increased rostered time off by 16 days a year. The extra leave was made
retrospective to 9 July 1975, creating a very large accumulation of leave at all airports. The
transfer of staff from secondary airports is not the only way of remedying this. This is not a
satisfactory solution to the problem because of the time required to give training in the
different procedures applicable to the major airports and centres, and to validate ratings.
The most effective answer lies in the recruitment of additional manpower. In December 1976
the Government authorised an increase of 23 staff for this purpose, but a normal air traffic
control cadet requires 3 years' training before being ready for full operational duties. The
training capability and capacity of the Ministry of Transport is at present fully extended. It
may still take up to 12 months to clear the present backlog of leave. However, I am satisfied
that all possible measures are being taken to enable as much leave as possible to be taken,
and that the transfer of secondary airport staff to major units is unlikely to become
necessary.
(16/8/77)

Nash Papers in National Archives
108. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui), on behalf of Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt), asked the
Minister of Internal Affairs: Why has access to the papers of Sir Walter Nash, held by the
national archives, been refused to students and others wanting to use them for serious
research or study?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs) replied: Although national archives has
Sir Walter's papers in its custody for safekeeping, it does not have control of them. Under
the terms of his will, control of access to the papers remains with his trustees and advisory
trustees. When the papers were deposited in national archives the trustees granted exclusive
access to the papers to Sir Walter's biographer for a period that has not yet expired. In the
memorandum of agreement at that time, they indicated that access should continue to be
restricted for at least 10 years—that is, until 1980-with the proviso that this period could be
extended to 1990, so that the papers can be properly sorted and recorded. On archival
grounds, the chief archivist strongly supports the view that the task of appraising, arranging,
and describing this vast collection should be undertaken before general access is allowed.
Most researchers who have expressed interest in working on these papers have accepted this
view.

On-shore Oil Prospecting Licences
114. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga), on behalf of Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone),
asked the Minister of Energy Resources: Do the on-shore oil prospecting licences which the


## p. 2590 (#228) ###########################################

2590
31 August
Questions and Replies
Government has issued to itself despite the provisions of section 47D of the Petroleum Act
contain the same conditions and terms as would have been required from any other licence
holder?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources) replied: It is unnecessary for petroleum
prospecting licences issued to the Minister of Mines to include conditions relating to the
payment of royalties or an annual licence fee. Nor is it necessary that the Minister, as the
holder of the licence, should deposit with the Secretary of Mines as security a deposit or
bond. This is because the Petroleum Act provides that terms and conditions which are
required to be included in licences issued to other licensees need not be included in licences
issued to the Minister on behalf of the Crown. I note that the question suggests that the
petroleum prospecting licences have been issued to me as Minister of Mines despite the
provisions of section 47D of the Petroleum Act. This section, however, deals with a
completely different and unrelated matter, and is itself subject to the section in the Act
under which these prospecting licences have been issued. The object of section 47D is to
prevent public servants who, on account of their position, may have access to confidential
information from using their position for personal advantage by acquiring an interest in a
prospecting or mining licence issued under the Act.

Trade Unions in United States and Canada-Penalties
128. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Labour: Do any figures available to his
department reveal either court fines or civil damages imposed on or awarded against either
United States or Canadian trade unions?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: The Department of Labour does not
keep statistics on this. However, I personally know of a case involving a wildcat strike by
members of the United Mineworkers Union in 1975. Judge K. K. Hall in Kentucky found
that the union was making "feeble attempts" to end the strike. He ordered a return to work
and assessed a fine of $500,000 with an additional $100,000 to be paid for every day the strike
continued. The amount payable increased to $1.2 million before the dispute was resolved.
The fine was set aside on resolution of the dispute. However, the union was found in
contempt of court and ordered to pay $500,000 to the coal operators. A similar case
involving teachers in New York City has also been reported.

Government taken to improve the collection and usage of economic and production statistics
from agriculture in order to make decision making by the Government, using up-to-date
information, more effective?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: The Government is very
conscious of the need for up-to-date and informative agricultural statistics as an aid to policy
formation. To this end efforts have been directed towards a greater degree of co-ordination
in the task of statistical collection and in the conduct of field surveys as well as the increased
use of sample surveys where appropriate. The same objectives can be secured in part by the
more rigorous analysis of existing statistics. An example is the work of the joint industry-
Government agricultural review committee which examined the latest production, cost, and
financial information early this year. The results of its work have been valuable as a guide to
policy formation, in particular in the development of policies based on selective incentives
designed to stimulate production.

1080 Poison with Apple Pulp Attractant
139. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Minister of Agriculture: Will he advise whether
his departmental officers are carrying out, or will carry out, investigations into the apple pulp
attractant or bait being used with 1080 poison by pest destruction boards that is apparently
causing secondary poisoning of native and other birds through the consumption of insects
attracted to the baits?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: Preliminary trial work by the New
Zealand Forest Service indicated that raspberry lure used with 1080 impregnated jam bait
may have been contributing to some bird losses. Use of raspberry lure has consequently been
discontinued by the pest destruction movement. My colleague the Minister of Forests and I
recently instructed our departments to prepare a comprehensive report on the poison 1080,
the terms of reference of which include reviewing the effectiveness of existing procedures
relating to the use of 1080 to protect adequately human health and non-target species such as
birds, and the adequacy of research into the use of 1080. This report will establish whether
additional research into any aspect of the use of 1080, including the use of lures with baits, is
needed.

Charge of the Inland Revenue Department. "The actual tax rates for taxable incomes up to
$2,000 were as follows: 1972-73 tax year, the rates of income tax were on the first $650,
7.85c in the dollar on the next $1,050, 21c in the dollar and on the remaining $300, 24.5c in
the dollar. The following changes were made in subsequent years: 1974-75 tax year-on the

19.5c and 20c in the dollar respectively. I should add that these basic rates are subject to the
deduction of special exemptions and rebates."

Sales Tax on Vehicles
148. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Customs: What changes
are proposed in sales tax on vehicles, and in particular on buses ?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs) replied: The proposed changes are as
follows: on 1 April 1978 sales tax on all vehicles other than motorcars and motor cycles will
be reduced from 40 percent to 30 percent; on 1 April 1979 sales tax on vehicles with a gross
vehicle weight exceeding 3.5 tonnes will be reduced from 30 percent to 20 percent, and this
will be further reduced to 10 percent on 1 April 1980; on 1 April 1980 the present decision
exempting the building and fitting of bodies to commercial vehicles will be withdrawn. The
body-building operation will attract the rate of tax applicable to the vehicle on which the
work is performed. Passenger service vehicles are already exempt from sales tax, and no
change is planned.

Unemployment Statistics
157. Mr COOPER (Otago Central) asked the Minister of Labour: What are the latest
unemployment figures for Australia, the United Kingdom, Canada, the United States, and
West Germany, compared with New Zealand?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: The latest available unemployment
figures for the countries mentioned are as follows: Australia had 332 793 registered as
unemployed with the Commonwealth Employment Service at the end of June; this repre-
sented 5.4 percent of the estimated work force. At the same time the United Kingdom had
1 400 000 registered as unemployed, a rate of 6 percent. The Canadian level of unemploy-
ment was 878 000 in July 1977, a rate of 7.9 percent. In May of this year the United States
had 6 800 000 unemployed, a rate of 6.9 percent. In West Germany the unemployment rate
in April was 4.4 percent, or 1 000 000 unemployed. In New Zealand 6590 persons were
registered as unemployed in July, a rate of 0.6 percent. These statistics are collected by
different methods, thus making inter-country comparisons of limited value. Australia has
two different statistical series of unemployment, one of those registering with the Common-
wealth Employment Service for employment. The other is taken from a quarterly survey
conducted by the Australian Bureau of Statistics. The United Kingdom also counts as
unemployed the numbers who register with the employment service for placement. In
Canada and the United States unemployment figures are estimated from a sample household

Tetramine Poison
164. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Minister of Forests: Would he advise what
research has been done on the systemic poison tetramine, and whether his department plans
to use the poison for controlling introduced animals?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: Between 1961 and 1965 the Forest
Research Institute made a study of all overseas literature related to the systemic poison
tetramine to assess its possible potential for the control of red deer. As a result, no tetramine
was imported and the poison has not been used in New Zealand. The Forest Service has no
plans to undertake any applied research on tetramine or any other systemic poison, and
there are no plans for using systemic poisons for the control of introduced animals.

Unemployment Comparison with OECD Countries
174. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) asked the Minister of Labour: How does New Zealand's
unemployment rate calculated on a total basis, Government work schemes included,
compare with the average OECD rate of unemployment and the worst and best countries in
the OECD?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: New Zealand's unemployment rate,
registered unemployed plus those on special Government works, stood at 1.2 percent at the
end of July 1977. Although differences in the methods by which OECD countries collect
unemployment statistics make rigorous comparisons difficult, New Zealand's rate of
unemployment is widely accepted as being amongst the lowest in the OECD membership.
For example, while New Zealand's rate including special workers has averaged about 1
percent this year, Sweden experienced an unemployment rate of 1.8 percent in April 1977,
and Ireland a rate of 12.8 percent in February 1977. These countries represent the best and
worst of the remainder of the OECD countries for which recent figures are available. No
average rate of unemployment is calculated for OECD countries.

URGENT QUESTIONS
Karitane Hospitals
181. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) asked the Minister of Health, as an urgent question: Has he
seen the report in last night's Evening Post that "the Plunket Society's six Karitane hospitals
are nearly all 'broke' because the Government has not paid its subsidy to their running costs
for 5 months", and, if so, (a) can he say why the subsidies have not been paid, and (b) will he
take immediate action to ensure that the Plunket Society is not forced to waste its funds on
an extension of its overdraft?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: Yes, I have seen the report in the Evening
Post. The Plunket Society is the recipient of four subsidies in respect of the operations of its
Karitane hospitals: a subsidy of $2.25 for each $2 raised by the society as voluntary
contributions; a subsidy on the salaries of medical staff; since 1972, an annually approved
grant towards the annual operating deficit of the hospitals; and private hospital benefit of $9
per day per patient. All of these subsidies, except the annual operating deficit, are paid up to
date, and for this financial year so far are over $200,000. Because it is a grant to meet a
forecast annual operating deficit, time is required to fully investigate the amount of the
subsidy sought. This is particularly so when one considers that for the year ended 31 March
1973 the actual deficit was $28,797, while in 1976-77 $363,000 was paid out. I am, however,
looking at ways in which the hospitals liquidity problems can be overcome, perhaps by an
interim advance on the grant, while the necessary investigations are being completed.
A condition of the grant is that adjustments, both up and down, are made in the following
year when the final accounts are available, and although these were sought by my depart-
ment early in May this year, the society was unable to provide this information in respect of
the 1975-76 financial year until mid-July, and final accounts for the 1976-77 financial year
are still not to hand. Although the grant has been approved earlier than this in some years, in
1975 when the Labour Government was in power it was not approved until 28 October. I
intend taking a paper to Cabinet on Monday, 15 August, seeking a grant for the operating
deficit for the year ending 31 March 1978, and any decision will be conveyed to the society
immediately.
(11/8/77)
Mercury Levels in Fish
182. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Health, as an urgent question, Is it
correct that some fish being sold in Auckland contain mercury in excess of the maximu rr
level permitted by the Food and Drug Regulations, and which may be harmful to human
health, and, if so, what action does the Minister propose to take?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: The Department of Health is aware that
large sharks, sometimes sold as lemon fish, contain mercury in excess of the maximum
permitted level of 0.5 parts per million. This maximum level in fish and fish products was
established in February 1971. Since that date, the Department of Health, in conjunction with
the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, has monitored samples of fish offered
for sale to the public. Generally, the permitted levels of mercury have not been exceeded.
The level of mercury in the shark is related to age and size of the fish. The older and larger
fish generally contain elevated levels of mercury, and should not be consumed by humans.
Present sampling indicates that excessive levels of mercury are limited to Auckland. The
Auckland Medical Officer of Health has issued a warning to all fish wholesalers that the
Department of Health will prosecute anyone who is found to be selling for human
consumption shark (lemon fish) which contains mercury in excess of 0.5 parts per million.


## p. 2607 (#245) ###########################################

31 August
2607
Questions and Replies
Control at this stage is being concentrated at the wholesale level, as it is in this area that non-
conforming fish are being sold to the retailer. Should officers of the Department of Health
have reason to believe that fish containing mercury in excess of 0.5 parts per million is
offered for sale for human consumption, the fish will be seized to prevent sale to the public,
and prosecution will follow. All medical officers of health are investigating the possibility of
shark (lemon fish) which contains mercury in excess of the legal limit being sold in their
districts, and appropriate steps will be taken to protect the consumer.

Prison Outbreak-Addington
183. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central), on behalf of Mr KIRK (Sydenham),
asked the Minister of Justice, as an urgent question: Due to the recent amount of public
concern over the violent outbreak of four prisoners from Addington Prison, what steps has
the Minister of Justice taken to: (1) make a full inquiry into the breakout; (2) satisfy the
public that the breakout was an isolated incident and is unlikely to be repeated in this or
other prisons; (3) reduce the number of prisoners being held in Addington to the 25 that it
was designed to take; (4) ensure in the future that prison officers will not be exposed to
excessive vulnerability which occurred in the recent violent example at Addington Prison;
and, (5) ensure that a breakout of the type experienced at Addington Prison will be guarded
against in the future interest of public safety?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Acting Minister of Justice) replied: In reply to the first part of
the question, an inspector visited Addington Prison within 24 hours of the escape. The
department awaits a full report from the superintendent. This has been delayed because
some of the injured officers could not be questioned at the time. Secondly, any comment on
the matters raised will have to await the report. Thirdly, all medium security prisons are
overcrowded. The muster at Addington Prison can be reduced only by increasing strains
elsewhere. However, it cannot be assumed at this stage that overcrowding caused the riot.
Fourthly, steps have been taken to reinforce the staff at Addington, but in most prisons, here
and overseas, the staff are vulnerable to concerted attack. Fifthly, all possible steps will be
taken to guard against a similar outbreak in the future.

COUNTIES AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. The Local Bills Committee considered five submissions on this Bill, but
decided to make only one change-an addition to clause 2, which I shall explain shortly. I
appreciate the committee's efforts, and I thank the members for the very careful and
thorough consideration they accorded the measure. I am grateful to the people and the
organisations that made submissions to the committee.
Members will see that the Local Bills Committee has changed clause 2 by adding a
further provision to amend section 191F(1) of the principal Act. That subsection empowers a
county council, having stopped a road, to offer to sell the land in the former road to the
owner of the adjoining land. If he does not want it, the council can sell or lease the land to
any other person. It was pointed out to the committee that a council can offer the land on
lease to other persons, but it cannot offer a lease of the land to the owner of the adjoining
land in the first instance. The committee quite correctly saw this as an anomaly, and the
amendment rectifies the position by allowing the council to offer the land to the adjoining
owner for sale or lease.
The other amendment made by clause 2, as I explained when introducing the Bill, is a
clarification of section 191F(3) of the principal Act. As previously framed, this provision
required an area of stopped road, which at some point touches on a river, stream, lake, or
the seashore, to be set aside as a public reserve. The original intention was to acquire a
reserve, but over only that part of the stopped road that actually abutted on the waterway,
lake, or seashore. Clause 2(2) introduces the flexibility necessary to enable this to be done.
Submissions to the committee expressed fears that the stopping of paper or unformed
roads would lead to the denial of public access to back-country areas, without there being
any opportunities for objection. The fears are groundless. The county councils proposing to
close roads must follow the procedure laid down in the Act, which is designed to allow for
objection to and public consideration of the proposal. First, the consent of the Minister of
Lands must be obtained, and, secondly, there are extensive requirements in the eighth
schedule to the Act for advertising the closure. The public has a right of objection to the
closure, and it must be considered by the council. If the council disallows the objections,
they must be referred to a magistrate's court or the Town and Country Planning Appeal
Board for a final decision. Clause 8 of the eighth schedule states: “The board or the court, as
the case may be, shall not confirm the decision of the council unless satisfied that adequate
access to the lands in the vicinity of the road is left or provided." No further safeguards are
necessary.
Clause 3 is a re-enactment of section 29 of the Counties Amendment Act 1961 with
some modifications. Section 29 provides for a county council to require reserves to be set
aside for recreation purposes in subdivisions, other than farming subdivisions, on the banks
of rivers or streams, and in all subdivisions around lake shores and the sea coast. The
council, with the consent of the Minister of Lands, could waive the requirement for the
lakeside or riverside reserve, or reduce that reserve to not less than 3 metres in width. The
Minister of Lands could waive the requirement for a seaside reserve only if the subdivision
was for commercial or industrial purposes, if access to the sea was essential for the purposes
of the subdivision, or in the case of an artificial boat harbour. Those provisions have been


## p. 2619 (#257) ###########################################

31 August
2619
Counties Amendment Bill
found to be too inflexible to deal fairly with a limited range of situations that cannot readily
or reasonably be expressly provided for in law.
The modification to section 29(1) of the principal Act extends the power of the Minister
of Lands to consent to the waiving of a reserve requirement on a coastal subdivision
regardless of the purpose of the subdivision. It has been suggested that this will result in the
reduction of public access to the sea. This suggests that a change in the policy followed by
successive Governments is intended. I assure the House that no such change is intended or
envisaged. The sole purpose of the modification is to provide an element of
flexibility-which is at present lacking-to deal with rare situations that cannot readily be
provided for in general statute law.
The other modification is the insertion of the new provisions shown in subsections (5) to
(9) of the new section 29, set out in clause 3. These provisions give statutory recognition to
the payment of compensation for reserves taken in farming subdivisions around lakes or on
the sea coast, and provide for the refund of the survey costs incurred in determining the
reserve areas to be set aside. Provision is made for the compensation to be refunded wholly
or in part, at the discretion of the Minister of Lands, if the land is further subdivided within 5
years. Compensation is payable only if the subdividing owner retains not less than 4 hectares
of the land adjoining the reserve areas, which he continues to farm, and the land is not zoned
for residential, commercial, or industrial purposes.
In the past 4 years, section 29 of the Counties Amendment Act 1961 has been
considered by the House on three occasions. The modifications now being made will
produce a practical and operable measure. Reserves will continue to be set aside as before to
ensure public access. A flexibility is provided to waive or modify this requirement in those
rare cases that cannot be expressly covered in law. The use of that power will likewise be
rare, and certainly its provision now does not imply any change in a policy consciously
followed by successive Governments. This is a good measure, and I have no hesitation in
recommending it to the House.
