DEVELOPMENT FINANCE CORPORATION AMENDMENT BILL (NO. 2)
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I move, That this
Bill be now read a second time. When I introduced the Development Finance Corporation
Amendment Bill (No. 2) last December, I made the following points: first, the Bill arose
from the Government's election pledge to establish a Small Business Agency; secondly, it
recognises the social and economic importance of small businesses in New Zealand; and,
thirdly, the Bill is intended to remedy a situation in which no single organisation is
specifically responsible for the special needs of the small business sector. It is appropriate
that my introductory remarks on the occasion of the Bill's second reading should elaborate
these points somewhat further, because they contain, in essence, the reasons for the Bill's
existence.
The Government's 1975 election manifesto contained a firm undertaking to establish
the agency; that statement was well read and studied by the commercial community. Now,
some 22 months after that statement was published, we see no reason to change our views.
Indeed, the extensive process of consultation and discussion that has been undertaken by my
Parliamentary Under-Secretary, the member for Tauranga, and me has served only to
reinforce our belief in a strong and vigorous small business sector. There has been a great
deal of interest about the Bill among business organisations, trade associations, individual
firms, and people in the academic and university field.
I come to my second point, which acknowledges the economic and social importance of
small businesses. Small business is a vital part of the New Zealand industrial, commercial,
and servicing scene. I suppose it can fairly be said that about 90 percent of New Zealand
companies employ fewer than 50 people, and small businesses therefore provide employ-
ment for large numbers of people, particularly in the provincial and suburban areas. They
contribute much to our industrial growth and development, but because they are small they
make their contribution while preserving an essentially human scale of values. The physical
size is seldom overpowering, and employees of a small company usually find it easy to
communicate. The individual can thus identify readily with his job, and with the objectives
of the business organisation as a whole. He is an important part of a team.
The scale of small businesses can also offer economic advantages. It used to be an article
of conventional wisdom that efficiency was the preserve of large companies, and it is true
that a large company can afford to invest more in advanced plant and methods, in research,
and in the training of staff. It is also true that the large-scale enterprise can exploit economies
of scale that none of its smaller counterparts could hope to match, and of course the large
company plays a vital role as an employer of labour, offering jobs to large numbers of
people. The small company has distinctive strengths in other areas. For example, it can
provide short production runs, and the kind of specialised service that a large company
would find uneconomic.
The relationship between big and small businesses is complementary, a situation
reflected in the fact that many small businesses act as suppliers or subcontractors to large
companies. As I move around New Zealand—although perhaps I do not do so as much as my
Parliamentary Under-Secretary-I find it fascinating and stimulating to visit smaller
companies and see how their technology and their products are often used as the essential
component for a larger company that is exporting effectively. One company in Tauranga is
making components for a chest freezer that is being exported by a larger company to Japan,
among other countries. Technology of this type is developing in the smaller New Zealand
companies.
That brings me to my third point. It is easy to take the small business for granted, and to
see it and the benefits it offers as simply an integral part of the New Zealand business scene,
and leave it at that. But to do so would be to take less than seriously our national ambitions


## p. 2621 (#259) ###########################################

31 August
2621
Development Finance Corporation Amendment Bill (No. 2)
for an efficient manufacturing and commercial sector, and our hopes for increased and
diversified export earnings. If we are to encourage the potential for innovation and growth in
the small business sector, the Government believes it is important to recognise the sector's
special needs and to provide an organisation that is responsible for meeting them. Hence the
provisions of the Bill.
I have mentioned some of the strengths of the small business, but it often has special
needs, which are rooted in the dominant fact that the small business is the distinctive
expression of an individual. More than any other characteristic, the common denominator of
small businesses is that, more likely than not, they are run personally by the owner. On the
one hand, this gives the small business owner the advantage of independence in making
decisions, but, on the other hand, he must work in isolation, without the benefit of the back-
up resources of many of the larger business organisations. With all the decision making, and
often a good deal of the shop-floor responsibility-particularly in the manufacturing
area-concentrated in the hands of this one person, he is usually under constant pressure.
There are other problems as well. The experience of the owner-manager is more likely
to lie in the practical aspects of his business-the practical aspects of manufacturing, for
example, or of providing a service-than in the specialised areas of management techniques
and knowledge, yet this knowledge is often essential if the business is to succeed and to
achieve its full potential. The small business also experiences distinctive problems in the
management of finance, and in raising finance. This can result in problems of equipping and
maintaining satisfactory production facilities, or perhaps in a total inability to finance the
development of potentially valuable and profitable operations.
In summary then, our investigations in New Zealand and the information we have
received from overseas show that the small business owner tends to require assistance in two
broad areas: first, general management advice and information, and secondly, assistance
with financial management and the raising of finance. The Bill has been drafted with these
two areas of assistance in mind.
The report of the chairman of the Commerce and Mining Committee, which considered
the Bill, has already been tabled. This report was based on the 13 submissions received by
the committee, which, as the House will have noted, have resulted in some amendments to
the Bill. These amendments are largely of a polishing nature, and the main provisions of the
Bill are substantially unchanged.
If I may speak for a moment or two on the clauses before I conclude, clause 1 provides
for the short title. Clause 2 inserts a new Part IA in the principal Act, and contains new
sections 9A to 9G. Section 9A relates to the interpretation of the new part. Section 9B
provides for the definition by the Minister of Trade and Industry, following a recommenda-
tion by the board of the Development Finance Corporation, of those businesses to which the
new part will apply. The section also empowers the board to limit the exercise of particular
powers of the small business agency to particular types of small business. No final definition
of "small business" has been included in the Bill itself, so that it can be modified more easily
in response to changing circumstances by notice in the Gazette. Section 9c requires the
Development Finance Corporation to establish and maintain the Small Business Agency,
and entrusts the conduct of that agency to the corporation's board.
Section 9D gives the agency the following functions: first, to encourage, promote, and
facilitate the establishment, carrying on, expansion, and development of efficient small
businesses; secondly, to liaise with, and to encourage co-operation and co-ordination
among, organisations that are concerned with the activities of small businesses; and, thirdly,
to collaborate with organisations and persons in developing financial and technical assistance
schemes and other services for small businesses. Section 9D has been amended, first, by
removing mention of specific organisations in section 9D(b) and 9D(c) in order to eliminate
any suggestion that liaison and collaboration might be limited to those mentioned, and,
secondly, by adding a subsection (2) which, for technical reasons, makes clear that in this Bill
the term "organisation" includes a Government department and a Government agency.
Section 9E prescribes the general powers of the agency, which include: first, the
establishment of regional information and referral centres in collaboration with local
organisations; secondly, the provision of advisory, consultancy, and other services in co-
ordination with existing services; thirdly, the arranging of suitable educational programmes
and dissemination of information; and, fourthly, the review of the performance and welfare
of small businesses in the light of the existing policies of the Government, and existing or
proposed legislation.
Section 9F(1) makes it a particular function of the agency to promote the availability of


## p. 2622 (#260) ###########################################

2622
31 August
Development Finance Corporation Amendment Bill (No. 2)
financial advice and suitable forms of financial assistance to small businesses. Subsections (2)
and (3) empower the agency, with the approval of the Minister of Finance, to guarantee
loans made for the purposes of a small business. Subsection (3) has been amended by the
removal of a proviso that empowered the agency to enter into a guarantee only when the

Agency, by removing the requirement that he first establish his inability to borrow elsewhere

charges any sum required to fulfil a guarantee to the Consolidated Revenue Account.
Subsection (2) enables the agency to take over a creditor's remedies against a debtor if it
discharges any liability under a guarantee.
Clause 3 amends section 10(1)(d) of the principal Act to provide for the appointment of
an additional director to the corporation's board. This is similar to the provision that was
made for the new ventures division, when an additional director was provided for that
purpose. Clause 4 consequentially amends section 15(3) of the principal Act, which relates to
a quorum for meetings of the board of the Development Finance Corporation. This clause
has been amended to provide for a lower quorum-three, instead of four-when the number
of appointed directors, excluding the chairman of the board, does not exceed four. This
amendment has been made to ensure that the board of the Development Finance Corpora-
tion can continue to function even though the number of appointed directors may not be at
full strength, for one reason or another, taking into account the other business commitments
of board members.
Clause 5 inserts a new section 20B in the principal Act, which requires the corporation to
establish a separate Small Business Agency Account and makes provision for payments into
and out of that account. This account is to be disregarded in determining the corporation's
annual surplus under section 20 of the principal Act. A new clause 5A amends section 22 of
the principal Act, and provides for the payment of fees, allowances, and expenses to
members of committees of the board of the Development Finance Corporation who are not
directors or officers of the corporation. This provision has been included largely to cover the
existing situation of members of a committee that is advising on the work of the new ventures
division, and does not relate solely to the Small Business Agency. The Government intends
to set up a committee outside the board specifically to advise the Development Finance
Corporation about the operation of the Small Business Agency, and this clause provides for
that.
Clause 6 adds a new subsection (4) to section 25 of the principal Act, and provides that
the finances and operations of the agency are to be reported on to the Minister and
Parliament separately from those relating to the other activities of the corporation. It is
desirable that the Small Business Agency should report separately from the other activities
of the Development Finance Corporation. The new clause 7 amends section 32A of the
principal Act, and provides specific protection for the Development Finance Corporation
against a liability to any action for damages taken on the grounds of its refusal to give advice
and assistance. This will enable it to make its own judgment of cases on their merits.
Although the powers conferred on the corporation by the Act are largely discretionary, it
was thought appropriate to make this explicit by including this new clause.
New Zealand's small businesses have demonstrated their potential ability to operate
successfully in a highly competitive business world, not only on the domestic market but on
the world market. One of the exciting facets of the job of Minister of Trade and Industry is to
observe what the small businesses are doing, and the new export ventures they are
undertaking. The Small Business Agency will encourage them to play an even greater part in
the development of industry and New Zealand's export earnings. The goods they produce,
which range from sophisticated electronics through to farm materials and handcrafts, not
only meet a wide variety of local needs, but, as I have said, can also be found in a growing
number of export markets. The services they offer touch the daily lives, in one way or
another, of most New Zealanders. Nevertheless, many small businesses require additional
assistance to ensure that they fulfil their maximum potential. The Government considers
that the Small Business Agency will assist this process.

CARTER OBSERVATORY AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Science and Technology): I move, That this Bill be
now read a second time. The Carter Observatory Act 1938, which this Bill amends, provides
statutory authority for the establishment of the Carter Observatory as a public astronomical
facility. Mr Charles Rooking Carter died in 1896, leaving £2,240 for the purpose of
establishing an astronomical observatory in or near Wellington. At the time that sum was too
small to finance the construction of a major building, and it was invested. It was not until
1938, when the funds had accumulated to about £13,000, that the Carter Observatory came
into being. Since then there have been all sorts of changes.
The purpose of the Bill is to amend the machinery which was set up to provide for the
growth and development of the observatory's activities. The amendment has two major
features. It declares the Carter Observatory to be a national astronomical observatory for
New Zealand, and in doing so recognises that the observatory has been effectively carrying
out such functions for many years. Members may be surprised to know of the wide variety of
functions undertaken by a national observatory. A national observatory provides reliable
astronomical data for government departments, industry, and citizens-for example, tables
of sunrise and sunset, phases of the moon, visibility of planets, and calculations for the
Nautical Almanac. The prime function of a national observatory is to maintain information
about navigation, surveying, accurate time keeping, and the like. Other functions include
providing a national link, contributing to an international network of astronomical observa-
tions and information and sponsoring the promotion and development of astronomy in the
country.
The Bill amends the provisions resulting from the original Carter bequest confining the
observatory's operations to Wellington, and authorises the observatory to establish and
operate outstations in other parts of New Zealand. The need for this arises from the
difficulties that have developed over the years in making astronomical observations from
urban sites, largely through the interference of town lights and the effect of the atmosphere
and vibrations. The headquarters of the Carter Observatory will remain in Wellington.
A number of other amendments relate to the two main features. The Bill expressly
authorises the observatory to carry out its functions in collaboration with other organisations
and people. This is important in New Zealand, where significant astronomical work is done


## p. 2631 (#269) ###########################################

31 August
2631
Carter Observatory Amendment Bill
by amateurs. The Bill also authorises the Carter Observatory to make grants and subsidies to
other workers in astronomy. In addition, the Bill provides for the alteration of membership
to the Carter Observatory Board in order to give additional representation to local
authorities, thus reflecting the wider sources of contribution to the board's income in recent
years. The Bill specifically authorises such contributions by interested organisations and
people. As a matter of interest, in 1938 the Government and the Wellington City Council
provided £1,500 and £500 respectively towards the operation of the Carter Observatory. In
addition, the Wellington City Council donated the land and the telescope. Today the total
requirements of the Carter Observatory are more than $83,000, of which the Government
contributes about $64,000, the Wellington City Council $8,600, and other local authorities
$6,000. The Bill gives these other local authorities representation on the board.
The Carter Observatory Amendment Bill is a machinery measure. It is a result of the
report and the recommendations of the national committee on astronomy of the Royal
Society of New Zealand. It has been discussed in detail with the Carter Observatory Board
and other interested bodies. The representation provisions have been agreed to by the local
authorities concerned. The amendment will tidy up the 1938 Act and allow the Carter
Observatory to carry out its functions more satisfactorily.

Astronomy occupies a unique place in man's intellectual ascent. The stars first triggered

RESERVES BILL
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I move That this Bill be now read a second
time. This Bill of 125 clauses is a consolidation and updating of the Reserves and Domains
Act 1953, and the amendments to that Act. The present legislation has therefore served our
needs for almost 24 years. The revision of the present Act is necessary because of the
changes in attitude to the preservation of open space, and the increasing pressures for the
use and development of reserves. These pressures were not envisaged when the present Act
became law in 1953. That Act contains definitions for only two categories of reserves-scenic
and historic. Reserves of other categories are mentioned in the present legislation, but not
defined. This is rectified in the new Bill.
The Reserves Bill establishes seven distinct categories of reserves, each with its own
management requirements. The seven categories are: recreation, historic, scenic, nature,
scientific, Government purpose, and local purpose. The nature reserve is a new description
for the existing flora and fauna reserves. However, I should like to mention one important
matter in respect of the new local purpose reserve category. In addition to such uses as
library, stock, plantation, etc., local purpose reserves will also include such community uses
as play centres, kindergartens, and Plunket rooms. The Reserves and Domains Act provides
that these are legitimate uses on recreation reserves, but in drafting the new Bill it was felt
that their inclusion would not be consistent with a recreation reserve classification. These
latter reserves are to provide for recreation and sporting activities, and the physical welfare
and enjoyment of the public. They also provide for the protection of the natural environ-
ment and the beauty of the countryside. Emphasis is on the retention of open spaces and
outdoor recreational activities, including walking tracks in the countryside.
Clause 16 requires all existing reserves as well as new reserves to be classified into one
or more of the seven reserve categories established under the Bill. These I described
previously. An investigation of all reserves will be undertaken to determine their correct
classification. Depending on use, there will undoubtedly be some existing reserves that will
be subdivided and given more than one classification. For example, part of a recreation
reserve may contain a play centre. That part will be classified as a local purpose reserve, the
balance as recreation reserve. Future use will also be investigated, and if it can be foreseen
that a reserve could have more than one use it too will be subdivided and classified into two
or more categories.
Clause 13 gives the Minister of Lands the power to declare any specified reserve or part
of a reserve to be a New Zealand reserve. This important provision is not contained in the
present Act. New Zealand reserves will be those which protect assets of national or
international significance for which specialised management is needed. In these cases the
reserves will be administered either by the department or by a reserves board, or in such
other manner as the Minister may decide. Few reserves will be thus categorized. Among
those that will are some which should have special protection because of their unique
qualities or value as habitats for rare or endangered species of flora and fauna. Such reserves
will be declared areas meriting special protection, and their reservations may not be revoked
or their classifications changed except by Act of Parliament. Examples of these reserves are
the white heron colony at Ökarito in Westland and the Cape Kidnappers gannet colony in
Hawke's Bay.
The provision for the appointment of boards, local authorities, and voluntary organisa-


## p. 2633 (#271) ###########################################

31 August
2633
Reserves Bill
tions to control and manage reserves is contained in clauses 26 to 39. Other general
provisions allied to this are also included. These provisions are mainly re-enactments of
similar provisions in the present Reserves and Domains Act. However, clauses 38 and 39 of
the Bill are new. Clause 38 provides for an existing administering body to control and
manage land that is not a reserve, and for the appointment of an administering body to do
likewise. In both cases the agreement must first be obtained from the owner of the land. The
owner of the land must also agree to its being used for one of the purposes specified in the
seven categories of reserves. The clause is designed to meet those cases where owners of land
wish to co-operate in a scheme of preservation, but do not wish to relinquish the title. There
are other clauses of the Bill which have a similar effect, but clause 38 relates to assistance by
administering bodies, and not the department. The power to spend public moneys in these
cases is contained in clause 85.
Clause 39 makes provision for technical advice, guidance, and related assistance to be
provided with or without charge to administering bodies. Clause 40 provides that the
administering body must control and manage the reserve in accordance with the provisions
of the Act. In clause 41 the administering body is given the responsibility to prepare within 5
years a management plan of the reserve. It is a requirement that the plan ensure compliance
with the principles laid down for the reserve classification, and also that it be under
continuous review to enable account to be taken of changing circumstances or increased
knowledge that may accrue to that reserve. The public is to be involved. Provision is made
for public notification of the intention to prepare a plan, and to invite comment from the
public. Subsequently, when the plan is prepared, the public will also have the right to lodge
objections if it is considered that there is a need to do so. Objections will be heard by the
administering body before the plan is submitted finally to the Minister for his approval.
Exemptions to the requirement to seek ministerial approval will apply in some cases.
Section 27 of the Reserves and Domains Act relates to leasing. In the Bill these powers
are extensively altered. Provision is made for distinct categories of leases, which follow a
consistent and logical pattern. Clause 54 of the Bill deals with recreation reserves, and
provides for leases for a number of purposes-for example, baths, camping grounds, parking
grounds, outdoor sports and games and other recreational activities, and for the carrying on
of any trade, business, or occupation. Leases of the open portions of a scenic reserve are
dealt with in clause 56. The first schedule to the Bill sets out the various classes of leases, and
the provision applicable in each case. A feature of the Bill is the various provisions designed
as alternatives to outright purchase or lease of land for reserve purposes where the public
interest requires action to be taken.
I referred earlier to clause 38 and to control and management of land that is not a
reserve. I said that it would permit an administering body to assist the owner of private land
with both expertise and finance. It will assist the private owner to protect and preserve that
land without the necessity for the Crown or a local body actually purchasing the property.
The Reserves and Domains Act provides for private historic and scenic reserves, and these
are now combined in the Bill and given the term "protected private land”. Clause 85, which
authorises the expenditure of money on land that is not a reserve, is also in the Reserves and
Domains Act, although in the Bill this has been widened to provide that the owner must
agree to his land being used for one of the seven reserve categories before any public money
can be spent.
A most important provision is contained in clause 77. Conservation covenants are a new
concept in the preservation and protection of our landscape. The clause provides that, for a
consideration, the department can negotiate a private agreement with landowners to
preserve the natural environment or landscape amenity without having to resort to acquisi-
tion. The consideration could be a lump sum, or a yearly payment. It could be a contribution
towards rates or payments for fencing off a bush area. It would be compensation to the
owner for the uses forgone on the land over which the covenant is granted. The covenants
can be for a specified period, or in perpetuity. It is intended that they be registered against
the title. It is to be hoped that landowners will take advantage of this provision. Many have
land that they know should be protected, but they have been loath to give up ownership.
This is understandable, and the conservation covenant will meet their wishes entirely. To
ensure that this kind of protection has the widest possible application, the Government has
also included the same provision in the Queen Elizabeth II National Trust Bill, in which it is
referred to as an open space covenant. However, its effect is exactly the same as a
conservation covenant.
The financial provisions of the Reserves Bill, in the main, re-enact the existing


## p. 2634 (#272) ###########################################

2634
31 August
Reserves Bill
provisions of the Reserves and Domains Act, with minor changes only. Domain boards are
abolished, and will become administering bodies of recreation reserves. The financial
provisions relating to domain boards are therefore altered to relate to administering bodies
generally. New clauses provide for the payment of rates on Maori reservations and protected
land subject to certain criteria. Apart from the penalty provisions, the offences section of the
Reserves and Domains Act has, in the main, been re-enacted without material change. Two
of the three new clauses relate to the seizure and forfeiture of animals, birds, and other
property, and the trespass of sheep, cattle, or other animals. These provisions follow similar
provisions in the National Parks Act, and it was considered worth while to include them in
this Bill.
Clause 99A deals with the stopping and searching of boats, and follows the introduction
of the Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Bill. The clause acknowledges the need
for strong powers to deal with suspected offences on the country's very important outlying
island reserves. Fishing activity in the general area of these reserves-which contain some of
the world's last remaining areas of vegetation unmodified by man or introduced animals-is
increasing. Landing rights are strictly controlled to guard against the introduction of foreign
plants, fires, the release of cats or rodents, or interference with nesting birds or nursing
mammals. Under clause 13 of the new legislation, all these outlying island reserves will
qualify for declaration as New Zealand reserves. Outlying islands will be classified basically
as nature reserves or scientific reserves. The prohibition of entry is strengthened in the
access provisions of these clauses.
In conclusion, I should mention the extensive provision in the Bill for public involve-
ment in decisions affecting reserves where there is some loss of freedom of access to the
public. Clauses 118 and 118A lay down the procedure to be followed when advertising is
required under the provisions of this new measure. The public is given the right to object,
and to be heard by the administering body of a reserve. Objection will be against specific
proposals, but must be made within 2 months. Where my consent to a proposal is necessary,
a summary of all objections and a statement as to the extent to which they have been
accepted or disallowed are to be sent to me by the administering body. The advertising and
objection procedure for revoking reserves is the only public involvement provision common
to both the Reserves and Domains Act and the Reserves Bill. The extension of the
advertising procedure to other provisions of the Bill is new, and was the subject of a number
of submissions to the select committee. It also recognises that public opinion favours the
disclosure of information as a part of the decision-making process. The Bill represents a
consolidation and updating of the reserves legislation, and is an integral part of the
Government's policy on the open spaces programme and the protection and conservation of
our land.

others were from Maori groups, the Historic Places Trust, and play centre organisations.
Fourteen submissions expressed the view that there was still a need for public participation
in decisions on reserves. That small deficiency was very important to those who made the
submissions, and I am pleased to see that it has been corrected in the Bill.
I come from an area that is oriented towards the development, enhancement, and
protection of reserves. However, it is a fragile area in regard to development work by local
government over a long period. I believe that the present Act provides insufficient flexibility
for the leasing of land, the designation of land, and the problems of domain boards and those
with designated right to make the right community decisions for the area, the region, and
New Zealand. The pressures on land development are known to everyone. They come from
subdividers and those who can see in the tremendous bank of reserves we have in New
Zealand a way in which to meet community needs by avariciously moving on to lands that
have been held in trust for future generations. Often the pressure from such sources is a little
overpowering for local authorities. With the new mobility of people, new concepts in town
and country planning, and new community patterns, there is a great need for an Act that
provides flexibility and a philosophy on which to base future decisions about the needs of the
community. I regret that these pressures will always apply in resorts and scenic areas. I think
of Auckland and other coastal areas, where too many restrictions or conditions are imposed
on community groups.
The seven categories of reserves given in the Bill will provide an important means of
identification, and enable communities to decide where best to develop play centres,
kindergartens, or other community facilities. The new categories of Government purpose
and local purpose reserves are very important. Although the right was contained in the
previous Act, libraries, stock, plantations, cemeteries, or play centres and kindergartens,
can now find a home.
On occasions it has been difficult to obtain permission from local branches of the
Department of Lands and Survey, from the department in Wellington, or from the Minister,
largely because of a lack of clarity about the leasing of land. I am pleased at the way the
legislation treats this problem. All land in New Zealand must be categorised, but at the same
time we must be careful, with a population of just over 3 000 000-at almost zero population
growth-that we do not fall into the hands of the extreme conservationists and environmen-
talists who believe that every block of unused land should remain unused. Although local
authorities will be extremely busy in the next few years designating these lands, in 5 years'
time it should be much easier for a person affected by the use of a reserve to look at the
categories and object, or apply to a local authority for the use of a reserve.
I am delighted to see that the word "domain" has been taken out of the legislation,
particularly when I think of the number of times we had to notify our local authority
members, who were members of the borough council, that they were expected to attend
statutory meetings of the domain board. Notices had to be sent out, when all the work could
have been done through the borough council. It was all a bit demoralising, particularly for
the small 6-monthly meetings which dealt with trivial matters. The reserves committees of


## p. 2637 (#275) ###########################################

31 August
2637
Reserves Bill
territorial local authorities will now be able to make recommendations and work within the
Act. Any problems can be put to the Minister, and members of the public will have a right to
appeal against any decision made by a local authority. Members of the public will be fully
involved, and that is very important, particularly when people are now much more
environmentally conscious.
I welcome the conservation covenants, the private agreements that can be arranged
between the owner of land and the local authority or the Crown. Potential reserves may be
on private or commercial properties. They could be pleasant little corners that should be
used as passive reserves, but generally they will be in the larger blocks where a farmer may
feel that overdevelopment will spoil the area. Under the Bill, however, he will still own the
land but not pay rates on it. That is an excellent policy, in that the land can be taken without
removing it from private ownership. I think particularly of land that is important for our
environmental or social progress. The Queen Elizabeth II National Trust Bill fits in
beautifully with this legislation.
One very important point I should like to raise relates to our off-shore islands. Although
people do not often get to them, at least they know they are there. Botanists can visit them
and study natural habitats and various ecosystems. Now, of course, we have the 200-mile
management zone, which means more pressure will be placed on those off-shore islands.
These islands will be protected from illegal entry, and penalties are set for the removal of
flora and fauna. I do not believe that people are irresponsible, but a person from overseas
ignorant of our laws might take some of the flora and fauna off the islands and allow the
infestation of rats and mice. I would be the last person to fall in with the extreme
conservationists, but I do believe the Bill will play an important part in the development and
protection of our off-shore islands.
The Bill contains much more than did the Bill introduced by the former member for
Eden, who was proposing to strangle our coastline completely. The former member for
Taupo offered his congratulations on the proposed Coastal Moratorium and Management
Bill. Those two members are hoping to return to the House, but I do not think they will be
successful. However, I hope that during their spell in the cold they have realised that New
Zealand now has a Government that believes in a property-owning democracy.
The member for Northern Maori spoke of the need to set up a fund to buy coastal
reserves. The Opposition has been crowing about the $2.6 million it spent on this while it was
in power. I think it was a miserable amount to spend, but that comment is all the Opposition
can find to make. Over the years I have watched the way in which the Department of Lands
and Survey has interpreted the Act, but the Bill clearly allows for the use of reserves by all
New Zealanders, whether passively, or for physical pursuits such as tramping, hunting, or
shooting. The Bill is a consolidating measure, and I support it.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori): Listening to the member for Otago Central, one would
have thought the House was discussing a local authority Bill. The Opposition accepts the
principles contained in the Bill, and believes that in its amended form it will play an
important part in protecting our reserves. The report brought down by the department
summarises the Bill quite satisfactorily. The matters covered in the report include the
relationship of the Bill to the Town and Country Planning Act, a wider public involvement,
the Maori viewpoint, mining, the extension of the Act to include, local authority land rights
for public purposes, and the provision of sites for play centres, kindergartens, Plunket
societies, and marine reserves.
The last four points have been dealt with by previous speakers and I shall confine my
remarks to the first three, particularly in connection with the Town and Country Planning
Bill, which was introduced into the House only last week.
Mr Birch: You can't refer to that Bill.
Mr WETERE: Well, I may say about the Bill before the House that it caused some

Tairawhiti District Executive. I think the amendments have cleared up the confusion felt by

concern can be cleared up. There is provision for wider publication in national dailies and in
libraries and places of public interest, so that people can become more informed about the
department's plans for management of reservations. If there is wider public involvement,
people will accept the amended Bill.
The submissions made to the committee by the Maori Graduates Association relate to
the acquisition of land, and are particularly concerned with clause 12. I read from the

Dr WALL (Porirua): I do not want to take up the time of the House tonight, particularly

drew attention to the fact that the Minister, when discussing the Counties Amendment Bill,
had said we were quite safe in passing the extended provisions for more flexibility in dealing
with reserve or potentially reserved land because one of the essential safeguards was that the
Minister of Lands must agree, as we were dealing with reserve lands. At that time I said that
the provision was only temporary, because of the provision in the Bill we are now dealing
with. Clause 10 makes provision for the delegation of the Minister's powers, which are
extensive, and deal not only with the naming but also the disposal of reserves. His powers
can be delegated not only to members of his staff but also by statute, so that reference to the
Minister does not then become necessary, and the safeguards mentioned by the Minister of
Local Government will not be present in many cases.
I draw attention to clause 10, which states: "The Minister may from time to time
delegate any of his powers and functions under this Act—not being the power to approve
any bylaw-to any individual, committee, body, local authority, or organisation, or to any
officer or officers of the department specified by the Minister, either as to matters within his
jurisdiction generally"—and it is that matter which concerns me-"or in any particular case
or matter, or any particular class of cases or matters, or in respect of any reserve or
reserves." The position may arise where a local officer of the Department of Lands and
Survey, who has certain powers delegated to him by the Minister, makes arrangements with
a local officer of the county council or the local body, the whole matter being jacked up
within the provisions of those two Acts without reference, except that provided for appeal to
a magistrate's court under the Counties Act. Potential and existing reserves may be
withdrawn without any representation being made to anyone outside the local scene.
I should like the Minister to explain the extent of his powers of delegation, the manner
in which they are limited, and the limitations of his authority to delegate power under the
Reserves Act when compared with the Counties Act. The fact that the authority is
mentioned in two Acts does not mean that there is a cross-authorisation in the two Acts
dealing with reserves. If the Minister says that his power of delegation under the Counties
Act is in any way affected by the Reserves Act, I should like to have a legal opinion justifying
that statement. If we have that assurance I think the degree of unanimity in the House on
this Bill will continue, but, in the absence of an assurance my reservations on the Counties
Act must remain.
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): When the member for Porirua referred to the
Counties Act I thought, as I did when the member for Northern Maori was speaking, that
the Counties Act is one measure that the Labour Opposition would prefer not to think about
because of its unhappy record with that legislation. We all know quite well, in spite of what
the member for Northern Maori said about the provisions of the Counties Act, that the
original legislation was substantially amended because of pressure from the National
Opposition and Federated Farmers. As a result, that legislation is now much more
acceptable to the farming community and to those who own land.
The member for Porirua referred to the provisions in the Counties Amendment Bill,
which I can refer to only in passing. He mentioned the responsibility of the Minister of Lands
in setting aside reserves where there is a subdivision, or where the land fronts on to the sea or
a lake. Following an approach by the local authority, the Minister is able to reduce the area
of the esplanade reserve set aside. The Counties Amendment Bill also provides for
compensation where the land remains with the Crown. The delegation provisions in clause
10 of the Reserves Bill allow the Minister from time to time to delegate any of his powers and
functions under the Act,—not being the powers or functions he is required to exercise by
notice in the Gazette or approved by any bylaw-to any individual, committee, body, local
authority, or organisation. Under this legislation, the Minister's responsibilities are very
wide, and cover not only the setting aside of reserves, but also the classification of reserves,
and requirements for the publication or otherwise of changes in classification.
When one considers the thousands of reserves in New Zealand-there are many large

Public Servants-Statistics
2. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) asked the Minister of State Services: In view of his reply to
question 3 for written answer on 19 August 1977, in which it is stated that the numbers of
public servants increased by 2404 to 79 199 from 76 795 during the period 1 April 1975 to
1 April 1976, could he inform the House of the numbers of those extra staff employed in
each quarter of that year?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I reply on behalf of
the Minister of State Services. His answer follows. I apologise that the reply is fairly detailed,
but it does stem from a written question. "The figures given in my reply to question 3 for
written answer on 19 August 1977 for total numbers of public servants were established on a
head-count basis. The figures are not available for each quarter of the year. However,
figures established on a full-time equivalent basis, and which exclude approximately 9000
wage workers under financial-as opposed to staff ceiling-control are available for most
quarters of the 1975-76 financial year. Those figures are: 31 March 1975, 64 342; 30 June
1975, 65 270; 30 September 1975, not available; 31 December 1975, 65 743; 31 March 1976,
66 733. The 31 March 1976 staffing figure is 2391 higher than the 31 March 1975 figure; 928
of the increase occurred in the quarter April to June 1975, 473 in the two quarters July to
December 1975, and 990 in the quarter January to March 1976.”
Mr T. J. Young: Are all those civil servants employed through the State Services
Commission; and, if not, could he tell me how the figures are made up?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The staffing figures which were quoted in the 19
August 1977 reply referred to by the honourable member were established on a head-count
basis. Each employee is counted as one, regardless of whether he works full time or part
time—that is, whether he is engaged under the State Services Commission procedures or
whether he is employed on a part-time basis.
Mr T. J. Young: This would include Railways staff, teachers?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: It includes quite a wide range of people who are
engaged on a temporary basis. The figures are obtained at 31 March each year, and are used
in the State Services Commission's annual report. All public servants are included. The
staffing figures which I quoted in reply to this question are those obtained for staff ceiling
control purposes, so that is the difference between this answer and the written answer given
by the Minister, which included all on this head-count basis.

Sheep Numbers
12. Mr LAMBERT (Western Hutt) asked the Minister of Agriculture: Can he confirm
the recent press announcement of a 3.5 percent increase in sheep numbers?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): The recent press report of a 3.5 percent
increase in sheep numbers at 30 June of this year compared with last year's figure is based on
an estimate produced by the Meat and Wool Board's economic service. My ministry's
estimate, however, is for a larger increase of 4.3 percent, on the basis of sheep numbers this
year being 2 410 000 higher than last year's figure of 56 400 000. This latter estimate takes
account of the pattern of this season's ewe and lamb kill, mortality, last season's lambing
percentages, and other factors. There is, indeed, good reason to believe that farmers, taking
advantage of recently introduced incentives, retained a higher proportion of ewe lambs last
season.

BAY OF PLENTY CATCHMENT COMMISSION AND REGIONAL WATER BOARD
ADMINISTRATIVE EXPENSES RECOVERY BILL
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): I move, That leave be given to introduce
the Bay of Plenty Catchment Commission and Regional Water Board Administrative
Expenses Recovery Bill. The Bill is a measure to resolve a very difficult situation that has
prevailed in the Bay of Plenty for the past 5 years. When the Bay of Plenty Catchment
Commission was established in 1962 the constituent local authorities-five counties and
seven municipalities-agreed to contribute to the commission's administrative expenditure
on the basis of about 63 percent by the counties and about 37 percent by the municipalities.
However, at the review date in 1972 the local authorities failed to agree on the apportion-
ment of costs. As an interim measure they agreed to contribute for that year on the old basis
without prejudice.
Since April 1973 all further attempts to reach agreement on the required contributions
have failed. Representatives of the National Water and Soil Conservation Authority and the
Soil Conservation and Rivers Control Council, successive Ministers of Works and Develop-
ment, an independent Treasury officer, the Local Government Commission, and a further
independent arbitrator appointed by the Minister of Works and Development have held
discussions with either the catchment commission or the local authorities involved, but have
failed to settle the dispute. Over the past 4 years all the local authorities have paid varying
amounts to the commission, but there has been a continuing shortfall that has been met by
the temporary and undesirable expedient of using funds from other accounts and by bank
overdraft.
The Soil Conservation and Rivers Control Council has directed that the catchment
commission make and levy a rate on a uniform scale of all rateable property in the Bay of


## p. 2650 (#288) ###########################################

2650
Bay of Plenty Catchment Commission and Regional Water Board
Administrative Expenses Recovery Bill
1 September
Plenty catchment area. This took effect from 1 April this year. The catchment commission
now has the problem of recovering revenue to cover administrative costs for the period from
April 1973 to March 1977. The Bill empowers the Bay of Plenty Catchment Commission to
recover from local authorities in the area, by way of a special levy, sufficient money to cover
the cost of its general administrative expenses for those years. The voluntary payments made
by the local authorities since 1973 are to be refunded or set off against the amount due.
It is intended that the expenses to be recovered from the local authorities include the
general administrative expenses incurred by the commission in its capacity as a regional
water board. It is intended that payments should be spread over 3 years, with the first
payment falling due on 28 February 1978. The Bill proposes that the share payable by each
constituent authority shall be calculated as if a rate had been made and levied on all rateable
property in the catchment area. Contributions will be assessed as if rated on the basis of an
equalised rateable capital value. The Bill also validates the deficits shown in the catchment
commission's accounts during the period covered to maintain compliance with the Local
Authorities Loans Act 1956.
I understand that the matter of payment of regional water board rates was tested by the
Supreme Court in 1975, but the cities of Rotorua and Tauranga and the Mt. Maunganui
borough have refused to pay any contribution in view of an appeal to the Court of Appeal,
tentatively set down for November of this year. I have been informed by the Clerk that that
does not prevent the introduction of the Bill.
Motion agreed to.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
ROTORUA COUNTY COUNCIL EMPOWERING BILL
Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): I am directed by the Local Bills Committee to
present the report of the committee on the Rotorua County Council Empowering Bill. The
committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed. I move, That the report do lie
upon the table. The committee added the following rider: that at the end of the 10 years
permitted extension the land must revert to public recreational use and that the present
occupiers and the council be notified accordingly.
The Bill amends section 3 of the Reserves and Other Lands Disposal Act 1955. That
section vested an area of land of more than 11 acres in Rotorua County as a recreation
reserve. Holiday and fishing cottages have been erected on part of the land and some of the
cottages have become permanent residences. The council was authorised to subdivide the
land and lease it to the occupiers of the cottages. The terms of the leases as fixed by
subsection (5) were 21 years without right of renewal. However, if the county council did not
require the land for recreation purposes at the end of the lease the land could be leased for a
further 10 years on the same terms and conditions as the former lease. The committee heard
an opinion substantiating that by the use of the expression “same terms and conditions" the
same rental provisions would pertain, which did not allow the county council to review the
rent payable even though the extension would be for a further 10 years.
After most careful consideration the committee has allowed the Bill to proceed. If the
Bill had not been allowed to proceed the leases would have expired on 31 December this
year. That would have put the lessees in a somewhat invidious position. The county council
did not require the land for a recreation reserve at this time, and there was an agreement
between the county council and the lessees that the empowering legislation should be
passed. The legislation will allow the leases to be renewed on terms and conditions
determined by the Minister of Lands. That provision safeguards the lessees and was
acceptable to the county council. The Minister of Lands, through his department, expressed
opposition to the passage of the Bill, but his opposition has been withdrawn following
consultation. The Local Bills Committee would, I know, want me to stress the serious intent
behind the rider to the report, and I repeat it: the committee wants to make it quite clear to
both parties that at the end of the 10 years permitted extension the land must revert to public
recreation use, the purpose for which it was originally granted.
Dr WALL (Porirua): Members on this side of the House are in agreement with what has
been done, but are particularly concerned about the rider. In the second reading debate we
shall make certain suggestions to the Minister on the way in which his discretion will be
exercised. I think the House may well find the suggestions helpful in furthering the aim
expressed in the committee's rider.
Motion agreed to.

Judicature Amendment Bill (No. 2)
JUDICATURE AMENDMENT BILL (NO. 2)
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Judicature Amendment Bill (No. 2). The committee
recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie
upon the table. Thirteen submissions were received on the Bill. The most substantial
objections came from several voluntary organisations—such as the National Youth Council
and the New Zealand University Students Association-all of which were concerned at the
possibility that the provisions of clauses 6 to 10 might make the decisions and actions of those
organisations the subject of some sort of review by the courts. Understandably, these
organisations viewed with some concern the possibility that a decision of, say, an executive
of a student's association might be challenged in the courts.
What the submissions did not appreciate was that the Bill makes procedural rather than
substantive changes to the Judicature Act, that no new right of action is created by the
amendments that are contained in the Bill, and that, in any event, previously such decisions
could be reviewed by the courts either by way of one of the prerogative writs or under the
provisions of the Judicature Amendment Act 1972. Accordingly, while the committee
appreciates the concern expressed by these organisations, having satisfied itself that no new
substantive right of action is created by the amendment it does not recommend any change
based on their submissions.
I have had a lengthy discussion with representatives of the New Zealand University
Students Association, and I believe that organisation is now satisfied that its fears about the
amendment are no longer justified. There was a late submission from the Federation of
Labour along very similar lines to those received from the voluntary organisations. This
submission was given very careful consideration by the committee, but, like others, it
appeared to be based on a similar misunderstanding of the law.
The committee recommends the deletion of clause 4. This provision would have given a
court that was hearing a civil action power to waive proof in certain cases, and was originally
recommended by the rules committee. The select committee questioned the need for the
clause, and subsequent discussions between Department of Justice officials and the rules
committee have led to our recommending its deletion. The select committee also recom-
mends deleting clause 6(2). This clause was originally recommended by the Solicitor-
General, who was concerned that the amendments to the Judicature Act contained in the
Bill might have permitted a judicial review of the administrative and investigative matters
leading up to the decision to prosecute a person. However, subsequent discussions with the
Solicitor-General have revealed that this question is at present before the courts, and both
he and the committee decided it would be inappropriate to amend the law until the case had
been determined. The committee also recommends certain changes to clauses 7, 8, and 10.
Finally, I refer briefly to the fact that the Acting Minister of Justice asked the committee
to look at a proposed Supplementary Order Paper setting out further amendments that
would increase the size of the Court of Appeal and permit it to sit in divisions. I understand
that the Minister will give fuller details of these proposed amendments during the second
reading debate. The matter requires only two observations from me. First, the Standing
Orders would probably not have permitted the committee to make the amendments
proposed in the Supplementary Order Paper, and in any event those amendments are of
some constitutional moment and would be better dealt with by the House than by a select
committee. Secondly, on behalf of the committee I should like to thank the Minister for his
courtesy in referring the proposed amendments for consideration. This enabled the commit-
tee to make certain recommendations that we hope will ultimately appear in the Supplemen-
tary Order Paper.
Mr HUNT (New Lynn): The Opposition does not oppose the reporting back of the Bill,
but we will have much more to say on the second reading. I deplore the reporting back of this
Bill on an estimates day. We do not really have adequate time to debate the report. The
member for Birkenhead referred to one matter of considerable importance, and I feel

allowed to look at were really outside the provisions of the Judicature Amendment Bill

The Government should have introduced a Judicature Amendment Bill (No. 3),
because the Supplementary Order Paper deals with increasing the membership of the Court

New Zealand to study or on business from those who had gone for pleasure, but, assuming
that the three categories were fairly evenly spread, in the March 1975 year the number of
New Zealanders departing on short-term trips had increased by 20 percent over that for the
previous year. But in the March 1977 year, that number had risen by only 1.7 percent. That
showed that the foreign travel tax had had a marked effect in slowing down the rate of
increase in travel spending.
It had been suggested that the foreign travel tax could be evaded by buying a single fare
to Sydney, and booking the balance of a trip to the United States there. If one bought a
ticket in New Zealand direct to Los Angeles, the cost was $753, including foreign travel tax,
whereas, if one broke the journey at Sydney, under the impression that it was the smart way
to avoid the foreign travel tax, the total cost would be $1,026. The tax had not been popular,
but popularity was not the name of the game; the name of the game was survival. The only
serious, organised attacks on the foreign travel tax had been from the travel industry and
from the Labour Opposition. The baggage hall at the new Auckland international air-
terminal, although larger and better arranged than the old one, was still not perfect in the
Customs Department's view, as it might not be fully adequate for all needs.
Sitting suspended from 5.30 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON said that the new international air-terminal at Mangere would
provide a better passenger flow, because passengers could be separated more effectively.
The closeness of its facilities would enable better surveillance, improved baggage handling,
and continuous staff deployment.
At present there was little evidence of any great demand for cocaine, but the position
could change. The evidence on the volume of drugs entering New Zealand was very erratic,
and depended considerably on the success of seizures in the year. The seizures statistics were
not necessarily any more than a suggestion of the trends in drug use and were a very fallible
guide. Cannabis resin appeared to be becoming more popular as an import, probably
because it was less bulky and therefore easier to smuggle. Another pattern had been noticed
with two other drugs, which might or might not be interrelated; seizures of lysergide or LSD
tablets had fallen markedly between 1975 and 1977, but unfortunately there had been a
parallel increase in seizures of heroin. Another pattern in drug use was the marked interest
in the drug trade by organised crime. Whereas narcotics had formerly been mainly smuggled
in by users in small quantities, the present pattern showed a much better organised
operation, with a high financial gain and a quick turnover rate.
Labrador dogs were used for drug detection work, and more Labradors would be
trained when the police training centre had the facilities available. It was planned to increase
the number of drug dogs to 20 over a 3-year period, depending on the availability of
resources. For each dog, it took about 12 months from birth before it attained operational
usefulness, and involved an investment of about $20,000. Overseas experience had shown
that dogs could be trained very effectively to be sensitive to more than one drug. The
department had two excellent pamphlets on narcotics. The first dealt with the appearance,
texture, smell, packing, different grades, and methods of administration of drugs, the slang
terms used to describe them, and the symptoms of drug users; it included coloured
illustrations to assist in identification. The second pamphlet, which would be available

The Customs report had stated that it was intended to introduce a positive list for sales
tax. That represented probably the biggest change in sales tax administration in 40 years, and
would lead to a very much more effective system and a great lessening of the difficulties
between the commercial community and the Customs Department. The existing basis for
sales tax liability was that all goods were taxable unless covered by a statutory exemption. It
was proposed to base future sales tax administration on a positive list of taxable goods and
any exemptions considered necessary. That would alleviate the situation considerably, as
departmental officers had to spend much time in determining and interpreting an ever-
increasing list of exempt goods. Furthermore, the descriptions would be more capable of
legal definition. It was most sincerely hoped that the result would provide a clear guide for
everyone, particularly those in the commercial community, as to their liability for sales tax
on specific goods.

a small newspaper advertisement.
The Navy and the Air Force had made a study of New Zealand's coastline, and had
recorded the areas in which ships had been fishing, the type of fish they had caught, and how
long they had been there. He admitted that New Zealand did not have sufficient vessels to
patrol the 200-mile zone, but said that that problem was common to all countries with a long
coastline. The Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries had its own vessels, as had the Navy,
and the job would be carried out efficiently.

The Police
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) paid a tribute to the Commissioner of Police
and his officers for the dedicated service they gave in protecting people and property. In his
annual report the commissioner had said that the incidence of crime and offences was
increasing. Decisive action was required. Resources had to be provided to enable the police
to do their job, and social policies that would build a better and more law-abiding society had
to be introduced. Salaries and conditions of service had to be improved to attract and retain
first-class officers.
The Labour Government had increased staff numbers by about 1000, but the National
Government had so far increased staff numbers by about 250. The number of vehicles in the
Police fleet had been increased by about 200 under the Labour Government, and about 600
new vehicles had been bought. Under the National Government the fleet had increased by
about 50 vehicles, and the number of foot patrols had not been increased. The concept of
police community liaison offices introduced by the Labour Government had been welcomed,
but although provision had been made for them in the estimates none had been
opened. A survey carried out by the Police had shown that 483 additional men were needed
immediately. The Minister had said he would be making submissions to Cabinet, and he
urged the Minister's Cabinet colleagues to support the request for additional staff. The
policies followed by the Government were helping to lift the crime rate, and if the police
were to be asked to clean up the mess they should be provided with the manpower to enable
them to do so.
Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North) said that the public should develop a relationship
with the police and give them the support they deserved in their responsible work. The
actions of the police had been criticised by civil liberties groups, minority groups, partisan
groups, the media, and individuals, but those who knocked the police should be more aware
of the job they did. Policemen had to deal with rapists, robbers, drug addicts, murderers; to
do their job fearlessly, but with firmness, fairness, and discretion; to seek information, yet to
be suspicious of people; to show doubt, but to challenge and apprehend the law breaker.
Many policemen were aware of authority and the number of interested groups they had to
satisfy, but they should not be inhibited by regulations or by public contempt for any law.
The public could create the attitude among policemen that the less they did the less they
would be blamed for.
In the past 12 months he had spent 17 nights between 7 or 8 p.m. and 2 or 3 a.m.
patrolling with the police in "I cars", and had found that alcohol had been present in 80
percent of the cases dealt with. Credit had to be given to the handlers of police dogs. This
year they had handled more than 10 000 cases, and more than 2000 cases had been
successfully prosecuted. Sixty-one dogs were in action and 27 were being trained. The three
dogs used for narcotics detection were in Auckland, Christchurch, and Wellington. He
commended the Minister for the increase in the vote of $17 million-more than 30 percent.

other honourable members. Procedures are available whereby honourable members and
other citizens can take up the issue of inaccurate statements made by television or radio
reporters. In the Broadcasting Act, provision is made for complaints to be lodged by writing
to the secretary of the Broadcasting Council.
With regard to this point of order, Standing Order 103 is clear. In providing that certain
notices are not allowed, it is stated that notices of motion shall not contain any statement of
facts or name of any person unless they are strictly necessary to render the notice intelligible
and can be authenticated. Therefore, statements of facts must be authenticated if they are
challenged. I shall certainly not challenge them myself, but other honourable members are
entitled to do so. The same principle applies whether the reports emanate from Radio New
Zealand, one of the television channels, a newspaper, or any other source; I do not see that
there is any great difference. In this case the authentication was carried out by me, in that I
asked for the transcript of the Radio New Zealand reports. One was provided for me by the
member for Hastings, and the other was provided for me by Radio New Zealand. Therefore
I have the transcript of the actual statements made, and I believe that is the appropriate way
of authenticating the alleged statement. I hope we do not have too many more of these cases.

NATIONAL PARKS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I move, That the National Parks Amendment
Bill be introduced. The prime purpose of this Bill is to reconstitute the Egmont National Park
Board on the expiry of its term of appointment on 31 March 1978 so that in future it will be
appointed much in line with section 18 of the Act, and the administration of the park will be
consistent with that of other national parks. The Egmont board is constituted in a way
peculiar only to this board. It was first established under the Egmont National Park Act
1924. This is a legacy from the days of limited transport, when each sector of the park was
predominantly the preserve of the local community. These early provisions have been
carried forward in section 17 of the National Parks Act 1952, but are no longer appropriate.
Other sections of the Act affecting the Egmont board are also dealt with. The National Parks
Authority, the Egmont National Park Board, and following discussions with me-the
Taranaki Local Bodies Association representatives support the general provisions proposed.
The Bill also deals with other amendments of a non-controversial nature, the main ones
being higher monetary penalties, and increased powers for rangers within the boundaries of
the parks.
Clause 1 relates to the short title and commencement, which is 1 April 1978 to bring into
statutory being the new Egmont National Park Board as the term of the present one expires
on the previous day.
Clause 2 repeals section 17 and substitutes a new section to constitute the new board as:
the Commissioner of Crown Lands for the Taranaki land district; two persons to be
appointed by the Minister of Lands on the recommendation of the Taranaki Local Bodies
Association; one person to be appointed by the Minister on the joint recommendation of the
dominion executive of the Federated Mountain Clubs of New Zealand Inc. and the New
Zealand Ski Association Inc., and five members also to be appointed by the Minister of
Lands on the recommendation of the National Parks Authority. The clause also repeals
obsolete sections and makes the necessary consequential adjustments to others.
Clause 3 amends section 19 in part to enable a member of any national park board to be
appointed for a term not exceeding 3 years. The National Parks Authority agrees that the
terms of all park boards should eventually expire on a common date. This will enable the
authority to call for nominations for all boards through the news media and other avenues,
and will be an effective way of providing for full public participation in the appointment of
national park boards. Clause 4 of the Bill repeals section 23, which established the north,
south, east, and west local committees-which have statutory powers-and now enables the
Egmont National Park Board to appoint one or more local committees which shall act in an


## p. 2673 (#311) ###########################################

2 September
2673
National Parks Amendment Bill
advisory capacity to the board on matters relating to park administration, and which shall
maintain the traditional link between the board and the Taranaki people. This clause also
vests the funds of the four existing committees in the park board.
Clause 5 repeals section 25 relating to expenses of members of the four existing local
committees, and substitutes a new section to provide for payment of expenses by the board
to any member of a new committee appointed. Clause 6 repeals section 40 and substitutes a
new clause providing for a monetary penalty of a maximum of $1,000-it was previously
$100 for a breach of any bylaw. This is consistent with the Reserves Bill that is at present
before the House. The clause also provides for a further fine not exceeding $20 a day for a
continuing offence.
Clause 7 amends section 52 to give wider powers to park rangers, constables, and other
officers within the boundaries of a national park. The existing powers are extremely limited,
and are restricted to acting to prevent any actual or intended breach and to requiring
offenders to give their names and addresses. The new powers to seize and search are similar
to those conferred on rangers by sections 39 and 40 of the Wildlife Act 1952. The
opportunity has been taken to consolidate section 52 of the present Act by transferring the
provisions for the disposition of seized articles from section 54, so that the powers of search,
seizure, and disposition are contained in one section of the Act. Clause 8 amends section 54
by substituting a new subsection (3) to increase the monetary penalty for an offence by an
individual within a national park to a maximum fine of $2,500, and for a continuing offence
to a maximum fine of $50 for every day on which the offence has continued. Where the
offender is a corporation the maximum fine is $5,000, with a maximum of $50 a day for a
continuing offence. This also is consistent with the Reserves Bill in respect of a New Zealand
reserve.
Clause 9 defines "animal" for the purposes of section 54 relating to offences. The term
now includes any marine mammal and any eel to protect these species within park
boundaries. While it would be possible to adopt a comprehensive biological meaning of the
term "animal", this would not be readily recognised by a lay member of the public, who may
be apprehended in terms of section 54, and it is preferable to adopt the familiar names of
specified animals. Clause 9 also provides authority for the Minister of Lands to declare any
other species of mammal to be an animal for the purposes of section 54 by notice in the
Gazette.
Clause 10 makes national park boards subject to the Public Bodies Meetings Act 1962,
and enables wider public participation in park administration. While some boards already
encourage public interest, park boards and the National Parks Authority consider that the
application of the 1962 legislation will give statutory effect to what is now, in most cases, a
matter of policy. This will ensure public involvement in park administration.

Mr ACTING SPEAKER: As the Minister of Energy Resources pointed out, my
attention was temporarily diverted. However, I was listening to the honourable member for
Auckland Central, and there is some validity in the point raised by the Acting Prime
Minister, as the member for Auckland Central was stating his belief that the land should be
returned to the original owners. The National Parks Amendment Bill contains no reference
to the ownership of land. However, I do not consider that the member for Auckland Central
was straying much further from the intention of a debate on the introduction of a Bill than
most members have done in this debate. Indeed, on practically every occasion that a Bill has
been introduced in this session, in this Parliament, and in Parliaments for some years back,
members have ranged widely.
The Standing Orders Committee in 1972 said, of the debate on the introduction of
Government Bills: "The committee considered this matter at considerable length❞—and, as
a member of that committee, I can assure honourable members that it did consider the
matter at considerable length. "There was general agreement that the introduction of a Bill,
except in exceptional cases, need not be a lengthy process, and that in general all that is
necessary is a brief explanation from the Minister followed by a limited period of questions.
It is unnecessary for the Minister at this stage to give a detailed analysis of the Bill, as this
material is contained in the printed explanatory note attached to the Bill, and it is also not
the appropriate time for members to make impromptu speeches which would be more
suitable on the second reading after they had had an opportunity to study the legislation. The
committee considered suggestions to restrict the number of speeches and also a proposal to
limit the total time for the debate. These were not approved as it was felt that the present
rights of members should be preserved to cover the comparatively few cases where matters
of conscience or local interest were affected, or where there was strong opposition to the
Bill." Therefore, no change was made to the Standing Orders.
The committee that met in 1974 made much the same comments, except that it finally
agreed to limit the time allowed for the introduction of a Government Bill to 2 hours-1
hour for the Government and 1 hour for the Opposition. The point honourable members
should bear in mind is that there is a question before the House, which I posed when the
Minister moved the introduction of the Bill, and that is that the Bill be introduced. Later on,
if the House agrees that the Bill should be introduced, we have the question that the Bill be
read a second time. At that stage, members are given the opportunity of debating in full the
principles involved in the Bill. A principle of debate in the Chamber is that every stage of the
debate on a Bill should carry the discussion a stage further, and that we should not repeat
ourselves and use the same arguments in each of the subsequent stages. At the moment, we
tend to have a second reading debate on the introduction of a Bill, and, fairly naturally, a
second reading debate on the second reading of the Bill. We also tend to have a second

reading debate when the Bill is reported back to the House from a select committee, and yet

I believe there is a very good case for a different procedure for the introduction not only
of Government Bills, but also of private Bills. On the introduction of private Bills we have
two second reading debates, because normally we have a second reading debate on the
introduction of the Bill, when each speaker is allowed 10 minutes, and, by convention, the
member who brings the Bill forward is normally given the right to a second reading debate of
limited time, and we then have another debate along the same lines. That is repetitious; and
the principles laid down for the conduct of the House do not provide for tediousness and
repetition. I invite honourable members to heed the Standing Orders of the House and to try
somehow to obey them.
