MARINE RESERVES AMENDMENT BİLL
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): I move, That the Marine Reserves
Amendment Bill be introduced. The Bill provides that fishing for recreational purposes in a
marine reserve can be authorised only by the Minister of Fisheries after consultation with the
management committee of the relevant reserve. At present fishing is totally prohibited in
reserves created under the Marine Reserves Act. That is considered to be too restrictive in
special circumstances, and the Bill will make it possible for the Minister of Fisheries to
permit fishing in certain circumstances.
The authority for such fishing will be by notice in the Gazette, and the Minister can
impose restrictions on the time and place of fishing, the methods and gear used, and other
conditions, to ensure that no fishing detrimental to the prime objective of the reserve is
undertaken. No person holding a permit issued under Part I of the Fisheries Act 1908, which
generally means a commercial fisherman, can be authorised to fish in a reserve. The
Director-General of Agriculture and Fisheries is given the initiative to declare a certain area
a marine reserve. One could cite the Poor Knights region, where reserves have been talked
about but not permitted. If the director-general makes an application for a marine reserve
and an objection is filed, the Minister may obtain a report on the matter from an
independent source. Clause 4 provides that inspectors of sea fishing appointed under the
Fisheries Act 1908 are to be rangers for the purpose of the Marine Reserves Act.

extend or create marine reserves. The present Act restricts the taking of shellfish, and I

Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): The member for Eastern Maori was
concerned about journeying up to the scientific reserve at Leigh. The purpose of the Marine
Reserves Act 1971 was to designate an area of coastline for exclusive scientific studies. At
present, under that Act, all fishing in the area is totally banned. Interested people can do
nothing but go and look at what is there. The Bill is to relax that slightly, and give the
Minister the power, after consultation with management committees and the like, to allow
some fishing that will not be detrimental to the scientific nature of the reserve. That is the
simple objective. At the moment only one reserve is so designated. The total prohibition on
fishing is a factor preventing the designation of other reserves, and if that can be relaxed in
some areas necessary scientific reserves can be established, with some amateur fishing that
will not harm the reserve. That is the sole purpose of the Bill. I believe the Bill is a good one.
Bill introduced and read a first time.

hearing of evidence be open to accredited representatives of the news media.

PRIMARY PRODUCTS MARKETING REGULATIONS VALIDATION AND CONFIR-
MATION BILL
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Associate Minister of Agriculture): I move, That the Primary
Products Marketing Regulations Validation and Confirmation Bill be introduced. The purpose
of the Bill is to validate and confirm the Egg Marketing (Production Entitlement) Regula-
tions 1972, Amendment No. 2, which was promulgated on 20 December 1976 when
Parliament was in recess. Honourable members will recall that these regulations were
brought in at the request of the industry to reduce from 1000 to 100 the number of laying
birds that any person could keep without entitlement. These regulations were made pursuant
to the Primary Products Marketing Act 1953, which required all regulations made thereun-
der to be tabled, but also to have a special confirming and validating Bill passed during the
session if Parliament is sitting. If this were not done, the regulation would lapse. Parliament
met on 28 February this year, and, technically, these regulations should have been tabled at
that session, and a Bill passed to confirm and validate them. The tabling of the regulations
and the passing of the Bill were not practical in the February session. Therefore, this small
Bill has been introduced to validate these regulations.
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram): The Bill confirms that regulations covering
production entitlement under the Egg Marketing Regulations have not been in force since 28
February 1977. As the Minister said, the purpose of the Bill is to state that, notwithstanding,
the regulations have been valid and in force all the time. I made representations to the
Minister on behalf of a constituent about an egg entitlement to which he claimed he was
entitled, but which had been ruled out on a technicality relating to regulations that this Bill
now confirms were not in operation at the time. Now the Minister is attempting to say that
the regulations were in force, so obviously that decision will stand.
In introducing the Bill, the Minister is attempting to introduce retrospective legislation,
which would validate an invalid decision. I can recall the Minister and his colleagues
objecting to retrospective legislation as though it was a major principle to them. That could
be construed from the arguments they advanced. If the Government's attitude towards
retrospective legislation is what it has been claimed to be, I am sure the Minister will readily
agree to some provision being included in the Bill enabling my constituent's claim to stand in
spite of regulations belatedly brought into force to deprive him of something he contends he
has a right to.
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Associate Minister of Agriculture): Unfortunately, I cannot recall
the details of the case of the honourable member's constituent, but, obviously, the
Government cannot bring in a proviso to exclude one person in circumstances like this.
When the Primary Products Marketing Act 1953 was introduced, the short formal session
that we had in February this year for Her Majesty the Queen was not envisaged. Technically,
as the honourable member said, these regulations should have been tabled and validated,
and the special Bill passed through all its stages. I expect that the members of Her Majesty's
loyal Opposition would not have been happy had the proceedings been delayed on that
occasion in order to pass a small Bill through all its stages. To answer the member's question,

Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Before I call questions for oral answer perhaps I should

## p. 2690 (#328) ###########################################

Questions-Admissibility
comment on today. It was suggested yesterday, when the member for Western Hutt asked
the Minister of Transport whether his department regarded car radios as a distraction to
drivers, that this was out of order as seeking an expression of opinion. My initial ruling was
that the question did not seek the Minister's opinion, though it might have involved the
opinion of the department. The Minister, of course, is entitled to give that opinion or
withhold it, at his discretion. However, on further consideration I did not regard that as the
real basis of the matter. The question seeks to discover the official departmental attitude to
the use of car radios-are they or are they not regarded as a distraction to drivers? The
matter is clearly one within the administrative responsibility of the department, and
therefore one of administration, for which the Minister is responsible. I rule, therefore, that
the question was admissible under Standing Order 75.
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert): A point of order, Mr Speaker. Before we proceed to
oral questions, I wonder if I could seek some guidance from you. Through the normal
procedures I submitted a question addressed to the Under-Secretary to the Minister of Trade
and Industry. It has not appeared on the Order Paper. I was seeking the reasons why he
talked about New Zealand being nearly bankrupt. I am aware that an Under-secretary is

procedure has developed in recent years quite justifiably-whereby Under-Secretaries
accept responsibility for certain sectors of administration.
My question is whether it is possible for a question to be directed to an Under-
Secretary, referring to his administration of that sector of a portfolio which is in his care. It
would be possible to ask the Minister of Trade and Industry, for example, for his
understanding of the remarks of his Under-Secretary, and whether he knew the basis on
which the Under-Secretary said that New Zealand is nearly bankrupt. However, I would
then be asking for an expression of opinion from the Minister, and, under other Standing
Orders to which you have just referred, an expression of opinion from a Minister cannot be
obtained. An Under-Secretary has made a statement that New Zealand is nearly bankrupt,

Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): We have had instances in the House when, for

Mr ACTING SPEAKER: The question was referred to me and perhaps I can help the

Hon. W. W. Freer: I have the letter here, and there is no question—
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I am not questioning the accuracy of the statement. It seems
to me that when Standing Order 75 refers to Ministers and a Minister, as it does, it is
referring solely to a Minister of Ministers of the Crown appointed pursuant to the preroga-
tive power of the Crown, and not to an Under-Secretary appointed under the Civil List Act.
I am fortified in this opinion by Standing Order 83, which deals with the absence of a
Minister from the House when a question is addressed to him. Standing Order 83 provides
that, in those circumstances, a Minister or Under-Secretary may answer the question on
behalf of the absent Minister. It may be that, having regard to section 16 of the Civil List
Act, this Standing Order is unnecessary, and that an Under-Secretary could answer a
question on behalf of a Minister in any case. However, the Standing Order makes it plain
that an Under-Secretary is not encompassed within the term "Minister" for the purpose of
having questions addressed to him. Under Standing Order 75, while he may answer a
question on behalf of a Minister, a question cannot be addressed to an Under-Secretary in
his own right.
That does not conclude the matter, however, because, under Standing Order 76,
questions may be addressed to members other than Ministers, and that clearly includes an
Under-Secretary. However, the subjects on which a member may be questioned under
Standing Order 76 are more circumscribed than those on which a Minister may be
questioned. They are limited to parliamentary matters—that is, questions relating to any

companies at Christchurch on 31 March. The fact that the prospectus has been registered is
prima facie evidence that the registrar was satisfied that it complies with the law. It is not a
function of the department to give financial advice and it would be irresponsible of him to
say whether a particular investment was adequately safeguarded. The legal requirements are
designed to provide a minimum standard of disclosure about the issuing company. Given
that information, the prospective investor or his professional adviser must form an opinion
based on past performance, profitability, the present state of the company, and the terms of
the current issue of shares or options. Safeguards depend on continuing disclosure, economic
factors, financial structure and controls, and above all good management. All a prospectus
can do is to disclose relevant information relating to the recent past. It can never guarantee
adequate safeguards for the future or eliminate informed risk taking, which is inherent in any
commercial investment.

12. Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) asked the Minister of Housing: Can he indicate

withdrawn?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): The variable mortgage repayment
scheme was introduced in 1974 to help lower income borrowers service repayments in the
initial years of home ownership and provide them with an opportunity to consolidate their
finances at a time when their income was under the greatest pressure. I confirm that the
variable mortgage scheme has been withdrawn, but this is temporary only to allow the
Housing Corporation the opportunity to evaluate altered repayment patterns following the
recent changes in its rate of interest to borrowers. The concept of this scheme has been
retained meanwhile by offering borrowers "interest only" repayments where the need for
assistance is established.

Transport Amendment Bill (No. 2)
TUESDAY, 6 SEPTEMBER 1977
Mr Acting Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
TRANSPORT AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That the Transport
Amendment Bill (No. 2) be introduced. This Bill consists of only six clauses, so my remarks
will be fairly brief. It is important for members to understand the mechanism of the
regulation of road-rail competition. The purpose of the Bill is to help implement the
Government's decisions on the mileage restriction governing road-rail competition, which
were announced in the Budget this year. This Bill will amend the Transport Act 1962, and
will come into force on 1 October 1977. The Bill is essentially of a machinery nature,
designed to amend the Transport Act 1962 to conform with the change to the distance limit
of 150 kilometres which will be made in the Transport Licensing Regulations, and to achieve
compatibility in other parts of the Act with that change.
I feel I should clarify just what is meant by the 40-mile limit, or the 150-kilometre limit
as it is to become, and how it is to be imposed. The restriction itself is imposed in the
Transport Licensing Regulations 1963, which are made pursuant to the Transport Act. It
takes the form of a condition in every goods service licence which, of course, a road
transport operator needs in order to carry goods for other people. Whether the restriction is
expressly stated in the goods service licence or not, the goods must be sent by rail if there is
an available route for the carriage of goods which includes at least a certain distance of open
Government railways. This distance is to be extended from 40 miles to 150 kilometres, which
is nearly 94 miles. Essentially this change of figure is the difference between the old system
and the new. The same provisos and exemptions remain, and, as before, the restriction will
not apply in cases where the route that includes the railway is more than one-third longer
than the shortest road route available for the carriage of goods; where the Crown owns the
motor vehicle; where the owner is a local authority or public body, and the carriage begins
and ends in that local authority's district; for the carriage of livestock, as well as in certain
other instances specified in the Transport Act.
The required changes to the distance limit stated in the Transport Licensing Regulations
will come into force when this Bill comes into force on 1 October 1977. The Bill itself consists
of a number of clauses to amend sections in the Transport Act which specifically refer to the
40-mile limit, and a few other matters including an enabling clause to provide for the making
of regulations concerned with goods service licensing and licensing districts.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): It will be appreciated that I have not had time to
study the Bill in detail, because the Minister has been rather brief in his introductory
remarks.
Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: He can't read.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: All right, the Prime Minister is back, and he wants to make
it obvious at the first available opportunity with an inane interjection which has nothing to
do with the Bill.
Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: Don't lose your temper.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: I have had occasion to tell the Prime Minister before that
members on both sides have a right to speak on the introduction of a Bill and to ask
questions of the Minister in charge, who on this occasion is not the Prime Minister.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Don't count on that.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: There may be a point in that. No doubt he will have
authorised whether or not the Bill should come in today. The legislation is not unexpected,
as it was announced in the Budget. Following that there was some criticism that the proposal
had been arrived at without consultation with the Transport Advisory Council or the Road
Transport Association. Both had virtually been given an ultimatum before the introduction
of the Budget that the limit would be increased to 150 kilometres or 93.5 miles.
The Minister assured me that the industry would be consulted before legislation was
introduced, and I should like to know what views the Road Transport Association has
expressed. A number of anomalies have already been highlighted-for instance, the distance
between Palmerston North and Gracefield is 150 kilometres, but one oil company's depot

6 September

might be within the limit, and another one just outside.
Rt. Hon. B. E. Talboys: It's the same thing as with the 40-mile limit.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: I am asking the Minister, not the Deputy Prime Minister.
Rt. Hon. B. E. Talboys: It doesn't change anything.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: Why introduce this Bill if it doesn't change anything? Will
there be flexibility to overcome the anomalies that have been highlighted by the Road
Transport Association and a number of manufacturers and retailers? A truck travelling from
Timaru to Christchurch will have to stop at Hornby, and, going south, the 150-kilometre
limit will be reached at Washdyke. During the Budget debate the Opposition made a strong
case for flexibility on a regional and commodity basis to either reduce or increase the
distance limit to avoid double or triple handling of goods. The transport industry must be
made more efficient, and the Opposition believes the best way to achieve that would have
been to phase in the increased distance limit, say from 40 miles to 70 miles, and from 70 miles
to 80 miles, and so on, because the difficulties would have been foreseen. Anomalies that
cannot be overcome should be cushioned where possible in the consumer's interest. If the
consumer does benefit from this flexibility then there is much to be said in its favour, but
what the Government intends is not to the advantage of the consumer.
The Minister mentioned the transport licensing regulations. Some problems could arise
with backloading where two transport licensing authorities are involved. Transport licensing
authorities must act together to ensure better utilisation of road transport, otherwise there is
no reason to extend the 40-mile limit. The licensing authority in Auckland must have an
understanding with his counterpart in Hamilton to allow a truck that has come from
Hamilton to be loaded in Auckland for its return journey.
The Minister did not mention the Transport Licensing Act. I should have thought an
amendment to the Act was necessary, but the Minister might have covered it by regulation.
The Minister has had discussions with the industry, and it would be helpful to the House to
know if agreement has been reached, and how the Government will overcome the difficulties
that are foreseen.

POST OFFICE AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General): I move, That the Post Office Amend-
ment Bill be introduced. The Bill gives effect to the measures announced in the Budget to
give flexibility in setting the structure of, and the interest rates on, Post Office Savings Bank
investment and other term deposit accounts. It also gives authority to the Post Office Savings
Bank to receive desposits into term deposit accounts, and provides for a simplification of the
current procedures for the calculation of interest on certain Post Office Savings Bank
accounts.
Clause 2 amends the classes of Post Office savings accounts into which the Postmaster-
General may receive deposits. At present the Act provides for deposits to be received into
ordinary accounts, thrift club accounts, school accounts, investment accounts, home layby
accounts, and such other accounts as the Postmaster-General considers expedient in the
circumstances.
Term deposits are a new type of account for savings banks, and their inclusion in section
113 of the principal Act permits the Postmaster-General to offer this class of security through
the Post Office Savings Bank.
Clause 3 amends section 121 of the Post Office Act 1959. The existing section 121
provides that the Minister of Finance shall, by notice published in the Gazette, fix the rate of
interest payable on money deposited in the Post Office Savings Bank. The amendment in
clause 3 provides for the rate of interest payable on money deposited in securities under
provisions made in other sections of the principal Act to be excluded from the application of


## p. 2704 (#342) ###########################################

2704
6 September
Post Office Amendment Bill
section 121. The amendment gives effect to the Budget announcement that the rates of
interest on investment accounts and term deposit accounts shall be fixed by the Post Office
Savings Bank, with the concurrence of the Secretary to the Treasury.
Clause 4 provides a change of a machinery nature aimed at simplifying interest-bearing
cheque account processing in respect of interest calculation, and will confer no significant
advantage or disadvantage on any depositor.
Clause 5 repeals section 127 of the Post Office Act, which empowers the Minister of
Finance to determine the rate of interest payable on investment accounts by notice in the
Gazette, and the Postmaster-General to set the structure of investment accounts. In
substitution, clause 5 in the Bill authorises the Post Office Savings Bank to receive deposits
into investment accounts and into term deposit accounts at rates of interest that shall be
determined by the Director-General of the Post Office with the concurrence of the Secretary
to the Treasury.
Clause 6 amends section 129B(8) of the principal Act to provide for every development
bond to be issued for such term as the Postmaster-General directs. The current section
129B(8) provides for every development bond to mature at the expiration of 8 years from the
date of purchase. Section 129B is further amended by the repeal of subsection (9) and the
substitution of a new subsection (9), which provides for every development bond to bear
interest from the date of its purchase at such rates as the Director-General, with the
concurrence of the Secretary to the Treasury, may from time to time determine.
Clause 7 amends section 129E of the principal Act by adding to subsection (1) the
proviso that every security issued under section 129E shall bear interest from the date of its
purchase at such rates as the Director-General, with the concurrence of the Secretary to the
Treasury, may from time to time determine.

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General): Once again members opposite are
confused as to what should be done about the Post Office Savings Bank. The member for
Onehunga was openly debating with himself whether the Post Office Savings Bank should be
encouraged. Two members opposite asked whether interest rates would increase, and then
asked if people would be encouraged to save. It is hard to follow the thinking behind their
questions.
Fears have been expressed about the recent trends in interest rates as they affect the
Post Office. I have here the latest figures on interest rates on Post Office Savings Bank,
trustee, and private savings banks investment accounts. Anyone is welcome to look at these
figures, which cover periods of 6 months, 1 year, 2 years, and 3 years. The interest rates
being charged by the POSB indicate that the bank is neither a leader nor a lagger. No one
could say that the Post Office Savings Bank will be used as a vehicle for pushing up interest
rates. If the POSB is to perform its function successfully, it should not become a lagger, so it
is only natural that a degree of flexibility should be given in setting the rates.
The interest rates charged by the POSB and the private savings banks on investment
accounts are much of a muchness. In each case, the Post Office interest rates converge at
about the average of the trustee savings banks and the private savings banks rates. The
average amount held in Post Office Savings Bank accounts is about $450, but I am sure that
the honourable member for Petone is aware that a much wider range is deposited in
individual accounts. The POSB must satisfy many depositors, because at present it has
$1,292 million in Government securities, which represents just under 30 percent of New
Zealand's total domiciled public debt. That gives an indication of the size of the operation.
A very large number of New Zealanders are attracted to the POSB for their short-term
needs or longer-term needs, or for their small loans, or big loans. The member for Petone
cannot derive any significance from the fact that the average deposit size is relatively low,
because many depositors want only small amounts deposited as a matter of convenience. I
am pleased that the member agrees with what the Government has done about bonus bonds.
I agree that the action taken should boost the popularity of this investment outlet. No
sinister significance can be read into the introduction of the term deposit accounts. Other
savings banks are offering the facility, and it was felt that the Post Office should, too. It is
merely an expansion of the range of services offered. We have not yet worked out details.
Finance companies do not come into it, because the type of market we are thinking of is not
significantly catered for by finance companies.
The member for Onehunga mentioned the retrospective legislation provision. The
commencement date is 1 September, ånd if one looks through Budget legislation in modern
times, under both National and Labour Governments, one finds there has always been some
degree of retrospectivity. That is the way it works; it is a question of the time involved in
preparation, of administration, and of convenience. It has no significance. The Bill gives
effect to the Budget undertaking to promote free competition among financial institutions,
to encourage the development of a more efficient and flexible financial system. We have
every faith in its ability to do this, and to continue to maintain the high popularity the Post
Office Savings Bank has enjoyed in the past through the very wide range of services it offers
to investors.

Overseas Loan, Mr David Northfield
3. Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition) asked the Minister of
Finance: What were the reasons behind the decision to allow the Auckland property
developer, Mr David Northfield, to raise a $2 million overseas loan for property develop-
ment purposes (as reported in the New Zealand Herald of 13 August), and how does the
Government reconcile this with the recent refusal of permission for local authorities to raise
an overseas loan for capital works programmes?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The recent approval referred to for
David Northfield Developments Ltd to borrow $2 million overseas was given by the
Overseas Investment Commission because the application complied with the commission's
existing criteria. Current and longstanding policy, apart from some minor changes, is that
overseas loans are approved if the following conditions are met: (1) the loan is for at least 12
months and has a fixed basis of repayment; (2) the loan is drawn down within 6 months of the
date of formal consent; (3) any interest payable is at a rate no higher than the appro-
priate market rate for the currency concerned; and (4) the proceeds are transferred to New
Zealand through a trading bank or used overseas for some approved purpose. The recent
Government decision to decline the applications by the Auckland Regional Authority and
the Auckland City Council to borrow money overseas for their capital works programme is
in keeping with the policy of successive Governments towards local authority borrowing
since the 1930s. This policy is that local authorities may be permitted to borrow overseas
only where the project involves major revenue undertakings and is in the national interest. A
recent example of such a loan approval is the 1976 loan of about $30 million for container
port development, which was arranged through a Government agency. As indicated by the
Associate Minister of Finance in answer to a question in August, the Auckland Regional
Authority and Auckland City Council applications were declined because the projects
concerned were purely local in nature and the particular loan offers were considered inferior
to the terms that could have been possible in the capital markets concerned.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Were the requests of the Auckland Regional Authority and the
Auckland City Council referred to the same Overseas Investment Commission, and did the

Neurosurgical Unit, Christchurch
4. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North) asked the Minister of Health: On what date did
the Otago Hospital Board ask that a subcommittee of specialists in the neurosurgical field be
set up to consider the application by the North Canterbury Hospital Board to establish a
neurosurgical unit, when was that application put before the Hospitals Advisory Council,
was the request of the Otago Hospital Board ever acknowledged, and, if it was, by whom
and when?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): On 7 June the Otago Hospital Board was asked
by the Department of Health for information about the Dunedin neurosurgical unit to assist
the Hospitals Advisory Council in its consideration of the application by the North
Canterbury Hospital Board for a neurosurgical unit at Christchurch. On 29 June in its reply
to the Department of Health the Otago Hospital Board, in addition to providing the
information requested, also suggested the need for a subcommittee. No acknowledgment
was called for as the board's letter was in response to a departmental request for informa-
tion. On 13 July the Hospitals Advisory Council met and considered the North Canterbury
Hospital Board's request, together with the information and suggestion from the Otago
Hospital Board. The council decided to recommend to me that approval be given to establish
a unit at Christchurch but made no recommendation regarding the setting up of a specialist
subcommittee. I accepted the council's recommendation and the two hospital boards were
informed accordingly.
Richard Walls: Has the Minister or his department had any discussions with the Otago
Hospital Board relating to this letter?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Yes, only today I received a deputation led by Mrs Fraser, Chairman
of the Otago Hospital Board. The deputation members represented to me that, while they
were concerned that the people in the South Island should have a neurosurgical service, with
the setting up of the neurosurgical unit at Christchurch there was some danger that the
Otago neurosurgical unit might be adversely affected. The evidence presented to me showed
that, unless the introduction of the Christchurch unit was done with care, such an eventuality
could take place. I undertook to ensure that there would be co-ordination of planning and
some discussion to see that all the necessary steps were taken to ensure that in the
development of the second service and in our efforts to provide a proper neurosurgical
coverage in the South Island we should make absolutely certain that any detrimental effect
to existing services would be kept to an absolute minimum.
Mr Hunt: Is the Minister aware that the Southland Hospital Board has also expressed its
concern about this matter; and will the Minister give an assurance that irrespective of the
approval granted the neurosurgical unit at Dunedin will not suffer in any respect?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: The Minister may answer the second part of the question. The
first is quite unrelated to the original question which contains nothing about the Southland
Hospital Board.
Hon. T. F. GILL: No, I cannot give an assurance that the Dunedin unit will not suffer in
any respect. The aim is to provide a neurosurgical service, particularly to the people of the
South Island, and it is inevitable that if a second service is set up some emphasis will be taken
off the Otago neurosurgical service which is, I think, the oldest established in New Zealand
and has a worldwide reputation. Every effort will have to be made to see that its reputation
and capability are safeguarded. However, since it has been decided to develop a second unit
in Christchurch I cannot say that there will be no adverse effects. We have to try to ensure,
by careful planning and action, that both units will fulfil the requirements in the community,
and in the case of Otago its requirement associated with the pre-medical school. There are
clinical schools in both cities, but Otago is in a special position and we will have to our best to
safeguard that position.

Teaching of Reading, Primary School Teachers
6. Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei) asked the Minister of Education: Has he seen the article
in the Dominion of Tuesday, 30 August, which quotes an American education expert, Dr
Alan Purves, as saying that New Zealand primary school teachers are terrific at teaching
reading, and, if so, can he cite any research findings which back up what Dr Purves said?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I have read the article in the Dominion
of Tuesday, 30 August, and am able to cite research that supports the statements made by Dr
Purves. In 1970 the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achieve-
ment, usually known as the IEA, conducted reading surveys in 15 countries. Results showed
that 14-year-old and 17-year-old pupils in New Zealand had higher scores than children in
any of the other countries, including England, Scotland, and the United States of America.
Dr Purves visited New Zealand to look for the reasons for this high level of achievement
among New Zealand children. In 1952 the New Zealand Council for Educational Research
standardised for use in New Zealand a set of reading tests prepared by the Australian
Council for Educational Research. Thirteen years later, in 1965, reading standards were
again surveyed using the same tests in the same schools. This showed that reading standards
had been maintained, and for 80 percent of the children surveyed had improved. In 1968 the
New Zealand Council for Educational Research standardised its own test of reading for New
Zealand schools. In 1974 NZCER staff carried out a check on standards using a comparable
sample of children from the same schools. The results showed comparable standards
between 1968 and 1974. On the basis of this survey the NZCER decided there was no need


## p. 2711 (#349) ###########################################

6 September
2711
Oral Answers to Questions
to restandardise its reading tests. These research findings are helpful because they provide
an international basis of comparison, and on these comparisons they indicate that New
Zealand standards of reading compare favourably. But there can be no room for compla-
cency or any resting on our laurels. My department and the teaching profession are
constantly striving to find more effective ways of teaching reading.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I should draw the attention of the Minister to Standing Order

Hon. L. W. GANDAR: As I explained in reply to the original question, in 1968 the New
Zealand Council of Educational Research standardised reading tests, and that is the
standard I am talking about. Six years later the council found there was no deviation that
required them to alter the standards on which reading was judged.

will be electrical blackouts in different parts of the country, with consequential loss and

Standing Order 90 states that the statement of the matter proposed to be discussed on a
matter of adjournment under Standing Order 89 shall not be framed in general terms but
shall deal with a particular case of recent occurrence which requires the immediate attention
of the House and the Government and which involves the administrative or ministerial
responsibility of the Government. It seems to me that the particular case of recent
occurrence contemplated in the Leader of the Opposition's letter relates to the action of the
Minister of Labour and his colleagues at a meeting with employers' representatives on
Thursday evening last week. This matter obviously involved the ministerial responsibility of
the Government, and can be considered a particular case.
As the matter occurred on Thursday evening, I considered carefully whether it can be
said to be of recent occurrence, having regard to the fact that it could conceivably have been
raised with me on Friday morning. However, while I feel that there must come a point at
which a subject is raised too late to constitute a matter of recent occurrence, and that this
point may be reached at a comparatively early stage, I do not think I should reject the
request on this ground. The requirement of "recent occurrence" under Standing Order 90 is
not so strict as the requirement when a member raises a matter of privilege-that it must be
raised at the earliest reasonable opportunity—and having regard to this fact, and the early
hour at which the House meets on a Friday, I find that this case is of sufficient recent
Occurrence.
Finally, the matter must require the immediate attention of the House and the
Government. In considering this factor, the notice of intention to strike on 20 September is
relevant and has persuaded me that the immediate attention of the House and the
Government is required in terms of the Standing Order. I therefore rule that the matter
proposed to be discussed is one contemplated by Standing Order 89, and I ask members who
approve of the proposed discussion to rise in their places.

Since there has been no free wage bargaining for some time, negotiations were protracted

An Hon. Member: Such as?
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING: Let me remind the honourable member of some of them.
First, the salaries of inspectors, linesmen, and electricians are almost invariably below the

others. They further indicated that all special payments would be increased by 9.4 percent.
Standby and long-service bonus payments were to be increased by 16.4 percent. All workers

authorities stepped out of line on the wages issue.” Understandably, in those circumstances
negotiations collapsed, and, more significantly, each of the employers' assessors resigned
that evening, and before that council.

could they fulfil their undertaking. Some free wage bargaining!

PERSONAL EXPLANATION
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): With the leave of the House, I wish to make
a personal explanation. The last speaker before the tea adjournment asked me to obtain the
tape-recording of the conciliation proceedings between the New Zealand Electrical Supply
Authorities Association and the union. If they were obtained, he requested that they be
tabled in the House. I have made inquiries during the tea interval, but no tape-recordings are
made during conciliaton proceedings. No record of the proceedings has ever been kept. The
conciliator makes personal notes. The proceedings are privileged. No Minister of Labour has
ever sought such a record, and I have no intention of doing so.

Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition) said that the National Party
manifesto had stated that a more flexible interest rate policy would be adopted, and the
controlled and uncontrolled markets would be brought closer together. What advice had
made the Minister of Finance change his mind on interest rates? What was the gap between
the controlled and the uncontrolled markets, and what was the ceiling of those markets?
House mortgages averaged an interest rate of about 11 percent.
Investment in the manufacturing sector had fallen under the present Administration,
and real private investment as a percentage of gross national product, which had reached an
all-time record of 19 percent three years ago, was 14 percent. In its market intelligence
report No. 3, the New Zealand Manufacturers Federation had stated that there was a grave
shortage of reasonably priced money, especially in term and overdraft facilities. Manufactur-
ers had to compete for finance with finance houses, which lent only in consumption areas.
Undoubtedly, there would be a rush of debenture issues from New Zealand companies and
very high interest rates would apply. The companies would lose their competitive ability,
particularly in overseas markets, and the cost to the New Zealand consumer would be
increased.
Who was making money out of the new system introduced by the Government in March
1976? The 1977 annual report of Broadlands stated that the company had made a profit of
almost $2.8 million-it was making money out of the new policy. The overall reserves and
retained profits of finance houses were up about 50 percent for 1 year, from $21 million to
almost $31 million. It was surprising that the companies were making such large profits,
when Auric Corporation Ltd had paid 13.5 percent interest for 2-to 5-year investments,
Broadlands and Challenge Finance Corporation had paid 13 percent, General Finance Ltd
had paid 13 percent for 3-to 5-year investments, and International Harvester Credit Co. had
paid 13.25 percent for investments for 4 to 6 years. The consumer was paying dearly under
the system.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) said that the Government had carried
out its election policy that it would bring controlled and uncontrolled interest rates closer
together. When the rate of inflation had been between 3 percent and 5 percent, a controlled
interest rate at about that level had been reasonable and desirable. Because of the Labour
Government's failure, the rate of inflation had risen from 5.5 percent in 1972 to 15.7 percent
in 1975; at that level a low interest rate policy meant that everyone who had saved money
and lent it at low interest rates was subsidising someone else. Unless people received after
tax an amount equal to the rate of inflation on the money they saved they were subsidising
somebody else, so why save? With double-figure rates of inflation, unless interest rates were
higher it simply did not pay to save. Who was making money? The saver was doing a little
better, but he was not making money.
Mr Hunt: Bob Jones is.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON said that the person referred to by the member for New
Lynn had done a great deal better under the Labour Government than he had ever done
under National. He had made his money by speculating on inflation—the opposite side of
the coin on the matter raised by the Leader of the Opposition. Under the Labour
Government the price of the average house and of the average farm had doubled, and
speculators had done very well by borrowing on mortgage at rates of up to 12 percent and
finding that the capital value of the properties they had bought had doubled. In the first half
of 1977 the price of houses had increased by 3.78 percent; interest rates had gone up, but the
price of houses would not double in 3 years. With the doubling of the price of houses under

about inflation the country was in trouble.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Fire Safety Legislation
1. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Internal Affairs: Has he seen
the comment of Sir Jack Hunn as reported in the Evening Post of 23 August 1977, where he
said that "Fire safety legislation must be put right with desperate urgency", and, if this is
indeed the case, is it the intention of the Government to take legislative action to tidy up the
situation?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I have seen the report in which Sir
Jack Hunn was repeating his well-known views that as a matter of urgency regulations should
replace bylaws for fire safety standards for building construction. Successive Governments
have preferred that these standards should be determined through the consultative process
of the Standards Association of New Zealand and then issued as model bylaws to be adopted
by territorial authorities. This procedure provides much more flexibility for amendments
made necessary by technological development and the requirements of individual districts.
Fire safety bylaws must be adopted by all territorial authorities and they must have the
approval of the Minister of Local Government. I do not consider that the present legislation

7 September

is in need of urgent attention along the lines suggested.

Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order!
Hon. F. M. Colman:-if the Minister could indicate-
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order! Perhaps the honourable member is not familiar with
the Standing Order that states that when the Speaker is on his feet all members will be seated
and all members will be silent. That is a fundamental rule of the House and I intend to see
that it is obeyed. I called the honourable member to order because he was making a speech
in the guise of asking a supplementary question. That is not in order. The Minister may
comment if he wishes.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: I am very happy to comment. The crux of the matter is that
bylaws are constantly undergoing revision and updating, particularly for existing buildings.
A building which would have satisfied the bylaw requirements when it was erected may not
meet the updated and more stringent standards. It would be unreasonable to suggest that
such buildings be demolished. The continuing problem will necessitate local administrative
flexibility, and that should be exercised by local government. Bylaws, being local laws, are
regarded as the appropriate vehicle for dealing with local circumstances.

Coal Mining, United States Bureau of Mines Research Reports
3. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Mines: In the light of the
department's view that new technology is needed to recover up to 70 percent of coal in a
seam 50 ft thick, is he aware that the United States Bureau of Mines has a contract research
programme with mining companies and consulting firms "oriented toward improved recov-
ery in underground mining of thick and pitching seams", and that in early August it was
said that these studies are essentially complete and final reports will soon be available
through the Government's technical information service, and, if so, what step is he taking to
ensure that this information is available and quickly applied in coal mining here?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I reply on behalf of the Minister
of Mines. His answer is as follows: "I am aware that the United States Bureau of Mines has
let research contracts with mining companies and consulting firms to find ways of economi-
cally recovering 80 percent or more of thick and steeply pitching seams of coal in certain
western deposits of the USA. The New Zealand Mines Department will receive copies of
reports on this work as soon as possible and the results will be considered to see if they are
applicable in New Zealand conditions. Tunnel driving and surface development at Huntly
will ensure that coal is accessible and that any new technology that is applicable can be used
without delay."
Hon. F. M. Colman: In view of the nature of the development of underground coal
mining in New Zealand and the statement by the Secretary of Mines that it may not be
possible to open new underground mines until the early 1980s, what urgency is being given to
obtaining the information and its application?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: It is not only a matter of urgency to obtain the material.
Several engineers have travelled to America and Germany, and the department is in touch
with Australia so that it can keep up with the new technology.

Liquor Act 1962. New wine put down during the year totalled 26 659 000 litres. Table wines:
grape wines, 13 666 000 litres; fruit wines, 148 000 litres. Dessert wines: grape wines,

GOVERNMENT BUSINESS-PRECEDENCE ON WEDNESDAYS
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Deputy Prime Minister): I move, That, on and after
Wednesday, 14 September 1977, and for the remainder of the session, Government business
shall take precedence on Wednesdays. The timing of the motion is sometimes directly related
to the time at which the House comes together, but I think the real measure is the number of
sitting days that have elapsed. In this decade, there has been no occasion on which the notice
has been moved after so many sitting days. I found it interesting to look back on former
occasions. In 1960 it was moved after 36 sitting days; in 1964, after 33 sitting days; in 1966,
32; and in 1968, 33. In fact, in the 10-year period from 1960 to 1969, the greatest time ever
allowed was 45 sitting days. On this occasion it has been 64, which is more than in any year
since 1970.
Motion agreed to.
MARLBOROUGH COUNTY COUNCIL RESERVES FUND EMPOWERING BILL
Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): I am directed by the Local Bills Committee to
present the report of the committee on the Marlborough County Council Reserves Fund
Empowering Bill. The committee recommends that the Bill be not allowed to proceed. The
committee further recommends that the Bill be referred to the Government for considera-
tion in conjunction with the Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 3). I move, That the
report do lie upon the table.
In the Bill the county council sought to provide for the maximum area of 2 acres for
residential subdivisions to be deleted from section 28(2) of the Counties Amendment Act
1961 for the areas of land controlled by the Marlborough County Council, to enable it to levy
reserve fund contributions on such subdivisions. The committee deliberated with a great deal
of sympathy for the plight of the county council, but finally agreed unanimously that the Bill
should not be allowed to proceed because it would be setting aside the general powers
contained in the 1961 amendment, for the benefit of only one county council, at a time when
the Government is amalgamating the Municipal Corporations Act and the Counties Act.
We had a great deal of sympathy for the Marlborough County Council, particularly in
respect of the Marlborough Sounds area, to which the county clerk-who appeared before
the select committee-made special reference. The preamble to the Bill indicates that the
council is thinking especially of the Marlborough Sounds area. If the Bill had been allowed
to proceed on the recommendation of the committee, there might well have been changes to
tighten the provisions, to make it quite clear that it could pertain only to that area of land.
But, finally, and on balance-and I agree with the recommendation-it was felt that we
should not allow the Bill to proceed. However, we drew it to the attention of the
Government in its consideration of the next phase of the merging of the two Acts already
referred to. The member for Marlborough made strong representations in support, and I
have no doubt that he would like to make some comment on the committee's recommenda-
tion, The departments that gave evidence to the Local Bills Committee were, in general,
against the specific provision contained in the Bill, and felt that it was a matter for
consideration when legislation was looked at in a general sense.
Mr LATTER (Marlborough): On behalf of the Marlborough County Council I thank
the committee for its full study of the Bill, and for its sympathy. Of course, I am
disappointed, as is the council. It has been a long fight. The council first took this issue to the
counties conference in 1972. It was agreed to there, but with two changes of Government the
council has not managed to get it through. So be it. The council will now await with interest
further consideration when the Government introduces the Local Government Amendment
Bill (No. 3), and certainly I will be making representations to the Minister.
There is a problem in the Marlborough Sounds-not in the whole county. It is not
peculiar. to the Marlborough Sounds; it must exist in other areas of New Zealand. That is
why I hope that after fuller consideration there will be provision for a flexible maximum in
certain areas of New Zealand. This is not a sudden brain-storm. Marlborough is not a
backward county. The Marlborough County Council is almost leading at the moment. It is
the only area in New Zealand for which a recreational plan has been produced by the
Department of Lands and Survey. Certainly the council has gone into its planning. It has had
23 000 objections to the plan, so a lot of work has been done. The problem will remain until

DISCUSSION OF MOTIONS
OECD Economic Survey
Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei): I move, That this House notes that the July 1977 OECD
Economic Survey reports "some important positive achievements" for the New Zealand
National Government which, despite inheriting a record level of inflation, a record internal
deficit, a record external deficit, and record unemployment levels, has made, according to the
OECD report, "exceptionally good" efforts in the employment field, has seen "inflation pass its
peak", and "the current external deficit reduced", none of which was achieved under a Labour
Government.
Two popular sayings have been associated with the third National Government. Both
are true. One is that nobody will be worse off under national superannuation; and that has
tended to overshadow the other one, which is also a beaut-the first 3 years of National
Government will be largely devoted to restoring our shattered economy. In a commentary
on the OECD report in July 1977, Mr T. W. Hall said in the Dominion of 22 August that it
reads rather like a mid-term report on a favoured pupil by a well disposed teacher.
The report states that New Zealand is doing well in countering problems not of its own
making. The Government and the manufacturing sector receive particular praise. The report
notes that the rate of inflation has passed its peak and is decelerating. It says that New
Zealand's record in employment is exceptionally good by the standards of most members of
the 24-nation OECD, particularly in view of the magnitude of the adjustment problem the
country has had to face. The report notes that the current external deficit has been reduced,
and its financing has not yet placed too great a strain on the country's future foreign
exchange earnings. It says too that, while external developments have played a role in this,
the Government's tight economic policies have made a significant contribution. For two full
years wage controls successfully kept pay rises below the rate of inflation. The report says
that monetary policy changes advanced by the Government must be carried further, and I
have no doubt they will be.
I now want to detail some of those successes with irrefutable facts and figures. Inflation:
On 29 December 1974 the then Minister of Finance, now the Deputy Leader of the
Opposition, was asked: "Can you predict what the rate of inflation will be in 1975?" He said,
"No, that is not possible"; but he estimated that, failing either greater co-operation from
New Zealanders or unexpected changes in price levels overseas, a 12 or 13 percent inflation
rate in the coming year might be a more realistic figure than 10 percent. In fact, the annual
rate rose to 15.7 percent before the change of Government, and was still rising; it rose to
over 17 percent before we grabbed it. Remember the sorry tale; it was 5.5 percent in 1972,
rose to 15.7 percent at the time of the change of Government in 1975, and was over 17
percent before we managed to grab it. As at June 1977 the rate was 14 percent—and that
includes the disappointing fourth quarter of the year at 4.8 percent. Therefore, as pointed
out in the OECD report, inflation is past its peak; it is 14 percent, and is falling right now.
What of the current account deficit? A current account deficit of $41 million was
recorded for the month of July 1977. A good trade surplus of $33 million was offset by a $74
million deficit on invisibles. The deficit for the year ended July 1977 was $490 million, a
decrease of $40.5 million on the year ended June 1977, an improvement of $210 million on
the year ended July 1976, and an overall improvement of more than $500 million on the year
ended November 1975 at the time of the change of Government. I remind the House that at
that time the deficit we inherited was almost $1,000 million. Let us look at the position in
another way.
Mr Hunt: It will not look any good that way either.
Mr ELLIOTT: The overseas exchange transactions deficit had reached the equivalent of
11 percent of the gross national product in mid-1975. I wonder if the member for New Lynn
is proud of that. It has steadily dropped under this Government. At the time of the change of
Government the deficit as a percentage of gross national product was 9.5, and by July 1977 it
had dropped to only 3.9-a remarkable recovery. The Prime Minister was told during


## p. 2743 (#381) ###########################################

7 September
2743
Discussion of Motions
discussions with major financial institutions overseas that New Zealand's financial standing
was high-a tribute to our efforts to restore our external balance.
I turn now to employment. The OECD report says that New Zealand's record on
employment is exceptionally good. The number of registered unemployed has been kept low
by the activities of the Department of Labour in placing people in jobs. I pay tribute to those
in the Department of Labour's employment service, for the way in which they have placed
people in positions and the priority they have given to special work schemes and the private
sector employment subsidy scheme. Although different countries collect their unemploy-
ment statistics in different ways, it is very clear that New Zealand is doing much better than
the other countries listed. For example, in Australia 5.4 percent of the total labour force is
unemployed, in the United Kingdom 6 percent, in Canada 7.9 percent, in the United States
6.8 percent, in West Germany 4.4 percent, and in New Zealand 0.6 percent. That
comparison proves that New Zealand is doing well by international standards.
According to the former Secretary to the Treasury, Henry Lang, as reported in the
Christchurch Press of 18 August 1977, New Zealand is the only Western country to have
maintained anything like full employment. He said the key to maintaining full employment
was the maintenance of a reasonable incomes policy, thanks to the National Government.
He also said he believed it was now dependent on whether the unions would accept
conciliation and arbitration, or whether the more militant unions would insist on using their
"full muscle". All sectors of the community must do their part. Labour promised more than
it could deliver on employment. In the Economic Outlook of April 1975 the then Minister of
Finance was reported as saying, "The Government regards full employment as an objective
of the highest priority"; but the former Labour Government failed to meet that objective.
One of the excellent moves made by the National Government to assist the unem-
ployed, and particularly recent school leavers, was the introduction of the private sector
employment subsidy scheme. Piloted last year in Northland and the East Coast, this highly
successful scheme has this year been reintroduced in those areas and extended to several
other areas. On 22 July last year the Auckland Star said, "The scheme is a commendable
attempt to grapple with a difficult social problem." The National Government is living proof
that the Labour Party has no sole claim to promoting social justice in New Zealand. Under
that scheme young men and women will be able to contribute to production on farms and in
factories rather than sit out the recession on the dole. The Government will save on
unemployment benefits and receive something back by way of taxation; and just as
important is the gain in self-respect and the feeling of usefulness to society that will be
engendered in the young citizens employed under the scheme.
Despite the assertion of the Deputy Leader of the Opposition, as reported in the
Christchurch Star in 1975, when he was Minister of Finance, that the Government had faced
the problems realistically, the people of New Zealand knew otherwise and they voted
accordingly in November 1975. We will continue to follow policies based on social justice
and sound economic management. Let me quote Mr T. W. Hall again: "The OECD report
on the New Zealand economy reads rather like a mid-term report on a favourite pupil by a
well disposed teacher." I suggest that the end-of-year report for the year 1978 will read in the
following way: "Leadership, excellent. Economic management, excellent. Social justice,
excellent. Outstanding term's work. Great progress. New Zealand is the way I wanted it.
Have another 3 years. Signed, John Kiwi.”

South Pacific Fisheries Agency
Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury): I move, That this House supports the setting up of a
South Pacific Fisheries Agency now being discussed at the South Pacific Forum in Port
Moresby, and commends the Prime Minister on his initiative in first promoting this concept
which in association with the declaration of 200-mile economic zones will lead to an increasing
percentage of the $250 million worth of fresh fish taken annually from Central and South
Pacific waters being caught and processed for the economic benefit of forum countries.
I hope Opposition members will give complete support to the Prime Minister for his
initiative at the South Pacific Forum. The developments taking place around New Zealand's
shores, and in the area of the South Pacific countries, will lead to the biggest economic
development for New Zealand since the first refrigerated cargo of meat left the country
nearly 100 years ago. I hope the speaker who follows me will second this motion, and will
endorse the views I have expressed about our biggest economic development in 100 years, a
matter about which the country is concerned, and which experts in the fishing world and
industry are talking about.
Shortly, New Zealand will have the fourth largest economic management zone in the
world. That zone, when combined with those of the other South Pacific Forum countries,
will be the largest in the world. The demand for fishing resources and fishing rights is
expanding rapidly. The Government is aware of this, and has moved with the utmost speed
to protect New Zealand's resources during the planning and expansion of its own fishing
industry.
Mr Hunt: When?
Mr TALBOT: The Government is doing it now in association with the other forum
countries. The member for New Lynn has been yacking too much in the House to know what
is going on. With the declaration by New Zealand of a 200-mile economic zone, and the
establishment of a South Pacific fisheries management area, there is no doubt that the forum
countries will have very strong bargaining powers in trade negotiations with friendly nations.
The dramatic changes taking place through the declaration of 200-mile economic zones
have resulted in increasing demands for fishing resources by the great fishing nations. Korea

The National Research Bureau confidence index suggests that economic confidence has
