ADJOURNMENT-FOREIGN AFFAIRS
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I move, That the time allotted to speakers
in the debate shall be 45 minutes for the first speaker on either side, 30 minutes for the second
speaker on either side, and thereafter 20 minutes for each speaker.
Motion agreed to.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): For the purpose of discussing
foreign affairs, I move, That the House do now adjourn. I want to say immediately how much
I welcome the opportunity for the House to debate the question, for there are great issues to
discuss. They are issues that are not remote from us here in New Zealand, however remote
our geography may be. They are issues that affect us, as they affect every other country in
the world. We are all, one way or another, caught up with the forces that are changing the
shape of the world we live in. Many aspects of that world that have become familiar to us are
changing, and we have to recognise the forces that are bringing about these changes and
come to terms with them if we are to look after our own interests and play an effective and
helpful part in the world at large.
The world, then, is changing fast, and we have to change with it. I want to emphasise
that this does not mean that we have to give up old friends, or abandon old traditions and
values. They will stay, and we will stay with them. We need them as points of certainty in a
time of search and of questioning—and, heaven knows, there is plenty of questioning around
the world today. We need to be adaptable. We need to be imaginative enough to see where
change is needed, and to take the initiative with our friends and neighbours whenever we
can, or, if necessary, take the initiative alone. We must be aware of the world beyond our
shores. We must be somewhat more self-reliant. Sudden and often violent change is the
spirit of the age in which we live. While there has been no major war for the past few years,
that must not be mistaken in any way for an absence of struggle-far from it. In every
quarter of the world we look at today people have been or are pushing for
change-sometimes peacefully, sometimes by violence-for what they see as a better and
more just way of life than that which they have experienced. We in a country like New
Zealand, who have a natural abhorrence of violence, must understand those forces if we are
to help to bring change by more peaceful means.
The struggle takes many forms. It is the conflict between rich and poor, between those
countries that have much-those countries that enjoy so much of the material benefit of
today's living-and those that have very little. We in New Zealand are caught up in that
struggle between developed and underdeveloped countries, for we are pledged to help our
friends and neighbours to get a better deal. We know something of their problems. In fact,
many of them we share. Indeed, I remember the experience at the very first UNCTAD. For
a brief period New Zealand was part of the group of 77. However, they discovered or we
discovered, or perhaps we both discovered-that we did not altogether fit there. Neither, of
course, do we fit in the other groups. The struggle is for a fairer share of the world's


## p. 2759 (#397) ###########################################

7 September
2759
Adjournment-Foreign Affairs
resources, for a better economic system, for a fairer system of trading, and for more
certainty in commodity arrangements. Let me add that we know a good deal about the other
groups because, although others may have greater needs, we too have seen the forces of
narrow self-interest close the door to trade in our face.
The struggle is also for identity, and in many cases it is a struggle for self-respect, a
struggle of people who want to run their own lives, whether it is the people of the Middle
East who are now taking charge of their own destiny, or Africans who demand a major say in
the running of their own countries. That, I think, is the highest priority in their quest-the
right to make their own decisions, the right to determine how their countries should be run.
That is not remote from us either, because it is a simple statement of fact that we have played
a major, a very considerable, part in bringing independence to the South Pacific and in
helping to sustain the right of our friends in South-east Asia to choose their own way of life.
Those are the issues that I thought to talk about tonight, and I want to relate them to
specific areas of interest that involve New Zealand immediately. In each case we need to
take those facts into account, both to advance our own interests and to help others. That
does not mean-and I emphasise this-that there are not other subjects of major import-
ance to us. There are, but it is not possible to cover them in a speech in these circumstances.
Many of the other questions I want to deal with have been dealt with extensively in recent
months, but there are two matters I want to refer to briefly.
One is ANZUS. As I see it, that is basic to all that we do. We can play our part in world
politics, and in helping others, only if we are confident of our own security, of the strategic
underpinning that ANZUS gives, assisted undoubtedly by detente. Let me underline the
point that we must never mistake what detente means. I shall always remember the words
spoken to me by a Foreign Minister I met in Europe; he said, "Remember that detente there
may be, but there will be no armistice in the battle of ideas." That is why this Government
has moved quickly to re-emphasise and re-invigorate the ANZUS relationship. If the recent
past has taught us anything, it is that the United States must continue to sustain the strategic
balance in our part of the world. I can say, after the recent ANZUS Council meeting held
here in these buildings, that the alliance is in good shape, that the Americans are determined
to maintain their presence throughout the Pacific, and that they value their continuing
partnership with Australia and New Zealand. This point was made abundantly clear by Mr
Warren Christopher while he was here.
The second matter is our relationship with the European Economic Community. That is
of the greatest importance to us, obviously, not only for our own economic well-being, but
also because we need Europe's partnership if we are to play our role in this part of the world.
There have been those who have said it is a waste of time seeking to continue a relationship
with Europe for our pastoral products, and that we should be out searching for new markets.
Well, of course, we are, but there is no other market at present for the dairy products, and
certainly the meat, that we sell in the community. Our economy must be strong if we are to
accept our full range of responsibilities, and I believe that the Europeans generally
acknowledge that. They know that New Zealand has a major economic stake in the British
market, as well as a growing economic stake in other markets within the European
community. The point I have continued to make to those Ministers with whom I have spoken
is that they should bear in mind the fact that, as the community expands, it stretches out to
embrace a market such as Greece, which is of very considerable importance to this country.
It is our task to translate that awareness so that they take practical account of New Zealand's
interests, and recognise that their decisions affect us, and that New Zealand's well-being and
stability are in their interests too.
There are still many decisions to be made. There is no denying that the going in Europe
will be tough, but we do have continuing British support; this was underlined by Mr John
Silkin when he was here just a few weeks ago. We do have the beginnings of a new and
broader relationship with Europe. We have had to work hard to maintain our position in
Europe, and we will have to work harder still to make Europe recognise that our well-being
and the well-being of the area we live in are of very considerable importance to them. It is
part, in fact, of the general struggle I talked about earlier, of persuading countries to look
beyond their immediate national interests and to recognise that partnership and co-
operation are as much in their interest as that of anyone else. That is what lies behind the
debate between the developed and the underdeveloped countries, the so-called north-south
dialogue.
It is also basic to New Zealand's relationship with Japan. We have reached a crucial
stage in our relationship with that major Pacific power. There have been some glib


## p. 2760 (#398) ###########################################

2760
7 September
Adjournment-Foreign Affairs
headlines. People have spoken in terms of "fish for butter" or "fish for beef", but these
expressions, in my view, are a gross oversimplification. They serve to distort the problems,
to misrepresent the tone of our dealings with Japan, for it remains true that we have built up
with Japan a relationship that in range, in content, and in variety is second to none.
Successive New Zealand Governments have urged the Japanese to take account of our
interests and of our difficulties when they impose their agricultural stabilisation and import
policies on products that are of major importance to the New Zealand economy. We have
pressed our case hard, for more than a decade. Japan, however, has continued to operate its
system in a way that treats our products-beef and dairy produce and forestry products
among them-as residual supplies. The Japanese Government has deliberately kept the
price of butter, milk powder, and beef as high as possible. It has done this to restrict
consumer demand so that production of these products in Japan will match the demand. It is
simple to attain a position of self-sufficiency if you keep the price high enough. Imports from
New Zealand are called in only to regulate that stabilisation system. This is not acceptable.
Over the last year or so the Japanese Government has made it clear that it wants New
Zealand to be sympathetic over the difficulties that confront the Japanese people because of
restrictions on Japan's fishing catches in foreign waters. We understand that problem, but
have asked that, first, the Japanese Government should do something about our problems.
We are looking to the Japanese Government to show the same concern for our difficulties as
the Japanese are asking us to show for theirs. I am content-the Prime Minister has made
this perfectly clear-that there should be no direct linkage between our problems and theirs,
and that each should be settled in its own context. We are not haggling in a bazaar. We are
emphasising the complementary interests that are at stake for us and for them, and are
simply asking if it is not reasonable that we should solve our problems first, particularly when
Japan will not, in practice, have to make major changes, and our requests have been on the
table for so long-for more than a decade. The position now is that we are waiting for the
Japanese Government to respond to our approach, and that response will be of the utmost
importance, because if, as I hope, it is a fair and satisfactory one, then the talks I am to have
in Japan next month will focus on future co-operation between our two countries; and I
know there is an interest there, as there is an interest here, in building that relationship.
I want to refer to another area where there has been a definite and constructive
response to the need for change, where partnership is gradually replacing what was at one
stage cut-throat competition, and where people are working together to make their countries
more self-reliant. It is an area where New Zealand has been playing, and will continue to
play, a constructive role-I refer, of course, to the five countries of South-east Asia that
make the Association of South-east Asian Nations-ASEAN. The Government
welcomes-in fact I am sure the House welcomes-the progress that ASEAN is making in
practical co-operation in economic matters. It is too early yet to speak of the emergence of
an ASEAN common market, but let there be no doubt-and in fact they have made this
perfectly clear-that what they intend to create is a preferential trading zone. That is the
direction in which they are heading. New Zealand will do everything it can to move closer to
ASEAN, not only because we recognise the need to expand our trade with the ASEAN
countries—and, heaven knows, that is vital to us-but also because we share ASEAN's aims
of achieving peace and stability in South-east Asia.
The very purpose, of course, is to achieve that through economic, social, and political
advancement. I want to emphasise that this is not an area for Government activity alone. I
have talked of change, and the need to adapt ourselves. We, as a community, need to adapt
our thinking to the importance of the role of ASEAN in our future. It is not only an area for
Government activity, but also one of opportunity for the business community. Governments
can create the climate for co-operation, but it is up to private industry to take advantage of
that climate. No doubt there will be risks, but nothing will be achieved without taking those
risks. New Zealand entrepreneurs have a great opportunity, which some have already
grasped. However, we must not look on ASEAN solely in economic terms, any more than
do the member countries themselves. We want a broadly based relationship, and that is what
they are setting out to create.
Right now we are looking at ways in which we can help ASEAN social and cultural
development. These are two specific areas in which our assistance has been sought, and we
shall give it, because the stability of South-east Asia, the growing strength of those countries,
and the peace of the area are of major importance to everyone. This is one part of the world
in which the demand for change is being met peacefully, sensibly, and through co-operation.
No doubt there will be struggles, but the main has been set, and is an area in which New


## p. 2761 (#399) ###########################################

7 September
2761
Adjournment-Foreign Affairs
Zealand can help, and, by doing so, help itself. It is a good example of mutual co-operation.
Turning closer to home, I want to say something about the South Pacific, not because it
is an area of primary importance to us-our home base, as it were-but because here, in an
area in which we play a major role, many of the dilemmas being faced by the world at large
are being worked out. Here, in a readily comprehensible form, are the same forces that are
changing the shape of the international community. We are fortunate, indeed, that in our
own area we have recognised those imperatives, and with our Island neighbours are working
to deal with them peacefully. It is on record that nearly 65 percent of New Zealand's bilateral
aid is now channelled to the South Pacific. More projects, more New Zealand equipment,
and more New Zealanders are in the Islands than ever before.
It is sometimes claimed that, because of this, New Zealand has an ugly face in the
Pacific. I want to stress that not only do I believe that such claims are groundless, but there is
also plenty of evidence to substantiate that belief. At the opening of the Cook Islands
Legislative Assembly in May 1977, it was recorded in the Speech from the Throne that, "It is
gratifying to know that after 12 years of independent government, the very special relation-
ship between the Cook Islands and New Zealand has grown richly in both understanding and
maturity." Obviously, there will be difficulties as there were in the past, but that statement,
with which we could all concur, emphasises the understanding and the maturity of the
relationship between our two countries. In a letter to me recently, the Prime Minister of Fiji
said: "We place a very high value on our relations with your country, and it is because of the
positive spirit that you have always responded to our aspirations and needs that we have
made this submission to you on our bilateral aid programme." The Prime Minister was
expressing some views, which I will indicate shortly, about the nature of the aid programme,
and I wanted to point out the way in which the submission was made. That statement is
typical of many others made to me when I visited the five South Pacific countries earlier this
year. The value of the New Zealand relationship was made clear by all the Island leaders I
met.
The aid relationships that we have with these countries must be kept under constant
review. The objective of the aid programme is to help Island governments to support the
achievement of social, economic, and political goals. This calls for the highest degree of
consultation and co-operation, but the point made by the Prime Minister of Fiji in his letter
to me, and to which I have referred, is that policies that guide our normal aid operations can
sometimes be too inflexible to meet the special needs of the South Pacific countries. Too
much paper work is involved; and that can be a problem. I recollect the observation made by
one honourable member during the consideration of the Foreign Affairs estimates, when he
sought to make the point that not only money should be given as aid. There was some
discussion about that. Every member is no doubt aware that the Auditor-General has
expressed some views, and considers that documentation is sometimes not comprehensive
enough. This criticism was expressed in his report. I do not doubt for a moment that our
internal procedures can be improved, but the demands we already make can place too heavy
a burden on the Island governments and their planning resources.
Frequently, in my discussions with them, Ministers in those governments have made the
point that, as we seek more information, we ask questions that they do not have a
bureaucracy capable of answering; and that when we seek that information they have to
decide whether they will divert people to find out the answers, or simply say that they cannot
provide them. I have explained to Pacific Island leaders that our requirements arise from our
accountability for the expenditure of Government funds. I have also said that we will look
for other ways of meeting this need better suited to Pacific Island conditions. The way to a
better aid relationship may lie, not in stricter demands on the recipient country, but in a
greater flexibility in our own approach.
One course I am at present looking at—and I say no more than that—is the possibility of
allocating funds to a particular sector of an Island economy, say, agricultural production,
and leaving the country to determine for itself the precise ways in which the funds would be
spent. That is the difference between programme aid and what we know as project aid,
which is the form taken by the greater part of our aid programme. However good and
however well administered, aid programmes will not solve the problems of the developing
world. What is true on a world scale is certainly true in the South Pacific. Aid will help, but
we all know that only increased trade opportunities will awaken a real desire to build up
production and increase local revenue. We have to face the fact that New Zealand has a real
and practical responsibility for many of the Island countries. Our market is the major outlet
for their exports, and for some it is the only market.


## p. 2762 (#400) ###########################################

2762
7 September
Adjournment-Foreign Affairs
The problem in those cases is the lack of stable and remunerative prices. For instance,
an Islands Minister said to me that it was one thing to encourage a grower to grow a certain
fruit and deliver it to the wharf of an outer island, but it was another for the grower to
discover that, in the market for which it was intended, no value whatsoever was attached to
the product. That is an issue that New Zealanders are familiar with from the other end, in
varying proportions, in our own exporting of agricultural products to the markets of the
industrialised countries. To help to overcome it in the South Pacific, we are now looking at
the contribution New Zealand can make to price-stabilisation measures. The Government
recognises that freer access is important to encourage productivity and promote trade. We
must look sympathetically at ways of reducing some of the existing barriers to those
traditional exports, in favour of imports from the Islands.
The Islands need to boost their agricultural sectors, and they also need to develop light
industry, to create more jobs. Here New Zealand can help. A beginning has been made
through the Pacific Islands Industrial Development Scheme, which is producing results, but
here again the question of access to the New Zealand market has arisen. Some of the
ventures proposed under the Pacific Islands Industrial Development Scheme will be to
provide the Islands' needs alone-no need for any other market. Some will aim at third-
country markets. A number, however, will look to access to the New Zealand market for
part of their production, and in those cases there can be requests as needed. There has
already been, in one case, a request for adjustment here to make room for the product. But
the adjustments required will be small compared with the benefits to the Island economies
concerned. Steps that benefit the Island economies benefit the South Pacific region as a
whole, New Zealand included.
In terms of the requests to make more money available, I have at times thought of the
mistaken belief that it is always better to give than to receive. This might well be an instance
where perhaps we have to think in terms of some willingness to receive. These steps, and the
progress in communications and transport, set a pattern which could well be followed
elsewhere. They show how co-operation can meet successfully the demand for progress felt
by people everywhere. I wish I could say that those lessons of co-operation and partnership
have been learned in Africa. They have not.
The history of relations between black and white, between those who exercise power
and those who, though an overwhelming majority, have had no say in their destiny, is
undoubtedly one of lost opportunities. Violence is already part of the pattern of life in
southern Africa, and the pity is that, unless the minority governments in those countries are
prepared to come to terms with reality, that violence will expand and bring in its wake
widespread panic, destruction, and suffering. The idea that one racial group is superior to
others, and therefore has the right to impose its own political system on other groups, is
quite untenable, but it is an idea that is still vigorously defended in southern Africa, and it is
an idea around which a way of life has been built. The stark reality is that the idea is wrong,
and that the way of life will have to be changed. The choice is literally between working
things out now, or being involved in a conflagration later.
In Rhodesia, time has almost run out. Everyone stands to gain from a settlement based
on the Anglo-American proposals that David Owen and others have worked so strenusouly
on. The proposals have been put forward, and there is no doubt that a willingness to accept
and act on those proposals can make a major change. But there must be some question about
whether those who seek to gain power on the one hand and on the other those who seek to
hold on to it can come together. A number of people have asked me about the possibility of a
United Nations peace-keeping force. The point I make is that there would have to be a peace
for that force to keep, before the force could be put into place.
The gravest problem is in South Africa itself. Unless the South African authorities
dismantle the system of apartheid-are prepared to start to move in that direction—the tide
of black resentment will sweep across the country. In discussions I had with Ministers when I
was in East Africa, a number of them made the point that it was a system they would not
tolerate. Certainly it is no easy thing for a white population to accommodate. After all,
South Africa is their home too. President Nyerere said there were those who asked, "What
do you expect us, the white people, to do? Where do you expect us to go?" His answer was,
"I do not expect you to go anywhere. This is your home." But change must come. I am
certain that there is no alternative. It is only a question of when and how.
As I said at the outset, many topics ought to be considered. The subject of our relations
with Australia could well be a debate in itself, because no two countries are closer together,
and no two have such an assured future if they work together economically, politically, and

Adjournment-Foreign Affairs
in dealing with the region around them. Indeed, the state of our relationship with Australia
is basic to our international approach, and it most certainly cannot be taken for granted. It
has to be nourished, developed, and kept in good order; and certainly it is the Government's
intention that it should be. I might also have touched on China, a great Asian country whose
impact on the area in which we find ourselves is bound to grow, or the Soviet Union-not
perhaps a traditional partner, but certainly a country which is fast developing into one of our
major trading partners.
I decided at the outset that tonight I wanted to bring into focus some of the main issues
facing the world, to isolate those forces that are working through the international commun-
ity, and to relate them to our own experience. If we recognise those forces, if we accept them
for what they are, and if we learn how to deal with them when they impinge upon us, then we
can face the future confidently. I believe we have shown, in our own immediate area of
concern, that we can deal with such forces confidently. We are fortunate that, unlike many
other parts of the world, we have no overwhelming immediate threat to our security, and can
marshall our resources, political and economic as we set the economic problems right, to
deal with those forces in practical, sensible ways. That is an experience we can share with the
rest of the world, for all countries, large or small, must learn somehow to cope with those
same changes that press upon us all.
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert): We on this side of the House are delighted that at

at the outset I must make it perfectly clear that we are a little disturbed that once again—and

a very complex subject. The Minister is well aware that Oppositions, including his own, have

It is correct that Japan is our second largest export market. It is getting close, although
not as close as some probably would like-including the Government-to the British
market, where 19.2 percent of our produce was sold in the year ended December 1976 as
against 13.7 percent in Japan and 12.48 percent in Australia. We have trade agreements with
Great Britain and Australia, but not with Japan, and that is what angers and irritates the
Prime Minister. But Japan does not have that type of trading agreement with many
countries.
New Zealand, as a minor trading partner, is seeking something that Japan has denied
her major trading partners. The United States buys 23.7 percent of Japan's exports, and sells
to Japan 18.3 percent of her total imports. The EEC buys 5.6 percent of Japan's exports, and
sells in return 10.8 percent of her total imports. New Zealand does not import or export 1
percent of the Japanese export or import market, so why should we expect special treatment
when other countries have been told by Japan that she does not trade on that basis? An
article in the Dominion of 22 July stated that after 3 days of talks in Tokyo the EEC
negotiators had accepted the fact that even though they were large trading partners they
would not be able to reach such an agreement. The Japanese have been told by the
Government that if they do not buy our meat they cannot have our fish. A cartoon appeared
in a paper recently showing a Japanese gentleman fishing in Lake Taupo against the limits.

cutlets for breakfast, amd therefore was entitled to fish. I think that illustrates the position

worked for the last 2 years to repair that relationship.
The member for Mt. Albert saw fit to attack the Government, and me personally, on
our attitude to ASEAN. He said that ASEAN is going to get less aid. The commitment I
made in Kuala Lumpur represents an increase of $10.6 million-not a decrease. I told the
five heads of the ASEAN countries, as I have told the people of New Zealand, that we are
deliberately going to switch a greater proportion of our external aid to the South Pacific,
where it is needed, where there are the people whom we know, where there are the people
who know us, and where we can be certain that it is going to be used effectively. The
ASEAN leaders accepted that. There is also the fact that among the ASEAN countries
Singapore, in particular, no longer needs the level of aid that was previously required; in its
place we put the co-operative organisation between Singapore and New Zealand to
exchange technology and establish industry. When I attended the New Zealand trade fair in
Singapore recently, I was told at stall after stall of new joint ventures between New Zealand
and ASEAN countries that had been arranged during that period.
Our relationship with ASEAN has never been better. Let me read a short extract from
the address I gave to the ASEAN heads of Government: "Since 1975 we have begun to
develop a programme of regional projects, ASEAN projects. As a supplement to our
continuing bilateral aid, these are designed to benefit ASEAN as a whole, and to promote its
unity and regional awareness. Apart from trade promotion through the joint trade study
group, these ASEAN-New Zealand projects cover timber marketing, forestry development,
animal health, veterinary services, and dental health. They will cost about US$2.5 million.
The first of them, a survey of the end uses of ASEAN timber in the main importing
countries, has just been completed and presented to ASEAN Governments. I believe this
project has been very successful. Its recommendations on market development and strategy
will be important for a commodity of major export interest to all five ASEAN nations.
Looking ahead, we are ready to do more. Exactly what is done will depend on proposals put
forward by your Governments. New Zealand prefers where possible, to match finance to
specific projects, rather than the other way round. But I know it would be helpful to your
planners to have some indication of the scale of assistance that can be expected from New
Zealand. Let me say, therefore, that provided suitable projects can be identified New
Zealand can expect to offer assistance amounting to at least $50 million within the next 5
years, 1977-82. This sum includes provision for our continued bilateral assistance to ASEAN
member countries. In deciding on projects, we want to concentrate on the things we do best,
the sectors where we have world-class technology, where we can build on foundations
already laid.”
At the conclusion of that address, the five heads of Government of the ASEAN nations,
one after another, said, "We have no questions. We have no requests. We are satisfied with
the statement of the New Zealand Prime Minister, and we warmly thank him and the people
of New Zealand for what they are doing for ASEAN.” Our relationship with ASEAN has
never been warmer, it has never been closer, and the criticism made by the member for Mt.
Albert is totally unwarranted. I was specifically thanked by the President of Indonesia and
the President of the Philippines for the successful geothermal investigations that we have
done in both countries as part of our aid programme; both countries have found steam on
which they can build geothermal power stations. That is practical New Zealand aid, and that
is the relationship we have.

The Japanese Prime Minister, Mr Fukuda, said that we could not discuss at the same
time the two questions of access to fish and the problems we have had for a number of years
in trade. My response was, “I can see your position. You do not want to create a precedent.
All right, let us not create a precedent. Let us deal with the outstanding issues in trade access
that have been there for a number of years, and, after they have been dealt with, we will talk
about fish; not together, but one after the other, in proper sequence in the order in which the
issues have been raised." We sent an aide-mémoire to the Japanese Government, I guess 6
weeks or 2 months ago; we are waiting for a response.
The position of the New Zealand Government remains as I have put it. We are getting 4
percent to 5 percent of the beef imports into Japan; in every other country our percentage of
beef imports is much higher than that. The reason for this low percentage is the conditions
under which the quotas are issued. All we want is a change in the terms of the quotas, more
notice, and more regular quotas, so that we can compete as we do in every other market.
That is not a big request, nor is it a difficult request. We want similar conditions for milk
products.
We should like the prices in Japan to go down. I have been told, but I have no official
information, that the retail price of beef in Japan is 10 times what the producer gets. In other
circumstances, the Labour Opposition would be screaming about something like that. We
should like to see the price to the Japanese consumer brought down, not held up, so that the
consumer would consume more and, of course the Japanese would import more and help to
reduce that surplus for the benefit of world trade, something to which Mr Fukuda has given
his consent since his return to Japan-a reduction of Japan's external surplus. The same
applies to milk products. Although Japan takes American timber, which is no better, it will
not accept New Zealand timber of the kind we build our houses with. We want Japan to
remove the 10 percent duty on New Zealand timber, and to also remove the 10 percent duty
on fish caught by New Zealand fishermen. If the same type of fish is caught in New Zealand
waters by Japanese fishermen, no duty is payable.
These are not large requests. The member for Mt. Albert said that nobody is removing
duty. However, when I was in Germany earlier this year, it was announced that the Japanese
had decided not to use cut-price methods in their shipbuilding industry, so that they would
not bankrupt the shipbuilders in the Common Market. There is no reason Japan should not
make such a move on New Zealand's products.
Ten nations, including Japan, want access to the fish in our extended 200-mile zone. As
recently as yesterday the New Zealand Government decided it would declare the 200-mile
economic zone on 1 October 1977. For the first 6 months the zone will be used for fish
management, because our information is that the fishing effort is increasing, and that fish
stocks are being overfished and could be slaughtered during the summer season. I hope
members opposite will not oppose that. I also hope that tonight they will say they support the
Government in its move to close totally the areas in the zone that are the spawning grounds
for our domestic species of snapper and terakihi. Certain limits will be placed on total
catches, but, obviously, in the short time before 1 October we cannot have a licensing system
in force. That system will commence on 1 April and licences will be issued on an annual
basis. Japanese applications for licences will be considered in the light of the discussions we
are having on the other matters. The Minister of Fisheries will no doubt talk about this in
greater detail, but I hope that, even though members opposite seem to want an antagonistic
and controversial debate on foreign affairs, they will see the benefit to New Zealand and

on which he based his notice of motion was abridged and did not give in full the Minister's

Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): The point raised by the member for

Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I will look at the notice of motion. I had looked at it before,
and it appeared that there was no suggestion that the member was breaking the law as such.
With regard to the point raised by the member for Heretaunga, the Standing Order reads:
"All imputations of improper motives, or unbecoming reference to a member's private
affairs, and all personal reflections, shall be deemed highly disorderly." That Standing Order
is modified to a certain extent by Speaker's ruling 77/2, which reads: "A reference to a
member's private affairs is not out of order, but it depends on the spirit or context in which it
is made. If it is used in an insulting or injurious way it is bad form and not in order."
NEW ZEALAND SECURITY INTELLIGENCE SERVICE AMENDMENT BILL
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I move, That the New Zealand Security
Intelligence Service Amendment Bill be introduced. The introductory remarks are rather
more lengthy than is normal, because I believe the Bill, at its introduction, should be seen in
a proper context. I apologise in advance for the length of my remarks. The report of Sir Guy
Powles, on which the New Zealand Security Intelligence Service Amendment Bill is based,


## p. 2782 (#420) ###########################################

2782
New Zealand Security Intelligence Service Amendment Bill 8 September
covers a great deal of ground. In introducing the Bill, I should like to recall the resolution of
appreciation sent by this House earlier this year to the Chief Ombudsman on his retirement.
Sir Guy's investigation into the Security Intelligence Service was typical of the thorough
and humane approach that characterised all his work and deservedly gave the office of
Ombudsman in New Zealand an international reputation. Sir Guy's investigation was
commissioned by the Leader of the Opposition when he was Prime Minister in 1975, and his
report was presented to me in classified form in May last year. Sir Guy's report to you, Mr
Speaker, was tabled in this House on 6 August 1976, a few weeks before the retirement of Sir
William Gilbert as director of the service. Sir Guy's conclusions are a tribute to Sir William's
leadership of the service since its inception in 1956.
Consideration of the report by the Government has therefore occurred during the
settling-in period of the new director, Mr Paul Molineaux SM, who will be responsible under
me, as Minister, for effecting any alterations. It is timely, therefore, that the process of
investigation, reporting, consideration, and implementation has straddled changes in both
Government and director. The report contains 8 findings, 15 recommendations requiring
legislation, and 28 other recommendations of an administrative character. The Bill before
the House incorporates those of the legislative recommendations that have been accepted by
the Government, as well as some further proposals to fill gaps that became apparent in the
consideration and the drafting of the legislation.
A first reading of a Bill should be limited to what is proposed. However, on this
occasion I believe the House would expect me to introduce the Bill in the broader context of
the former Chief Ombudsman's report. I therefore seek your indulgence, Mr Speaker, to
indicate the Government's responses to the findings and administrative-type recommenda-
tions, as well as to the legislation recommended in the report. In doing so, I wish to place on
record the Government's concurrence with the view expressed by the Leader of the
Opposition on 10 March 1975, when he was the Prime Minister, that "Any State, however
small, and however far removed from world nerve centres, needs some form of security
service. It is needed in New Zealand to protect our own interests: for example, to keep a
check on international guerrilla movements, to check on the reliability of people working in
sensitive Government areas, and to ensure that foreign nationals living temporarily in our
country do not go beyond their legitimate fields of activity."
As the late Rt. Hon. Norman Kirk remarked on 21 August 1969, when speaking to the
Bill leading to the principal Act, "In the present way of life throughout the world this type of
thing is essential in an otherwise free society." He was referring to the service. Later in that
same debate Mr Kirk said: “We are discussing a service which is essential in an open
democratic society. There are tremendous advantages and also some risks attached to having
a free and open society. The proper purpose of a security service is and always has been to do
with the maintenance of a democratic open society, but we have to remember that the
freedom conferred by such a society creates the opportunity to abuse the privileges of or
destroy that society. This Bill"—the 1969 Act-"should be a protection against such abuse,
and against both those who would overthrow our free and open society and those who could
in fact inhibit those rights in the name of its protection."
The Bill now before the House follows the principles enunciated by Mr Kirk. It is my
belief, therefore, that much of the Bill will be supported by both sides of the House, and that
debate on its various clauses will be aimed at securing a bipartisan approach in matters of
security which safeguard our fundamental freedoms in a parliamentary democracy. The
Government generally welcomes the findings in the former Chief Ombudsman's report,
which acknowledged that a security service is essential; that surveillance of known or
suspected espionage activities is of the highest national importance; that the service is
justified in keeping under close scrutiny organisations that pursue doctrines calling for the
revolutionary overthrow of the State, and that in informing itself about organisations that
have fallen under a substantial degree of subversive influence its method of obtaining
information is basically sound; that vetting is a prime function of the service; that the security
screening of people coming to New Zealand is in the national interest; and that, in general,
the service's current relations with the press and non-governmental organisations are within
proper bounds.
In the recommendations requiring legislation, the report deals with terrorism but makes
no legislative recommendation. In the opinion of the Government, terrorism is a growing
and frightening phenomenon. Unfortunately, New Zealand is no longer geographically
remote. Recognising this new situation, the Government has recently established a Cabinet
committee on terrorism to co-ordinate activities to meet the threat. It is therefore approp-


## p. 2783 (#421) ###########################################

8 September New Zealand Security Intelligence Service Amendment Bill
2783
riate to update the principal Act in this regard. Clause 2 thus provides for a definition of
terrorism, and also includes the word "terrorism" in the definition of security in section 2 of
the principal Act. It should be noted too that this is the first time that terrorism has been
included in our legislation.
Perhaps one of the most important recommendations requiring legislative action is that
on page 30 of the report. The former Chief Ombudsman recognises the difficulty of assessing
"subversive potentiality" at any given point, place, and in any given circumstances.
Although this question can be very much a matter of subjective opinion, we now have a
judicial officer as director of the service. Having such an officer at this stage will provide a
period in which judicial attitudes and impartiality can be brought to bear on developing and
establishing satisfactory guidelines for the service. The director is acutely aware of the thin
line between potential subversion and a free expression of political views, but he must
continue to have the discretion to exercise surveillance and thus be in a position to ascertain
when to begin or cease inquiries into fringe areas. The director, who is also a member of the
reconstituted New Zealand Intelligence Council, is moreover able to inform the council of
any new area of potential subversion and, as he sees fit, to seek the advice of the council on
such new areas.
It would, however, be wrong in principle and impracticable administratively for the
director, as this recommendation proposes, to have two masters—that is, the Minister and
the council-by obliging him to seek the advice of the council before acting. Furthermore, to
introduce such a statutory obligation would undermine the concept of ministerial responsi-
bility and ultimate accountability to Parliament. The Government is, therefore, unable to
accept this recommendation in the form in which it is submitted in the report. Nevertheless,
the Government believes that much of the spirit of this important but problematical
recommendation can be reflected in a modified provision that ensures that the service will
operate with the benefit of local, New Zealand, and top-level advice—as emphasised on
pages 29 and 30 of the report. Clause 3 has been drafted with that objective in mind. It is
therefore proposed that the functions of the service included in section 4 of the principal Act
should be enlarged by adding to subsection (1) the following paragraph: “(d) To inform the
New Zealand Intelligence Council of any new area of potential espionage, sabotage,
terrorism, or subversion in respect of which the Director has considered it necessary to
institute surveillance."
I refer next to the recommendations on pages 44, 59, and 60 of the former Chief
Ombudsman's report, which spell out an amendment to the principal Act to provide
authority for the service to intercept communications under specific conditions and subject
to satisfactory control. It should be stressed at the outset that this power would be used only
sparingly. Clause 4 reflects what the Government proposes to do in implementing this most
important recommendation. In making his recommendation Sir Guy stated, "The Minister
should have the power first and principally, because as I have stressed throughout this
section he is responsible for the service; secondly, because-unlike the situation where a
judicial officer grants a warrant-the grant is likely to be part of an ongoing intelligence
exercise not resulting in court proceedings; thirdly, because of the problems of properly
briefing a person issuing a warrant; and fourthly, because judicial officers should not be
involved in what is essentially executive business."
The report covers in much detail a subject which is fraught with difficulty. I should
illustrate the problem in respect of one significant aspect. To put the matter beyond doubt,
subclause 5 of the Bill contains a saving provision which gives protection to any person acting
in pursuance of an interception warrant without making it "legal" to commit offences against
the property rights of individuals, which conduct might otherwise be construed as breaking
the law in a technical sense. In short, the possession of an interception warrant might
authorise breaking and entering, but would not absolve the person named in the warrant
from committing, for example, a theft; he will still be answerable to the law.
The Government has considered very carefully the limitation of 90 days suggested by
the former Chief Ombudsman on the validity of a warrant, but has not adopted this
limitation. The Canadian legislation on which Sir Guy modelled his suggestions has no such
limitation. Nevertheless, the Government sees great value in a review by the Minister of
warrants issued for the preceding 12 months prior to the preparation of his annual report to
Parliament. The report would, however, cover only interception warrants to detect domesti-
cally implied activities prejudicial to security referred to in the proposed new subparagraph
4A(1)(a)(i); the report would not cover the foreign activities in subparagraph (ii).
The report could also include information under the four heads suggested by the former


## p. 2784 (#422) ###########################################

2784
New Zealand Security Intelligence Service Amendment Bill 8 September
Chief Ombudsman-in line with the Canadian model-provided that information prejudi-
cial to security is not disclosed. The Government believes this is a sound approach. It has,
therefore, included further checks and balances in subsections (3), (5), (6), and (7) of the
proposed new section 4A which will effectively control the actions covered by the intercep-
tion warrants, grant a reasonable degree of immunity to persons authorised to make
interceptions, and override other enactments that may be contrary to the provisions of this
clause. For example, if the former Chief Ombudsman's recommendation is to work at all, it
is clearly undesirable in matters of security that the conditions upon which the Minister may
issue a warrant should be subject to judicial review or in any other way.
The Government recognises, however, that inevitably there will be dilemmas in this
area, which can only be resolved case by case. While there may be grounds for the view that
warrants should be issued by an independent person, the Government sees no option but
that he should be the responsible Minister. The former Chief Ombudsman has argued
cogently that this power should be wielded by an executive rather than a judicial authority.
This follows the pattern in the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia, where the issuing
authorities are all of ministerial rank. The Bill also provides in clause 2 for a definition of
"intercept" and "interception warrant".
Clause 5 is an amendment of section 5(2) of the principal Act which is proposed by the
Government. It is similar to a provision in the Broadcasting Act 1976, and would update the
mode of appointment of the Director of Security. With the retirement of Sir William Gilbert,
it is also proposed that subsection (4) should be dropped from section 5 of the principal Act.
Clause 6 implements the recommendations at the top of page 80 of Sir Guy's report to
provide against the unauthorised disclosure of information by a member of the service, and
widens it to include unauthorised disclosure by a former member of the service—as well as
by co-opted persons, referred to in clause 4, covered by interception warrants. Clause 7
implements the recommendation on page 82 of the report. It inserts a provision, similar to
section 23 of the Act, restricting and making it an offence to publish in the media the fact
that any person is a member or former member, or connected with a member, of the service
except with the written permission of the Minister.
The recommendations on pages 84 and 85 of the report, among other things, make the
Commissioner of Security Appeals in section 14(1) of the principal Act, the same person
who is appointed chairman of the Security Review Authority in section 38 of the State
Services Act 1962. This principle is accepted by the Government. That being the case, it is
proposed to amend only the principal Act rather than both Acts. This would mean that the
Minister of State Services rather than the Minister in charge of the service would formally
recommend the commissioner's appointment to the Governor-General. Clause 8 is designed
to reflect the spirit of these two recommendations.
The former Chief Ombudsman, on pages 87 and 88 of his report, suggests an amend-
ment to section 19 of the principal Act that would require the Commissioner of Security
Appeals to inform the complainant of the reason for refusing to investigate a complaint, and
would remove the discretion that the commissioner now has to refuse to hear a complaint
from a person who is not a New Zealand citizen. The Government sees no good reason why
the commissioner should be bound to inform the complainant of the reasons why he has
decided not to proceed with his inquiries. However, it believes the commissioner should not
refuse to hear complaints from New Zealand residents. The latter change is the subject of
clause 9 of the Bill.
Although on the face of it the redraft of section 20 of the principal Act on pages 90 to 92
of his report may look complicated, only six changes are recommended by Sir Guy Powles.
These amplify the provisions governing the procedure to be followed by the Commissioner
of Security Appeals in relation to complaints. The Government proposes to accept four of
the recommended changes. These are embodied in subclause (1) of clause 10 of the Bill as
follows. First, the proposed new subsection (2A) spells out the duties of the commissioner in
terms of security requirements-including consultation with the director—and directs him in
the new subsection (2B) to examine all relevant files and obtain all information relevant to
the inquiry. Secondly, the proposed new subsection (2C) is a modified version of the change
suggested by the Chief Ombudsman that a complainant should be furnished with a statement
of the opinions, if any, of the service. The modification reflects the Government's belief that
such a statement must be prepared by the service if its sources are to be protected. The
acceptance of this change requires the inclusion, as recommended by the report, of a
contingent provision in a new section 20A, which is the subject of clause 11 of the
Bill-disclosure of certain matters not to be required.


## p. 2785 (#423) ###########################################

8 September New Zealand Security Intelligence Service Amendment Bill
2785
Thirdly, subclause (2) of clause 10 contains a modified version of the change suggested
by the former Chief Ombudsman regarding the commissioner's power to summon witnesses
and to receive evidence. The Government believes he should have powers similar to those of
a commission of inquiry, including a sanction against a person who refuses or neglects to
answer a summons to witness. Fourthly, subclause (3) of clause 10 adds "except on the
ground of lack of jurisdiction" to section 20(9) of the principal Act. The two changes which
are not adopted by the Government relate to: (a) the omission of the requirement in
subsection (3) of section 20 of the principal Act that evidence shall be heard separately and
in private; and (b) the conferment in a redrafted subsection (6) of an express power for the
commissioner to summon any person to produce documents. The former must be retained to
avoid the possibility of any confrontation between the complainant or his counsel and the
service, and the latter is adequately covered by the powers of the commissioner now
included in subclause (1)—proposed new subsection (2B)—and subclause (2) of clause 10 of
the Bill.
The Government accepts the recommendation on page 93 of the report which redrafts
section 21 of the principal Act regarding action by the Commissioner of Security Appeals to
forward his findings to a complainant. The Government also proposes that the director as
well as the Minister shall be informed of any breach of duty or misconduct on the part of
service personnel. The whole redraft is set out in clause 12 of the Bill. The recommendation
on page 94 of the report makes two changes to section 23(1) of the principal Act relating to
restriction on publication and broadcasting of proceedings before the Commissioner of
Security Appeals. The Government accepts the removal of the word "application", but not
the words "or of any decision of the commissioner or the Minister". It is important, with
regard to the latter point, that correct and undistorted accounts of the commissioner's
findings should be published. Clause 13 covers these matters.
Finally, clause 14 implements the recommendation in the middle of page 80 of the
report to include the service as an organisation named in section 31 of the State Services Act
1962. This would facilitate movement between the service and the Public Service, and
enhance recruitment prospects for the service. The Public Service Association has been
advised of this clause.
There are only three legislative recommendations in the report that the Government has
not adopted in some way. I shall now comment on these. The Government believes that the
service must maintain flexibility to operate efficiently. This is better achieved if the terms
and conditions of its officers are not laid down by regulation as has been recommended on
page 79 of the report. The Government does not propose, therefore, to implement this
recommendation. In the middle of page 86, the former Chief Ombudsman proposes to
replace the words “career or livelihood” in section 17 of the principal Act with the words
"personal capacity". However, the Government believes that "personal capacity" is incap-
able of any consistent definition, and is far too wide. When the principal Act was enacted in
1969 it was considered that appeals should be restricted to those where there might be
genuine grievance, and that the Commissioner of Security Appeals would be the best judge
of that. For these reasons, the Government does not accept the recommendation. Nor does
it propose to accept the recommendation at the bottom of page 86 of the report, to abolish
the payment of a fee provided for in section 18 of the principal Act. There is no reason to
suppose that the very small fee of $2 has deterred anyone from submitting an appeal.
With the indulgence of the House I shall now indicate how the Government has
responded to the 28 administrative-type recommendations in Sir Guy's report. On page 25 is
a recommendation on how the term "counter" should be construed. There is no misunder-
standing within the service regarding the use of this term. The director and his officers are
fully aware that the service's function is intelligence gathering and advisory only, as laid
down in its statute. On page 31 it is recommended that higher priorities be given to
espionage and terrorism, and lower priority to subversion. The priorities are reviewed
systematically within the service, which is now allocating more of its resources to the study of
terrorism. The Intelligence Council is continuously aware of the service's priorities.
On page 32 it is urged that student sources should not supply information to the service
relating to activities within a university. The Government cannot accept the claim, when or
where national security may be at stake, that a university is a special sanctuary. The service
would be failing in its statutory duty if, for instance, it did not investigate an attempt by
foreign intelligence officers to recruit agents at universities. Such cases have occurred.
On pages 35 to 43 there are 10 recommendations, plus another on page 50, covering
classification of information and the vetting of personnel who handle classified information.

This bracket of 11 recommendations has implications for the State services generally, and is

A bracket of five recommendations on migration and citizenship are contained in pages

Zealand should, whereever practical, be screened on both criminal and security grounds.
The Government also agrees that there is a need to adopt a more comprehensive set of
criteria with regard to those who wish to reside permanently in New Zealand in line with

Following a decision by Cabinet, it is the Government's intention to publish as much

form has become the subject of clause 3 of the Bill. The director is now a member of the

I turn now to the question of warrants being in the Minister's hands. Sir Guy, who
fortunately came into the issue with a lifetime of support for what are euphemistically
called liberal causes, after mature consideration came down firmly on the side of warrants
being in the hands of the Minister, and he gave several reasons for doing so. The first and
principal reason is that the Minister is responsible for the service, as is the case in other
countries like ours-Britain, Canada, and Australia. In each case the Minister is responsible.
Secondly, unlike the situation where a judicial officer grants a warrant, the grant is
likely to be part of an on-going intelligence exercise not resulting in court proceedings. This
means that the officer or the person granting the warrant must have a continuing familiarity
with the particular situation-something that is extremely difficult in the case, for example,
of a Supreme Court judge, because he is not able to obtain such information and in the
nature of things could hardly be briefed on continuing situations that may or may not lead to
a request for warrants. From an operational point of view it is clear that the Minister is the
one who can be briefed on a continuing basis and has the background at the time the warrant
is applied for. Thirdly, there is the problem of proper briefing and I referred to that as a
continuing exercise. The fourth reason is that judicial officers should not be involved in what
is essentially executive business. That is an argument of principle and needs no elaboration.
We have given the issue very deep thought indeed, and come down on the side of Sir
Guy's recommendation. We considered a time limit on warrants, and for practical reasons
decided against it. Part of our difficulty in this area, where we will be reporting to
Parliament, arises from the fact that the number of warrants in New Zealand will be few
indeed; there could be years in which there are none and there could be years in which there

I now ask what I consider to be a very important question: why has this Bill come
forward, particularly at this time? In asking that, I am not in any way seeking to deny or
denigrate the powerful arguments the Prime Minister has put forward for some form of
legislation dealing with the activities of terrorists. Indeed, as I acknowledge and he is very
well aware, we ourselves promoted legislation that bordered on a similar aspect, and I shall
turn to that in a moment. What is the exact evil that needs a cure now?
I use as a parallel the Bill with which he will doubtless be familiar-the Listening
Devices Bill that I introduced into the House. That Bill was referred to a committee, which
heard evidence in public on it, and there it was allowed to languish and die by the present
Administration. The main purpose of the Bill was to deal with an evil that was then known to
exist and to be on the increase, and in the absence of its passage presumably the problem is
still increasing. It was aimed at preventing the use by private inquiry agents and others of
bugging devices. The polite name of "listening devices" was given to it, but the object and
main thrust of the Bill was to prohibit the sale or use of bugging devices.
To enable the Security Intelligence Service and the police to use these devices for
proper and strictly limited purposes, and within a carefully limited time scale, provision was
made for that authorisation to be given. However, they were to use it simply for particular
purposes in respect of particular people, and to prevent the commission of particular crimes
or offences against the interests of the State. For the rest no authority was given. There was
no right to use the Post Office to intercept mail or to tap telephones, and nothing of that kind
was done. There was an immediate evil which needed to be guarded against-the use of
bugging devices-and that was to be remedied with the allowance that the Security
Intelligence Service or the police could, on application to a proper authority, be granted the
right to use those devices.
The authority was to be an ombudsman-like character, and it was the intention of the
then Government that somebody holding the position of ombudsman or one of the other
semi-judicial officers would be the person to grant that authority. I do not accept the
argument put forward by the Prime Minister about the Minister in charge of the service
14


## p. 2790 (#428) ###########################################

2790
New Zealand Security Intelligence Service Amendment Bill 8 September
being the right person to grant authority of this kind, that he is the one responsible for the
service, and that it is part of an ongoing procedure. I knit those arguments together. That is
one of the very reasons why I do not think the Minister in charge should be the authorised
person, simply because he is part of the operation; and I feel he is not equipped to give to the
question of whether a warrant should be issued the detached consideration that is important
and necessary. For those reasons I do not accept the force of Sir Guy's argument, and indeed
to me it points in the opposite direction.
The problem of briefing is a different one, and in this connection I believe the issue of
this kind of authority is like the issue of a search warrant, although on a much grander scale.
None the less it calls for the same kind of consideration that was analysed by the Supreme
Court in connection with the issue of a warrant against the Auckland Medical Centre. Then
the familiar principles of the law were restated, and it is clear that it is an obligation of the
issuing authority-in the case of a search warrant a justice who in fact combines administra-
tive and judicial roles; and by that very fact answers the fourth argument put forward by Sir
Guy, but indeed it is necessary-that the semi-judicial officer of this kind be convinced of the
need to issue a search warrant before he is authorised to issue one; the same argument
applies here.
There ought to be a need for a person of integrity, judicial experience, and detachment
to be convinced of the need to issue any such authority before it is issued, and that is why I
think the issuing authority-if there is to be one should be neither ministerial nor judicial
in character, because the judge may ultimately—if the legislation is the way it ought to be, if
it is allowed at all-be called upon to review the procedure in due course.
I do not want to go into this at great length. I want to give sufficient time to my
colleagues to speak about some of the views that they hold very strongly. I am sorry that the
time taken by the Prime Minister may eat into the time of some of his colleagues who I
know, from my reading of the press, have broadcast very strong views and strong antipathy
to what is in this Bill. I hope there will be time for them to say what I am sure they will say.
I draw attention to the somewhat peculiarly oblique manner in which the powers to
issue interception warrants are set out in the proposed new section 4A. This simply
authorises the interception or seizure of mail, and telephone tapping, and states that any
such interception warrant shall state certain things and may include certain things. Then in
the proposed subsection (4) the service is required to report to Parliament. I would have
thought the operative subsection would be (5), yet the Prime Minister has told us that is
there for another person. He explained that it was there simply to render the executor of this
warrant liable for excessive zeal or jurisdiction, if for example he commits theft in the course
of executing a warrant then he is liable. That seems to be the only authority for acting on a
warrant. Normally legislation of this kind authorises certain things to be done and then states
the effect of granting such authority shall be so and so, but I cannot find that in this Bill.
There is simply the oblique phrase justifying the person for doing what he is authorised
to do. Why do we have this rather peculiar and indirect way of vesting the individual
concerned with the authority to do whatever this Bill enables him to do?
I could refer to a number of other matters, but I do not wish to pre-empt the time of my
colleagues. However I have one further reservation-in regard to the Bill's going to a
committee. The Prime Minister has emphatically said that it will not, and he has justified his
refusal with arguments that have been repetitive and, to a degree, contradictory. First, he
was reported as saying when he was intimating that the Bill would be coming before the
House, "No, it is certainly not going to a committee. I will not give the opportunity of
providing a sounding board to minority fringe groups to voice their opinions." Indeed, that is
somewhat similar to the activities of Mr Bjelke-Petersen, a person for whom the Prime
Minister professes some admiration but who is going even further in prohibiting the
opportunity for those people he would call fringe groups to even demonstrate at all, let alone
give evidence.
His first reason was that he did not want groups that would make the committee a
sounding board for their views. The second ground stated today was that he would not
expose the Security Intelligence Service to cross-examination. That seems to be somewhat
contradictory to the procedure on two previous occasions. When the Bill which is now the
principal Act was introduced by the National Government it went to a select committee
where we heard the Security Intelligence Service, and in the Listening Devices Bill
introduced by the Labour Government evidence was heard from the Security Intelligence
Service when that Bill went to a committee. Both times that happened in public, and I do not
see why this Bill should not go to a committee.

The third reason seems to be a counter reason, because on the radio today the Prime

Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I did not think the member would do
anything to facilitate the passage of this Bill. I had not the slightest doubt that he would
oppose it at every tick of the clock, knowing his attitude to these matters. I have not the
slightest doubt he will oppose it vigorously and totally. I should like to deal with one or two
of the comments he made. First, he slandered the Premier of Queensland—and he sits there
chuckling and laughing away-by totally misrepresenting the action he referred to. The
Premier of Queensland did not prohibit demonstrations as the member has claimed. He
prohibited demonstrations in the streets while providing a place in a public park where they
could take place. So the member slandered the premier by saying he totally prohibited the
demonstrations, but then he is not renowned for his accuracy.
The member spoke about the proposed new section 4A(5). He is correct. Perhaps in the
very lengthy speech I made he did not realise that I confirmed what he said about it, and then
went on to deal with the qualification that otherwise people are liable for any unlawful acts.
The principal purpose is the one he took, and which I mentioned in my introductory
remarks. A search warrant is not analagous to an interception warrant in terms of
authorisation. One of the difficulties mentioned by Sir Guy Powles was the briefing of a
judicial officer. Apart from members of the Security Intelligence Service and the Intelligence
Council, only the Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister are fully classified to obtain
Security Intelligence Service information. New Zealand receives a great deal of intelligence
information from other countries, and it is received with the strictest conditions about who
may have access to it. In my view, and in the view of the people who advise me, it would be
undesirable for that classification to be extended unless it was absolutely necessary.
If the police need a search warrant they go along to the court and outline the
circumstances that suggest they should have a warrant, and that is the end of the matter.
However, interception warrants would be sought in an on-going situation after a build-up of
activity over many months, on which the Minister may well be briefed but on which it would
not be possible, and certainly not desirable, to brief a Supreme Court Judge. It is a practical
difficulty rather than a difficulty in principle, and Sir Guy clearly saw it in that light. This has
also proved to be the case in the three countries I mentioned that are closest to New Zealand
in the type of search procedures used. I can see no reason why the warrant could not be
issued by an independent person other than the practical difficulties mentioned.
The member for Henderson mentioned the Listening Devices Bill, but he, more than
anyone, knows the difficulties caused by that Bill and the Bill on privacy. Those Bills which
had been promised for a while were introduced towards the end of the Labour Government's
term, because of the difficulty of bringing them together. The member asked why the Bill
had been introduced at this particular time. Immediately the report was tabled the Govern-
ment set out to consider it and implement legislation based on its recommendations. It has
taken this long to grapple with the very difficult concepts and bring them together in
legislation. I would have been happy to introduce it earlier, but it has not been easy
legislation to draft, and there is nothing more sinister than that in the timing of its
introduction. The member for Henderson seemed to approve of the use of listening devices
by the police. The police asked that they be given power under the Bill to get such warrants.
I was unhappy about that and I consulted the Leader of the Opposition who, after
consideration and discussion with the police, came back to me and said he was unhappy
about it. I had forgotten that power was contained in the bill introduced by the Labour
Government.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: No telephone tapping.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: But listening devices?
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Yes.

Mr HUNT (New Lynn): The Prime Minister has said the Bill covers a delicate subject.
For that reason alone this controversial and potentially divisive measure should be accorded
the widest possible scrutiny and comment before it becomes law. Therefore, it must be
referred to a committee. Our democratic process demands the greatest possible public
participation in the framing of legislation, particularly when it has implications that go to the
very heart of the rights of the individual. The Bill is another step to separate the Government
from the people by a wall of secrecy. The Bill is introduced by a Government with 55
members, but only one person has spoken on the introduction, and that will interest a lot
more people than the 32 members of the Opposition.
The Prime Minister has been quoted as saying: "It would be illogical for the Opposition
to fight the Bill, as it originated from a Labour Government directive." He should be
reminded that in 1975, as already mentioned by the member for Henderson, the Labour
Government introduced the Listening Devices Bill, which approached the problem of
electronic surveillance in a very different and less political way. In reply to the member for
Invercargill, who is trying to say something, I advise him, on his way through Bulgaria and
other European countries, to look at some of their legislation. He will probably find that the
legislation in Bulgaria is much the same as the Bill we are considering.
Mr N. P. H. Jones: Probably worse.
Mr HUNT: It might well be worse, but that does not make this Bill very much better.
The Opposition believes that the method of control advocated in the Listening Devices Bill
was better. That Bill went to the Statutes Revision Committee and the hearings were open to
the public. For the benefit of the Prime Minister, the so-called minority fringe groups that
presented evidence included the New Zealand Law Society, two civil liberties groups, the
National Council of Women, the editor of the New Zealand Law Journal, the New Zealand
Police Association, the New Zealand Legal Association, the International Commission of
Jurists, and the widest of all fringe groups—the Security Intelligence Service itself!
It would be a good idea to send this Bill to a committee and invite the Security
Intelligence Service to comment on it. The Prime Minister has said that the Bill will not go to
a select committee, because he has no urge to provide a sounding board for the fringe
elements that "in my view get far too much publicity anyway". That is another attack on the
news media. By not sending the Bill to a select committee the Prime Minister treats
responsible, hard-working people with contempt. In his report Sir Guy Powles spoke highly
of the submissions made to him. He said, "I have been impressed by submissions made to me
by moderate and sensible people who are concerned that suspicion of the service has been
and is continuing to have an inhibiting effect on free expression of political views in New
Zealand." The Prime Minister may have difficulty recognising moderate and sensible
people, but the Opposition does not.
Issuing an authorisation to undertake bugging, electronic surveillance, wire tapping, or
the interception of mail is analogous to issuing a search warrant. It should be a judicial
decision made after balancing the rights and establishing the grounds. A politician should
not issue a search warrant; a politician cannot make an independent, judicial-type decision
while he holds office. The Prime Minister cannot make a non-political, non-partisan
decision, and, if he is to give authorisations, when will he be in the country to give them? The
Prime Minister said that only the Prime Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister were
entitled to highly classified material. When the Prime Minister and the Deputy Prime
Minister are out of the country who will give the authorisation? It will be given by the acting
leader, and that could be any Cabinet Minister. It is presumed that the Deputy Prime
Minister will give authorisations while the Prime Minister is away, or perhaps they could
emanate from Singapore, South Korea, or wherever the Prime Minister may be. It could be
worse the responsibility could be left to the Prime Minister's Department, that ever-large
and increasing body.
New Zealand does not have a constitution like the United States, which protects the
rights of the individual. New Zealand does not have a bill of rights, and an individual's right
to privacy is not guaranteed. The Human Rights Commission Bill contained a watered-down
version of the privacy commissioner legislation, rendered toothless by the Government. The
Opposition believes in the individual's right to privacy and also believes that any interference
should be made only after careful, independent, non-political consideration. The Prime
Minister should not be authorised to interfere in sensitive matters that are controversial and
potentially highly political.

asked the Minister of Labour: Has he any statistics of "moonlighters" or people doing two
jobs, and, if so, what are the latest?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): There are no statistics available on such
people in New Zealand. Employment statistics collected by the Department of Labour do
not record the number of jobs held by employees.

result of those studies?

have been studied, and some information would be available through the returns made to
the Inland Revenue Department. It is possible, although I cannot vouch for it, that a
question addressed in that direction might get some information.
