Housing-Second Mortgage Lending by POSB
5. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Postmaster-General: Can he confirm that to
qualify for a second mortgage through the recently introduced Post Office scheme the total
outgoings under first and second mortgages must not exceed 33 percent of the income of the
applicant, or, if both parties are working, 33% percent of the income of both applicants?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General): Generally, a person wishing to borrow
under the Post Office Savings Bank's personal housing loans second mortgage scheme must
not be overcommitted with regular payments for items such as mortgages, rates, insurance,
hire purchase, and so on. However, no percentage figure that these payments bear to income
is laid down, each case being considered on its merits by the Post Office Personal Loans
Board. There is no 33 percent limit for housing loans. The member appears to be referring
to unsecured personal loans. Approval to authorise unsecured personal loans within
prescribed limits has been delegated to district officers. In the case of an unsecured personal
loan, if the level of commitment exceeds 33 percent of the net income of the applicant, or
the joint net income in the case of an application from two people jointly, the application
must be forwarded to the loans board for decision.
Mr Prebble: Is there any second mortgage limit, and if so, does it go up to the total cost
of the land?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: There is a limit. I cannot give the honourable member the
exact figure offhand, and it is not strictly germane to the question. However, if he writes to
me I will give him the actual limit.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Exports to Australia
14. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: What was the
value of exports to Australia for the years ended June 1975, June 1976, and June 1977, what
were the trade imbalance figures for those years, and what percentage of this trade is under
NAFTA arrangements?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I have answered
the question as briefly as I can, but I apologise for the length of the answer to a
comprehensive question on a broad subject. The value of New Zealand exports to Australia
for the years ended June 1975, 1976, and 1977 were as follows: June 1975, $166.8 million;
June 1976, $263.7 million; June 1977, $365.6 million. The balance of trade figures for those
years were: in 1975, 1:3.01 in favour of Australia; in 1976, 1:1.95; and in 1977, 1:1.79. We do
not have available schedule A figures for the year ended June 1977. In the year ended June
1976, however, A$172.2 million, or 68.7 percent of New Zealand imports into Australia,
were covered by schedule A of NAFTA. In addition, there was NZ$35.58 million of trade
carried on under company-to-company article 3:7 arrangements. Thus for the year ended
June 1976 the total amount of our exports to Australia covered by the NAFTA agreement
was 78.8 percent. Since the 1975-76 trade year furniture and luggage products have been
brought under schedule B of NAFTA, and in April 1977 a 3:7 arrangement was concluded
on apparel.
Mr Downie: Are the exporters who are not included in the figures for the NAFTA
arrangement able to extend their exports, unlike those who are at present restricted on a
numerical basis?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: That supplementary question is wide of the original question,
but the Minister may comment if he wishes.
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The answer is yes, exporters not under the schedules
can increase their exports unless world or global quotas have been imposed. At that point
they have an opportunity of competing under the global quota, which is more difficult. If
they are subject to a global quota, they can also negotiate for a special arrangement for New
Zealand, but that would obviously mean that the Australians themselves would want access
to this market if they did not already have it.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Are any additional items being considered for inclusion in either
schedule A or schedule B?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I can say yes, but I am not in a position to give the
honourable member the individual items. We are having discussions with our officials, and
will shortly be approaching the Australians about the items that we wish to have included in
schedule A.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Is the Minister satisfied that the imbalance ratio is likely to continue
to improve in New Zealand's favour in the immediate future?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: That question is seeking an opinion, but the Minister may
answer it if he wishes.
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I am not prepared to predict that it will continue to
improve, but I have been delighted with the considerable improvement over the past several
months. We have achieved more than I thought we would. Having regard to the statements
and criticisms Opposition members have made, I believe our manufacturers have done
exceptionally well.

been accepted. Whether that can be interpreted as purchased and an order placed I do not
know, but a tender has been accepted.

URGENT QUESTION
Wairua-Seamen's Strike
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Transport, as an urgent question, What
steps are being taken by his officials to: (1) deal with the strike of seamen on the Stewart
Island vessel Wairua; (2) ensure that supplies of essential foodstuffs and fuels are delivered
to Stewart Island; and (3) ensure that the Wairua sails as scheduled tomorrow, 9 September
1977?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I apologise for the length of the
answer. Discussions have been held between the Ministry of Transport and the South Island
area secretary of the Seamen's Union in an endeavour to resolve the matters in dispute, and
considerable progress has been made. The dispute has been referred to the Shipping
Industry Tribunal, which conducted a hearing attended by representatives of the ministry
and the union this morning. The tribunal instructed the union representative to inform the
members of the union on board Wairua that the ministry is endeavouring to remedy the
problems the union complains about, and that they should load cargo this afternoon and
comply with the master's orders to go to sea on a normal scheduled sailing tomorrow. If the
members of the union do not do this the tribunal will issue directions. Settlement of the
dispute will ensure that Wairua delivers essential foods and fuel to the island. If the dispute
is prolonged, permits may be issued by the ministry to allow fishing boats to carry essentials.
Directions issued by the tribunal will require the members of the union to perform normal
duties, including the loading of cargo and taking the vessel to sea.
CONTRACTUAL MISTAKES BILL
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Contractual Mistakes Bill. The committee recommends
that the Bill be allowed to proceed without any further amendment. I move, That the report
do lie upon the table. The House will recall that this Bill was first reported back some weeks
ago. At that time the Minister of Justice indicated through me, as chairman of the
committee, that, because of the complex nature of the legislation, it would lie upon the table
for some time to enable interested parties-particularly and fairly obviously the legal
profession-to consider and comment upon the amendments proposed by the committee.
The value of this course of action was clearly shown when the Law Society approached
the Minister and indicated that it had some comments that it wished to make on the Bill as
reported back. It will be remembered that originally the Law Society had told the committee
that it did not wish to make any submissions on the Bill. Following a brief discussion between
the Minister of Justice, the member for Kapiti, the Law Society, and myself, it was agreed
that the Bill should be referred back to the select committee to enable members on both
sides of the House to give careful consideration to the Law Society's views, and that was
done by a motion agreed to by the House. The committee has now heard the Law Society
and has received a further report from the Department of Justice and has discussed the
matter in detail with Mr Iles, Chief Parliamentary Counsel, who was also a member of the
Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee-on whose report the original Bill was
based.
It should be emphasised that the Law Society made it clear to the Statutes Revision


## p. 2804 (#442) ###########################################

2804.
8 September
Contractual Mistakes Bill
Committee that it had no fundamental objection to the Bill, and that the points raised in its
submissions were matters of drafting and emphasis only-or, as the society called it, "fine
tuning". The society expressed the view that, if anything, the Bill did not go far enough, but
that initially at least it would be a worth-while reform to enact the Bill in its present form.
The society's representatives described the Bill as "a bold and innovative move". They
emphasised that the present law is "a mess", and said that the Bill had great potential to
bring about greater justice to parties to a contract where a mistake has arisen.
The Law Society's submission raised five issues, two of which the committee considered
to be of a minor nature. The society suggested that it was inappropriate to confer powers
under the Bill first on arbitrators and secondly on small claims tribunals. The society thought
such bodies might experience difficulties in correctly applying an entirely new system of
legislative relief. The committee was not attracted to either of those two suggestions. It was
generally conceded that most arbitrators have for many years been exercising, on a quasi-
legal basis, powers similar to those contained in the Bill. Committee members anticipate that
arbitrators will have no greater difficulty in dealing with the new law than they have had in
applying the present case law.
Small claims tribunals were established under the Small Claims Tribunals Act 1976, and
have a limited jurisdiction to deal with certain types of claims involving sums of up to $500.
Even though such tribunals are obliged by section 15(4) to determine disputes according to
the substantial merits and justice of each case and to have regard to the law in so doing, and
are not bound to give effect to strict legal rights or obligations or to legal forms or
technicalities, the committee does not accept that such tribunals will have any difficulty in
dealing with the new law, particularly bearing in mind the limited jurisdiction exercised by
such tribunals in the first place.
The Law Society's third submission centred on the committee's recommendation to
limit by amendment the definition of mistake in clause 2. The society was particularly
concerned at the committee's decision to delete the reference to erroneous opinion,
erroneous calculations, and errors in the manner in which a document is expressed. The
committee had been concerned that the definition of mistake in the Bill as first introduced
could lead to a much greater number of actions based on contractual mistakes than has
previously been the case. The Law Society conceded that this was a possibility, but expressed
the view that the present paucity of cases could be attributed to the present inflexible
remedies available at law. Despite this submission, the committee is of the opinion that it
would be unwise to extend the definition of mistake beyond a fairly limited category at this
early stage in the development of a new category of legal remedies. Accordingly, the
committee recommends no change to clause 2.
The Law Society's fourth submission related to clause 5, and considered that the use of
the words "influenced in his decision"-an amendment suggested by the
committee―unnecessarily widened the court's jurisdiction to grant relief. The use of those
words in preference to "relying on mistake"-which were the words in the original
Bill-resulted from confusion expressed by those who gave evidence at the first hearing of
the committee as to what could constitute "reliance" upon mistake. The new words were
inserted by the committee to clarify this point and further to make it clear that one or both of
the parties to an agreement would not have entered into the contract if the true state of
affairs had been known. Again, the select committee is not persuaded that the change
suggested by the Law Society is necessary.
The society's fifth and final comment also related to clause 5, and concerned the extent
of knowledge of a mistake that was required by one party of the other party's mistake. To
overcome this difficulty the committee had proposed to redraft clause 5 to make it clear that
one party's mistake had to be known to the other party, and also had to be material to the
party making the mistake, although this materiality need not necessarily be known to the
other party. This matter is of particular significance in cases of mistaken identity. The
committee is of the opinion that complications could arise if specific reference to materiality
were included in clause 5(1)(a)(ii) and (iii), and does not favour any amendment to these
subclauses.
Accordingly, it is the recommendation of the Statutes Revision Committee that it is not
necessary to change the Bill in any way from that which was reported back on the previous
occasion. Members of the committee particularly appreciated the verbal comments of the
Law Society on clause 3A, which the committee has recommended should be included in the
Bill to make its purpose that much clearer. Some Opposition members of the committee
have expressed doubts as to the suitability of this clause. The Law Society made it clear that


## p. 2805 (#443) ###########################################

8 September
2805
Contractual Mistakes Bill
it had no objection to such a clause; to quote one of the representatives who appeared before
the committee, it is a good idea. After careful reconsideration of the Bill, the committee
does not recommend any further changes to its provisions.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): The chairman failed to report that Her Majesty's
Opposition and alternative Government is opposed to the Bill. The Law Society's submis-
sion argued against the Bill. One of the members of the Law Society told the committee that
the Bill was a bold and innovative step, but the member for Kapiti said that he thought the
Bill was a codification of the present law. It cannot be both. The Law Society's submission
consisted almost entirely of submissions received from lawyers. Some of the most prominent
lawyers in the country appeared before the committee, and in all sincerity said what they
thought the Bill meant. Individuals expressed differing views, and they were divided on what
the Bill meant.
A series of very expensive Court of Appeal cases will follow the enactment of the Bill,
because it will create uncertainty in the law. The Law Society felt that some of the matters it
raised were important enough to warrant a meeting with the Minister and the chairman of
the Statutes Revision Committee. The Bill was sent back to the committee, which is a most
unusual step. When the measure was before the committee for the second time the members
of the Law Society were not certain whether the Bill contained matters of substance, and one
member went so far as to say that it was a matter of "fine tuning". The lawyers of the country
have shown that they do not know what the Bill means. The evidence of the Law Society
should be set against the evidence received by the committee.
The professional people representing the developers, quantity surveyors, and
engineers-the people the Bill will affect-told the committee that the present law is well
known and the system works well. The confusion arises out of possibly one of the most
complex and contradictory parts of the law. The people who build know what they are doing,
and when they have a dispute they go to arbitration. Arbitrators told the committee that they
were confident they could make the present system of law work. The lawyers are the only
group who have said that they are unhappy with this part of the law. Disputes surrounding
this aspect of the law are not sent to the courts, but are settled by arbitration. When the Bill
has been enacted no one will know what the part of the law relating to building contracts
means. The Law Society does not know what it will mean.
Mr Brill: Yes it does.
Mr PREBBLE: The Law Society is not happy with the Bill. Another objection to the
Bill would be that a builder or developer who made a mistake would be able to go to court to
rectify his mistake. That would mean that we are setting up a system of social welfare for the
incompetent businessman. No member of the committee saw any reason to protect the
incompetent businessman from the forces of the free market. The present law drives the
person who makes mistakes-the incompetent-out of business. What is wrong with that?
The sooner the incompetent builder stops building the better. The Bill will enable the
builder to go to his lawyer, who will say that no one knows what "mistake" means. There
will be a series of mistakes, and the more incompetent the builder the more mistakes he will
make. The case could be taken to the Court of Appeal.
The member for New Lynn has said that the Bill will give the law student a field day. I
predict that contractual mistakes will be the No.1 subject on next year's examination paper. I
believe that the House is legislating for the sake of legislation. Not one professional body
associated with the building industry has requested changes to the legislation. I asked every
organisation appearing before the committee whether it had asked for the changes, or
whether the changes had been requested at the annual general meeting. I was told that no
association had asked for the change, and they were shocked when they heard the Bill was
being introduced. The organisations appeared before the committee to oppose the legisla-
tion.
What great evil will the Bill rectify? Why are we wasting the time of the House passing
legislation that has not been asked for and does not appear in the National Party manifesto?
Why are we going ahead with legislation that no one understands? The Bill is proceeding
because eminent lawyers have given opposing meanings to clause 2. One lawyer's interpreta-
tion was contrary to another's. No doubt the matter will be argued in the Court of Appeal.
Academics will be very interested in the outcome of the Bill. The Bill will cost the country a
fortune. I predict that the only good thing about the Bill is that people will be able to opt out,
and that every competent builder will contract out of the Bill immediately. Any lawyer who
does not advise his client to contract out of the Bill is incompetent and is liable to have a
negligence action brought against him if his client loses money. The Opposition will oppose

the Bill and vote against the reporting back. It should be sent back to the committee and

Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I regret to have to inform the House that what the member
for Auckland Central has said about the proceedings of the select comittee, the evidence
given to it, and the attitude adopted by various witnesses before the committee, is simply not
correct. He said that he asked witnesses whether they or their organisations had asked for
the Bill. He certainly asked those questions, and it was conceded that the particular
organisations that were giving evidence had not asked for the Bill. But I did not hear one
witness say to the committee that he had been shocked to find the Bill had been introduced,
which were the words used by the member for Auckland Central.
The Bill is based on a report of the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee
published in May 1976. The member for Auckland Central is today being consistent with the
attitudes of the Labour Party to law reform, particularly its attitude towards those reforms
proposed by the various law reform committees. The Labour Party has always been hesitant
about law reform-so hesitant that it was left to the National Government to deal with a
backlog of law reform committee reports that for 3 years had gathered dust on the shelves of
the Department of Justice. The present Minister of Justice has taken up these reports and is
proceeding to implement them.
The member for Auckland Central said that the Law Society had not understood the
Bill that was reported back from the select committee. That is completely incorrect. The
members of the Law Society who appeared before the committee, and the members of the
Law Society's legislation committee who drafted the submissions that we heard, all made it
quite clear that they clearly understood what the Bill was designed to achieve. They did say
that they were making suggestions of a drafting nature only, and that the suggestions related
only to the emphasis of the Bill; I took these words down from members of the Law Society.
The Law Society called its proposals "fine tuning”.
The member for Auckland Central, who is interjecting, mentions arbitrators. Does he
now agree with the Law Society's submissions on arbitrators? At the select committee, the
member for Auckland Central described the Law Society's submissions on arbitrators as
"ignorant". The member acknowledges; he nods his head. Now he suggests that in some way
the Law Society, in its submissions, did not understand the Bill. Clearly the member for
Auckland Central does not understand the Bill. He said it was nothing but a codification,
and he took the member for Kapiti to task about something he had said by way of
interjection. The member for Auckland Central does not understand that there are two
distinct aspects of the Bill. The first is clearly nothing more than a codification, and that is
the definition of "mistake", but the clause that prescribes the new remedies-that will soften
the effect of contractual mistake-is new, and those are the remedies that the law reform
committee recommended. It is that aspect of the law that is new, and the member for
Auckland Central should clarify his understanding of it before the second reading debate.
The member for Auckland Central also said that leading lawyers had disagreed on the
intent and purpose of the legislation. That is complete and utter nonsense. Some lawyers
came to the select committee before the Bill was reported back on the first occasion, and
expressed doubts as to the form and intent of the original Bill, but there was no such
misunderstanding about the Bill as reported back. The Law Society did nothing more and
nothing less than recommend some "fine tuning"-certain drafting changes. In all the
circumstances, the arguments put forward by the member for Auckland Central have no
substance whatever. It is clear that the Labour Party will make an election issue of
contractual mistakes next year-well, let it do so.
The House divided on the question, That the report do lie upon the table.

ADJOURNMENT-FOREIGN AFFAIRS
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): For the purpose of further discussing
foreign affairs, I move, That the House do now adjourn. I understand that it has been
arranged that we continue from where we finished last night.
Motion agreed to.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): Last night the first foreign affairs debate of this
session was commenced, and we heard speeches of various types, with outstanding contribu-
tions by the member for Mt. Albert and the member for Roskill. We had a contribution from
the Prime Minister, which I think even he would be happy to forget. The Minister of Foreign
Affairs, who opened the debate, found himself in a role that he must now be accustomed to:
mending fences that the Prime Minister has barged through in the course of his international
journeys, which are becoming more numerous, and repairing fences in the arena of
international and overseas trade. A pause in the debate was provided by the member for
South Canterbury, who offered nothing more than what I would refer to as a lot of mumbling
humbug.
In mentioning the difficulties being experienced by the Minister of Overseas Trade and
the Minister of Foreign Affairs, I refer particularly to our trade relationship with Japan, and
the possibility of negotiated access to New Zealand fishing grounds. The Prime Minister has
rushed in here, as he did at Gleneagles, and is again trying to find some sure ground and
international respectability. If there was one notable comment in the speech by the member
for South Canterbury, it was his reference to the triumph of Gleneagles that the Prime
Minister had emerged from. That was no triumph. Had it not been for the actions of this
Prime Minister and this Government, there would have been no need for the discussion at
Gleneagles that almost wrecked the British Commonwealth as we know it. The Prime
Minister and his colleagues claim as a diplomatic victory what could have been New
Zealand's ultimate shame. He dragged himself out of a bog into which he had pitched
himself head first.
On the question of trade between New Zealand and Japan, the member for Mt. Albert
warned last night that the bullying tactics being adopted were doomed to failure, and he
reminded the Prime Minister and the Minister of Overseas Trade that the representatives of
bigger countries do not go around the world publicly haranguing the Japanese or anybody
else if they hope to finalise a successful trade settlement. Japan has not agreed to guaranteed
long-term access to her markets for her major trading partners, and, while we have a strong
bargaining point in access to our fishing grounds, the whole matter must be kept in
perspective. The Prime Minister has adopted a ridiculous stance, and, as with sporting
contacts, is desperately trying to retain some credibility. Japan's total fish catch is 12 000 000
tonnes a year. From New Zealand waters it takes 80 000 tonnes, 0.8 percent of its total catch.
Let us relate that to our total trade relationship with Japan. No one is selling New Zealand
down the drain, but let us see ourselves in the total trade perspective. It is no good going
around the world with swollen heads. We have to consider realistically the total situation.
Let us look at the total Japanese trade figures. New Zealand's exports to Japan
represent 0.6 percent of that country's total imports. New Zealand's import share is 0.7
percent, which shows how small we are in terms of total Japanese trade. We have an
important bargaining point. We have a trump card. Let us play it to its maximum value, but


## p. 2808 (#446) ###########################################

2808
8 September
Adjournment-Foreign Affairs
if we overplay it we do so at the expense of our trade possibilities with that country. Japan
also has several trump cards. We have to keep trade as a two-way deal. While Opposition
members are all for New Zealand's getting the best possible deal, the total situation from the
point of view of those on the other side of the negotiating table-in this case the Japanese—
has to be appreciated. The Prime Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister would be wise to
adopt a conciliatory stance in future negotiations, because the figures I have given of the
percentage of our exports to Japan in relation to its total trade, compared, for instance, with
the United States and the EEC bloc, indicate the real situation. However, the Deputy Prime
Minister's future negotiations will be more difficult because of the Prime Minister. We hope
that the Deputy Prime Minister will do better than the Prime Minister, but his job has been
made much more difficult by the ham-fisted standover attitude adopted by his leader, who,
although he will not admit to it, now seems to recognise that a costly error of judgment was
made.
Last night the member for Mt. Albert put the question of New Zealand-Japanese
relationships in its proper perspective. He tried to give much-needed advice to the Prime
Minister, based on his long experience in trading matters. The Prime Minister responded
with a blatant personal attack, based on National Party propaganda and hearsay, which was
quite uncalled for. The Minister of Overseas Trade, when opening the debate, said, “Japan
wants us to understand its problems"—we can understand that—“and its need to have access
to the fishing zones, including waters adjacent to New Zealand with our 200-mile economic
zone." The Minister was referring to future New Zealand-Japan trading relationships. He
said there had been some sensational headlines-I think that was the right
word-overstating the vital need for New Zealand and Japan to come to trading terms. It is
not just headlines; the spoken word and the fine print are causing concern in this country and
in Japan. There was no doubt about the Prime Minister's attitude at the Pacific Basin
Economic Council conference in Christchurch in May. The Christchurch Press of 11 May
printed a direct quotation from the Prime Minister's speech, in which he said that New
Zealand would not sign any agreement with Japanese organisations until it could be assured
of regular access for New Zealand farm products to the Japanese market.
Hon. L. W. Gandar: What's wrong with that?
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: We have to be realistic. We cannot stand over a country
when we account for less than 0.1 percent of that country's import and export requirements.
Recently, when the Prime Minister returned from the ASEAN conference at Kuala Lumpur
and his meeting with the Prime Minister of Japan, Mr Fukuda, it was patently obvious that
he had not succeeded in getting across to Mr Fukuda the need for Japan to give access to
more New Zealand produce, and the fact that, before coming to terms about access for
Japanese fishing boats to the New Zealand economic zone, New Zealand expected a
reciprocal consideration. I listened to a radio interview, because I was interested in what the
Prime Minister had to say on his return from Kuala Lumpur, and he said bluntly that unless
Japan takes more of our produce, particularly beef, it will get no fish. Those were strong
words. I can understand his feelings, on having to return home without even the basis of a
deal. No doubt that made him very testy; he never conceals his dislike of radio and television
interviewers, and the fact that they were the first people he met when he came off the plane
probably did not improve his ulcer. However, that is the situation as it is.
Just how realistic is his statement that if Japan does not trade with New Zealand it will
get no fish? How will New Zealand police the 200-mile economic fishing zone? That is
something we want to have a close look at. I want to refer back to the Pacific Basin
Economic Council conference in May, when the Prime Minister talked about trade deals and
New Zealand exports to Japan. At that time, Mr Hasegawa, a representative from Japan and
a very good friend of New Zealand, was talking in a very different voice. It is very
important that the good relationship existing between Mr Hasegawa and New Zealand
should continue. After all, he is the President of the Japan-New Zealand Economic Council.
He referred to the power agreement the Government has with Comalco, in which the
Japanese have a very sizable interest. While the Prime Minister was saying that New Zealand
wanted Japan to import more New Zealand goods in return for access rights to this country's
200-mile fishing zone, the Japanese were talking about Comalco having to pay more for the
power it used, as a possible deal when discussing access to New Zealand's 200-mile fishing
zone. Japan does not see the access for New Zealand imports as a negotiating basis for
fishing rights. Instead, it offers technology, research knowledge, and co-operation, which
New Zealand could consider.

Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: I am only trying to put the whole argument into perspective.
You cannot isolate beef or mutton for fishing access rights, but have to consider the matter in
its totality. Japan is offering us some alternatives. The Prime Minister has tied his own hands

Widely conflicting statements have been made about the policing of the 200-mile zone.
On 9 April, the Minister of Fisheries was reported in the Timaru Herald as saying that he
believed the Orion aircraft and the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries vessels, augmented
by the Royal New Zealand Navy, would be able to meet requirements, but that much would
depend on arrangements with foreign nations. On 25 May the Minister of Fisheries was again
reported in the Timaru Herald as saying that, in addition to the air surveillance available
from the Royal New Zealand Air Force Orions and the new Andovers, New Zealand would
be able to monitor accurately who was in the zone. He was very confident! On 5 September
the Minister was reported in the Timaru Herald as saying that the policing of the vast new
zone posed problems. He did not consider that this would be as difficult as had been
believed, although he admitted that New Zealand would have to deploy all its resources.
The Minister of Defence had different views, and is reported in the Evening Post of 28
March as saying that New Zealand could not afford to use Skyhawks every time it wanted to
arrest a fishing boat that might come into its waters. Although the Prime Minister said in the
House last night that the 200-mile economic fishing zone would come into force from 1
October, the Minister of Defence, when questioned later in Christchurch, said that he knew
nothing about it. He is reported in this morning's Christchurch Press as saying that he
considered fishery law enforcement to be the secondary role of the Navy. The Minister of
Fisheries, when visiting the United States and Canada, said he could see no problems with
patrolling such an area. Those countries have a 200-mile economic zone about the same size
as that which New Zealand will have.
Hon. J. B. Bolger: How many boats do they have?
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: That is a very good question. The United States Coastguard
has 18 high endurance cutters, 15 medium endurance cutters, and 79 patrol boats to police an
area of 1 600 000 square miles, whereas New Zealand has four frigates-if the one in reserve
is recommissioned-one survey ship, four patrol craft, and one research vessel to police an
area of 1 400 000 square miles. The American endurance cutters are very efficient vessels of
1780 tons, with a speed of 19.5 knots. New Zealand needs this type of vessel if it is to police
its 200-mile fishing zone.
We must come to reasonable trade agreements with countries that can assist our fishing
industry by buying New Zealand fish caught by New Zealand fishermen. New Zealand must
co-operate. I am not against New Zealand; nor are any other members on this side of the
House. However, we have our feet on the ground, and, unlike members opposite, we do not
have our heads in the sand. We realise that New Zealand is a small country and that it must
enter into joint agreements with other countries. We cannot say to one of our greatest
potential partners, "Buy our beef, or you will get no fish." That is no way to do business.
Will members opposite please tell the Prime Minister to stay at home and give the Deputy
Prime Minister a chance, when he goes to Japan, to mend some of the fences that have been
so badly damaged by the Prime Minister dropping bricks in his usual ham-fisted way when he
travels overseas?

While speaking of Japan, I should like to place on record a new development this year,
following a parliamentary delegation to Japan led by my colleague the member for Franklin.
Discussions were held with parliamentarians in Japan, and the suggestion was made and
adopted that a friendship league be established between the Parliaments of the two
countries. In Japan a New Zealand-Japan Parliamentarians League was established in April,
comprising some 90 members of the Diet. Following that, 52 members of this Parliament
formed themselves into the Japan-New Zealand Parliamentarians League at an inaugural
meeting in New Zealand on 9 June. I believe that augurs well for a continuation of the very
close ties we have had at various levels with Japan, and extends those ties into the
parliamentary sphere.
I refer to the principal article of the regulations of the league: "The purposes of the
league shall be to promote mutual friendship between the parliamentarians of Japan and
New Zealand, and to co-operate in the cultivation of a friendly relationship between the two
countries." I believe that is further evidence of the close co-operation and friendship
between our two countries. Opposition members during this debate have not contributed to
that friendship, but I am sure it will survive, in spite of their attacks. The same type of
argument that was in evidence during the debate on the Territorial Sea and Exclusive
Economic Zone Bill has, just as unhelpfully, been introduced into this debate.

Our whole approach to foreign affairs must change dramatically. The third Labour
Government, under the impetus of Norman Kirk, shook the country out of its insular
attitude and convinced people that decisions must be made in Wellington, not in London or
Washington, that our relationship with the Pacific countries and China and South-east Asia
had to become much more positive, and that diplomacy was not something to be practised by
professional diplomats at cocktail parties. Foreign affairs include everything that touches on
our relations with other countries, regardless of whether we like those countries, or have
formal relationships with them. Foreign affairs mean trade, transport, cultural relationships,
defence and sporting contacts. They mean the responsibility of countries with a surplus of
any kind to countries that know nothing but shortage; a moral responsibility towards fellow
human beings regardless of colour, religon, race, or politics; and a relationship based not on
the past, as is the policy of the National Government, but on the long-term future.

have gone even further. Sometimes one wonders if there is a bipartisan approach among
Government members. Some people would welcome a bipartisan approach by the Prime
Minister and the Minister of Foreign Affairs.
I should like to make one or two general comments about Parliament's attitude to

enough. I have a couple of suggestions to make, which I have already put to successive
Ministers. The first is that we upgrade the status of the Foreign Affairs Committee. As far as
I can gather, the committee is of far less importance than it was in its earlier days and than
the late Peter Fraser intended it to be. It needs a much wider range of input, not just that
from the diplomatic corps and from our own foreign affairs staff and members of Parliament
who return from overseas trips. There are many other people in the community with
expertise in all aspects of foreign affairs whose assistance would be helpful to members of
Parliament. That is one way in which I should like to see the role of the committee enlarged.
For as long as the committee meets at 9 a.m., jammed in before other more important
committees, nobody will take it very seriously.

Speaking of the South Pacific reminds me of the area where we now have our greatest
commitment in overseas aid. The late Norman Kirk did more than anybody else in the
country to make this an issue, first as a back-bencher, then as president of the Labour Party,
and finally as leader and Prime Minister. That commitment, which was to increase overseas
aid substantially and to give a new perception of what overseas aid means, was carried on by
the present Leader of the Opposition in his term as Prime Minister. The 1976-77 Budget, the
first Budget of this Government, slashed the overseas aid commitment by 10 percent; that I
guess amounts to a cut of about 25 percent in real terms. The amount provided this year, $51
million, is the same as that of last year, but again that means a loss in real terms, in spite of
the fact that there has been a 19 percent increase in total Government expenditure.
The figures for overseas aid as a percentage of gross national product make interesting
reading. In the Labour Government's last year, overseas aid reached 0.58 percent of our
gross national product, having stood at about a third of that figure for most of the term of the
previous National Government. Last year it dropped to 0.44 percent, and this year to 0.36
percent.
The Government has again deliberately cut the proportion of aid spent on multilateral
aid. In 1975-76, under the Labour Government, 25 percent of our aid was multilateral. Last
year the figure fell to 18 percent, and this year it is down to 14 percent. Most people who
follow international aid discussions and arguments appreciate that multilateral aid is
recognised as being more useful to the recipient countries, because, unlike bilateral aid,
which is often tied, it enables them to take advantage of competing supply sources and
technology.
Aid to the South Pacific this year is still adequate, but only because cuts have been made
in other areas. Aid to Asia has been cut, although the area contains some of the largest and
poorest countries, those most affected by world recession and rising world prices-India,
Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka. Those countries ought to have major international priorities for
aid. When we talk about reductions in aid to Asia it is interesting to reflect on the much
publicised commitment of $50 million in aid recently made by the Prime Minister at the
ASEAN conference. In fact, the present Government's aid to the ASEAN countries is
slowly decreasing. The $50 million promised over 5 years will be only slightly more than
those countries would have received in normal bilateral aid, and it will be considerably less
than they would have received under the level of aid given by the previous Labour
Government. I am sure that the ASEAN countries realise what that commitment of $50
million is: much less than they would have got had they had the good fortune still to be
dealing with the Labour Government in New Zealand.

growing recognition of their value, especially in the small communities such as those of the

been my opinion, and I hope it remains so, that the goal of our foreign policy is to preserve

relations policy. Our traditional guidelines are all changing: the guidelines of history,
tradition, and customs; the guideline of geographical location, and our distance from
everywhere else; the guidelines set up by trading patterns based on a seller's market—we are
no longer in a seller's market; the guideline of overseas aid, which was created exclusively
from moral concern; and the defence and security arrangements that came out of our
traditional background.
I want to say only a few words about the last point, because I know that the Minister of
Defence will be speaking later. However, the traditional guidelines of our defence and
security have changed only very recently. It is often said that New Zealand was born in the
bloodshed of the 1914-18 war, and that is correct. However, there was no real difference in
our defence and security outlook up to and after the second world war. It could be said, with
a lot of truth, that the first dramatic thing New Zealand did as a nation was to take part in the
1945 San Francisco conference. But even that did not change our outlook on defence and
security, which still maintained the age-old concept that we would train people and send
them to the Middle East if they were needed, but that they would be equipped by the "Old
Country".
That concept quietly changed about 1958. From then on, as part of our foreign affairs
policy, we had to pay for our security and defence ourselves; we had to buy our own
equipment, and stand on our own feet. There was no answer other than a collective defence
arrangement. ANZUS is the cornerstone of the security and defence part of our foreign
policy. I hope I did not hear the Opposition say that it would not stand behind ANZUS. Co-
operation with allies is the only answer and will remain the key factor.
The member for Mt. Albert asked what the Government's policy was on the neutron
bomb; whether the Prime Minister would raise the matter with President Carter when he
went to Washington; and, if so, what he would say. That was quite a leading question. I have
asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs. I will not read out the entire answer, but make the
point that, first, we should realise that the neutron bomb differs from the conventional
atomic bomb. The conventional atomic bomb has three effects: the shock wave, or the
blowing down of buildings; the heat and fire; and the nuclear fallout. The neutron bomb
does not have those three effects to anything like the same extent, but it has a fourth and
nastier one: it has an initial high radiation. To put it in simple language, it is inclined to kill
people instead of blowing down buildings on top of them.
Is it therefore a dreadful weapon to have? Any weapon is dreadful. I note the
Passchendale plaque above me. Half a million men were drowned or killed before breakfast.
I do not suppose it was any more pleasant dying in the mud of the trenches there than dying
by radiation. I am not sure that we are right in bringing in this emotion about weapons. Any
weapon in any war is unpleasant. It is clear that the bomb is intended to be a deterrent.
People might ask, can we have a nasty weapon like that as a deterrent? But some members
will remember that gas masks were issued at the beginning of the last war, because gas was in
fact a deterrent. It was not used. Whether or not we like it, atomic warfare has been shown
to be a deterrent—and long may it stay.
I shall read from the answer given to me by the Minister of Foreign Affairs: "There is no
final judgment on this complex issue. Because of the concern that has been expressed in New
Zealand on the subject, the Minister of Foreign Affairs raised the matter with US officials
during the recent ANZUS meeting, and conveyed the sense of public unease in New
Zealand. The US therefore knows of the concern felt here." The issue is not a simple one.
The Minister said: "I have no doubt that President Carter and the US Government are
aware of its implications." I hope that members on the other side will pass that on to the
member for Mt. Albert.

country. We have far too great an opinion of ourselves. Because we are right on the
perimeter of world affairs geographically, we tend to dissipate our resources everywhere
around the globe, instead of concentrating them, as we possibly would if we had an

agencies, it would be a matter of concern and publicity everywhere, and no doubt we would
have established an attitude according to the demands of what would certainly be a
considerable international furore. However, because this is a small group of people in a
country that is little bigger than the islands we have so generously helped to independence,
and because the land those people have is coveted by a nation that has been strongly
protected by the American mineral and oil lobbies in both the United Nations and
Washington, so that any move on our part to try to protect these people from massacre will
upset the financial gain of some of the major international concerns, we are not prepared to
act and, in fact, are not even allowed to ask direct questions. On that basis, how can there be
a bipartisan approach?
What happened in that place has been portrayed in many guises. It has been portrayed
as a noble suppression of communism by the Indonesian Government, as the stopping of a
local terrorist group or a group unjustly usurping power, but none of those descriptions has
taken cognisance of the fact that the conflict most closely resembles a good, old-fashioned
jihad, or a religious war involving the Muslims. There are religious overtones there that have
political counterparts in most of the causes of the fighting. After 300 years of Portuguese
domination, the Portuguese territory that was East Timor was naturally almost entirely
Christian in its culture and in the religious aspirations of its people. Indonesia was almost
entirely Muslim in its outlook. I am not saying that this is the sole cause of the conflict,
because colonialism and territorial greed are undoubtedly major factors, but one of the
things that has undoubtedly distorted the whole picture has been the jihad aspect of the
fighting there. However, that has not in any way reduced the most urgent need to establish
peace.
I say to those Government back-bench members who are anxious that there should be a
bipartisan approach to important foreign policy matters that we should consider our
responsibilities in this field, and join with those in Australia who are so desperately
concerned, not only because of the question of justice, but because, from an internal and
international point of view, the matter closely touches the security of their own borders.
Both our countries should invite representatives of the South Pacific, possibly from Fiji, to
accompany representatives of the Australian and New Zealand Governments to East Timor
to find out what is happening to these long-suffering people. This is a matter of considerable
concern to Australia and every Pacific country; because of the signs of brutal injustice, it is a
cause of concern to every human being.
East Timor is still the responsibility of Portugal, who is unable to exercise her authority;
and so, without meddling in the internal affairs of Indonesia, Australia and New Zealand
should see that law and order is being maintained. If the position is as bad as we are led to
believe by those who support the local people, the United Nations should be asked to take
the necessary steps to protect the lives, the property, and the liberties of the people. If New
Zealand initiated that inquiry, we could all hold our heads up high once again. No
declaration would have to be signed, but if we acted as we should we might live down some
of the disgraceful behaviour and the double dealing of our representatives with regard to the
Maputo Declaration.

Honourable members know that about a year ago I had the opportunity to visit South-
east Asia to discuss developments in the region with the leaders of Singapore, Malaysia,
Thailand, and Indonesia. I had visited that area in 1972, and the contrast was profound. In
the period between my visits the anti-communist regimes in South Vietnam and Cambodia
had fallen. United States forces had been disengaged in Vietnam, and had been withdrawn
from Thailand. The last British forces had gone from Singapore, ending a military involve-
ment of about 150 years' duration. The Australian ground forces in Singapore had returned
home, although Australia still continues to station an air force unit at the Butterworth base.
The decision was taken, as we all know, to phase out SEATO completely by June this year.
The ASEAN Governments have in recent times made impressive progress in their
efforts to develop co-operation and harmonious relations within the region. At last year's
Bali summit, and at the recent meeting in Kuala Lumpur, the member countries demon-
strated their growing sense of unity, progress, and determination to act together to achieve
greater economic strength and political stability within the area. The effort of the ASEAN
countries to develop their economies and move towards common goals can only contribute
to stability in South-east Asia. This is important to us, because our interests, too, are best
served by a South-east Asia that is stable and is growing economically.
Although progress has been impressive, there are some economic problems that will not
be easily resolved. There are also unsettling security problems of greater or less severity in


## p. 2829 (#467) ###########################################

8 September
2829
Adjournment-Foreign Affairs
each country in the region. These are disruptive of economic progress, which is essential to
political stability. In each of the countries I visited last year, I was briefed on the nature of
the security problems confronting that country and on the steps being taken to counter them.
In Thailand, I was told of increased insurgency in the northern and southern parts of the
country, problems with a separatist movement, problems with a disaffected minority, and
problems on the border with Laos and on the border with Cambodia. There had been an
increase in communist terrorist activities in Malaysia, which had heightened the Govern-
ment's concern with internal security problems that had been worrying it for a long time.
Indonesia was concerned with social and economic difficulties that offered opportunities for
mischief-making by disaffected groups. It was made very clear to me by all concerned in
Indonesia that they had had all they wanted of a communist regime and were watching every
step to see that the communists could not get a toe in.
Wherever I went, Ministers expressed concern that internal problems must not be
exploited by unfriendly states within the region or powers outside the region. They were
worried about the possibility of assistance from outside to insurgents and subversives.
Security and economic progress were, and still are, of fundamental concern to all those
people. Our programme of defence co-operation is therefore welcomed by the Governments
and the armed forces in those countries. New Zealand's efforts across the board in South-
east Asia are aimed essentially at promoting conditions of confidence and security. This is a
two-way relationship. Trade, aid, and political activities have all played a part, together with
defence. This has been an interrelated national effort.
The defence contribution is important, because defence and security are national
problems of fundamental concern to all those countries. Our contribution in the defence
area is limited by our size. It is nevertheless welcome, and I know it is appreciated. The
general objective of our mutual assistance defence programme is to assist all these countries
to improve the capability of their armed forces, and to provide New Zealand servicemen
with training, experience, and deployment opportunities. It is not just a one-way street. We
try to help in a small way to promote the stability of this region, and we hope that we are
playing our part there.
We have an exchange programme with Malaysia, and officers on secondment to the
Singaporean armed forces. Contingents of Malaysian and Singaporean troops come here for
training and exercise with our armed forces, and we exercise regularly with units of each
branch of the Malaysian and Singaporean armed forces. Personnel from several ASEAN
countries attend courses of instruction at various establishments here. In addition, senior
officers have visited New Zealand for discussions, and the contacts made in this way are
valuable in the general context of our relationships with the various countries. Our defence
activities are an integral part of our overall foreign policy. Through the mutual assistance
programme, our armed forces have a constructive role to play in support of our general
foreign policy. This region is of strategic importance to us.
The armed forces are also playing their part in the South Pacific, an area of no less
importance to us—an importance that has increased in recent years. Our forces are helping,
through training, to build up the effectiveness and self reliance of the defence forces of both
Fiji and Tonga, and are giving assistance in many other ways. Many servicemen from Fiji
and Tonga are trained in a wide variety of fields in our training establishments. Military civic
action programmes are also organised with these countries. The armed forces have assisted
greatly with disaster relief. Under the bilateral aid programme Army and Navy teams have
been undertaking tasks requiring special skills that our people have the training to be able to
perform. In addition, the Royal New Zealand Air Force carries out maritime surveillance
patrol, and provides air transport and other bilateral programmes.
The extent to which the armed forces provide effective and wide-ranging support to
New Zealand's overall national interests and policies in these other areas is all too seldom
given the recognition it deserves. On many occasions the assistance is given by these
servicemen at considerable personal risk, and I think they deserve more recognition than
perhaps they sometimes get.
Mention was made tonight of the importance of our relationship with Australia and the
United States, which has formal expression in the ANZUS alliance; I am sure all would
agree that this is the keystone of our collective defence policy. I was recently privileged to
attend the ANZUS council meeting in Wellington, and I want to say that this Government
has proved to the member countries that New Zealand is playing its full part in the ANZUS
alliance. I recall that in the 3 years of the Labour Government, which had a policy of non-
alignment, it was going to dissociate itself from countries associated with nuclear power or

nuclear warfare. If the Labour Government was going to take that attitude, it would have

problems in Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, Timor, and throughout Africa. No matter how
much we try, such conflicts will continue. In years gone by, communications and transport
were slow and, although the smaller countries had their problems and military conflicts, they
seemed to be able to overcome them between themselves in a reasonable time. However,
today, because of rapid communication and means of transport, the major powers can take
part in such conflicts; often, one of the conflicts, which would formerly have petered out in a
matter of days, flares up.
It is interesting to note that in many of the countries that have gone through these
conflicts in the past 10 years, the opposing parties have all been supplied with sophisticated
arms by the East. These countries have been stirred up by communist aggressors, who start
the fight and supply both sides with sophisticated weapons. Unless the powers-that-be take a
realistic attitude, we will be in real trouble. The conflicts are not those between nation and
nation or tribe and tribe such as have occurred for generations. If we are to bring a peaceful
solution to the world we should tell these people that they should not put weapons into the
hands of others, thereby causing chaos and suffering. In Mozambique, Angola, and other
places, both sides are being provided with sophisticated weapons by the Eastern countries.
It is time we had a good look at these problems, and took a stronger view to try to overcome
them and to bring a little more sanity into the world today.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): As I am the last speaker in the debate tonight I
want to discuss what New Zealand's foreign policy should be rather than to criticise previous
speeches. A successful New Zealand foreign policy should contain 10 elements. The first is
that it is essential that our foreign policy should have a firm moral base. "It may be said that
the only basis for a sound foreign policy is the national interest. I see no contradiction. I
believe that to secure our foreign policies on moral principles is the most enlightened form of
self-interest." Those are not my words, but the words of the late Norman Kirk. I agree with
them completely. Statements made by President Carter echo the sentiments of the late
Norman Kirk.
The present Prime Minister's much vaunted pragmatism is another word for expe-
diency. Perhaps the most damaging criticism that can be made of New Zealand's present
foreign policy is its short-sightedness. For example, last year we opened our ports to United
States nuclear warships, in the hope, I understand, of getting beef sales. Only a few months
later, President Carter, a Democrat, was elected, and he has said that he is in favour of
nuclear-free zones. That was the.very policy that the Labour Government put forward and
the National Government abandoned. President Carter has said that he is in favour of such
zones as being a step towards peace. The National Government should consider adopting a
nuclear-free zone in the South Pacific.
The second element our foreign policy should contain is that of independent policies.
Our policies must start in Wellington, not in Washington, Moscow, or Tokyo. We should
look at whether we believe a policy is right, not at whether some other country believes it is
right. Thirdly, our foreign policy should reflect our moral values, not those of anyone else. It
is a strange contradiction, which many New Zealanders have commented on, that it is illegal
in this country to discriminate on racial grounds, yet we have allowed ourselves to be
associated with a nation that is built on racial discrimination. Parliament this year has passed
a human rights Bill, yet our foreign policies do not appear to reflect concern for human
rights. When has the Government, for example, stood up on behalf of the people in French
Polynesia and in the French New Hebrides, who are calling out for independence? The
National Government has said the opposite-that it welcomes the French presence, because
apparently French warships might help to monitor the 200-mile zone. That is a short-sighted
policy which is not in the best interests of the Pacific.

rich nations and the poor nations is widening rather than narrowing. That is one of the great

other countries has only one flag, and on foreign policy, although we may disagree, basically

understand the problems of its neighbours better.

BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): Next week I propose to take 2 days of
estimates, Tuesday and Thursday. There will be a Supplementary Order Paper on Ministers'
replies to questions on Wednesday afternoon, and local Bills on Thursday. Otherwise we
shall deal with legislation. There might be some slight rearrangement of the Order Paper
depending on the availability of Ministers. I have in mind, although I am not firm on it yet,
that we might start sitting-as we sometimes do-until midnight on 1 night a week to take
the pressure off the end of the session. I have in mind that we might sit until midnight for the
first time next Wednesday. I shall look at the weight of legislation. We are starting to get into
the main body of legislation, and if we sit until midnight 1 night a week it might enable us to
move more smoothly to the end of the session without too many late nights.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): The Prime Minister has said
that there will be 2 days of estimates next week, and I presume 2 days each week thereafter.
Has any action been taken to expedite the tabling of annual reports? The committee's main
problem is that it is jammed up against the timetable because reports have sometimes been
introduced almost on the day it is sitting. One recently came in after the committee had
sat-the Prime Minister's own report from the Reserve Bank. It has been noticeable that
reports are running very much later this year than in previous years.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): That is true, and, as I think the Leader of
the Opposition knows, the problem is new equipment in the Government Printing Office,
which has been having a difficult time in the last year or two. It has introduced computerised
typesetting, and it is well known that whenever you introduce a computer of any type you
have endless difficulties. The difficulties are continuing, and even if they are not in the exact
area of the printing of the reports they throw the printing schedules out. That is the principal
reason for the delay, but I have been keeping in touch with the position for some time now,
and the annual reports are coming forward reasonably well. I have checked with the select
committees, and in general the work is going ahead, and we should get enough estimates
from this time on to have them 2 days a week if we wish. I do not think we will have 2 days
every week, but things are in reasonably good shape now apart from the printing delays.
Somebody has just asked me about today. If by any chance we are still sitting at 1 o'clock we
shall have a lunch break. It would be civilised to do so; there is no point in sitting through the
lunch hour.
NOTICE OF MOTION-ADMISSIBILITY
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I give notice that next sitting day I shall move, That
this House invites the country to contrast the actions of the New Zealand Attorney-General
who last year, for the first time in New Zealand's legal history, for political reasons stopped a
criminal prosecution based on the Prime Minister's unlawful action in halting the New
Zealand superannuation scheme-
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): A point of order, Mr Speaker. Obviously
this notice of motion has been scrutinised, but I suggest it has not been scrutinised
sufficiently closely. It contains an imputation of improper conduct, and is clearly out of
order. To say that a prosecution was stopped for political reasons by the Attorney-General is
highly improper, and it should not be in a notice of motion.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I do not see that the implication necessarily
follows. It is open to a member to place his own construction on the motivation behind an
act, and to say it was motivated by one reason or another does not, I suggest, bring it outside
the Standing Orders.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Attorney-General must act in the
public interest, as I am sure the member for Henderson would agree. If it were made clear
that the word "political" had no party connotations, or if the member giving the notice

Notice of Motion-Admissibility
referred to the public interest, then the Attorney-General would have acted properly. By the
way in which the member presented the notice of motion it was quite clear that he meant for

imputations should not be made in the House.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): Speaking to the point of order, the notice of motion

make what was unlawful lawful. I believe that that is a political reason for stopping a

normally stopped on the grounds that they are vexatious, or that there have been three such
prosecutions before. I freely admit that the Attorney-General last year said that he was
making the decision independently, but that does not mean he was not acting politically as

Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I looked at this notice of motion very carefully indeed when it

politics"-those sort of words—and that is the generally accepted broad meaning. However,
as has been drawn to my attention this morning, “political" has another meaning, which is
probably uppermost in members' minds-party political. Since my attention has been drawn
to that sense of the word "political" in the House, I think I must accept that that is the way in
which at least some members consider the word is being used.
I draw the attention of honourable members to Speaker's ruling 53/5, by Mr Speaker

that it is not conducive to the order of the House if members indulge in the use of words that
have a sinister as well as an innocent meaning. I believe that not only should they be avoided
but also that if there is a risk of there being disorder or impropriety they will be avoided. The
Minister of Justice was perfectly correct in drawing my attention to Speaker's ruling 79/3,
which states that a member may not impute improper motives to the Government. I

Broadcasting of Racing and Trotting Commentaries
2. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Broadcasting: In view
of the concern expressed by numerous clubs as to the financial and other consequences for
them and the Government of the decision to reduce the number of racing and trotting
commentaries on the Radio New Zealand network, will he discuss with the Broadcasting
Council the need to review this decision urgently, with the objective of restoring the status
quo?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): The chairman of the Broadcast-
ing Corporation has kept me informed of the corporation's thinking on this matter, and I
have conveyed the views of many members of Parliament and of the public to the chairman.
The chairman has already taken steps to ensure consultation on the matter with the racing
conferences, and will monitor very closely the effect of changes. As review is in effect taking
place, I do not propose to take action in what is a programme matter. As the member will
recall, the Broadcasting Act places the responsibility for decisions on programme matters in
the hands of the Broadcasting Corporation.
Hon. Michael Connelly: If the change is an adverse one, and will have an impact on the
funds available for club stakes, why does the Minister have to wait until that adverse effect is
readily apparent before acting?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I repeat what I said in the answer to the question. The
corporation is monitoring the matter very carefully. It is not inflexible on this matter. It will
check the effect on betting, consult closely with the racing clubs and the conferences, and
assess whether any changes are needed. In what is a programme matter, I think it is only fair
to give the corporation the opportunity to assess the situation before making any changes.
Mr Malcolm: Does the Minister have any evidence that the status quo referred to in the
question—that is, the financial consequences for racing and trotting clubs-has been
affected in any way by the decision of Radio New Zealand?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I have asked the chairman to check the matter. I understand
that the initial assessment suggests that so far there have been no effects on off-course
betting, but it is early days yet. I also understand that the council and the conferences would
like more time in which to assess the longer-term effect.
Mr Malcolm: Has the chairman of the Broadcasting Council indicated whether market
research was done on how many people wanted these programmes, and, if so, does the
Minister know what percentage of the public was actually listening to these programmes at
any given time?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: That question goes far wider than the original one.

Body Scanners
3. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North) asked the Minister of Health: Is there any
revision to the original estimate that New Zealand would need seven body scanners in all to
service a population of 3 400 000?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): No, there has been no revision. It must be
realised that this is only an estimate, based on overseas findings that one machine, properly
used and with other adequate pre-scanning procedures such as ultrasound and radionucleide
imaging, can service a population of 500 000.
Mr Hunt: Was the estimate that one body scanner could service a population of about
500 000 provided by those people who construct and make the body scanners?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I am not quite sure where the estimate came from. I do not place
much reliance on it, and neither is the Government's policy formulated on it. The estimate
was a serious one, but has not been revised or even contemplated.
Mr Hunt: As the policy will not be based on the estimate, could the Minister explain
why seven body scanners are planned for New Zealand?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I know of no statement having been made about seven body scanners
being planned for New Zealand. As we have three major neurosurgical units in New
Zealand it is planned to have three body scanners at present. On the basis of our own
experience we will formulate plans and a policy for any necessary expansion.

4. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue

he give any indications as to whether or not it might be favourable?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue Department): I

completes its research on the subject. Nevertheless, in view of the Government's emphasis

grounds for giving this proposal very careful consideration.
Mr Hunt: In view of the Minister's encouraging reply, will there be any report on the
matter, and, if so, will he be prepared to let all members have a look at it?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: Obviously, in a complex area such as taxation, where I must
have the full confidence of my department, I would need to give that matter very careful
consideration. I do not think that at this stage I would be prepared to give a ruling.

Wanganui Computer Centre
5. Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth) asked the Minister of State Services: To what
extent is there a backlog in supplying New Zealand citizens with their "stored file informa-
tion" from the Wanganui Computer Centre?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services): The question is basically not one
within my field of responsibility as Minister of State Services, because the Privacy Commis-
sioner is an officer of Parliament. In an endeavour to obtain an answer to the member's
question I made inquiries of the Privacy Commissioner's office, and was informed that 1050
applications have been received, and that 239 applicants have been advised of the informa-
tion, if any, stored about them on the computer system. Of the remaining 811 applications,
information is awaited in respect of 763 from the user departments, and 48 applications are
in the process of being referred by the Privacy Commissioner to the user departments to
obtain the information. Additional staff has been assigned to this work, and I understand the
Privacy Commissioner expects the backlog to be overtaken within a few weeks.

the case of the New Zealand Meat Workers Union and the Auckland Freezing Workers
Union, I will be inviting national and branch officials, and a union representative from each

of the key requirements within the industry at present is better and more efficient communi-

presentation of stock on the grating or the sticking chute could be one of the vexatious issues
raised. In that case, I would hope that the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries could play
whatever role is necessary from the hygiene or meat inspection point of view. I want to try to
confine it to a family affair of those involved inside the gate.

Overseas Currency from Visiting Skiers
9. Mr COOPER (Otago Central) asked the Minister of Tourism: What was the
estimated amount of overseas currency received from visiting overseas skiers in 1976-77, and
what is the estimated amount of overseas currency from the same source this season?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): Because separate statistics are not
available on the specific activities which visitors to New Zealand on holiday or vacation
intend to undertake, and as the present ski season is not yet over, a precise assessment of the
amount of overseas currency spent by visiting skiers is not possible. However, information

number of ski visitors was 4000, and in the 1977 season it was 10 000. In 1976 the estimated

million, and in 1977 it was $4.75 million. In addition, total revenue generated trans-Tasman
for Air New Zealand and Qantas, which is shared under a pool arrangement, is estimated
at about $1 million for 1976 and $2.5 million for 1977.

Creche at Yendarra
18. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Minister of Education: In view of the
widespread use by students at Manukau Technical Institute and the Otara Community
Education and Recreation Group of the creche at Yendarra homestead, what immedate
measures does he plan to take to ensure that the creche does not have to close because of
lack of premises?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): There is no policy which allows creches
attached to educational institutions to receive financial support through the Education vote.
Some educational institutions however, of which the Manukau Technical Institute is one,
have permitted buildings or rooms which are temporarily surplus to requirements to be used
as creches. The Yendarra homestead was offered by the institute to a group previously
operating a creche nearby when their premises were no longer available. This was to be a
temporary arrangement until the homestead building was demolished. The homestead was
used for a creche in the first and second terms this year. The creche closed at the end of the
second term. Demolition is now completed. The site is required for the institute's new
library.

We are living in a rapidly changing world; it is not the world of the status quo, as the
National Government would have us believe. It is not a conservative world. It is a world of
dynamic change, and the nations that are increasing their standard of living fastest are those
that, through able leadership, are adapting to take advantage of the changing tastes, the
changing incomes, and the changing growth patterns we see around the world.
New Zealand in the last 10 years has failed miserably to cope with the changes that have
taken place in world trade. Thirty years ago, the people of this country probably enjoyed the
highest standard of living in the world. Even a few years ago, around 1960, we still ranked
fourth in the world's standard of living table. Today, New Zealand has dropped from fourth
to about twentieth, and our rate of growth is even further down the scale. We have
plummeted in the last 18 years, during which the National Party has mainly been in office,
despite the fact that we have sold every pound of butter, every lamb, and every pound of
cheese we have produced.
The reasons for that decline are not hard to find. Despite all the talk about the need for
change, we still depend overwhelmingly for our export income on a narrow range of basic
and traditional primary products, and it is a matter of economic history that the prices
received for primary products have suffered over those years when measured directly against
the prices received for industrial products. The main factors responsible for that phenome-
non should be well known to us all, but they have been ignored by successive National
Governments. They include the general low elasticity of demand for agricultural products,
the rapid growth of synthetic substitutes during this period, the more efficient use of
industrial materials due to technological processes, and the adoption of protectionist policies
by advanced industrial countries. All these add up to a worsening in the terms of trade for
most of our basic commodities.
I suggest that that worsening will continue for as long as New Zealand relies on a narrow
range of basic and traditional primary products. It is, therefore, dangerous nonsense to
suggest, as some members opposite have, that all we have to do is find new markets for the
quantities of butter and cheese that will gradually be excluded from the British market. As
the New Zealand Planning Council said this morning, during the past few years—and I
would say the past 10 years-New Zealand has got itself into a hole. The reason is clear. In
the past, under the present Minister of Finance, New Zealand has faced a succession of
economic problems, and the Government's main contribution has been to talk about them.
In the late 1960s there was the National Development Conference, which has now been
replaced by the Planning Council.
