more than 70 percent of its export income will probably come from farm-based products. If
forest products are included as part of farming, the farming contribution will still be about 80
percent in the 1980s. As long as our export income is based on a narrow range of virtually
unprocessed farm products, our relative living standards will continue to fall as they have in
the past. Therefore, our products should be processed in a more sophisticated form, which in
turn will require both an increase in investment and a channelling of that investment into
essential areas.
That will not be achieved under the present Government's financial policy of free
interest rates and the channelling of money directly through finance houses. One has only to
read the 1976-77 report of the New Zealand Finance Houses Association to see who has
taken control of this country. In one year the association's assets have increased by about 40
percent. However, the implications of the type of investment are even more important.
Where has this increased money in loans, advances, and leasing from the finance houses
gone? Twenty-six percent, or $53.7 million, has gone into property speculation, and $14.8
million into leasing. No longer can the small manufacturers go to the insurance companies or
to their banks to raise money to help build their factories. They have to trot along to the
finance houses and pay interest rates of 20 percent to 23 percent, instead of the traditional
rates of 8 to 10 percent. Commercial vehicles took $47 million, and other loans and advances
$35.6 million. Only 21.8 percent, or $44 million, of the $175 million in new expenditure
through the finance companies could be said to have gone into productive areas such as
industrial and agricultural machinery and equipment. The capital of this country is being
harnessed by the finance companies, because they are prepared to offer a higher rate of
interest; they are accumulating small savings and charging an extra 10 percent.
New Zealand must control more of the end marketing of its processed products, to take
its future exports off the international auction block. It should start now with the basic
products of wool, milk, meat, meat by-products, and timber, and seek profitable markets for
new products. At the same time, we need to plan now for the long-term diversification of
both markets and products. All this entails a basic programme of market research carried out
by competent people overseas. We must stop the fiddles in this country, and encourage
manufacturers and others to increase production.
In a recent copy of the New Zealand Herald I saw this advertisement: "Exporters:
Unlimited finance can be made available to exporters who have tax losses or excess exports.
Substantial cash premiums will be paid for exports handled through a third party, giving a
cash advantage now, rather than a tax loss in the future. Exporters should have annual
exports in excess of $50,000." In other words, the incentives in this country are being paid
not to people who produce, but to those who can work the system. The Rangitikei Dairy
Co., for instance, because it was not allowed to claim export tax deductions, put its exports
through New Zealand Breweries. We will have to change that procedure.

PRIVILEGE
Mr BIRCH (Franklin): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I take this first opportunity of
raising with you, Sir, a matter that appears to be a prima facie case of a breach of privilege. I
refer to an article on the front page of the Auckland Star last evening, which was headlined
"New crossing rules may be scrapped". I should like to read part of the article: "The much-
criticised new law governing pedestrian crossings may be scrapped soon. This is revealed in a
letter from former Transport Minister Sir Basil Arthur to Mr G. C. Leatham, chief instructor
of the Auckland Motor Cycle Riding School. Sir Basil is a member of the select committee
on road safety which has been studying reaction to the controversial law. In his letter, Sir
Basil says the law on pedestrian crossings will revert to what it was before the change came
into effect on February 1. This will be the only change to the traffic regulations until at least
February 1 next year. The select committee had decided, by a majority, to postpone any
further amendments to the regulations until that date, Sir Basil said."
not
I believe that represents a very serious breach of the Standing Orders of the House. I
refer to Standing Orders 366, 367, and 368. Standing Order 366 states: "Evidence, etc.,
to be published or divulged-The proceedings of, or the evidence taken by, or the report of
any Select Committee, or any summary of such proceedings, evidence, or report shall be
strictly confidential and not published or divulged by any member of the Committee or by
any other person, until the report of such Committee has been presented to the House . . .”.
Standing Order 367 states: "Divulging proceedings or evidence a breach of privilege-Any
person committing a breach of Standing Order 366 shall be deemed guilty of a breach of
privilege, and may be dealt with by the House accordingly."
Standing Order 368 provides for exceptions to non-publication of evidence, but I have
read that Standing Order closely, and I do not believe that the provisions apply in this case,
although I remind the House that in some instances a chairman of a committee may in his
discretion refer to comments made before the committee, and a select committee chairman
may also make a press statement to inform the public of the nature of its inquiry. I do not
believe that the article falls into either of those categories.
I am informed by members of the committee that the House has referred several
petitions to the Road Safety Committee. The petitions request action on the new regula-
tions, particularly those applying to pedestrian crossings. I am informed—without divulging
the proceedings of the committee-that the committee has discussed the subjects of the
petitions, and that some aspects of them have been referred to the Minister. The committee
is now awaiting a reply from the Minister, but, as far as the records of the proceedings of the
committee show, there was no authority for either the chairman or any member of the
committee to divulge the proceedings of that committee.
Clearly, Sir, it presents a serious breach of the Standing Orders, and, because it appears
to be a very blatant breach also, I have brought it to the attention of the House, although I
am mindful of the comments made by the Speaker earlier this year. I feel that this instance
falls within those categories of breaches of privilege that the House should deal with, and I
ask you, Sir, to rule on the question of whether a prima facie breach has been established.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): I am taken completely by surprise by the charge
laid by the Senior Government Whip this afternoon; firstly, because I understand it is
customary-if a charge such as this is to be made against a member-to inform the member.
This has not been done, and I am not in a position to give the House any information this
afternoon on the breach alleged by the Senior Government Whip. I challenge his contention
that it was a blatant breach of privilege. If there is in fact a breach of privilege, it is not a
blatant one. I have not seen the article in question. I wrote down that it was from the
Auckland Star of last night. Is that correct?
Mr Birch: That's so.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: I have not seen it, and the member will perhaps understand
that, being a South Island member who arrived in Wellington on Tuesday morning, I did not
have the opportunity to see the paper, and the article has not been referred to me. If it

Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): Probably there is a prima facie breach

committee passed about public statements about its activities. The breach of privilege is not
the publication in the newspaper, but the communication by way of correspondence to Mr
Leatham. That would be the breach of privilege initially, and the member may find on
looking at his correspondence that he has done that without possibly realising that it is a
breach of privilege.
I make the point that it has not been customary to notify the member concerned. I recall
an occasion some years ago when a breach of privilege was alleged against me, and the first I
heard of it was in the House when the Senior Labour Government Whip made the
allegation. It is not customary, although in some ways it is not a bad idea to do it so that the
matter can be dealt with immediately. I know the background to the activities of this
committee, which has corresponded with the Minister of Transport, who in turn has brought
the matter to Cabinet. It probably is a breach of privilege, but I would not consider it a
serious one. It may well have been done quite inadvertently.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): Speaking briefly, I draw

practice'-this refers to the House of Commons-‘as a matter of courtesy to give him notice
beforehand. If a member who makes a complaint against another member has failed or been
unable to give the member notice of his intention to do so, or if although the latter has been
given notice he neglects to attend, the more regular course is to adjourn further considera-
tion of the matter of the complaint to a future day and to order the member whose conduct is
impugned to attend the House in his place on that day.'
Obviously, the member for Timaru is here today. The matter at issue is that, quite apart
from what Erskine May might or might not say, common courtesy should have suggested to
the Senior Government Whip, who raised the matter, that he might advise the member for
Timaru. Even more relevant-if I might make one further comment in the light of the
statement made by the member for Timaru-the House might well take note of Speaker's
ruling 126/1, which states: "If the House is satisfied with the explanation of a member as to
publication of proceedings of a Select Committee, it may not be necessary to deal with the
question of breach of privilege; the House may content itself with coming to a resolution not
to proceed further in the matter." Quite frankly, in all the circumstances prevailing, I believe
that would be the wisest course, and would certainly be in line with the admonition of Mr
Speaker Jack in 1976.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Deputy Prime Minister): Whatever the argument about

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Boilermakers Union, Wellington
1. Dr WALL (Porirua) asked the Minister of Labour: What have been the beneficial
results of the deregistration of the Wellington Boilermakers Union?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The honourable member will be well aware
of industrial disruption on the Bank of New Zealand site, the No. 2 container crane site, at
William Cable's, and at the Union Steam Ship Company, to which the Wellington Boiler-
makers Union was a party prior to its deregistration. While some industrial action did
continue for a while following deregistration, it lessened in intensity, and indeed, in recent
months, Wellington boilermakers have not been a party to any major industrial disputes. In
a series of negotiations with the Wellington Trades Council about boilermakers' union
coverage, a desire by the men concerned to regain recognition has been obvious. I believe
the work force has found that the loss of unqualified preference within the workplace has
weakened union activity. The eventual outcome of the negotiations has yet to be reached,
but they are continuing.
Dr Wall: I wonder if the Minister could elucidate which of those varying results he sees
as being beneficial.
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The first, and most obvious, is the amount of work being done in
Wellington.
Dr Wall: Could the Minister tell us when structural steel work will recommence on the
Bank of New Zealand site?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The member's electorate is a lot closer to the site than mine. As
far as I know, it has been going on for the last 4 months at least.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: In view of the Minister's comment that the union has not been a
party to a dispute for several months, could he tell how it possibly could be, since it no longer
legally exists?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: It can be in two ways. We have accepted that the Wellington
Trades Council, as a body affiliated to the Federation of Labour, represents the men on an
understanding between the men, the Wellington Trades Council, and the Government-and
that has been working very well. The men could have approached me, and indeed at one
stage in the negotiations a suggestion was made that I should recognise them under Part X of
the Industrial Relations Act.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Oral Answers to Questions
Housing Corporation Assistance to Doctors
2. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Minister of Housing: Can he outline the
nature of the scheme whereby Housing Corporation assistance is available to doctors wishing
to practise in urban areas where general practitioner shortages exist?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): This scheme-which involves loans by
the Housing Corporation to local authorities at local body rates of interest where the
sanction of the Local Authorities Loans Board has been obtained-was introduced in 1969,
and was originally confined to rural areas. More recently, it has been extended to urban
areas where the Department of Health confirms that there are problems in obtaining or
retaining doctors because of a lack of house and surgery facilities. In practice, the local
authority builds the facilities and leases or rents them to doctors.
Mr Wellington: Can the Minister give an indication of the general response to the
scheme, particularly in the last year, and especially in new mass housing suburbs?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I cannot give the honourable member all that information,
but I can indicate that loans have been made to eight local bodies between 1970 and 1976,
and that the total amount lent has been $219,000.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Is the Minister in a position to confirm or otherwise whether any
application has been received from the south Auckland area for such a loan?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I am unable to confirm or otherwise the inquiry made by the
honourable member. The list I have does not show that a loan has been made to the south
Auckland area.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Housing Corporation Loan Freeze
3. Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) asked the Minister of Housing: Why did he not make
public until August 1977 the findings of a survey carried out in September 1976, and referred
to in the Housing Corporation's 1977 annual report, which confirms that the Government's
decision to freeze the basic Housing Corporation loan at $13,000 has not only created the
biggest "deposit gap" in the corporation's lending history, but has led to a situation in which
"outgoings on home ownership have . . . doubled inside 2 years"-in other words,
during the term of this National Government?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): The survey was limited in scope and
carried out for the corporation's own purposes. The honourable member should be well
aware that the basic loan provided by the Housing Corporation is not frozen and that the
Government's policy is to adjust loan limits as and when economic circumstances permit.
The Government has concentrated on helping those most in need, and has made significant
improvements to the loan supplement scheme whereby both the range of those qualifying
and the amount of supplements have been increased. Supplements up to $6,000 are now
available, and in addition, in its August package, an additional supplement of $3,000 for
single-income one-child families was introduced. In brief, these adjustments are to be seen
as steps in the process towards achieving a larger basic loan.
Hon. W. A. Fraser: When were the results of the survey conveyed to the Minister; and
did the Housing Corporation indicate to him at the same time that two incomes were
increasingly being required to meet the total ingoing, and that in the corporation's opinion
adjustments in that area remained a first priority?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I cannot inform the honourable member when the findings
were conveyed to me. If he had listened to my answer to the original question he would have
heard me say that the survey was limited, and carried out for the corporation's own
purposes. The honourable member referred to the need for a family to have two incomes if it
was to afford housing. He will be aware that we have taken steps in the latest package to give
increased assistance to single-income families.
Mr Bell: Can the Minister advise the average size of loans granted by the Housing
Corporation in comparison with the maximum loan quoted of $13,000; or, if not, can he con-
firm that the average loan made available is well over $13,000 when one takes into account
the supplementary loans mentioned in his answer to the original question?

2883
Oral Answers to Questions
Mortgagee Sale-Threat by Trustee Company
7. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) asked the Minister of Justice: Has he considered the
implications of a letter he will have received from Messrs Gazley and Black, solicitors,
relating to a threatened mortgagee sale by a trustee company, and can he take any action to
prevent the company from using its financial position to secure an unjustified profit by
evicting a widow and family from a home that provides ample security for a renewal of the
existing loan at market rates?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): On behalf of the Minister of Justice I
apologise in advance for the length of the reply. This is a complex matter and entails a fairly
lengthy reply which, with the leave of the House, I shall give. The Minister has given
preliminary consideration to the letter from Messrs Gazley and Black, and, from my
understanding of the situation, there is no way in which he can intervene. The honourable
member's information is obviously far from complete. The brief facts are that about 2 years
ago the widow purchased a property for $97,000. The purchase was financed by taking over
the existing first mortgage of $30,000 to the executors trustees, and by raising a second
mortgage for $10,000 through her solicitor's nominee company. The balance of $57,000
consisted of her own cash contribution.
The first mortgage had been raised in 1972 by the prior owner of the property. The 5-
year term was due to expire on 7 July 1977, and as the conditions of the mortgage did not
require regular repayments of principal this meant that only interest at 9.5 percent had to be
paid. This is not a case where personal circumstances have changed after the property was
first purchased, nor does it involve a widow and a young family. The house is plainly in the
high-price bracket. I understand that the widow and her married daughter's family both live
in the same home, and indeed her son-in-law is a covenantor to the mortgage. At the time
the contract was entered into the owner and her solicitor would have known that there was a
possibility that refinancing would be necessary once the balance of the term had expired.
The company is not evicting the family. As long ago as last February it was made clear
to the owner that repayment had to be made on due date. Despite further reminders, the
only response was a request for a 2-year extension. At no stage was any explanation
regarding possible difficulties mentioned, and since there was no dialogue the company had
no alternative but to follow its present course. As the honourable member will appreciate,
moneys lent on mortgage by trustee companies represent in the main investments with them
by their clients, in accordance with whose instructions the companies must at all times abide.
If the worst did happen and there was a mortgagee's sale, the company itself would make no
profit at all from it. Naturally, I sympathise with any person in this predicament, but on this
occasion it is simply not true to label the trustee company as the villain of the piece.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Economic Stabilisation
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) said that, when in Opposition, National members had
told the people that subsidies meant that the people would pay twice, implying that if
subsidies were removed taxation could be reduced. That argument had been false, because
the people were now paying the highest taxation in the country's history. Subsidies were a
social and collective acceptance of the need to assist production and consumption, and the
Labour Party had tried to get stability by the use of a subsidy scheme.
Although Government members gave the impression they were opposed to subsidies,
many votes provided for substantial payments from the Consolidated Revenue Account in
subsidies or grants to groups in the community as incentives to increase production or for
research. This year, agricultural subsidies alone amounted to more than $100 million.
Scientific subsidies were substantial, and the Stabilisation vote included continuing subsidies
for milk, shipping services, the gas industry, and the Railways Department. Under the
National Government, the continuation or abolition of subsidies appeared to have a political
basis. How could the Minister justify increasing subsidies to the Railways when he had cut
consumer subsidies?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) said that in 1972-73, the last year of
the former National Government, subsidies had cost $36,195,000. As a result of Labour's
promises to freeze postal, electricity, and rail charges, subsidies in 1973-74 had cost
$112,185,000; in 1974-75, $148,152,000; in 1975-76, $182,553,000; and would have cost $200
million the following year if the National Government had not reduced them in December
1975. In 1976-77 the cost of subsidies had been down to $58,321,000, and this year it was
$89,950,000. On 21 March 1975 the member for Heretaunga, the Minister of Railways and
the Minister of Electricity at that time, had said that if the Labour Government were
returned to power it would look at the possibility of raising rail charges and bulk electricity
charges, but, although it had had the opportunity to do so, it had never said by how much the

charges would be raised. Even the Prime Minister at that time had admitted in March 1975
that subsidies could go only so far. The 1975 Budget had stated that charges would be

Admittedly, the National Government had doubled the price of milk in December 1975, but
it was still only half the price of Coco-cola, and New Zealand's milk was still the cheapest in

PRIVILEGE
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Yesterday a matter of privilege relating to the honourable
member for Timaru was raised by the Senior Government Whip. On 26 July the Road Safety
Committee voted, at the request of the Minister of Transport, who was not present, to make
a recommendation on certain regulations he had referred to the committee, at the same time
recommending that the secretary write to the petitioners-those who had petitioned the
committee on the regulations—after the Minister had advised his approval of the proposed
change regarding the prayer of their petitions. The honourable member for Timaru was
absent from the next select committee meeting on 23 August, but his colleagues reported to
him that the committee had dealt with other regulations referred to it by the Minister. It is
recorded in the minutes of the committee's meeting on 23 August that the chairman read out
a letter from the Auckland motor cycle riding course, dated 21 August, requesting an
interview before the Road Safety Committee. It was agreed that a senior official from the
Ministry of Transport discuss the matter with them, obtain their views on the regulations,
and report back to the committee. Apparently the member for Timaru was not informed of
this.
On 1 September, Mr Leatham, chief instructor of the Auckland Motor Cycle Riding
School, wrote to the honourable member for Timaru asking him for confirmation of a
statement he said had been made to him over the telephone on 30 August by Mr Emerson of
the Ministry of Transport, Auckland, to the effect that the select committee had agreed to
certain amendments to the new road regulations. I cannot go into great detail on those,
because I might be breaching privilege myself. However, on the basis of his knowledge of the
committee meeting on 26 July and of the report from his colleagues of the meeting on 23
August, and assuming that the Minister must have issued a statement on which Mr Emerson
had based his comments to Mr Leatham-whereas Mr Leatham's approach had resulted
from the discussion Mr Emerson had had with him at the request of the select
committee-the member for Timaru confirmed that the committee had agreed to certain
recommendations, which he then outlined for the sake of clarity. These were subsequently
reported in the Auckland Star of 12 September, and are now the subject of an alleged breach
of privilege.
I find that quite properly, under Standing Order 368(d), the committee-and not just
the chairman exercising his discretion, as is laid down in the Standing Order-referred a
submission to Mr Leatham, through Mr Emerson, for his comments for the purpose of
assisting the committee in its inquiries. In turn, Mr Leatham sought confirmation of certain
facts from the member for Timaru, who gave this information because he believed he could
properly do so, as he thought, mistakenly, that the Minister had issued a statement.
Nevertheless, the member for Timaru was entitled to make that comment, because the
committee had referred the matter to Mr Leatham. The member for Timaru did not know
that. I find that, in spite of this mix up, no prima facie case of privilege exists.
I should like to comment on one other point raised during yesterday's discussion on this
point of order. It was drawn to my attention that the member for Timaru had not been
informed beforehand of the intention to raise a matter of privilege involving him. I draw the
attention of honourable members to the ruling given on 10 August 1976 by Mr Speaker Jack,
reported in Hansard, Volume 404, at page 1423, and by me 2 days later, reported in
Hansard, Volume 405, at page 1579, in which the rule of practice contained in the 19th
edition of Erskine May, on page 170, was reiterated. Consonant with Standing Order 429,
which requires the matter to be raised at the earliest reasonable opportunity, a member
raising a matter of privilege involving another member must take reasonable steps to inform
him beforehand of his intention. If he cannot do this because of the absence of the member,
the proper course spelled out in Erskine May and adopted by the House on 6 August 1976, as
reported in Hansard, volume 404, at pages 1390 to 1391, is that the House is to adjourn
further consideration of the matter to a future day to give the member the opportunity to be
present.

2. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Minister of Health: What salary arrange-

Security Council and the international community generally that an essential element of any
settlement of the Arab-Israeli dispute would be the withdrawal by Israel from territories

supported Resolution 242.

QUESTIONS AND REPLIES
[Covering period 25 August to 7 September]
WRITTEN QUESTIONS
Motor Vehicles Confiscation and Sale
1. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Justice: (1) How many
vehicles have been confiscated and sold under the provisions of the Criminal Justice
Amendment Act (No. 2) 1976; (2) what arrangements were made for their sale and custody
pending sale; (3) what happens in the event of a successful appeal; and (4) in which, if any, of
the cases in the answer to question (1) above could the same result not have been attained by
invoking powers vested in the court prior to the passing of the Criminal Justice Amendment
Act (No. 2) 1976, in particular the power of attaching conditions to a probation order?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: The information sought is as
follows: (1) one vehicle has been confiscated and sold under the provisions of the Criminal
Justice Amendment Act (No. 2) 1976 and confiscation orders only made in respect of five
motor cycles. No further action has been taken pending the outcome of appeals; (2) the
motor vehicle was stored on the court premises and sold by public auction. Four motor cycles
have not yet been surrendered. The fifth one (allegedly rebuilt from stolen parts) is held by
the Police while its ownership is determined; (3) in the event of a successful appeal against
the making of a confiscation order or against conviction the order would be of no effect. In
those cases involving the five motor cycles no subsequent action will be taken until the
outcome of the appeals against conviction and sentence is known; and (4) the owner of the
confiscated motor vehicle was fined and disqualified from driving for 6 months. The owners
of the motor cycles were either fined or sentenced to imprisonment or borstal training. In no
cases were the offenders placed on probation by the court. Had the offenders been placed on
probation it would have been open to the court, if it wished, to impose a special condition
that they should not either alone or jointly own or have in their possession any specified
article or article of any specified class.
(25/8/77)

2. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) asked the Minister of Education: What progress has

discriminate against women by reason of sex or marriage, or treat women in a paternalistic
manner. The recommendation has been followed whenever possible subject only to those
areas which involve conditions of employment and thus become matters for negotiation with
the appropriate employee organisations under the State Services Remuneration and Condi-
tions of Employment Act 1969.

Éducation-Human Relationships in the Home
4. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) asked the Minister of Education: What progress has
been made by the Department of Education in the implementation of recommendation 3,
chapter 5, of the report of the Select Committee on Women's Rights?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: Teachers are encouraged to

Pacific Island Immigrants-Stay of Proceedings Scheme
15. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Immigration: Has he
received a letter from the Pacific Islands Housing and Welfare Association dated 19 July
1977, stating that people have been informed that under the stay of proceedings scheme
they have been accepted for permanent residence, only to be told some weeks later that they
must return, and, if so, is this the case, and, if it is, how many of the people who have been
informed that they can stay are likely to be advised later to leave?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration) replied: I have received the letter from the
Pacific Islands Housing and Welfare Association referred to, and I have informed the
association that if it cares to supply me with the names and addresses of the persons
concerned I will investigate the matter further. I should like to remind the honourable
member that the approvals were in fact provisional, and are subject to the satisfactory
completion of normal immigration requirements with regard to health and character. In
addition, since applicants were informed of whether or not they had been provisionally
approved for permanent residence it has become evident that in a few cases applicants had
misrepresented their situation to the committee-for example, by not declaring the existence
of a spouse or dependent children or by not disclosing previous criminal convictions. In such
cases the provisional approval has been withdrawn and the persons concerned have been
asked to leave the country.

Railway Wagons-Utilisation
16. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) asked the Minister of Railways: Are railway
wagons ever empty when they return to Auckland from further south, and, if so, are cut
rates ever given so that empty wagons will be filled?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: Different railway wagons are
used for different types of loads. In addition, there are seasonal trade imbalances in the
freight traffic moving both intra- and inter-island and a degree of empty haulage is inevitable
to position wagons at loading points. Because there is no constant empty haulage pattern it is
not practicable to advertise special rates for goods as back loads. However, the pattern of
wagon loading is one of the factors taken into account when setting special or scheduled
rates.

Herbicidal Sprays-Toxicity
22. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) asked the Minister of Agriculture: In view of the
fact that insecticides cannot be used while plants are in flower, will he consider the banning
of herbicidal sprays during the same period of plant life to prevent the possibility of
contaminated honey?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: The Apiaries Act prohibits the
application of any substance toxic to bees to any fruit trees, raspberries, strawberries,
loganberries and boysenberries when they are in bloom and to any cruciferous or leguminous
field crops during the period 1 September to 3 March next following without a permit from
the Director-General of Agriculture and Fisheries. The limitations under this Act are due to
toxicity to bees, not because of contamination of honey. Herbicides, even if they were toxic
to bees, would not be sprayed on the above crops during the flowering period. Most
herbicides are relatively non-toxic to bees, but by kiling weeds they may exert an indirect
effect on honey production by removing some plants which later may be a source of honey. I
have no reports of honey being contaminated by herbicides following field use of these
chemicals. I do not propose to limit the use of herbicides on flowering weeds.
(1/9/77)

32. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Transport: Will he list the countries that

from its obligations under the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic. However, separate
agreements have been made with a number of countries allowing bona fide visitors from
these countries to New Zealand, and allowing bona fide New Zealand visitors to them, to be
able to use their respective valid domestic drivers licences.

35. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Justice How many prosecutions have

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Attorney-General) replied on behalf of the Minister of Justice: I
presume that the provision to which the honourable member has referred is in fact the
amendment to section 259 of the Sale of Liquor Act 1952 as provided in the 1976 Sale of
Liquor Amendment Act. This amended provision came into force only on 26 November
1976. No statistics are maintained that will allow offences committed by barmen to be
identified. The provision in section 259 (2) of the Sale of Liquor Act makes it an offence for
any person other than the licensee or the manager to supply liquor to any person under the
age of 20 years. There is no provision specific to barmen. Statistics of prosecutions under this
provision for this year will not be available from the Department of Statistics until some time
towards the end of 1978 at the earliest.

Tourists-Comparative Financial Statistics
40. Mr BLANCHFIELD (West Coast) asked the Minister of Finance: What is the
difference in value between the amount New Zealand tourists take annually out of the
country and that which overseas tourists spend in New Zealand?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance) replied: Overseas funds taken out
of the country by New Zealanders travelling abroad as recorded by the Reserve Bank's
statistics of overseas exchange transactions amounted to $268.5 million in the year to June
1977, while travel receipts amounted to $162.2 million, an excess of payments over receipts

travel receipts to $149.6 million, an excess of payments over receipts of $58 million. There is

tourists and other short-stay travellers on accommodation and other services and purchases
of goods, but exclude fares for international travel.

Flood Relief
45. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister in Charge of the Earthquake and
War Damage Commission: Does he propose to consider the suggestion of the Earthquake
and War Damage Commission on the desirability of some further form of relief for flood
victims as advanced in the commission's annual report recently tabled, and, if so, what form
is this likely to take?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister in Charge of the Earthquake and War Damage Commis-
sion) replied: The commission has submittted a scheme whereby relief could be made
available to home owners for landslip, flood, or other disaster-induced problems affecting
developed residential sections. The scheme is intended to provide assistance for damage on
sections of the very nature for which insurance protection is not available. The commission
has recommended that local authorities be empowered to set up local relief schemes funded
and administered at local community level and tailored to meet the special needs of the
community-flood, landslip, sea erosion, and the like. The scheme will principally, provide
relief to homeowners, but it is envisaged it could also provide assistance for the local
authority for repair of damage to public property and services. Each local authority relief
fund would be financed by a special disaster rate, levied on the basis of land value, and each
local fund invested to the credit of that local authority with the National Provident Fund to
be available on demand. I have asked that the scheme proposed by the commission be fully
investigated with a view to implementation, and I understand the proposal is now being
examined by the Territorial Local Authority Council.

Children's Health
46. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) asked the Minister of Health: When health
problems-either by way of disease or diet deficiency—are detected among schoolchildren
as a result of surveillance in the schools by health nurses, what remedial measures are
undertaken, what steps are taken to ensure that there is parental awareness of the situation,
and what subsequent checks are made to avoid recurrence of such health problems?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: The child's condition is assessed by the
public health nurse, who may make referral to the Department of Health's medical officer or
a general practitioner, as appropriate. The nurse, may, in such cases as head lice or minor
dietary problems, advise the parents and institute treatment herself. Where necessary,
repeat visits are made by the nurse to review the situation and prevent recurrence.

Rural Bank Lending Rates
53. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister in Charge of the
Rural Banking and Finance Corporation: Has he seen the statement on page 2 of the Nelson
Evening Mail of 19 August, in which the president of Nelson Federated Farmers stated that
"new rural bank interest rates announced in the Budget would make life difficult for young
farm settlers, and that the increase "could add up to $1,000 more in repayments a year",
and, if so, does he intend to take any steps to reduce the additional burden that the increased
rates impose?
Hon D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation)
replied: I have seen the statement in the Nelson Evening Mail. If the president of the Nelson
branch is correctly reported, he would appear to have overlooked the very worth-while
concession announced in the Budget that a new settler obtaining a loan from the Rural Bank
pays only 72 percent interest for the first 3 years. Thus he is not called upon to meet the
higher rate until he has had a period to consolidate his new purchase. I note from the report
that the $1,000 more in repayments" statement was made in relation to the special
settlement scheme where loans of up to 85 percent of the value of the farm may have been
borrowed. Even there the increase would apply only after the first 3 years. In any event, this
increase in the prime rate of interest of only 1 percent, when expressed as a monetary sum,
would approach $1,000 per annum in less than 5 percent of loans made for settlement
purposes in any recent year.

Inflation-Comparative Statistics
66. Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth) asked the Minister of Statistics: Has he seen the
comment of the Labour member for Wanganui in the Wanganui Herald dated 10 August
1977, under the heading "57-year target", in which the Labour member claims "The
National Government's ambition of single-figure inflation would take 57 years to accomplish
at the present rate of improvement"; and, if so, is his claim correct, and how does the
present National Government's handling of the rate of inflation compare with the Labour
Government's record?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics) replied: I have seen the statement
referred to, and the honourable member for Wanganui has ignored the reductions in the rate
of inflation that the Government had achieved by the June quarter 1977, when the inflation
curve had declined to an annual rate of some 14 percent. Had he used this June quarter
figure he would have come up with a totally different answer, much closer to that of the
OECD survey report, which records a clear deceleration in the rate of inflation in 1976 and
early 1977 in New Zealand. Whereas the Government, in the 18 months since it took office,
has made significant reductions in the annual rate of inflation, the second Labour Goven-
ment in its first 18 months permitted the annual rate of inflation to treble, from some 1.9
percent to 5.8 percent, which is very close to the performance of the third Labour
Government, when the rate rose from 5.5 percent in December 1972 to 15.7 percent in
December 1975.

National Superannuation and Concessions
70. Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: Has he
seen the comments of the member for Wanganui, as recorded in the Wanganui Herald dated
10 August 1977, in which the member is reported as claiming "there were many snags in the
scheme (national superannuation) only now being felt by different sectors of society. Many
old people were alarmed to find that concessions on telephones, television sets, and rail
travel had been removed¨, and, if so, what was the National Party's published policy on
concessions, which section of beneficiaries, if any, has lost these concessions, and have
beneficiaries been adequately compensated by increases in the rate of national superannua-
tion?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: Yes, I have seen the article
referred to. The Government's 1975 election manifesto and the associated publicity material
dealing with national superannuation made it quite clear that telephone and television
concessions will continue to be available to national superannuitants at the same rates and
with the same income tests as applied when National took office. This is exactly what the
Government has done. At the time the Government took office, the income limits for the
concessions, under the former age benefit scheme, were $88.20 a week for married couples
and $60.80 a week for unmarried persons. In accordance with our manifesto undertaking,
these income limits still apply. The only section of beneficiaries who no longer qualify for
concessions are those national superannuitants whose income exceeds the qualifying limit.
All these people have had substantial increases in their cash-in-hand payments under
national superannuation. The New Zealand Railways travel concession is still available to all
former age beneficiaries now receiving national superannuation, and will not be withdrawn
until August 1978 when the rate of national superannuation will be based on 80 percent of
the average ordinary-time weekly wage for a married couple. Several public statements have
been made to this effect. When national superannuation reaches 80 percent of the average
ordinary-time weekly wage for a married couple, the relationship between the benefit and
the average ordinary-time weekly wage will be such that further concessions will no longer
be justified.

able member will be aware that the problem of model proliferation in the New Zealand

an accident, but he may not have been the one at fault.

Maori Employment Incentives
94. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) asked the Prime Minister: In view of his statement
in the New Zealand Herald of 18 August urging companies to employ more young Maoris
in the professions, trades, and other skilled occupations", and warning that "an already
grave social problem would become dangerously worse unless rapid improvement was
brought about", what incentives is he proposing for companies to ensure that this is done,
and what steps is he taking to ensure that the young Maoris receive the training necessary to
fill these positions?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied on behalf of
the Prime Minister. I must apologise for the length of the answer to this question, but it is a
very important question and the member for Northern Maori may wish to submit a further
question for written answer to obtain more details. The Prime Minister's answer is as
follows: "To take the second part of the question first, a number of substantial developments
in the area of job training for young Maoris are either being studied or being implemented.
For example: first, an inter-departmental committee is presently engaged in examining
programmes for raising the socio-economic status of the non-European population. This
involves job sponsorship, bursaries, and scholarships to encourage professional training and
promotion of various Maori activities. Secondly, the Vocational Training Council is
currently conducting research on the attitudes and behaviour of the multi-cultural work force
by initially studying five New Zealand companies. Thirdly, Cabinet has approved for 1978
pre-employment courses for young Maoris from areas where no apprenticeship oppor-
tunities exist. The courses, which will be concerned with introducing young rural Maoris to
the urban life and urban employment, have a target intake for 1978 of 90 boys and 125 girls.
Trainees will be able to pass the first qualifying test for the Trades Certification Board
examination, which will become the main attraction to an employer. Fourthly, the trade
training schemes will be extended in 1978 with the addition of four new courses, provision
for 56 more trainees, and the establishment of the scheme at the Taranaki Polytechnic, New
Plymouth. This will mean that 16 different courses will be offered to 370 trainees at 5 centres
throughout New Zealand in 1978. Fifthly, on 29 July 1977 the Minister of Labour announced
the extension of the private sector employment subsidy scheme, which is virtually concerned
with arming young people with skills, qualifications, and work qualifications needed to
enable them to enter the labour market. If these employment schemes and studies presently
under way are successful, it is my hope that there will be little need for the Government to
provide any company with further incentives to employ young Maoris."
(26/8/77)
Inter-island Freight Rates-"Iron Bridge" Concept
95. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) asked the Minister of Railways: Has he seen the
statement by Mr C. W. Campbell, president of the Canterbury Manufacturers Association,
in the Christchurch Star of 16 August advocating the "iron bridge" concept for inter-island
freight rates utilising the Cook Strait rail ferries, and, if so, will he undertake, after
consultation with the Minister of Regional Development, to investigate this concept with a
view to its implementation?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Defence) replied on behalf of the Minister of
Transport. "Yes, I have read the statement referred to. The "iron bridge" concept has been
advocated on several occasions in the past, even during the term of the last Labour
Government, which adopted a limited alternative scheme, known as the unit rate scheme,
under which the North and South Island rail portions of the journey are treated as a single
journey for charging purposes and an additional charge is made for the transport across
Cook Strait. The Government is fully aware of the need to foster regional development in
the South Island, and this has been recognised in the 1977 Budget, which provides for the
introduction of a differential between north-bound and south-bound inter-island freight
charges in the net freight rate review. I understand from the Minister of Regional Develop-
ment that details of this proposal, which will be designed with the object of assisting South
Island industries supplying North Island markets, have not yet been finalised, but the matter
is currently being studied by the Department of Trade and Industry."

Ocean Beach Co.-Breach of Wage Freeze Regulations
96. Mr N. P. H. JONES (Invercargill) asked the Minister of Labour: Would he advise
whether prosecutions have been authorised against the Ocean Beach Co. freezing workers,
and would he also confirm that a prosecution may be taken against the Ocean Beach Co. for
a breach of the Wage Freeze Regulations?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: I propose to deal separately with each
part of the question since two separate matters are involved. In respect of the first part of the
question, I set forth the position in some detail to avoid confusion over the meaning of the
word "authorise". On Tuesday 14 June 1977 an incident at the Ocean Beach Freezing Works
resulted in the condemning of several hundred carcasses. I asked the Department of Labour
to investigate the incident and take appropriate action should there appear to have been
breaches of the law. On 12 July the Solicitor-General gave authority, pursuant to the
appropriate rules-SR 1958/205-for the department to instruct the Crown Solicitor in
Invercargill. As is normal in cases where there is a substantial number of possible defen-
dants, the Solicitor-General pointed out that the department, as prosecuting authority, must
be satisfied, in respect of each individual defendant, that there is sufficient evidence to
establish a prima facie case. On that point, the prosecuting authority must be guided by the
advice of the Crown Solicitor. On 20 July instructions were forwarded to the Crown Solicitor
in Invercargill. Since then, he has made a procedural application to the registrar of the
Industrial Court concerning the form of proceedings to be used. That application has been
granted by the registrar. The Crown Solicitor is required to examine the briefs of evidence,
and prepare the necessary documents. At present he is engaged upon completing those
tasks. I expect that proceedings will be commenced by the filing of informations in the near
future. I am unable to give an exact date, nor can I give an exact number of defendants. I
point out that all informations need not be filed on the same day. Turning now to the second
part of the question, I reply that investigations by the department are still continuing in
respect of the alleged breach by the Ocean Beach Freezing Co. Ltd of the Wage Freeze
Adjustment Regulations.

Container Ports-Congestion
97. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Transport: Is it correct that the main
New Zealand exporters fear major congestion at New Zealand container ports when the new
export season begins, and, if so, what corrective measures are being taken?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Defence) replied on behalf of the Minister of
Transport. "There is some concern amongst exporters that congestion will be a possibility
later this year, and probably into 1978. I have repeatedly impressed on harbour boards and
terminal operators the need to be prepared, and the necessity for completion of their
planning and infrastructures. Some delays have been experienced over the year, and I know
that the shipping lines feel that the present facilities will be sorely tested over the next 15
months or so. The lines do say, however, that they are confident that once the current
developments are completed there will be adequate facilities for the expected levels of
container services. In the meantime, the lines are throwing their weight behind the transport
co-ordinating committees which either have been, or are being set up in each container
terminal area to plan the most effective use of berthage and facilities. The lines are also
endeavouring, where possible, to rationalise the services to minimise berthage congestion. I
am, however, still concerned that more may need to be done, and to that end both my
officials and I are keeping the matter under review with a view to taking any necessary
action."

Trade Union Trust Fund-Payments by Non-union Workers
109. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Labour: Is he aware that the
National Party's election manifesto states on page 6 of the industrial relations section for
those who are allowed to opt out of compulsory unions the appropriate fees will in future be
paid into a trade union trust fund, and, if so, is it still the Government's policy that those who
vote against compulsory unions, and leave, will still have to pay the equivalent of union fees
to the trade union trust fund, and, if not why not?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: The member is confusing two distinct
areas of policy. On the one hand, there is the question of ballots on the unqualified
preference provision. If the majority vote is against the unqualified preference provision,
then there would be no compulsion to belong to the union. Persons who subsequently leave
the union will not be required to pay the equivalent of the union subscription to any other
authority or fund. On the other hand, there is the question of persons who are bound by the
unqualified preference provision seeking exemption from union membership. As yet there
has been no change to the provisions of the Industrial Relations Act 1973 relating to
exemption from union membership on conscientious grounds. The trust fund has its
constitution in draft form, as I indicated in answer to question 107.

Forest Service-Planting of Native Trees
118. Mr LAMBERT (Western Hutt) asked the Minister of Forests To what extent is the
Forest Service planting native trees for either production or conservation purposes?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: The Forest Service has planted more
than 600 hectares with indigenous species for conservation, amenity, preservation, and
enrichment purposes. It should be noted that many thousands of hectares have been
restocked in native trees by natural regeneration in production forests of beech, tawa, and
podocarp species. For the kauri forests, a policy of enrichment planting has been in practice
since 1932, and 48 000 seedlings are being planted each year to cover some 130 hectares. In
podocarp forest areas of the Rotorua, Wellington, Nelson, Westland, and Southland
conservancies some 200 hectares are being planted annually mainly with rimu, with smaller
areas of totara, kahikatea, and matai. The total number of seedlings used is about 70 000. In
addition the Forest Research Institute is to plant some 20 hectares of podocarp species at
Tihoi, Horohoro, and Whirinaki this year, and will use some 8000 seedlings in a variety of
research trials in those ares. As a result of the indigenous forest policy, logged forests, in
which regeneration is more difficult, are being retained as native forests, rather than cleared
for pasture and plantation, and planting of native trees in such areas could increase. In
addition, the Forest Service provides indigenous species to a wide range of organisations for
amenity, ornamental, and conservation planting. These include other Government depart-
ments, schools, environmental societies, and the Chatham Islands.

ship of the offeree company prior to the newspaper offer, and where there is much doubt as

without actually giving notice of or making that offer, will be regarded as an attempt to
create a false market in either share." It remains to be seen how effective the takeover code
will prove without legislative sanctions.

an offer of overseas loans at low interest rates, as reported in the Dominion of 12 August?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance) replied: Overseas offers of funds
were made in Auckland and the Auckland local authorities sensibly sought the views of the
Government on financing capital works by overseas borrowing. The Government indicated
that it would be unable to agree to overseas borrowing for the following reasons: first, the
works proposed to be undertaken by the two authorities, the Auckland Regional Authority
and the Auckland City Council, were purely local in nature. Secondly, they contained little
or no overseas content; and thirdly-and this reason is of more importance-the Govern-
ment's information suggested that the terms proposed were less favourable than were
generally available on the market.

Gear Meat Company-Borthwick's Takeover Proposal
139. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister of Agriculture:
How does he reconcile the statement by the Prime Minister on 20 May that the proposed
Borthwick takeover of the Gear Meat Co. was "aimed at streamlining and rationalising the
throughput of meat, and that's a desirable thing" with the same Minister's statement last
week that "Cabinet had accepted the view that approval of the Borthwick proposal would
have meant a high degree of monopoly in the southern part of the North Island"?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: By taking two small quotations
out of quite long articles one can play any tune. However, I see no conflict in the Prime
Minister's statements of 20 May and 22 August. I agree with the Prime Minister's remarks in

desirable thing. However, the disadvantage, as pointed out by the Prime Minister in the
statement last week, was shown by the full investigation made by the Meat Industry
Authority and the Meat Producers Board in their recommendation that a Borthwick's
takeover would have meant a high degree of monopoly in the southern part of the North
Island. On balancing the pros and cons, the Government accepted the recommendations of
the Meat Producers Board and the Meat Industry Authority that the application should be
declined.

Sheep Numbers

the recent press announcement of a 3.5 percent increase in sheep numbers?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: The recent press report of a 3.5
percent increase in sheep numbers at 30 June of this year compared with last year's figure is
based on an estimate produced by the Meat and Wool Boards economic service. My
ministry's estimate, however, is for a larger increase of 4.3 percent, on the basis of sheep
numbers this year being 2 410 000 higher than last year's figure of 56 400 000. This latter
estimate takes account of the pattern of this season's ewe and lamb kill, mortality, last
season's lambing percentages, and other factors. There is, indeed, good reason to believe
that farmers, taking advantage of recently introduced incentives, retained a higher propor-
tion of ewe lambs last season.

Home Loans Fùnd (NZ) No. 2 Ltd
147. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Minister of Justice: Has he seen
prospectus No. 1, dated 31 March 1977, of Home Loans Fund (N.Z.) No. 2 Ltd, and, if so, is
he satisfied that it meets legal requirements and that investors' money is adequately
safeguarded?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied on behalf of the Minister of
Justice. He has seen the prospectus which was registered by the district registrar of
companies at Christchurch on 31 March. The fact that the prospectus has been registered is
prime facie evidence that the registrar was satisfied that it complies with the law. It is not a
function of the department to give financial advice and it would be irresponsible of him to
say whether a particular investment was adequately safeguarded. The legal requirements are
designed to provide a minimum standard of disclosure about the issuing company. Given
that information, the prospective investor or his professional adviser must form an opinion
based on past performance, profitability, the present state of the company, and the terms of
the current issue of shares or options. Safeguards depend on continuing disclosure, economic
factors, financial structure and controls, and above all good management. All a prospectus
can do is to disclose relevant information relating to the recent past. It can never guarantee
adequate safeguards for the future or eliminate informed risk taking, which is inherent in any
commercial investment.

Housing Corporation Variable Mortgage Scheme
155. Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) asked the Minister of Housing: Can he indicate
when the Housing Corporation's variable mortgage repayment scheme was introduced and
why it was thought necessary to have such a scheme, and can he confirm that it has now been
withdrawn?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: The variable mortgage repay-
ment scheme was introduced in 1974 to help lower-income borrowers service repayments in
the initial years of home ownership and provide them with an opportunity to consolidate
their finances at a time when their income was under the greatest pressure. I confirm that the
variable mortgage scheme has been withdrawn, but this is temporary only to allow the
Housing Corporation the opportunity to evaluate altered repayment patterns following the
recent changes in its rate of interest to borrowers. The concept of this scheme has been
retained meanwhile by offering borrowers "interest only" repayments where the need for
assistance is established.

Native Forest Desecration
156. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Forests: Has he read the article
entitled "Desecration of native forest by logging must stop" in the August issue of Forest and
Bird, in which evidence of a programme of clear felling, widespread erosion, and soil dams is
presented, and, if so, can he say whether any action has been taken to stop such practices
employed by C. and A. Odlin Timber Co. Ltd and D. Elliott, and, if not, why not?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: I have read the article and the area
described is in private ownership. The Forest Service has no power to prevent the sale of
timber from privately owned land. The possible risk of erosion that may result from the road
construction mentioned in the article is a matter for the Manawatu Catchment Board. The
local committee of the Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society has commented on an
excellent stand of forest alongside the logging road, but the article does not make it clear
whether the stand is in the area being logged or in the land owned by Odlins through which
the logging road passes, but which has not been logged. There is very little prospect of
stopping the present logging at this stage. Most of the private forest land in the area is owned
by Odlins Ltd, and the Forest Service has been negotiating with that company since early
1976 to see if some exchange arrangements could be made. However, there are problems in
locating sufficient suitable land, and exotic wood supplies from State forests as an alternative
form of exchange are limited. Negotiations are continuing with Odlins.

## p. 2952 (#590) ###########################################

2952
14 September
Questions and Replies
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: The recent approval referred to
for David Northfield Developments Ltd. to borrow $2 million overseas was given by the
Overseas Investment Commission because the application complied with the commission's
existing criteria. Current and longstanding policy, apart from some minor changes, is that
overseas loans are approved if the following conditions are met: (1) the loan is for at least 12
months and has a fixed basis of repayment; (2) the loan is drawn down within 6 months of
the date of formal consent; (3) any interest payable is at a rate no higher than the
appropriate market rate for the currency concerned; and (4) the proceeds are transferred to
New Zealand through a trading bank or used overseas for some approved purpose. The
recent Government decision to decline the applications by the Auckland Regional Authority
and the Auckland City Council to borrow money overseas for their capital works programme
is in keeping with the policy of successive Governments towards local authority borrowing
since the 1930s. This policy is that local authorities may be permitted to borrow overseas
only where the project involves major revenue undertakings and is in the national interest. A
recent example of such a loan approval is the 1976 loan of about $30 million for container
port development, which was arranged through a Government agency. As indicated by the
Associate Minister of Finance in answer to a question in August, the Auckland Regional
Authority and Auckland City Council applications were declined because the projects
concerned were purely local in nature and the particular loan offers were considered inferior
to the terms that could have been possible in the capital markets concerned.

Questions and Replies
Teaching of Reading, Primary School Teachers
164. Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei) asked the Minister of Education: Has he seen the article
in the Dominion of Tuesday, 30 August, which quotes an American education expert, Dr
Alan Purves, as saying that New Zealand primary school teachers are terrific at teaching
reading, and, if so, can he cite any research findings which back up what Dr Purves said?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: I have read the article in the
Dominion of Tuesday, 30 August, and am able to cite research that supports the statements
made by Dr Purves. In 1970 the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational
Achievement, usually known as the IEA, conducted reading surveys in 15 countries. Results
showed that 14-year-old and 17-year-old pupils in New Zealand had higher scores than
children in any of the other countries including England, Scotland, and the United States of
America. Dr Purves visited New Zealand to look for the reasons for this high level of
achievement among New Zealand children. In 1952 the New Zealand Council for Educa-
tional Research standardised for use in New Zealand a set of reading tests prepared by the
Australian Council for Educational Research. Thirteen years later, in 1965, reading stan-
dards were again surveyed using the same tests in the same schools. This showed that reading
standards had been maintained, and for 80 percent of the children surveyed had improved.
In 1968 the New Zealand Council for Educational Research standardised its own test of
reading for New Zealand schools. In 1974 NZCER staff carried out a check on standards
using a comparable sample of children from the same schools. The results showed compar-
able standards between 1968 and 1974. On the basis of this survey the NZCER decided there
was no need to restandardise its reading tests. These research findings are helpful because
they provide an international basis of comparison, and on these comparisons they indicate
that New Zealand standards of reading compare favourably. But there can be no room for
complacency or any resting on our laurels. My department and the teaching profession are
constantly striving to find more effective ways of teaching reading.
(6/9/77)
Overseas Loan, Mr David Northfield
165. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Minister of Finance: Was an investiga-
tion carried out into the financial backing of Mr David Northfield before permission was
given for him to raise a $2 million overseas loan for property development purposes, and
what protection is ensured for purchasers of sections should Mr Northfield for any reason be
unable to meet his commitments?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: No investigation was carried
out into the financial backing of Mr David Northfield before consent was given by the
Overseas Investment Commission to borrow $2 million overseas. The commission's function
is to determine whether overseas borrowing is desirable, and whether the terms of the
particular loans are acceptable. The question of the financial standing of the borrower is a
matter for the lender to assess, and protection for the purchasers of sections is similarly not a
matter which the Overseas Investment Commission is required to supervise.

Railways Signalmen-Appointment of Women
167. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga), on behalf of Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon), asked
the Minister of Railways: Has he read the report in the Dominion of 26 August 1977 about
the difficulty the Railways Department has in hiring signalmen, and, if so, could he inform
the House if the department would consider women for these positions and whether the
department's advertisements are worded in a manner that would attract both sexes?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: I have read the report in the
Dominion of 26 August 1977 about the difficulties experienced by the Railways Department
in filling vacant signalmen's positions. The Government Railways (Staff) Regulations
governing appointments to positions of signalmen require appointees to have been desig-
nated as shunter and to have served as a shunter for not less than 6 months. Only existing
Railways staff who qualify in terms of the regulations are eligible for appointment as
signalmen. The advertising of vacant signalmen's positions by departmental circular does not
discriminate against women. At present there are no females employed who qualify in terms
of the regulations for appointment as signalmen. As I have mentioned in reply to a previous
question, a working party is investigating ways and means of resolving the problems the
department is experiencing in filling signalmen's positions.

Fire Safety Legislation
169. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Internal Affairs: Has he seen
the comment of Sir Jack Hunn as reported in the Evening Post of 23 August 1977, where he
said that "Fire safety legislation must be put right with desperate urgency, and, if this is
indeed the case, is it the intention of the Government to take legislative action to tidy up the
situation?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs) replied: I have seen the report in which
Sir Jack Hunn was repeating his well known views that as a matter of urgency regulations
should replace bylaws for fire safety standards for building construction. Successive Govern-
ments have preferred that these standards should be determined through the consultative
process of the Standards Association of New Zealand and then issued as model bylaws to be
adopted by territorial authorities. This procedure provides much more flexibility for
amendments made necessary by technological development and the requirements of indi-
vidual districts. Fire safety bylaws must be adopted by all territorial authorities and they
must have the approval of the Minister of Local Government. I do not consider that the
present legislation is in need of urgent attention along the lines suggested.

AGRICULTURAL WORKERS BILL
Mr LUXTON (Piako): I am directed by the Labour Committee to present the report of
the committee on the Agricultural Workers Bill. The committee recommends that the Bill be
allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie upon the table. I shall
summarise some of the committee's amendments. In clause 1 the commencement date will
now be 1 November. The definition of agricultural worker in clause 2 has been amended to
clarify exactly who is covered by the Bill.
Under the provisions of clause 9, which deals with the application of Part II and Part IV,
State employees are not covered by the existing Act in regard to wage fixing and conditions
of employment. That position will be retained by excluding the application of Part II and
Part IV to workers whose wages were prescribed by the State Services Commission
immediately before the commencement date of this legislation. Part II refers to classes of
agricultural workers and Part IV to the settlement of disputes.
Three amendments have been made to clause 10. It will now be mandatory for the


## p. 2968 (#606) ###########################################

2968
14 September
Agricultural Workers Bill
registrar of the tribunal to require copies of any application under this clause to be served on
those organisations he considers will be affected by the application. Previously only
agricultural organisations could receive copies. In addition, only agricultural organisations
would appear and be heard as a party to an application. This was considered too narrow, and
discretion has now been vested in the president of the tribunal to allow other organisations
or persons to appear and be heard if he considers they might be affected by the result of the
application.
Clause 14 makes it clear that the basis on which membership strength of the agricultural
organisations is to be compared is the financial membership in the recognised categories for
which registration is held or sought. An amendment has been made to this clause, and
organisations registered under the Bill will now be required to provide in their rules for
purging their membership registers by striking off unfinancial members. Clause 14A is a new
clause inserted by the committee to spell out the effects of registering an agricultural
organisation. Registration renders an organisation and its members subject to the jurisdic-
tion of conciliation councils, the Agricultural Tribunal, and the Industrial Court. The
jurisdiction of the Agricultural Tribunal to interpret awards has been removed from clause
21. This was in conflict with the jurisdiction given to the Industrial Court under clause 28 to
decide any interpretation disputes.
Clause 29 covers conciliation. The number of nominated members of conciliation
councils has been amended. Instead of 6 persons with a maximum of 10 from each
organisation, membership will now be up to 4 with provision for a maximum of 6. The
applicant organisation will determine the number of members. Under clause 31 the Agricul-
tural Tribunal will now have the option of deciding to make an award in any case. Although
not likely to be used frequently, this is a very important power which will enable the tribunal
to retain the status quo in an appropriate case.
Clause 32 has been amended to prevent the parties themselves from varying the terms of
an award in an individual case. If the terms of the award are inappropriate, the parties will be
able to apply to the tribunal for a total or partial exemption. The tribunal could grant the
application either wholly or partially, and either unconditionally or subject to conditions, or
refuse to grant an exemption. An amendment has been made to clause 34 to prevent the
backdating of awards prior to the date of expiry of the previous award. Clauses 38, 38A and
38B have also been amended.
Under clause 40 penalty actions under Part IV of the Bill, apart from actions for the
recovery of wages, will now be subject to a limitation period of 12 months. Under the Bill
originally introduced actions for the recovery of arrears of wages were to be taken in the
same manner as actions under the Industrial Relations Act. To clarify the position, clause 41
has been amended to spell out the method of recovering such moneys without reference to
the Industrial Relations Act.
Clause 49 covering the safety of workers was discussed at length, and has been slightly
modified to make employers responsible for the safety of their workers only, and not for
other persons lawfully on the land or premises. The term "employer" for the purposes of this
section will include agricultural contractors. The fines have been reduced to $1,000 and $50
respectively.
Some amendments have been made to the schedule to bring it into line with existing
circumstances. The schedule is intended to cover only those classes of agricultural worker
that have already been defined by Orders in Council under the Agricultural Workers Act.
As originally drafted the schedule did not reflect the present position. The amendments
ensure that agricultural organisations retain their present coverage.
I thank the parties who appeared before the committee. The committee was able to hear
all those who wanted to make representations to it, and it also studied written submissions.
The Opposition has voiced its objection to the principle behind the Bill, but Opposition
members of the committee assisted greatly as the clauses in the Bill were examined, and I am
very grateful for their assistance.
