FINANCE (INFLATION-ADJUSTED BONDS) BILL
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. I move the second reading with a good deal of pleasure, because this legislation
is a very important part of the National Party's election policy. As members know, it is very
similar to the two private member's Bills introduced by the member for Piako during the
term of the Labour Government, which were hotly opposed by that Government and not
permitted to proceed. Doubtless, during this debate we will be given the reasons for that. It
may be that Labour members will have changed their minds, but certainly the Government
sticks to the view it held in 1974, that this is good legislation at a time of high inflation.
The Bill's sole purpose is to authorise the issue of inflation-adjusted savings bonds. It
provides that the bonds will be issued under Part III of the New Zealand Loans Act 1953,
which relates to the issue and registration of Government stock. Suitable modifications have
to be made so that Part III of that Act can apply to the bonds. The Bill, therefore, provides
that the bonds will be non-transferable, may be issued to individuals of or over the age of 7
years, and that, in addition to interest, there may be payable to holders of the bonds at
redemption a premium calculated on the basis of the inflation occurring between the issue of
the bonds and their redemption.
The interest, which at present is proposed at 2 percent, will be paid annually by cheque
on 1 July. The premium, or the inflation-proofing, will be paid at the end of the term the
bond carried, not necessarily the minimum period of 5 years, but possibly longer-and will
be calculated at the time the bond is redeemed. It will represent the difference in the
consumer price index between the time the bond was taken out and the time it is
redeemed-which effectively inflation-proofs the bond. The purchasing power of the bonds
at the date on which the funds are lodged will be retained.
The terms of issue will provide that, subject to certain exceptions, the bonds will not be
repayable until 5 years from the date of issue have elapsed. The inflation premium, payable
at redemption, will be calculated on the basis of the movement in the all-groups consumer
price index published by the Government Statistician-in other words, the index that is
published quarterly—and the nearest completed quarter to the date of the transaction will be
taken for the calculations. The bonds may be repayable at an earlier date than the end of the
5-year period where the bondholder is aged 60 years or more. The proceeds of the bonds are
to be used by a bondholder towards the acquisition of a dwelling, farm, or fishing vessel in
the manner provided by the Home Ownership Savings Act 1974, the Farm Ownership
Savings Act 1974, the fishing vessels ownership savings legislation that is to be introduced as
a result of the Budget announcement, or where application for repayment is made by the
administrator of the estate of a deceased or bankrupt bondholder.
The terms of issue of the bonds provide that applications must be made for a minimum
of $100 and in multiples of $50 thereafter. The maximum amount for which application may
be made in any one year is $1,000, and the maximum amount that may be held by any one


## p. 2973 (#611) ###########################################

14 September
2973
Finance (Inflation-Adjusted Bonds) Bill
individual is $5,000. The inflation premium payable on redemption of the bonds will be free
of income tax, and an appropriate amendment will be included in the Income Tax
Amendment Bill (No. 2), which will be introduced shortly. In addition to the inflation
premium, interest will be paid on the amount of the bonds at the rate of 2 percent per
annum, commencing from the date of lodgment of application. This interest will be liable for
income tax. The bonds will be available from the Reserve Bank, trading banks, post offices,
trustee banks, and sharebrokers; and will be available shortly after this legislation receives
the royal assent.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): Obviously, English does not
mean the same today as it did in 1974 or 1975, because the Minister of Finance said that this
Bill is very similar to the two introduced by the member for Piako. I have one of those Bills,
as well as the Bill we are discussing, and I find that, although the Bill that members are asked
to discuss and adjudicate on has two clauses, an analysis, and an explanatory note of nearly
two lines, one of the Bills introduced by the member for Piako has one and one-third pages
of explanation and six and a half pages of text-and we are told that they are similar.
We are being asked to legislate on a kind of IOU basis, and to leave everything to the
good faith of the Minister of Finance. Some of my colleagues will have quite a lot to say
about that, but at this stage I want simply to draw attention to what the Prime Minister-the
Minister of Finance-said in Budget press statement 56, which comprised nearly two pages
and ended up by stating: "The Government will be keeping a close watch on their progress
and may amend their terms or conditions of issue should the need to do so become
apparent." We therefore have a sort of E & OE Bill, with nothing very much in it. Most of
the matters will be dealt with by regulation, on principles that will be decided from time to
time by the Minister of Finance. In case anyone has any illusions about what is intended, the
Minister said that the legislation will be changed if the Government wants to do so.
Let us have a look at the Bill, and some of the comments made about it by members
opposite. The only clear definition is that individuals of or over the age of 7 years may
purchase these bonds, which are non-transferable. Beyond that, nothing is definite. Clause
2(1) states that at the time the bonds are redeemed, a further amount may-not "shall”—be
calculated on the basis of the inflation occurring between the issue of the bonds and their
redemption. Why the difference? I presume this is another area that can be changed if the
Minister of Finance thinks it is appropriate. Although we have heard quite a bit about these
bonds, no mention has been made of the amount. Who will benefit from the bonds? From
the very limited information in the Bill, it would seem that the Government either does not
know at this stage, or does not want the public to know.
I draw the attention of Government members to the difference in the statements—not
in the Bill-about the purpose of this Bill and of those introduced by the member for Piako.
In the Budget press statement, reference was made to a minimum contribution of $100, and
then multiples of $50. In the Bill on which this Bill is allegedly based, the minimum sum was
$10, and then multiples of $10. It was claimed that this Bill is an attempt to inflation-proof
small savings. As I understand it, that is what the reference in the National Party's manifesto
pretty clearly indicated. Of course, we do not know whether we are looking at the slim,
glossy manifesto, or the fat, dull version. But there is a world of difference between the two
Bills. One provides for $10 bonds, and $10 subsequent increments. That would provide some
assistance to small savers. But the Budget statement announcing $100 to start with, with $50
increments, would hardly come into the small-savings category, unless it is for a particular

Mr LUXTON (Piako): I welcome the Finance (Inflation Adjusted Bonds) Bill. It

The Minister of Finance, in opening the second reading debate, said that the sole purpose of

The Bill provides that the bonds will be issued under Part III of the New Zealand Loans

have known that this is just an empowering Bill to allow the issue of the proposed bonds

## p. 2976 (#614) ###########################################

2976
14 September
Finance (Inflation-Adjusted Bonds) Bill
the past? However, the Bill provides that only those people who are prepared to invest their
money for for 5 years will receive a 2 percent return.
At this stage the scheme must be viewed in comparison with other types of investment
available. The Post Office national development bonds return 5.98 percent per annum over a
period of 8 years. The Post Office also introduced savings certificates during the time the
Deputy Leader of the Opposition was Minister of Finance, and under that scheme people
receive a return of 6.96 percent on their investment. More recently, the series B savings
certificates have been introduced, giving a return of 10 percent. The important point about
each of those investments is that after a 5-year period the investors are entitled to $500 tax-
free income. I consider that represents a really high return for any investor.
The savings bonds provide an avenue of investment for the very small saver, and ensure
that his purchasing power is retained. The Bill provides for an initial investment of $100 with
multiples of $50 for each subsequent investment. Secondly, it provides for a maximum
investment of $1,000 per person in any one year. Thirdly, it provides for a total investment
limit of $5,000 by any one person. Fourthly, bonds are issued only to those of 7 years of age
and over. Fifthly, the bonds are not transferable. Sixthly, the inflation premium is calculated
from the date of issue to redemption.
Mr Marshall: The ones in the member's Bill were transferable.
Mr LUXTON: Yes, and I hope that some time in the future we may have transferable
bonds. That would be a cost to the person, but there would be a market value attaching to
them which would encourage such an investment. However, this is a step in the right
direction for people who do not want to trade in this type of commodity. The inflation
premium is calculated on the change in the all-groups consumer price index over a 5-year
period, when the purchasing power will remain constant. Seventh, there is a 2 percent
interest rate on the initial investment. In anyone's language that is not a very high return, but
there is 2 percent annually for those who are prepared to save for capital development.
The bonds will be available throughout the country at trading banks, savings banks, the
Post Office Savings Bank, and sharebrokers, as has been stated by the Prime Minister on
previous occasions. Once acquired they must be held for 5 years, but an opportunity is
provided for early redemption in certain circumstances—such as if the person holding the
bonds is over 60 years of age; for providing for a first home or a first farm; on the death or
bankruptcy of the holder. Under such conditions the bonds can be released.
I introduced a Bill in 1974 which provided for a 2 percent interest rate. Those bonds
would have been inflation-proofed, adjustable annually, and transferable for a fee. In 1975 I
introduced another Bill which provided for a nil interest rate but gave a guaranteed return of
5 percent. In any year in which inflation was higher than 5 percent it provided for a nil
interest return. Therefore, I believe that the scheme proposed in this Bill gives a better
return than the 1975 legislation would have—on the assumption that we will have inflation at
the rate of 5 percent or greater.
In studying a scheme such as this, one has to forecast from experience. Then you can say
what the interest rate would have been had the scheme been operating for some years. Two
years ago, when I introduced my Bill, I calculated figures for a 20-year period. They gave a
return of only 5.88 percent, but that was at a time when things had been stable under a
National Government for many years and that Government had been able to contain
inflation at acceptable levels. Knowing the trend that was being set in 1973 and 1974, I was
anxious that people who had not the skills to deal in money in an inflationary situation
should have some opportunity of providing for themselves, and I believe this measure will
make everyone in the community more conscious of his responsibilities. People will know
about costs no matter where they fall.
It is as well to remind the House that in 1972 the cost of living increased by 5.5 percent.
In 1973 the figure was 10 percent; in 1974 it was 12.6 percent, and in 1975, 15.7 percent. The
movement was onwards and upwards. We hope we can bring that back, but in considering
legislation like this we have to look at what is happening now and what has happened in the
immediate past. When I introduced my Bill 2 years ago the member for Manukau gave
several reasons why he believed it should not proceed. However, the Minister of Finance has
grappled with those problems.

at a time when the rate had to be held. However, in fact we have not had any improvement
in the inflation rate over that time. He also claimed that the scheme would divert savings

## p. 2982 (#620) ###########################################

Finance (Inflation-Adjusted Bonds) Bill
Let us take a more realistic example, a husband and wife with four children over seven.
They could invest $30,000 over a period of 5 years so that they would receive an annual and
largely tax-free payment every year. That seems to me to be a great deal higher advantage
than anybody in the lower brackets could possibly attract to himself.
What I want to talk about mostly is the terms of the Bill before us. Sometimes we are
accused of being too verbose in the way we cast our statutes. The economy of language in
this Bill is just about the ultimate; it is just about as laconic as it could be. More information
was provided in the Budget as to the objects of these so-called inflation-proof bonds. The
Budget stated that the bonds would have a minimum term of 5 years, and that their
redemption value would be increased in line with the increase in the consumer price index
over the period of the bond. This adjustment will be exempt from income tax, and in
addition interest will be paid at the rate of 2 percent per annum, and the interest will be
taxable.
Only private individuals aged 7 years or more will be entitled to hold the bonds, and
purchasers will be limited to $1,000 per annum for each individual, with a maximum holding
of $5,000. Of all that verbosity, the only detail that appears in the Bill is the 7 years of age
requirement, and I understand that appears simply because the principal Act has a limit of 10
years, and in order to change that there has to be a statutory alteration bringing it down to
seven. All the rest is not to be found in this minimal Bill of about half a dozen lines, and we
must imagine it ourselves.
The details available to us and to the public are to be found in a ministerial statement:
press statement No. 56. No matter how magisterial or domineering the Minister of Finance
may think his words are, they do not yet have the force of legislation. The statement that he
made contains some assurances, none of which is binding, and some disconcerting—and to
me quite frankly alarming-aspects. Let me turn first to the assurances. There was, first of
all, the provision that there will be a minimum subscription of $100, with multiples of $50
thereafter, a maximum investment of $1,000 in any 12-month period, and a maximum
holding by an individual of $5,000 at any time. The bonds may not be transferred.
At the end of 5 years the bonds will remain on issue until repayment is required by the
holder, and the inflation premiums will be determined by the movement in the all-groups
consumer price index over the period the bond is held. Additionally, it is said that
redemption will be available only where the registered holder is aged 60 or over. This is
another interesting development of the gratuities—the benefits-that the present Govern-
ment is conferring on people of 60 and upwards. Already they are entitled to national
superannuation, and it appears that if they subscribe to these bonds they will have an
entitlement that is not generally available to the rest of the community; so long as they are 60
or over, they will have the right to redeem these bonds within the period of 5 years that
applies to everybody else. This is another benefit to be conferred on the 60 to 65 age group
regardless of income.
Additional provisions are that the bonds may be redeemed if the proceeds are used for
the purchase of a first home or a first farm, or where the registered holder is deceased. Those
are the assurances. There are some other provisions that are not quite so assuring. If we
come down to the last paragraph of ministerial statement 56 that accompanied the Budget,
we find the provision that the Government will be keeping a close watch on the progress of
these bonds, and may amend their terms of conditions of issue should the need become
apparent.
I know it is not customary to write into legislation the terms upon which Government
bonds may be issued, but, if the Government is not prepared to confer statutory rights on
holders of these bonds, I think they and we are entitled to ask that the Government exhibits
to Parliament the terms of the contractual rights contained in the prospectus that becomes an
integral part of the bond. It seems that these bonds will be issued to people in terms of a
prospectus that will contain the provision that at some time during the currency of the bonds
the terms might be altered. In what way they might be altered we have not been told, and I
think that, as members of Parliament, we are entitled to know the provisions upon which
changes may be made to the terms and conditions of these bonds, as are the people who may
be induced into investing in them. I suggest that the least the Minister of Finance-who is the
Minister in charge of the Bill-can do is to table the prospectus upon which people will be
invited to subscribe to these bonds so that we know before they are exhibited to the public
the terms upon which there may be a change during the currency of the bond, and how the
terms may be altered.
I know the Minister of Finance said, echoing my words, that there might be a

who decide not to start a family for several years will have an opportunity to save the
necessary deposit for a house, because they will now have a real incentive. It is unrealistic to
expect that inflation will be reduced in a short time. The bonds will be a vital and important

designed to help the small investors, because the individual plays an important part in our
society.

measure. As has been pointed out, the compensation for the rate of inflation-whether it be

will be quite high, one has to compare the attraction of this investment with some of the fly-

Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau): It is obvious that Government members should
thank me for the speeches I made in 1974 and 1975, because without those speeches they
would have had some difficulty in finding anything to say this evening. It is true that while I
was a member of the Labour Government I made a number of criticisms of the measures
proposed by the member for Piako in 1974 and 1975. We should consider some of them to
see whether they are still as valid today as they were at that time.
A number of speakers have mentioned that I said then that if the principle of index
linking was established it would be difficult to limit its application, and that this could lead to
distortion. In support of that argument I want to quote from a report of the OECD
Committee on Financial Markets. Unlike a recent OECD report on New Zealand, this one
has not been tinkered with, and is the original version. On the principle of index linking the
report stated: "Partial data suggests strongly that the savings of the lower income groups


## p. 2988 (#626) ###########################################

2988
14 September
Finance (Inflation-Adjusted Bonds) Bill
tend to take a predominantly liquid form with few investments in long-term bonds. In other
words, this type of investment would not really have any benefit for the lower income
groups, while older age groups on all income levels are more concerned about the yield from
their investment, and may be likely to hold a large share of their financial investments in
long-term bonds. It follows from the consideration in the preceding paragraph that if the
prime aim is to protect certain income levels or age groups, indexation of long-term bonds
would be at best a rather imperfect instrument to use. Indexation of the principle forms of
small savings would be needed as well."
Marilyn Waring: Who wrote that?
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS: That means that the lower income groups, who are already
disadvantaged, would be under additional pressure. The member for Raglan asked who
wrote this. This is a report from the OECD Committee on Financial Markets, and it is one
report that has not been tinkered with on the instruction of the Government.
The second criticism I made was that inflation-proof bonds could well have psychologi-
cal repercussions by increasing the expectation of inflation at a time when it must be held.
On this particular point the OECD committee said: "A concern of Governments must also
be to guard against the risk that recourse to indexation would be interpreted by public
opinion as a sign that authorities were less firm in their determination to bring inflation
under control, and that a widespread use of indexation could fuel inflation." Government
members have attempted to ridicule the criticisms I made in 1974, but have not attempted to
answer the point I made, which is echoed by the OECD committee.
The third point I made was that this scheme could divert savings from non-indexed
financial assets to indexed financial assets. Again, the OECD committee had something to
say on this point: "If Government-sponsored indexation was perceived by savers as affording
more attractive yields for medium term than traditional non-index assets, such index savings
vehicles could drain off a growing body of funds to the detriment of the latter." Is the aim of
the Bill to divert savings from traditional non-indexed assets into inflation-proof bonds? If it
is, I should like the Government to say so. If it is not, let us have the reasons that will not
Occur.
The fourth point I made in 1974 was that uncontrolled interest rates on non-indexed
financial assets would tend to increase, and that that would lead to further pressure for
higher interest rates in controlled areas. I still believe that to be true. If the inflation rate
continues to be 15 percent to 20 percent, I am sure that finance companies will not sit back
quietly and allow inflation-proof assets to return 20 percent while they offer only 12 percent
to 13 percent on their debentures. I am sure they will increase the rate of interest they offer.
If that is not so, let us hear the reasons that it will not occur-and maybe Government
members will tell us how they will control those interest rates.
The next criticism I made was that higher interest rates could lead to higher costs in
some sectors, including housing, which might be hit if this occurred. Where is the money to
pay the interest on inflation-adjusted bonds to come from? If a person borrows $20,000 to
buy a house and the inflation rate is 15 percent, does that mean that if the $20,000 is
borrowed from the money invested in inflation-adjusted bonds the borrower will have to pay
back $23,000? If he does not have to pay back $23,000, who will make up the difference?
Will it be the taxpayer? If the money is invested with the Post Office, which in turn invests it
in the National Loans Account, does that mean that the Electricity Department will be
charged on its drawings at the annual rate of inflation, and, if so, will the price of electricity
be increased? That question must be answered. If the borrower does not pay the inflation
then who does? Obviously, it will be the small taxpayer and the small income earner and the
small saver, who cannot afford to take advantage of the bonds.
I also said in 1974 that there would be a risk of making more difficult and complicated
the implementation of the anti-inflationary policies that were being followed at that time.
The OECD report states: "The Finnish experience suggests that the introduction of
indexation on a wide scale complicates the task of Governments in fighting inflation when
faced with sizable inflationary cost impulses." Obviously the Government does not agree
with that comment; if so, I think we should be told.
I have a question for the next Government speaker to answer. Is it not a fact that for the
small saver inflation-proof bonds are the best investment he can make only if the rate of
inflation exceeds 12 percent? Once the inflation rate falls below that figure, the small saver
would be better off investing his money in debenture stock, which is returning 13 percent
interest at present. In fact, if the rate of inflation dropped below, say, 8 percent the small
saver would be better off investing in Government stock. I might add that, with the policies

Bill read a second time.
TRANSPORT AMENDMENT BILL (NO. 2)
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That this Bill be now read
a second time. Members will recall that when I introduced this Bill I explained the
mechanism of the mileage restriction which governs road/rail competition for the carriage of
goods. The restriction is contained in the goods-service licence that road transport carriers
need to operate their businesses. The necessary basic changes to the actual limit from 40
miles to 150 kilometres will be made by an amendment to the Transport Licensing
Regulations 1963, which will come into force at the same time as this Bill comes into
force on 1 October 1977.
The Bill is essentially of a machinery nature, designed to amend the Transport Act 1962
to conform with the change to the distance limit of 150 kilometres which will be made in the
Transport Licensing Regulations, and to achieve compatibility in other parts of the Act with
that change. On other occasions I have described the process by which the Government has
arrived at the 150-kilometre decision. The decision has not been taken lightly, but only after
studies, consultations, and discussions over several years, culminating in more intensive
deliberations in the last few months. Consultation has continued to take place since the
presentation of the Budget. We have all endeavoured to continue a system whereby any
inherent anomalies are as few as possible, and where the advantages of the change outweigh
them.
Clause 2 deals with section 109 of the Transport Act, which is concerned with people
who carry their own goods long distances. When a road carrier carries goods for other
people, he needs a goods-service licence. Section 109, as it stands at present, requires
persons such as manufacturers who carry their own goods with vehicles of over 2 tonnes, or
farmers with vehicles of over 5 tonnes, to have a goods-service licence. The amendment
contained in this Bill has the effect of bringing such persons under the same 150-kilometre
limit as the operator who carries other people's goods. This is done by deeming carriage over
long distances to be a goods service where over the route there is at least 150 kilometres of


## p. 2997 (#635) ###########################################

14 September
2997
Transport Amendment Bill (No. 2)
open Government railway not more than a third longer than the shortest available road
route. Thus a licence is required. Existing provisions allowing certain classes of goods to be
carried up to 75 miles will now be covered by the new general 150-kilometre provision.
However, the protection of the Murupara-Kawerau railway line for the carriage of logs will
be continued.
Clause 2 also amends the weight of a vehicle below which a goods-service licence is not
necessary and hence the distance restriction does not apply. A definition of weight for this
purpose is included. The vehicle weight has been raised from 2500 kilograms to 3500
kilograms. As before, the limit will remain at 5000 kilograms for persons carrying out
business as farmers, carrying any goods other than lime, which are owned by them and
carried in connection with their business. Licensing administration would be eased by this
change, and there would be some improvement in small vehicle use in such fields as retail
distribution, the movement of small scale builders' and contractors' plant, and the move-
ment of small urgent consignments. For the purposes of interpretation of what is meant by
"available route", clause 3 deems the Kaimai tunnel deviation to be open Government
railway.
Clause 4 amends part of section 113 of the Transport Act, which deals with specific cases
of carriage which are exempt from transport licensing. This amendment applies to the
carriage by cordial and carbonated-water manufacturers of cordials and carbonated waters
and other related goods. The 75-mile restriction that is now imposed will be raised to 150-
kilometres through the requirement to have a goods-service licence if there is available for
the carriage an available route that includes at least 150 kilometres of open Government
railway. The effect of clause 5 is to remove from the Transport Act the power of a public
body or the Secretary for Transport, when fixing charges for the carriage of goods, to
prescribe a minimum charge. As before, a fixed charge or a maximum charge may still he
prescribed. The minimum charge is being deleted to allow operators to take advantage of
economies of operation arising from the back-haul of goods. The savings that would result
could well lead efficient operators to offer rates below the present minimum.
Before I explain the intention of clause 6, I should like to comment on some features of
the new system as well as on the consequences of the fact that under the present system road
transport operators are confined to one licensing district except in special circumstances. Not
surprisingly, much discussion over the last few weeks has been about the actual level of the
distance restriction. The arbitrary nature of such a limit will always cause some anomalies to
arise, both within city boundaries and between certain centres; I have pointed that out to the
House before. The Government has carefully considered how any such anomalies might be
dealt with. It has discussed with the interested parties a range of options that attempt to solve
the anomalies. In each case, however, the options create more problems than they solve.
Therefore, we have decided that the 150-kilometre limit will be measured from the railway
station nearest to where the goods are loaded, just as the 40-mile limit did. Under the 40-
mile limit, licensing authorities have been able to cope with the sorts of anomalies that any
arbitrary mileage limit gives rise to, and should continue to be able to do so under the 150-
kilometre limit, on a case-by-case basis. There is no indication at this stage that this approach
would be unsatisfactory.
The other point I want to discuss is licensing districts. Members will no doubt be aware
that the Transport Licensing Regulations confine operators to specific districts, unless they
have a special licence. When the 150-kilometre limit comes into force many operators will, of
course, be entitled, on distance grounds, to cross district boundaries to eradicate this
potential anomaly in the transport licensing system. Clause 6 provides regulation-making
powers to solve this issue. As from the time the Bill is enacted, road transport operators will
be able to apply for an automatic amendment to their goods-service licences to authorise
them to carry on the goods services in all adjacent licensing districts provided the operation
is within 150 kilometres. This will stimulate economies of operation by encouraging road
transporters to carry back-haul loads. It will not, however, increase the area in which
licensees can operate in the same way as they do in their home districts. Any goods picked up
in the new districts into which the licences can now go will have to be destined for the home
district, or, in some cases, the home districts. Members will not find the details of these
regulatory measures in this Bill. What is necessary here is to provide enabling powers to
amend the Transport Licensing Regulations in the way I have just described.
In conclusion, I should say that our policy stated that we would co-ordinate
transport-and that is what we are doing-so that we could get the different modes of
transport doing what they can do best. We are giving people the right of choice so they can


## p. 2998 (#636) ###########################################

2998
14 September
Transport Amendment Bill (No. 2)
choose the way their goods shall travel. Despite the attempts made by the previous
Government, nothing major in this field has been done since 1936. Now we have placed
before Parliament what we believe to be good legislation. Road taxation is not dealt with in
this Bill, but will be the subject of other legislation yet to be introduced. This Bill merely
takes action to get rid of what the Government believes are needless restrictions that are
costing the country dearly. The railways are ready to compete in this field. The restrictions
have been costing the railways dearly, and they will be able to meet the public demand. It is
just a lot of piffle to say-
Mr Kirk: What!
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: It is what the honourable member for Sydenham usually
talks about-piffle. This will be beneficial to the New Zealand railways. They will be better
because they will be carrying out the mode of transport they can operate best, while the road
transport operators will be operating in the way that they do best.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): We have just heard the Minister introducing
legislation which I can describe only as a sledgehammer to crack a nut. The Bill essentially
implements the Budget statement that the 40-mile limit would be increased to 150
kilometres, and therefore the legislation was expected. As the Minister has said, I have
questioned some aspects of the legislation. I did so when the Budget was introduced and
when this Bill was introduced. I and my colleagues would certainly have preferred legislation
to phase in the proposals over a period of 2 or 3 years, thereby avoiding some of the obvious
anomalies which we are now experiencing through the introduction of an across-the-board
mandatory limit of 150 kilometres. I must say that I am not opposed to extending the limit,
but it should have been done in smaller stages, and then some of the anomalies we now see
would not exist. For example, at first we could have extended the limit to 60 miles, or the
equivalent in kilometres-say 95 kilometres. Then after 12 months it could have been
extended further, so giving an opportunity to survey the country from North Cape to the
Bluff to find out where anomalies were likely to arise. Perhaps a little distance could have
been added here and a little taken somewhere else, but I am sure that some of the difficulties
we will experience with a blanket 150-kilometre limit could have been avoided.
The Minister said that consultations and deliberations had gone on over a number of
years—and that is true-but consultation during the last 12 months has been almost non-
existent. It is the only time for a number of years that that has happened, and I regret it. We
have always had on-going consultations with the industry through the Transport Advisory
Council, but this time we have had this long gap between August of last year and June of this
year. If consultation had taken place then some of the anomalies that we see and which will
arise on 1 October could have been avoided. The Government should have listened
particularly to the men in the industry, but it preferred to take the advice only of the
economists or the desk jockeys in Government departments. It should have listened to the
advice which the practical transport operators were ready to give it; but that is now all in the
past.
The Minister has given me an assurance that there will be on-going consultation before
the distance charge comes into effect, and I only hope he will ensure that there is. I know
that some discussions have taken place, but I hoped there would have been more. I should
like the Minister to tell me, when he replies, if an opportunity will be given to interested
organisations to have further discussions with him and his officers before the regulations
under clause 6 are drafted. There is not much time between the passage of this Bill and 1
October. This is only the second reading. We have still to have the Committee stage and the
third reading before we can see the regulations. Perhaps they are in draft form now. Will the
road transport industry be consulted by the Minister about them?
I am surprised that the Minister introduced the mandatory distance provision in clause
2. He said in Ashburton on 17 June last year that, because of different locations and the
features of different areas, an across-the-board relaxation could hurt not only the Railways
and road transport operators, but also the areas. He said he needed 4 or 5 months to deal
with such matters, and I am sorry that the Minister was not successful in continuing with that
concept. He was absolutely right 12 months ago in his opposition to the mandatory extension
from 40 miles to 150 kilometres; he was quoted in the Christchurch Press on 17 June. The
Minister would have had much more support, not only in this House but throughout the
country, if he had provided for some flexibility within the industry, as he intended doing 12
months ago.
Members on this side of the House do not believe that the setting of an arbitrary limit
will solve the problems of road and rail competition, no matter at what distance the plug is

2999
Transport Amendment Bill (No. 2)
put in. Factors such as commodities in the various regions, regional characteristics, seasonal
demands, warehouse operations, handling facilities and so on, and two-way loading oppor-

should have been the keynote in drafting the legislation to introduce this new concept. That

the "think tank" to decide that a blanket limit is appropriate.
The reality is that there are wide variations in the pattern of industrial development, and
the needs of various regions, transport demands, and commodities. Some of the anomalies
of this blanket extension are known already. Many of the smaller towns with perhaps only
one major industry will be unable to take advantage of the new extension because they might
be just beyond the 150-kilometre limit, while the arteries into the big centres will be wide
open and overserviced by road and rail. Half-empty trucks and railway wagons could be
running side by side; that is not in anybody's interest. The Bill makes a mockery of planned
regional development, and will only accelerate the process of decay in the small centres. The
problem would not arise if relaxation had been on a regional or a commodity basis. A great
deal of discussion and consultation would have been necessary, but a solid foundation for the
changes would have been laid—and changes are needed.
I turn now to clause 5, which causes me some concern. Dangerous consequences could
arise if the clause is not amended or removed. The explanatory note states: "The effect of
this clause is to remove from section 145(3)(c) of the principal Act the power of a public
body or the Secretary for Transport, when fixing charges for the carriage of goods, to
prescribe a minimum charge." The Minister said that clause allowed efficient companies to
operate below the existing minimum.
Hon. C. C. A. McLachlan: Why shouldn't they?
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: Because it is rate cutting, and could drive a lot of the smaller
transport operators out of business. With no minimum charge the door is wide open for large
monopolies to take over the road transport industry. It is essential to maintain this minimum
charge to protect the small provincial operators who have done such a good job for so long.
The Government is ringing the death knell of those operators in the interests of the larger
monopolies, who, once they have all the trade, will increase their rates. If the Minister will
not agree to remove clause 5 altogether, I hope he will consider amending it by deleting the
words or a maximum charge". That would ensure that the law of the jungle did not operate
in the road transport industry. It is not scaremongering to suggest that unless this protection
is given then within perhaps 12 months, small operators, in an attempt to be competitive, will
drop their rates below the level at which they can operate economically, and it will not be
long before they are out of business.
The Minister knows that the largest road transport companies in New Zealand have a
large overseas ownership content. These companies will remain in business, and the small
New Zealand company will not be able to compete unless clause 5 is amended or removed
and we revert to the status quo. The Ministry of Transport is opting out of its responsibility
to police this area, and in a short time companies such as Allied Freightways, Transport
Nelson, Brambles-Burnett, and others will have all the trade to themselves.
Whom do these companies comprise? Let us look at Allied Freightways, which is the

company, and it in turn is wholly owned by TNT. Clause 5 is a sell-out to overseas monopoly

The following quotation from the report of the Committee of Inquiry into Overseas
Interests in New Zealand Road Transport-which came out in 1971-sums up the
position: "The foothold of the overseas companies in the field of freight forwarding,
especially over long distances and for inter-island traffic, is major, secure, and growing. It
seems clear, therefore, that the principal overseas transport companies exert a control over
the industry appreciably in excess of what might be expected on the basis of numerical
strength alone." The real risk is that those companies will continue to grow and, as they
grow, the overseas holding and overseas control of road transport in New Zealand will grow.
The committee of inquiry also recommended that someone should keep an eye on what was
going on. It said: "That the Ministry of Transport maintain a continuing surveillance over
trends towards consolidation of ownership and the possibility of monopolistic practices in the
road transport industry; that the Ministry of Transport institute procedures to enable
evaluation of the consequences of participation in internal road transport by overseas
shipping interests."
The Bill will worsen the position. I go into this detail because I want the Government
and the Minister to realise-perhaps they do not realise-just how serious the situation is
likely to become unless clause 5 is amended. Opposition members would go along with a
satisfactory amendment to ensure that the existing situation prevails; or clause 5 should be
taken out, because it has no real base. It is an orphan, because it has no real association with
the rest of the Bill. The Labour Party will not have anything to do with legislation that
creates a monopolistic situation. I come back to the green paper.
Hon. C. C. A. McLachlan: Oh, not the green paper-I've torn that up.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: On page 19 of the green paper there is this statement: "New

should be established. There are four freight forwarding companies operating in New
Zealand at the present time. They are all privately owned. Three have an overseas
ownership content. The participation of a public agency in this area should not only be
profitable to that agency but should also act as a competitive stimulant to the privately
owned freight forwarders." Why does the Government want to create a private monopoly

subsidising the transport industry. Rail transport is not subsidised in the same way, as the
losses every year clearly show. New Zealand depends on its exports, and that hidden subsidy

Notice of Motion-Admissibility
THURSDAY, 15 SEPTEMBER 1977
Mr Acting Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
NOTICE OF MOTION—ADMISSIBILITY
Mr HUNT (New Lynn): I give notice that next sitting day I shall move, That this House
notes the claim of the Prime Minister on TV2's programme, "First Edition", on Tuesday, 13
September 1977, that the member for Hamilton West has the right to vote in the House
against caucus decisions, and also notes his assertion that this was in contrast to what the
Labour Party did; points out to the Prime Minister that the last person to so vote on any issue
other than the usual conscience issues was the former Labour member for Awarua, Mr
Aubrey Begg, in 1973, on the issue of compulsory acquisition of wool, and notes finally that
on this subject National members in 1972 had all been instructed to vote by a caucus majority
for this legislation, and in 1973 by a caucus decision all voted against it.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): The notice of motion contains errors of
fact and, for that reason, is out of order. No such instructions were given. The fact that it
contains blatant errors of fact should rule the motion out. I realise that it could be debatable,
but it goes beyond what is debatable, and is simply an error of fact. No instructions were
given, because the rules of the National Party caucus do not permit instructions to be given.
It is simply an inference by the honourable member. He knows very well that the Labour
Party has formal caucus rules, and that the member for Awarua was given permission by his
caucus; whereas on this side of the House no such procedure is possible, because it is quite
impossible under our rules for any member to be instructed how he should vote.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Are you debating, or raising a point of order?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: Yes, I am raising as a point of order that the notice
contains two statements that are totally incorrect. You of all people, Mr Speaker, will know
that that is so, because you know the rules of the National Party.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I am sorry, the right honourable gentleman cannot bring me
into the debate, even by implication.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I am sorry, Mr Speaker, I take you out again.
Mr HUNT (New Lynn): If the Prime Minister would like, I am quite happy to change
the word "instructed” to “agreed”, but the only points the Prime Minister mentioned were
not errors of fact-he did not state any-they were differences of opinion; and after all that
is what this Chamber is all about. Some members have one opinion of an action, and others
have another opinion. It seems that, once again, the Prime Minister is confusing fact with
opinion.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): The honourable member is wrong. He
used the word "instructed" twice. Those are errors of fact because, not only was no one
instructed but it is impossible on this side of the House to instruct members. So those are
clearly errors of fact, not matters for argument. The notice of motion must be out of order. It
is not competent for the member to change his wording in midstream as it were. He should
resubmit it.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): This is purely a case of the
Prime Minister attempting to debate a notice of motion against his own resolution—moved a
couple of days ago that such motions be not debated. It is apparently his conception that
when 32 members of the National Government-or whatever number it is-come into the
House and all vote one way, it is more likely to be coincidence than instruction. This is a
matter for debate, and should be left to the opinion of both sides of the House, rather than
an attempt being made to raise a point of order against it.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I do not need any further assistance. When the notice of
motion was submitted to me, I debated very carefully whether I should allow it to be
introduced. I thought it would be best to allow the member the right to move it, and that if
there was any objection taken to it I would hear the objection, not from my own knowledge
of the situation, but from the knowledge of members who would bring it to my attention. It
would seem to me that the course of action proposed by the honourable member himself is
probably the proper one, and I would be very happy to discuss with him later the notice of
motion, and possible amendment to the words.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
OECD Economic Survey Draft
1. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Minister of Finance: Is he prepared to
table the draft of the OECD economic survey of New Zealand so that it can be compared
with the final version?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The OECD draft economic survey of
New Zealand is a confidential OECD secretariat working paper circulated to all member
countries, including the country under review. The final document is issued under the sole
responsibility of the OECD secretariat, after being considered at the annual review, which,
on this occasion, took place on 20 June. New Zealand, was, of course, represented. Since the
text in question is the first draft of a confidential report of an international organisation, it
would be wrong to table the draft. This is precisely the procedure which has obtained in
previous years, including 1975, when the honourable gentleman asking the question was a
member of the New Zealand Cabinet. Exactly the same procedure took place on that
occasion, and similar amendments were made.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: If the Minister is not prepared to table the original draft, is he
prepared to indicate to the House how many changes were made?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I have not counted the number of changes, and, indeed, I
have not compared the drafts, because this is a normal procedure, and is the way the OECD
operates with all the 24 member countries. The changes emanating from New Zealand are
principally to errors of fact, and the changes that come from the meeting in Paris-
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Like the free vote in the National Party?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: Well, of course, we do have a free vote and the Labour
Party does not. Would the Deputy Leader of the Opposition like me to make public the
Labour Party's caucus rules?
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Providing it is a true report.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order! When we have interjections or other comments that
are irrelevant it does not help the question before us. At the moment we are having
questions for oral answer. A supplementary question has been asked by the member for
Manukau and the Prime Minister is answering it.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: This matter is of some interest, and I think I should explain
it carefully. The suggested amendments emanating from New Zealand are in the nature of
changing errors of fact, but other changes to errors emanate from the meeting in Paris, at
which New Zealand is represented and at which all member countries discuss the report and
decide on the amendment. That is the normal procedure, and it was followed when the
former Labour Government was in office. Of course, the final report is the considered report
of the 24 nations after sitting and discussing the draft. Some suggestion has been made that a
draft is sent to New Zealand and someone in the New Zealand Treasury alters it and sends it
back, and that is the final draft. That is a total misconception or misunderstanding by the
journalist concerned.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: It would be a powerful amendment coming from a Treasury
official, though, would it not?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: No, not with the OECD, because at this level the OECD is
in fact foreign service and Treasury officials themselves. What we do from here is say: "You
say that so-and-so is the position, and in fact the position is so-and-so." That must be
accepted as a matter of fact, but matters of opinion are settled at a mecting in Paris, where
they all sit around a table and finally, if necessary, vote on what goes into the report. Any
suggestion that the report was altered to assist the New Zealand Government is ludicrous to
anyone who understands the situation. I should have thought that the member for Manukau
would know that, as he was a member of Cabinet—and, I thought, interested in economic
affairs in 1975 when exactly the same procedure took place.
Mr Hunt: Is the Minister prepared to table the changes he made if we table the changes
we made in 1975?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I can very readily table the changes I made, because I did
not make any. In fact, I did not see the draft report at all; but I shall have a look at the
changes made in 1975. I think the honourable member is a little unwise in taking this line,
because he was not in Cabinet in 1975 and would not know whether any changes were made.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: I happen to know that I made no changes either, and I did not even

Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: There you are; I have it confirmed by no less a person than
the Deputy Leader of the Opposition that in fact the Minister does not see the draft and does
not make any changes. I thank the Deputy Leader of the Opposition for confirming what I
have just said. It was very kind of him to help me in that manner, as he seldom does assist
me. What happens is this. In both 1975 and 1977 the New Zealand Treasury has looked at
the draft and said, "That is wrong"-and obviously, as a matter of fact, it must then be
changed. Then there is a meeting in Paris. The two New Zealand representatives in Paris this
year were Mr White, the Governor of the Reserve Bank, and Mr Martin, the Assistant
Secretary to the Treasury, and in 1975 they would have been the holders of those respective
offices. They sit around the table with members of the Paris Embassy, the London High
Commission, and representatives of the other 24 nations. They look at the report and say,
"Now, is that right, or should it be amended in some way?" That is the way the final report is
made. A total misconception has arisen from a report in a weekly newspaper by a reporter
who did not understand the matter at all.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: We have spent a long time on one question.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: We have had very long answers.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order! I should perhaps draw the Prime Minister's attention
to the fact that answers to questions ought to be concise.
Hon. M. Rata: Can the Prime Minister give an assurance that the changes made to the

revised, altered, or changed to take account of the political climate here?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I can give that assurance absolutely, because in this country,
we have a non-political Public Service and the only people who saw the draft were public
servants.
Mr O'Brien: Can the Prime Minister tell us how it came about that the National
Business Review published in the third week of July-I do not know the exact

phrase it is stated that the Government has clearly contributed to if not led the recession in
the last 2 years. If that information was available to the National Business Review from
another source, is it not right that members of the House should see the initial draft?

confidential international document. I think it is deplorable that any journalist in New
Zealand should have seen such a document, and I would have been of the same view and
made a similar statement had a Labour Government been in power. As to the changes
referred to, as the document originated from a visit in February and the statement made is
that the Government's activities led to the recession over the last 2 years, the member for
Island Bay will realise that the Government referred to was the Labour Government, not the
present Government. If one goes back 2 years from February, one is in the time of the
former Labour Goverment. It could well have been that New Zealand's public servants said,
"This is ambiguous, and it is a criticism that should probably not be made in a document of
this kind." However, the statement did not refer to this Government; it referred to the
former Labour Government. Why members of the Labour Party should take exception to its
excision is beyond me, because it was their Government that was being criticised.

Professional Charges-Complaints
3. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: How many
complaints has his department received relating to professional charges since the freeze on
these charges was lifted, and how many of these complaints have been found to be justified?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): My department
has received 78 complaints since the freeze on professional charges was lifted on 15 August
1977. Professional charges are now subject to Amendment No. 6 of the Stabilisation of
Prices Regulations 1974. The provisions of these regulations do not stipulate the basis on
which professional charges should be set. Instead they provide for my department to
investigate increases that have occurred and to carry out surveys of charges. The secretary,
who has statutory authority, estimates that about half of the 78 complaints require investiga-
tion, and this work is now being undertaken.
Mr Hunt: As it was reported in the Dominion on 8 September-just one week ago—that
the Government had received 39 complaints, is the Minister concerned that another 39
complaints have apparently been received in a week?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I have not seen the report, and I am not prepared to
concede that it was correct. The information, properly given to me by the secretary, is that
the number of complaints received is 78, and that about half of those justify further
investigation.
Mr Hunt: In what fields were these complaints?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: About 40 professional organisations are concerned,
but most of the complaints refer to medical fees.

Teachers Colleges
11. Mr HUNT (New Lynn), on behalf of Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui), asked the
Minister of Education: Does he expect the rolls of teachers colleges to continue to fall, and, if
so, will this have any influence on the future of the colleges?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): In line with the declining birthrate I
expect the rolls of teachers colleges to fall. On the planning information at present available,
the rolls of teachers colleges are expected to decline from 7200 students taking teachers
college courses in 1977 to 6750 students in 1980, after which rolls are expected to be stable.
The effect of the decline in rolls up to 1980 is being assessed by means of an accommodation
survey carried out by my department. The influence of these roll changes on the future of the
colleges may result in further opportunities for the continuing education of teachers and for
colleges to offer courses for other occupational groups.
Mr Hunt: Can the Minister give an assurance that North Shore Teachers College will
not be closed at the end of this year?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: As I have said, a survey is being carried out at present. I cannot
give any assurance about anything in particular, but it is very unlikely that North Shore
Teachers College will be closed.
Mr Hunt: In view of the Minister's encouraging answer to the people of North Shore,
can he give an assurance that the decline in numbers will be spread over all the colleges
roughly equally rather than closing down an existing training college?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: The only information I can give is that in 1977 there were 7200
students in the system. It looks as if we will have 6800 next year. That is only 400 students
fewer. Therefore, it is unlikely that any teachers college will be closed and it is highly likely
that the diminishing rolls will be spread over all the institutions.

ROTORUA COUNTY COUNCIL EMPOWERING BILL
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. This is a short Bill of three clauses that amends the Hamurana Springs
recreation reserve leases. It has been asked for by the Rotorua County Council to enable the
lessees of the Hamurana Springs recreation reserve to have a further 10-year lease of their
sections. In 1955, about 47 leaseholders were granted leases for 20 years, with a right of
renewal for a further 10 years at the same rental. In the intervening years the value of the
land has increased considerably. All the money collected from the leases is spent by the
Rotorua County Council on the development of the reserve, and the council feels that the
small amount of revenue collected under the original legislation is quite inadequate and
unrealistic compared with today's costs. The leaseholders are willing to pay an increased rent
for a further 10 years' security and the right to lease for that period.

Clause 2. Inflation-adjusted Savings Bonds.
(1) Notwithstanding anything in the New Zealand Loans Act 1953, the Minister of Finance may
issue, to individuals of or over the age of 7 years, non-transferable bonds (in this section referred to
as inflation-adjusted savings bonds) in respect of money borrowed under that Act upon terms that,
in addition to any interest payable on them, there shall be payable to the holders thereof at the time
the bonds are redeemed a further amount that may be calculated on the basis of the inflation
occurring between the issue of the bonds and their redemption.

TRANSPORT AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Adjourned debate on the question, That this Bill be now read a second time.
Miss DEWE (Lyttelton): When this debate was adjourned last evening, I had been
listening with great interest to the arguments, which I thought were inconsistent, put forward
by the Opposition. The member for Timaru lauded the proposals in the Labour Govern-
ment's green paper on transport. I am sure that members, as well as those people involved in
the transport industry, will recall that green paper with abhorrence, because it suggested the
building of another Government-backed finance corporation to compete with private
carriers. The member for Sydenham had obviously not listened to the comments made by
the member for Timaru, because he insisted that the Bill would spell the demise of the small
carrier, and build monopolies. I do not know how he reconciled his attitude to the green
paper and a Government corporation. There is no unified thrust in the arguments put
forward by members opposite. I see no justification in their continuing this debate.
Mr Isbey: Sit down then.
Miss DEWE: Government members are prepared to match speaker for speaker in
support of the Bill, which is worthy and certainly due for implementation. Last night the
member for Timaru said that if the Labour Government had been re-elected it would have
extended the road limit. However, during the 1960s the National Government set up the
National Development Council. The transport committee attached to that council recom-
mended a major study on transport, to which the Transport Advisory Council agreed. As a
result, the Government set aside about $800,000, and called for tenders. The successful
tenderer was the firm of Wilbur Smith and Associates, which produced the Wilbur Smith
report-a major study on New Zealand transport. In 1973, the report was presented to the
Labour Government, which let it lie on the shelf, but then produced its own green paper,
completely ignoring the cost and the expertise of the report.
The member for Marlborough quoted from a paper which was a summary of a summary
of a summary of the Wilbur Smith report, which stated that: "The 40-mile limit restricting
road freight transport competition with rail, should be abolished and replaced by a special
road tax on long distance road transport, competing with over 40 miles of principal
Government railway." Basically, this is what the Bill does-it implements the report's
recommendations by increasing the restraining limit of 40 miles to 150 kilometres, or, in the
old-fashioned terminology that I confess I still prefer, 93½ miles. Last night, the member for

Transport Amendment Bill (No. 2)
Auckland Central spoke about energy utilisation, a subject more appropriate for an energy
debate. He spoke about the comparison of costs and use of oil and fuel-both very costly and
precious in New Zealand today—with rail transport, and was trying to convince the House
that rail was far more economical.
I have a paper-which I would be happy to show the member for Auckland Central, if
he were interested-which gives the fuel consumption costs of a journey between Auckland
and Wellington. The paper, which was researched and presented by Mr Duncan, the
Managing Director of Mobil Oil, to the Bus and Coachmen's Association conference held in
Auckland on 24 August 1977, was also reported in the New Zealand Herald. Mr Duncan
gives some very interesting comparisons. He talks about the cost in fuel consumption of
different types of vehicles taking various numbers of passengers from Auckland to Welling-
ton. He first uses the figures for a 4-cylinder 2000 cc car carrying 4 passengers, and the
estimate is that it would use 59 litres of fuel, or roughly 14.8 litres each passenger, at a cost of
$4.38 per passenger. His next comparison is a bus carrying 32 passengers, using 165 litres of
diesel fuel, and the consumption per passenger on that journey would be 5.2 litres, at a cost
of 89.5 cents a passenger. So there is a remarkable decrease using a bus, as we all know. For
his next comparison he uses the Silver Star, carrying 107 passengers and using 2324 litres of
fuel-that is, 21.72 litres a passenger, at a cost of $3.04 a passenger. The member for
Auckland Central's arguments obviously were not based on any sound research or documen-
tation.
Another argument put forward by the member for Timaru was that the easing of the
restrictions should be phased in over a period. Further legislation, in conjunction with this
Bill, relates to provisions for sales tax, and also a different method of funding on an axle-
weight basis. The Wilbur Smith report made recommendations on both of those issues. On
page 116 it stated that consideration should be given to replacing sales tax and customs duty
on trucks with a usage tax, and it also stated, on pages 96 and 97, that the National Roads
Board should continue to derive most of its revenue from dedicated roading taxation. The
Budget implemented both of those provisions, and legislation will come before the House
shortly.
This is a simple Bill, enacting provisions of the 1977 Budget relating to the lifting of the
40-mile restriction. When the Bill is passed, road carriers will be able to operate up to 150
kilometres on a journey in competition with the New Zealand Railways. This does not mean
that the Government wants to run down the railways, which it fully supports, but it wants to
ensure that the railways can compete with carriers without protection. One could ask, why
150 kilometres-or 93.5 miles; why not 100 kilometres or 200 kilometres? Why was it ever 40
miles? I believe it was brought in at 30 miles in 1938, and in 1961 or 1962 was lifted by an
extra 10 miles, and has been 40 miles ever since. It has created anomalies, and no doubt the
150 kilometres will create anomalies; but, just as solutions were found for the 40-mile
difficulties, so will they be found for the 150-kilometre difficulties.
Licensing authorities have coped with the 40-mile limit for many years, and will have no
difficulty in coping with applications for licences relating to 150 kilometres. I cannot see any
insurmountable problems. Since 1961 the distance road carriers could transport goods in
competition with the railways has been 40 miles; and do not forget that it was 30 miles before
that. The 30-mile limit was brought in in 1938 to ensure—
An Hon. Member: Before you were born.
Miss DEWE: Unfortunately it was not before I was born, but it was not long after. It was
brought in to ensure that the railways were not disadvantaged as the road transport industry
grew. In those days, the industry was in its infancy. Members should reflect on the changes
that have taken place since 1938 in the vehicles used by the industry, as well as in the variety
and volume of goods carried-whether imported, exported, or produced and consumed in
New Zealand. It is an entirely different country-some say it is not as good-and it is an
entirely different industry from what it was when the original limitation was placed on road
carriers. There is hardly a process in any industry which has not changed over the past 40
years; or, if the process has not changed, certainly the methodology has. Road transport is a
typical example of those changes, and it has been restrained in its growth for 40 years.
Revision is long overdue. It has been sought by the carriers, and it was promised in the
National Party manifesto.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Which one?
Miss DEWE: The true one, the big one with the blue cover; the one from which
members opposite are reluctant to acknowledge how much has been implemented. The
National Party's 1975 election manifesto transport policy stated: "National believes the

Dr WALL (Porirua): The first observation I make is that the Bill will be very damaging
to the rural community. When the debate went off the air last night, not one
of the so-called farmers' friends on the other side of the House stood up to defend the
Government's policies. It is clear that they did not wish to speak on the Bill. However, now
that the debate is again being broadcast we are hearing a tirade of inconsequential and
unrelated arguments, such as we have just heard from the charming lady from Lyttelton. She
gave us a story about the cost of shifting passengers from Auckland to Wellington in
different ways, using transport varying from a car to a train, and claimed that in some ways
that refuted the very strong argument put forward last night by the member for Auckland
Central. The facts he gave the House were supported by some of the most reliable transport
authorities in New Zealand, and related to the transport of goods, which is what the Bill we
are now considering relates to.
What on earth the cost of shifting passengers in trains, buses, or cars has to do with the
costs involved in the carriage of goods, I just do not know. If the member for Lyttelton came
to Porirua and saw the different loadings of the Silver Star and the goods trains as they pass
through, very close to my door, she would realise that the points she made do not relate to
the Bill any more than do the flowers that bloom in the spring. However, as she attempted to
divert the attention of the House from the very sound arguments put forward by the member
for Auckland Central, I think it would be as well if I were again to draw attention to the fact
that a large truck and trailer with a gross weight of about 33 tonnes has four axles, each
bearing 8.2 tonnes, and causes as much pavement wear as 20 000 or 30 000 cars. That is a
very significant factor, quite apart from the large fuel costs involved.
Road transport operators complain that they bear 27 percent of roading costs. We all
know that throughout New Zealand the backlog of bridge repair and replacement work is
increasing. Much of that work would be unnecessary if it were not for the heavy traffic used
by road transport operators. I think immediately of one of the bridges in Porirua, that now
has a weight restriction placed on it because it has developed some rather alarming waves.
Heavy trucks are now prevented from crossing that bridge, which was constructed about 35
years ago. If it had not been for the heavy transport operators it could have been expected to
last for about another 50 years, but it is now due for urgent replacement. Heavy axle weights
are now going over almost every bridge in the country, and the Bill will bring about even
heavier wear and tear, because more heavy transport will be covering longer distances. Any
additional taxes that may be levied will very quickly be eaten up by the earlier replacement
of bridges and the extra upgrading of roads.
Just this week we have heard Government members trying to defend the abolition of
subsidies—and particularly consumer subsidies-which has placed a very heavy burden on
those who are suffering from the present financial policy, but no Government member
appears to appreciate the difficulties created by subsidising road transport more heavily than
it has been subsidised in the past. I point out that the big transport companies are very

For 3 years the Labour Government examined the transport industry, and at the end of
that time produced a green paper. It took no action, and produced no solution to the
problems facing the industry. The National Government has tidied up the political control of
the transport sector that existed under the Labour Government, which had separate
Ministers for transport, railways, and civil aviation. In addition, there was an Under-
Secretary for transport-interestingly enough, the member for Grey Lynn. Towards the end
of its period in office, the Labour Government set up a committee on transport, chaired by,
of all people, the member for Manukau. I assume that he was the author of the green paper.
Members opposite are still confused, and still have no policy.
Decision-making in the transport area is complex. The National Government commis-
sioned the 1973 Wilbur Smith report, which was available to the Labour Government. But,
because it posed decision-making problems, the Labour Government took the easy way out
and deferred making decisions, as it did in so many areas. Soon after it assumed office, the
National Government recognised that unless it tackled the issues presented by the
report—and the problems of the transport sector-and made decisions, any improvements in
the economy and efficiency of the transport industry would be impossible.
We are determined to improve the cost efficiency of the transport sector, and, far from
clashing with energy conservation, greater efficiency will make more effective use of
resources. Despite the pessimistic prognostications of members opposite, we on this side
believe that the Railways Department will respond in a healthy way to competition. The Bill
enshrines part of the most fundamental and historic changes in the transport sector for many
decades. It is in accordance with the National Government's philosophy, and the policy
enunciated in the 1975 election manifesto. We are determined to put into effect what we
promised, and that is another difference between the National Government and the Labour
Government. The National Party manifesto stated—
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Which one-the untrue one, or the true one?
Mr WELLINGTON: I quote from the section on the 40-mile limit on the restriction of
road transport: "National believes the transport user must be given a choice of mode in
order to use that which proves most economical and efficient. Accordingly, the road
transport industry will be given relief from legislative restrictions in line with recommenda-
tions made by the Wilbur Smith report and in progressive stages with the environmental
impact being assessed at each stage.'
""
The original 30-mile restriction on road transport was introduced in 1936, against a
background of economic depression and expansion in the road transport industry. In 1960,
the limit was increased to 40 miles. In 1973, Wilbur Smith concluded that overall transport
costs in this country were higher than they needed to be, because, for some transport tasks,
rail was less suitable and more costly than road transport. The report went so far as to
recommend the total abolition of the road-rail restriction. But the Government considered
that it had a clear duty, and while some relaxation of the 40-mile limit was needed in the
interests of efficiency, it was made to ensure that the railways did not become a declining
force.

secondly, to bring greater economic rationale to the future development of the transport
sector.

has made a decision. It has not been easy, and those of us who are members of the caucus

concerned about is the fact that a decision has been made. I do not believe they have any real

1972-75 period, not only to formulate a policy but, more importantly, to implement it. They
were elected to do that, but failed to take any action or even make a decision, and that is why
they are no longer on the Treasury benches.

The fear of the Opposition, of the small businessman in the retail or the manufacturing

Bill facilitates a move in that direction, which in the long term will be detrimental to the
opportunities and freedom of the smaller operators. That has been the National Party's

our staff." That carrier in a small central Waikato town is associated with the primary
industries of agriculture and forestry. That town has sustained small transport carriers for as
long as I can remember. Any Bill that puts companies and staff at risk requires more
consideration than some manifesto promise, whether in the true or untrue copy. One cannot
on the one hand say that one believes in regional development and on the other put small
operators at risk. The social and economic damage is more traumatic in a small town than in
a larger centre.
The Bill is not a simple matter. I have some idea of the difficulties, and know the
arguments put forward by Wilbur Smith before oil increased in price. The department has
not tested the principles under the new oil prices, because the people who could have done
that are no longer with the department. I challenge the Minister to show the cost-
effectiveness, taking into account the need to conserve energy. Is this the wisest time to
move as rapidly as the Government has moved?
I now turn to the impact that the Bill will have on the Railways. I am idealistic in these
matters and believe that the Government's first responsibility is that of a good trustee of the
nation's assets. The railways are a national asset. They are not always economic, but are a
great service to areas where there is a low tonnage of freight. National Governments have
always brawled with their supporters when branch lines have been ripped up. In the old days
that work was done for very low rates of pay. Even although something is not well utilised, it
should not be removed in haste if it is the basis from which people make a profit and pay
revenue. I have no doubt in my mind that the Bill will damage the viability of the Railways.
