INCOME TAX AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be
now read a second time. As I mentioned when the Bill was introduced, its main purpose is to
give effect to the Budget announcement to increase the amount of young-family rebate for a
family with a child under 5 from $6 to $9, and, secondly, to extend the allowable income of
the claimant for an income up to $150 a week. The Bill also introduces the new single-income
family rebate for families with a child under 10, and extends the allowable income of the
spouse for purposes of the spouse rebates.
Clause 1 relates to the short title. Clause 2 is the general application provision. The
amendments to the young family and wife rebates as well as the new single-income family
rebate are to apply for the full current income year ending 31 March 1978—that is for the full
1977-78 financial year. For PAYE purposes, the amendments to the young-family and wife
rebates will be incorporated in new tax tables that will apply to tax deductions on earnings
derived during pay periods ending on or after 1 October 1977. The single-income family
rebate will be allowed by way of adjustment in the annual assessment.
Clause 3 sets out the qualifying criteria relating to the new single-income family rebate,
which amounts to a maximum of $208. Basically, the rebate, which is in addition to the
young-family rebate, will be allowed where the commissioner is satisfied there is a child
under 10 years of age who is cared for and living as a member of the family with the claimant,
or the claimant and any other person, either of whom is entitled to receive the family benefit
for that child. Where two persons care for the child, the rebate will be allowed to the
principal income earner, and will diminish by 30c for each complete $1 by which that other
person's income exceeds $1,040. This means the rebate will extinguish when that income
reaches $1,733. For the purpose of this abatement, social welfare benefits, other than
national superannuation, will be deemed not to be income. The rebate will apply equally to
solo parents. Only the one rebate is allowable where there are two or more children under
the age of 10 in the same family. Where more than one person is entitled to the rebate in
respect of the same child, it will be apportioned equitably between them. In determining
entitlement to the rebate, the commissioner may obtain the advice of the Director-General
of Social Welfare in appropriate cases. Where the commissioner is satisfied that arrange-
ments have been made between taxpayers to obtain an unfair advantage under this
provision, he is authorised to make the necessary adjustments to correct the position.
Clause 4 amends the rebate for a married man supporting his wife, and increases from
$375 to $520 a year the income a wife may earn before the rebate is affected. Where the
wife's income exceeds $520, the rebate diminishes by 30c for each complete dollar of that
income, so the rebate is extinguished where the spouse's income amounts to $1,040 for the
year. At present, the rate of abatement is 40c in the dollar, so the rebate is extinguished
when the wife's income reaches $763. To enable this extension to the allowable income, and
to reduce the rate of abatement, the rebate has been fractionally increased to $156.
Clause 5 is complementary to clause 4 and similarly adjusts the rebate allowable to a
married woman supporting her husband. Clause 6 increases the amount of young-family
rebate, and extends the qualifying income of the claimant. The rebate will be $9 a week, or
$468 a year, on incomes up to $150 a week, or $7,800 a year, and replaces the present $6 a
week, or $312 a year, on incomes up to $100 a week, or $5,200 a year. The rebate will
diminish by 10c for each complete dollar of income over $150 a week, or $7,800 a year,
derived by the claimant, so that no rebate will be allowed when that person's income reaches
$240 a week, or $12,480 a year. At present, the rate is reducible by 15c for each dollar of
income over $100 a week, or $5,200 a year, to be extinguished when the taxpayer's income
reaches $140 a week, or $7,280 a year.
Clause 7 increases the housekeeper rebate fractionally to $156, to keep it in line with the
spouse rebate. Clause 8 is a consequential amendment to section 57 of the principal Act,
which ensures that the total tax rebates allowed do not exceed the total tax otherwise
payable. Clause 9 is an amendment for PAYE tax code purposes following adjustments to
the spouse and housekeeper rebates. A taxpayer may not operate tax code "M" if he expects
his wife's income to exceed $520, or if he expects to pay a housekeeper less than $390 during


## p. 3039 (#677) ###########################################

15 September
3039
Income Tax Amendment Bill
the income year. Clause 10 provides that an employee may not use the tax code of "M+F"
or "S+F" if he knows or anticipates that his assessable income for the year will exceed
$12,480. Clause 11 amends section 356 of the Act, and relieves from the obligation to furnish
a return of income, those taxpayers whose income is solely from national superannuation.
Clause 12 amends the weekly PAYE tax tables to incorporate the increased young-
family and wife rebates from 1 October 1977, and also consequentially amends the special
basis of calculating tax deductions on the earnings of shearers. Amendments to the young-
family rebate covering the period 1 April to 30 September 1977 will be allowed as an end-of-
year adjustment. This means that taxpayers currently operating a tax code "M-F” or
"S+F" will receive an additional end-of-year adjustment of $78, while that adjustment for
persons first qualifying for the rebate on 1 October 1977 will be $234. As previously stated,
the single-income family rebate of $208 will also be allowed as an end-of-year adjustment,
and is not incorporated in the new PAYE tables.
To summarise, the provisions in this Bill implement the Budget decisions which provide
additional tax relief for those on low incomes, a measure first introduced in 1976, and now
adding families relying on one income. Married taxpayers with a child under 5 years who
qualify for both rebates will pay no tax if their taxable incomes are less than $82.63 a week.
At present they would pay tax if their taxable incomes exceeded $57.65 a week. If their
taxable incomes are between $80 and $180 a week, their after-tax incomes will be increased
by between 8 and 12 percent. It is estimated that approximately 156 000 families will be
eligible for the single-income rebate, and approximately 160 000 will be eligible for the
expanded young-family rebate-an increase of 70 000 families receiving that rebate. In total,
it is expected that about 218 000 families will benefit from these provisions through either
one, or both, rebates. These measures show that the Government is prepared and concerned
to use tax measures to assist where the need is greatest. It will keep the system under review
to meet changing circumstances.

burden that taxpayers are being called upon to pay merely because of the increases in wages
or salaries granted partly to compensate for increases in the cost of living.
When wage increases were given last year and early this year, they were subject to the
Government's stabilisation policy, which provided that wages were not to increase at the
same rate as prices. For that reason, the wage increases were inadequate to cover increased
costs. The Government ought to have taken complementary action through the taxation
system by increasing personal exemptions to ensure that all of the limited increase in wages
would be conserved for wage and salary earners. However, the Government took no action.
Because of that, wage and salary earners have been forced on to higher rates of taxation,
which means that they have paid additional tax on increases designed to compensate them
for the increase in living costs.
Then those same people have been hit by inflation in all directions. Costs have increased
by 25 percent, and are continuing to increase by going on for 30 percent, under this
Government. The family man has been hit because the family benefit has declined in its
effective purchasing power as a result of the ruinous inflationary policies followed by the
Government. He has been hit again by the failure of the Government to increase the family
benefit to take account of the impact of increased costs on its purchasing power. Last
November the Government's own Council of Social Service submitted a report pointing out
the deterioration in family incomes, and called on the Government to increase the family
benefit, but the Government took no action.
If we consider just those two areas—the increase in tax paid because of wage increases
designed to compensate wage and salary earners for increased costs, and the need to upgrade
the family benefit to ensure that its effective purchasing power is the same today as it was
when the family benefit was last increased-the family benefit should be $5.50. It is $3. In
other words, a man with three children is receiving $7.50 a week less in family benefit than
he should receive.
Let us consider wage increases and the tax on them. A man who earned $100 a week in
1975 is today, because of wage increases, on an income that would result in his paying $7.65
more in tax. He is entitled to look to the Government for an increased personal exemption to
offset that increased taxation, so as to conserve his wage increase which is needed to help his
family budget. However, he has listened and looked in vain to this Government. Today, that
man needs tax relief of over $15 a week. Under the Budget he has received a rebate of only
$13.
Mr Latter: What is his wage?
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY: In March, it would have had to be $119.
Mr Latter: What is it?
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY: That is what his wage would have had to be relatively,
and increased tax would have been $7.65. Let us consider a taxpayer on $150 a week, which
is the level at which the exemption starts to be whittled away under this legislation. That
person would need a reduction in taxation of nearly $14 a week—in fact, $13.82—to offset
the increased taxes caused by the increase in salary given to offset increases in living costs. If
that taxpayer has three children, he would require in addition an increase of $7.50 in family
benefit. That taxpayer was looking to this Government for an increase in benefit and a

For a long time New Zealand has had a progressive tax structure in which people on
higher incomes pay a higher proportion of tax. If the tax system is not altered in inflationary
times, the extra money becomes an increase across the board and everyone moves into a
higher tax bracket. Unless the Government alters the tax scales, people will pay a higher
proportion of their earnings in income tax. They are not better off, they are paying more tax

points. When I first read the Bill and realised that it provided income rebates for some
people, I tended to scream, "Hooray, at long last the Government has recognised that some
family people are so badly in need of relief." It is unfortunate that those people had to be on
the poverty line before they got any recognition, but one must be thankful for small mercies,
and for the fact that they have at last been recognised. The Bill provides for a rebate for
single-income families with children under 10 years of age. That is great. It provides for a
young-family rebate that applies to children under 5 years of age. That is great stuff, too.
However, the Bill does not go far enough. Now that the Government has recognised
that there are families in New Zealand who need relief, I hope members opposite will open
their eyes a little more, and recognise that some families have children over 10 years of age,
and over 5 years of age. What we need is not the propping up of a system that is not doing the
job, but a completely new look at the taxation system, so that we can give relief to all
families who are in need, rather than having a cut-off point when a child reaches a certain
age. I am pleased that the young-family rebate has been increased, as that shows that
Government members have at least one eye partly open. One can only hope that in the
future they will open the other eye a little and recognise that this is a very small step. It is so
small that I am not sure whether it is actually a move forwards, but, as long as it is not a move
backwards, one must be a little grateful.
The Bill provides that superannuitants whose sole income is national superannuation
are to be relieved of the requirement to complete an annual income tax return. I should jolly
well hope so. Indeed, one of the Government's most thoughtless actions was to create a
situation where elderly people who had not completed an income tax return for years
suddenly found themselves having to complete taxation forms to receive their superannu-
ation. I know from the number of people in my electorate who have contacted me just how
badly that decision has affected many of our elderly people. I am sure I am not the only
member of Parliament who has spent many Sundays visiting pensioner cottages to assist
beneficiaries to complete their returns.
Clause 7 increases the housekeeper rebate from $155 to $156 a year. My word, what
great thinking! I had not realised that the Government was so daring that it could increase
the housekeeper rebate by a whole dollar a year! It makes one wonder about the exciting
measures it will introduce next. That is great stuff, and I am sure it will win votes!
Apparently, Government members fail to realise that only very few people are able to
employ a housekeeper, and that the money would be better spent on providing child care
facilities for those who require a housekeeper to look after their children while they are at
work. Let us face the situation. The conditions under which one can claim the housekeeper
rebate are so tight that very few people indeed will receive any benefit at all from that
provision. However, it looks good, and I am sure some people are really excited that they
will be able to claim a whole dollar a year extra as a housekeeper rebate.
As the member for New Lynn said, the Bill represents the maximum the Government is
prepared to do to relieve hardship in areas where there is a great need for relief, but it
actually turns out to be the minimum it can do. I find that attitude rather unhelpful. I am
sorry that the Government, in considering the needs of families and those on low
incomes-basically, the workers and those who are tomorrow's generation of workers—
realises that politically it must take some action, but can provide only the very minimum
relief possible. I was also interested to hear the member for New Lynn mention the
statement in the newspaper just 2 days after the presentation of the last Budget; that
statement showed clearly that the National Party itself does not believe that the Government
has gone far enough in providing taxation relief to single-income families. I am rather
surprised that more was not done, because there is a great need for more to be done. On the
other hand, I am not surprised that more was not done, because I recognise that the
Government's policies are not aimed at helping those in the most need.

Income Tax Amendment Bill
The tax burden on families is becoming greater and greater. There is no longer any
justification for trying to prop up a system that is obviously not doing the job it should do. I
do not profess to know much about figures. I am not an academic, and I have not been
terribly involved in the income tax field. I am not an accountant; I am more concerned with
people than I am with figures. I understand that the Government expects to collect an
additional $742 million in income tax this year; that surely means that there will be $9 extra
collected for every $1 handed out. What will happen to that $9? If the Government is to
collect so much more in income tax, why cannot it give more relief in those areas where it is
needed? This year, income tax is expected to rise by 26.2 percent and wages may rise by
perhaps 15 percent. That is not good enough. It means that the people we are supposed to be
looking after and caring for are paying more of their income in tax under this Government
than they did under the Labour Government. Does the National Government think that that
is good? Is the Government not aware that the money it gathers in taxation must be given
back and shared out equitably?
Is the Government sure that needy people are receiving the relief they should? Are
those who were identified in the Social Development Council report receiving the relief they
should? When the report came out, there were headlines in the Christchurch papers such as
"One earner families on poverty line". Surely in the 1970s we should not have headlines such
as that. Does this not cause some concern to Government members? Are they not aware of
what is happening? If they are, what do they intend to do about it? What about the families
with children over 10 years of age, which will not receive relief? In fact, they will have to take
a cut in their standard of living. Is the Government not concerned about them? Once a child
has turned 10 the second parent is forced to go out to work; while I have no hesitation in
saying that if the second parent wishes to work she should be able to do so, she should not be
forced to go out to work because of financial need.
Many of those who will receive assistance under the provisions of this Bill will be worse
off than they were before it was introduced. Why is it necessary to postpone the relief until
next year? Why could it not be introduced now? It is now that these groups need help, not
later. With inflation as it is just now, by the time those people receive their rebate they will be
much worse off than they are now, anyway. We are really fiddling with a situation that needs
to be completely reassessed. A person on a wage of $130 a week-the average wage, if you
include overtime-will receive an extra $7.50 from the young-family rebate, but he is
probably spending that much extra to pay off the increase in his mortgage, so it does not
really mean a great deal to him.
I am more concerned about what should be done to help those people. Why is some
effort not being made to hold interest rates, to freeze rents, and to hold back the increases in
Government charges and basic cost-producing items? Why is there not some taxation relief
to remove the disincentives to increased production? Why is there not effective price
control? If something were done in those areas there would be no need to single out certain
families for relief, which means that many who are not eligible will be penalised. It is
pleasing that some assistance will be given, but how can one be entirely happy when some
families are treated better than others? The assistance needed is the same, regardless of how
many children a family has.
While there is some good in the Bill it does not go far enough. I am surprised that the
Government does not recognise that it is being unfair to many families. It discriminates
against people who have children over a certain age. However, children grow up, and I
wonder if the Government considers that children should be put out to grass when they reach
a certain age. People are upset about the discrimination; families living next door to each
other will be at loggerheads because one family will be in a better position than others,
because it just so happens that one has a child who is 9 years of age, and the other has a child
who turned 11 yesterday. The Opposition is unhappy that the Government has not seen fit to
look at the rates of taxation, and to do something that will help families to live above the
poverty line.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): Listening to the Opposi-
tion, I was not quite sure what was wanted. Some Opposition speakers simply wanted more,
which appeared to be a resurrection of the baby-bonus mentality, while others wanted it to
go to the most deserving. The Government has moved to assist the most deserving within the
resources available. Any Bill that assists about 220 000 families in the average wage bracket
is a good Bill. I want to make a very brief comparison with the position under the Labour
Government. In 1975 and 1976, a family on the average wage with one child under the age of
5 years would have received only $156 in family benefit. In 1977 that family will receive $156

Income Tax Amendment Bill
in family benefit and $192 in young-family rebate, making a total of $348. In 1978, under this
Bill, that family will receive $156 in family benefit, $468 in young-family rebate, and $208 in

The young-family rebate could not be included in the PAYE tables until 1 October
1977, because two rates are at issue-the $6 rate up to $100 runs up to 30 September, and
after that the $9 rate applies up to $150. It would have been too complicated to bring this into
the PAYE tables in any other way. It would certainly be impracticable to include the single-
income rebate in the PAYE tax, as it would have involved too many and too complex
additional codes for both employers and employees. That is why we have had to work
towards an adjustment at the end of the tax year. This Bill is a carefully thought-out means
of assistance to meet real social needs, and I recommend it to the House for endorsement.

NURSES BILL
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I move, That the Nurses Bill be introduced.
Members will recall that a Nurses Amendment Bill was introduced in 1975 and referred to
the Social Services Committee. The committee reported back in 1976. However, following
further representations from the Nurses Association and the Nursing Council, the House
decided that the Bill should be referred back to the Social Services Committee to enable the
committee to re-examine the provisions for the registration of registered nurses (assistant).
The committee agreed with the further representations that instead of a register of registered
nurses (assistant) a roll should be established by the Nursing Council to cater for this group
of nurses who hitherto had been registered as community nurses. I undertook to introduce
legislation to Parliament this year to implement the views of the select committee.
The 1975 amendment Bill also made provision for the removal of any discrimination in
nursing on the grounds of sex. The present Act makes provision for private charitable
institutions to be approved as schools of nursing. For some years there have been no such
schools, and as these institutions do not wish to establish schools of nursing the provision is
being omitted from this Bill. The Bill makes provision for the registration of comprehensive
nurses-that is, nurses who have undergone training as such. It also makes provision for
nurses who are currently registered as general nurse and maternity nurse, and either
psychiatric nurse or psychopaedic nurse, to be registered as comprehensive nurses.
The opportunity is also being taken, in view of the substantial amendments to the
registration provisions, to consolidate the 1971 Act and its 1975 amendment. Apart from the
changes I referred to earlier, there are no substantive changes to the original Act, but some
minor matters of clarification have been embodied in the Bill. I propose to move that clauses
16 and 17, relating to registration and enrolment of nurses, be referred to the Social Services
Committee. I realise that this is an unusual procedure. However, the remaining clauses of
the Bill are a re-enactment of the 1971 Act or are clauses accepted by the select committee
last year in the 1975 amendment Bill.
Mr HUNT (New Lynn): I received a copy of the Bill only two or three moments ago. I
am very pleased that clauses 16 and 17 will be referred to a select committee. I presume that
the hearing of evidence will be open to the news media. The Minister acknowledges that. I
shall make no other comment on the Bill until I have had a chance to study it.
Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga): I compliment the Minister on the attitude to this Bill. As he
pointed out, a lot of time was spent last year in trying to sort out the various titles of nurses.
The move to differentiate between registration and enrolment is of considerable importance.
Can the Minister highlight enrolment and registration?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The Bill is no particular credit to the Minister. It
has not moved along as party legislation, but with the complete agreement of both sides of
the House. The Social Services Committee thought that community nurses should continue
to be registered. When the measure was before the House last year I said that it was not a
matter for parliamentarians. If the nurses clearly demonstrated what they wanted they
should have it. They gave clear evidence to the select committee that they wanted a special
roll set up, as is done in the United Kingdom. It has caused considerable administrative
work, but judgment of whether the move is right does not rest upon whether it will be a
nuisance. The move is toward what the Nurses Association and the Nursing Council want.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I move, That the Bill be referred to the Social
Services Committee for consideration of clauses 16 and 17, and that during the hearing of
evidence the committee be open to accredited representatives of the news media.
Motion agreed to.
WAIKATO VALLEY AUTHORITY AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): I move, That the Waikato
Valley Authority Amendment Bill be introduced. The Bill is a short one of only three clauses,
and deals with two matters, both uncontroversial. The first is the membership of the
authority, and the second is the general administrative expenses of the authority. The Bill
amends section 4 of the principal Act, which sets out the entitlement of the local authorities


## p. 3058 (#696) ###########################################

3058
16 September
Waikato Valley Authority Amendment Bill
within the Waikato valley to representation on the authority.
The amendment deletes from the Act the provision detailing the number of members
that each local authority or group of local authorities are entitled to elect to the authority.
The Bill provides for not more than 14 members to be elected to represent constituent
districts, either separately or as part of a combined district. The representation of the
Ministry of Works and Development, the New Zealand Electricity Department, and the local
drainage and river boards, which are each entitled to one member, remains unchanged. The
Bill also provides for the representation of the local authorities on the Waikato Valley
Authority to be determined by Order in Council in accordance with any agreement between
the authority and the councils of the constituent districts. If the local authorities fail to agree
as to their representation the clause sets out the criteria by which the representation is to be
determined.
The amendment is required as a consequence of the amalgamation of Te Kuiti Borough
and Waitomo County, now the Waitomo District Council, and of Otorohanga Borough and
Otorohanga Council, now known as Otorohanga County. In view of the coming local body
elections it will be necessary to expedite the passage of the Bill.
Clause 3 amends section 10, subsection (3), of the principal Act, which provides for the
payment of the local authorities' share of the general administrative expenses of the
authority. At present one half of the liability of each constituent local authority for its share
of the administrative expenses is determined by reference to adjusted rateable values, and
the other half by the assessed loading of the proposed works and services in its district. The
clause provides that in future years these expenses will be apportioned among the
constituent local authorities solely on the basis of adjusted rateable capital values.
The Bill has the full support of the Waikato Valley Authority, its constituent councils,
and the National Water and Soil Conservation Authority, and will provide a much needed
updating of representation on the Waikato Valley Authority and an improved method of
determining and apportioning the authority's administrative expenses among the constituent
councils.

TENANCY AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): I move, That the Tenancy Amendment
Bill be introduced. This short Bill is consequent upon the Government's decision to transfer
legislation relating to tenancies and rentals from the Department of Labour to the Housing
Corporation. The effect of the Tenancy Act is to protect a very limited number of tenancies
that have existed since before 1955, and in particular to give security of tenure to the tenants.
The Bill will in no way affect the rights of these tenants either now or in the future. It simply
does what I have said-transfers the administration of the Tenancy Act from the Depart-
ment of Labour to the Housing Corporation.
Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn): The Minister's explanation seems to be entirely inadequate.

away the supervision from a more independent body, the Department of Labour. In my
opinion there has not been sufficient explanation for the change. One should appreciate the
Department of Labour's enormous experience in this field, and in the supervision of all sorts

cannot be calculated with certainty. Most tenancies coming under the aegis of the Tenancy
Act are State rental house tenancies, of which there is a fair number. Between 12 000 and

security of tenure, as well as a formula by which the rentals can be calculated. Sooner or
later, with the effluxion of time, the Tenancy Act will overtake itself, and no tenancies will
be covered by it.

affected in any way by the transfer from the Department of Labour to the Housing
Corporation. The same rules, the same law, the same security of tenure, and the same
method of rent calculation will apply as apply today. For example, the Housing Corporation
calculates the rental for a State house to which the Tenancy Act applies according to the
Tenancy Act, and that is that—and there will, of course, be no change.

Rent Appeal Amendment Bill, which deals with tenancies not covered by the Tenancy Act.
It was stated in the National Party's election manifesto that the administration of that Act
would be transferred from the Department of Labour to the Housing Corporation. It would
clearly be inappropriate to have two Acts dealing with tenancies administered by different
departments. Therefore, the administration of both Acts is being transferred from the
Department of Labour to the Housing Corporation.

RENT APPEAL AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): I move, That the Rent Appeal
Amendment Bill be introduced. This short, five-clause Bill fulfils a promise in the National
Party 1975 election manifesto, by transferring administration of the Rent Appeal Act from
the Department of Labour to the Housing Corporation of New Zealand. Clauses 2 and 3(1)
are directly consequent on this decision. At the same time, the opportunity has been taken to
make a number of minor changes, all designed to improve the operation of the Act, and the
efficiency of rent appeal boards. Experience since the Act was passed in 1973 has shown that
there is an almost complete lack of uniformity and consistency in the manner in which the
boards operate, and the methods by which they present their findings, so clauses 3(2), 4, and


## p. 3063 (#701) ###########################################

16 September
3063
Rent Appeal Amendment Bill
5 propose changes that will help to improve those aspects.
Clause 3(2) provides that the Director-General of the Housing Corporation, or an
officer of the corporation whom he delegates, will be the secretary of each board. In this
way, I am sure that the desired uniformity and consistency of operation as to method,
decision making, and presentation will result. Clause 5 makes a number of minor changes to
the second schedule, which details the routine to be followed by the boards. The changes
are: first, a fee may be prescribed to accompany applications. This may be refunded in part
or in full if so ordered by the board, and I would expect this to be the case except where
applications had been judged by the board to be frivolous or vexatious, or of a similar
nature.
Secondly, in its written assessment, the board shall state three matters: the value of the
premises; the existing rent, if any; and the landlord's return. Those are three factors which
must be taken into account in every case, and by requiring them to be shown when the
assessment is given, some consistency will exist in the way the boards present the results of
their deliberations. At the same time, the board may dismiss an application if it is not
proceeded with with reasonable expedition, and an applicant, similarly, may withdraw his
application at any time before it has been determined.
Clause 4 introduces the concept of assessment by consent. Provided both the landlord
and the tenant agree, the Housing Corporation may refer a preliminary assessment to the
rent appeal board, which, at its discretion, may agree to it without a formal hearing. The Bill
makes no changes of principle. We believe, and we said so in our manifesto, that the
Housing Corporation of New Zealand is better equipped to handle matters of rent and rent
appeals.
Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn): The Bill poses certain problems. In introducing the Bill, the
Minister repeatedly said that it was part of the National Party's election manifesto. Looking
at some of the clauses, the Bill appears to be a gift from the Government to landlords. It
dilutes the effects of the rent appeal boards and their work throughout the country until now.
For example, the Minister went to great pains to tell us that the provisions of clause 3(2)
would prevent any inconsistencies, but he did not elucidate what those inconsistencies were.
He said that the simple way to end inconsistencies was to make the Director-General of the
Housing Corporation the secretary of each board, but he will not be, because he has the right
to delegate that responsibility to people in different metropolitan areas and they will make
their decisions in the same way as they have in the past. So, really, there is no change.
The supervision of the enforcement of the rent appeal legislation is being taken away
from the Department of Labour-an independent body—and given to the largest landlord in
the country. So the rent appeal boards will now come under the control of the largest
landlord in the country. By giving responsibility to the Housing Corporation, the Govern-

BEER DUTY BILL
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): I move, That the Beer Duty Bill be
introduced. The purpose of the Bill is to modernise and consolidate the legislation relating to
the control of brewing operations and the collection of duty on beer brewed in New Zealand


## p. 3068 (#706) ###########################################

3068
16 September
Beer Duty Bill
for sale. The present law is largely covered by the Finance Act 1915, and has not kept pace
with various major changes in brewing techniques that have taken place in more recent
times, particularly those relating to continuous brewing and continuous fermentation. The
objective of the departmental study, which has led to the introduction of the Bill, has been to
switch the point of duty collection from the wort stage to the point where the beer is in a
consumable state and is delivered from the brewery. It is also intended to substitute an audit
check of the companies' records for the present cumbersome system of measuring quantities
and specific gravities of wort at the time it is pitched and the fermentation process begins.
Factors which needed to be taken into account in the departmental study were, first,
that the level of revenue from this form of taxation should remain unaltered, and, secondly,
that the incidence of the tax as between the brewery companies should be maintained as far
as possible. The proposed system classifies beer into three categories: first, beer not
exceeding 4.35 percent alcohol by volume-standard beer; secondly, beer exceeding 4.35
percent, but not exceeding 5 percent alcohol by volume-medium beer; and, thirdly, beer
exceeding 5 percent alcohol by volume-strong beer. Duty will be levied on the three
categories as follows: on standard beer, 15.94c a litre; on medium beer, 19.93c a litre; and on
strong beer, 25.1c a litre. These rates provide virtually the same amount of revenue as is
currently received from this form of taxation, and there is virtually no significant change in
the incidence of the tax as between the brewery companies. I emphasise that this means
there will be no change in the price of beer. The structure of the tax and the proposed form
of the legislation have been discussed with the brewery companies, which have indicated that
they are in general agreement with the proposals.
The Department of Justice, which is responsible for the control of alcoholic liquor, has
also been consulted about the provisions of the Bill. Apart from a new basis for collecting
duty, all but one of the clauses are machinery items from existing customs legislation, and
are now brought together under one roof for the administration of beer duty. The exception
is clause 15(2), which provides that exporters of New Zealand beer will no longer have to pay
duty before export, and then have to apply for a refund. It is proposed that the Act will come
into force on 1 April 1978.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): Where the liability of the
exporter to pay the tax has been removed, is the procedure to be changed to make sure that
the beer is exported when it is stated that it is for that purpose? That point was not covered
by the Minister. In the past there have been various rates of duty. I understand the three
categories of duty are to be imposed on draught beer, ordinary bottled beer, and strong
beer. The categories must have some effect on different brands, because they are not all
identical. The change in duty will not affect all brews equally if the strength is not the same.
What will happen if a brewer changes the strength of his beer to meet the limits? Will this be
covered by price control legislation? Does the drop to meet the standards bring back price
control? From information I have received I understand that the previous allowance for
wastage has been changed. There has been a reasonable allowance for wastage under the old
brewing and duty assessment procedures. I ask the Minister to answer those questions.
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): I draw the member's attention to clause
16, which provides that no beer brewed for export may be delivered from any brewery
without the permission of the collector. This would deal with the situation where a brewer,
under the guise of exporting the beer, did not pay the duty. I do not for one minute suggest
that any brewer would do this, but it pays to provide for the possibility. There are differences
for brewers who, for whatever reasons, want to make a stronger beer. Leopard has a
lagerisation process that involves storage under controlled temperatures and conditions for
up to 24 days. In some cases under the existing basis of payment the company has paid duty
on the beer when the yeast was added to the wort, whereas other companies would have sold
the beer by that time. Leopard would have to wait longer to recoup the duty. The new
system will give that company a slight advantage over the current system, because the duty
will become payable at a later stage, giving an improved cash-flow position.
Under the present legislation the wastage allowance is 10 percent. The new legislation
makes no provision for wastage, because it is not necessary to do so. Under the present
system, duty is assessed at an early stage in the manufacturing process. Under the proposed
system, duty will not be assessed until the manufacture is completed, so no allowance for
wastage is needed. I hope the member will accept my assurance that I will give him the
information about price controls at the second reading.

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): First, I am surprised--but I accept that

the brewery companies, and they are satisfied. I should also repeat that there will be no

The member may not have heard me say that one of the basic terms of reference of the
departmental study that brought the legislation into being was that the level of revenue
should remain unaltered. As an example to prove that that was achieved, I point out,

payment of tax been left as they were there might have been a fairly substantial cash-flow
advantage to the brewery companies. As it is, there will be very little advantage to most of
them, because we have reduced the deferment period and in effect eliminated any real
advantage with regard to cash flow.
The final point is what would happen if one manufacturer lowered his quality. Brewing
is a competitive business, and the average New Zealand man—and I am sure this applies to
members of the Woolston Workingmen's Club referred to by the member for
Sydenham-knows the difference between good beer and bad beer. They will know,
whether the member for Sydenham realises it or not, that any brand that lowers its quality
will quickly find itself suffering severely with respect to sales. So a reduction in beer quality is
unlikely, but if it did happen the effect of this Bill would be neutral in regard to price. Any
price reduction consequential upon a fall in quality would be determined by the regulations
dealing with price.
I think I have basically covered the points raised. Perhaps I could add that we are
moving, with this new base of computation-which uses alcoholic content rather than
specific gravity as the basis for payment of duty-to a system that is widely accepted
overseas. I should perhaps add that this will eliminate a large amount of labour-intensive
work that currently involves a number of Customs officers, and will leave them more time
for other duties. It falls in line with overseas practice, and with modern manufacturing
processes, and will have a positive effect on administration inside the Customs Department.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
ESTATE AND GIFT DUTIES AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): I move, That the Estate and
Gift Duties Amendment Bill be introduced. This Bill makes miscellaneous amendments to the
Estate and Gift Duties Act 1968. The amendments made in clauses 3, 5, and 6 of the Bill give
effect to the principles of the Human Rights Commission Bill at present before the House by
removing, where appropriate, discrimination between males and females. The other amend-
ments are of a comparatively minor nature, and deal with such matters as fines for offences
and remissions of duty.
Without dealing in detail at this stage with each specific clause, I will briefly outline the
amendments in the Bill to make these general points clear. Clause 2 is a machinery
amendment as a consequence of the Government Actuary taking over from the Commis-
sioner of Inland Revenue the responsibility for approving group superannuation schemes.
Clause 3 extends the $2,000 a year exemption for pensions payable from group superannua-
tion schemes to apply to widowers in addition to those paid to widows. Clause 4 increases the
amount of duty, interest, and penalty the commissioner may remit without the prior


## p. 3071 (#709) ###########################################

16 September
3071
Estate and Gift Duties Amendment Bill
approval of the Minister of Finance from $500 to $1,000. Clauses 5 and 6 exempt from gift
duty certain payments to a widower from a deceased's former employer or from a group
superannuation scheme. At present the exemption applies only to payments to widows.
Clause 7 increases the maximum fines that can be imposed for offences against the Act. This
clause will apply from 1 January 1978. All the other clauses will apply from the date of
introduction, 16 September 1977.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): My only questions refer to

being raised. I do not remember a significant number of these requests for exemption

whether there has been any increase in the number of requests for remission?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): There has not been any
particular increase, but it is part of a general updating of figures. We are updating an Act
passed in 1968, so I think responsibility for it will have to be taken among us. It was thought
sensible, while updating the Act, to provide for a reasonable level of increase.
Bill introduced and read a first time.

Shipping Services, New Zealand and Singapore
1. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson), on behalf of Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt.

Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): As I advised members recently,

trade requirements. However, I believe it would be premature for me to comment further at

Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Can the Minister indicate when he will feel free to make a public
statement?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: Shipping companies, which are companies quite apart
from the Government or Government control, inform me when they intend to start, and
sometimes give me information about certain routes. I have to choose the time when I
should make a comment on behalf of the Government, and I cannot indicate that at the
moment.

discussions with the Singapore Shipping Company on this matter?

routes and are surveying them, I do not want to make any statement that might prejudice

Defence Expenditure
4. Mr H. N. AUSTIN (Hobson), on behalf of Mr BRILL (Kapiti), asked the Minister of
Defence: What proportion of total Government spending is outlaid on defence in New
Zealand, and how does this figure compare with the proportions expended in Sweden and
Switzerland respectively?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I reply on behalf of the Minister of Defence.
Differences in the scope of the Government sector invalidate comparisons. However, the
following information shows national trends. New Zealand: 1974, 4.5 percent; 1975, 4.3
percent; and 1976, 4.3 percent. Sweden: 1974, 10.3 percent; 1975, 10.5 percent; and 1976,
9.6 percent. Switzerland: 1974, 19.2 percent; 1975, 19.3 percent; and 1976, 19.1 percent.
Hon. David Thomson: Is it significant that the two countries mentioned-Sweden and
Switzerland-have, for many years maintained a policy of armed neutrality?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Yes, that is quite significant. The demands on countries with common
borders, to keep up with sophisticated modern equipment and stockpile that equipment, is
very great.

WILLS AMENDMENT BILL
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Wills Amendment Bill. The committee recommends that
the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie upon the table. The
House will recall that this Bill makes three changes to the Wills Act 1837 of the United
Kingdom Parliament, an Act that still has legislative force in this country to a limited extent.
Clauses 3 and 4 of the Bill make changes to the general laws relating to wills. These changes
were of such a nature that they required no attention from the committee; in fact, no
submissions were received on the two clauses. However, the committee's attention was
directed towards clause 2, which gives effect to a recommendation of the Property Law and
Equity Reform Committee in its report of November 1973. At present a will is automatically
revoked by a subsequent marriage. However, a similar rule does not apply where the
spouses are divorced after the making of a will. The effect is that a will made during the
marriage, which probably names the other spouse as a principal or sole beneficiary, would
continue to have effect after the divorce from that spouse unless specific steps were taken to
revoke that will.
In its report, the law reform committee cited several examples of injustices that resulted
from this rule of law, and recommended a change. Clause 2, as introduced, seeks to amend
the Wills Act to provide that, where a testator is subsequently divorced, his or her will shall
be read in all respects as if his or her former spouse had predeceased him, unless the will
expressly provides otherwise. The effect of clause 2 would be to nullify a gift by will to the
other partner of a former marriage, and to nullify the appointment of that former spouse as
an executor or trustee of the will. The New Zealand Law Society, the Public Trust Office,
and the New Zealand Trustee Companies Association indicated that they did not wish to
make any submissions on the Bill, and the select committee correctly assumed from this their
support for these provisions.
One detailed submission was received from a Wellington barrister. This submission
raised some substantive questions, and it, together with additional advice received by the
select committee from the Department of Justice and from parliamentary counsel, leads us


## p. 3084 (#722) ###########################################

3084
16 September
Wills Amendment Bill
to recommend certain changes to clause 2. The first change to subclause (1) is intended to
clarify the status of divorce decrees, etc. The second change that we recommend is the
deletion of clause 2(1)(a)(iii). The purpose of this subclause had been to nullify any direction
contained in a will absolving a former spouse from payment of death duty on any part of the
dutiable estate of the testator that might in fact belong to the former marriage partner. This
subclause refers to property commonly known as the notional estate, usually that which has
been disposed of by one spouse to the other, often by way of gift, in the 3 years immediately
preceding the death of the testator. The officials assisting the committee suggested a further
change to this clause, intended to make clearer the responsibility for payment of death duty.
Committee members entertained some doubt as to the suitability of this amendment, and,
for that matter, the original subclause. Subsequent discussions between parliamentary coun-
sel, the Inland Revenue Department, and the Public Trust Office indicated that the whole
subclause was probably unnecessary. With this advice in mind, the select committee
recommends that the subclause be deleted.
It was pointed out that in certain circumstances a testator might still wish to make
specific provision in his or her will in favour of a former spouse, and that, as drafted, clause 2
did not permit this to be done. Accordingly, we recommend certain changes to subclause (2)
to enable a will to be made in anticipation of divorce, in much the same way that a testator
can at present make a will in anticipation of marriage. The select committee also recom-
mends the deletion of subclause (2)(c) and subclause (3), and the insertion of a new
subclause (3) that will make clearer the status of wills that have been confirmed by a
subsequent codicil on the one hand, and also the status of wills that have been re-executed or
revived on the other hand.
Finally, we recommend that the Bill should come into force on 1 July 1978, thereby
enabling its provisions to be well publicised before they take effect. All these changes are of
a somewhat technical nature. They are all consistent with the original report by the law
reform committee, and with the Bill as introduced, but they clarify certain points that
emerged from the one substantive submission received by the committee, and also overcome
certain problems that emerged during the committee's deliberations on the Bill.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): This is a routine law reform Bill that originally
arose out of a matter mentioned by the former Minister of Justice, the member for
Henderson. It is worth while that members should know how this reform came about. I am
opposed to the Bill, not in a party sense as it is not party legislation, but because I believe
that Parliament should take a careful look at what we are doing today.
I read from the first page of the report by the Property Law and Equity Reform
Committee: "The Minister of Justice received a letter from a practitioner arising out of a
case in which he"-the practitioner-was involved. In that case the testator had made a will
during the last war, leaving his whole estate to his wife. They were divorced some 8 years
later, and he died some 20 years after the divorce, survived by his former wife. He had not
altered his will, and accordingly his whole estate, which happened to be quite substantial,
passed to the woman who had not been in his life for some 20 years." As a result of this, the
Minister wrote a letter to the law reform committee, asking whether the law needed to be
reformed. In reply, the committee stated: "In light of this case, the majority of the
committee considers that some amendment to the present law would be desirable." What
the majority recommended, and the reasons for the recommendations, are set out in the
report, which we are more or less talking about in this legislation. "On the other hand, some
members of the committee doubt—and I think this is important-whether there is a need to
change the present law. In their view, the circumstances where hardship or injustice is likely
to occur are so few that legislative intervention is unnecessary."
This matter is not one of party politics, as it was not mentioned in the manifestoes of
either party. However, should Parliament be spending its time altering the law in this way? I
believe that the change that will be made will cause as many injustices as those occurring at
present. My objection arises partly because of my experience as a solicitor, when I appeared
for a case that occurred as a result of similar circumstances. The parties had divorced, and
the husband was killed in a car crash. Admittedly my client was the former wife, and,
although she had remarried, her previous husband had not. As she was looking after the
child of her first marriage, she collected the estate. I do not think that any great injustice was
done, because obviously the money would go to that man's child. The other factor that
should be taken into account is that there was a will in existence at the time the man died.
Although he could have changed his will, he had chosen not to.
I accept that Parliament should help some people, but I do not accept that it has to re-


## p. 3085 (#723) ###########################################

16 September
3085
Wills Amendment Bill
write the wills of every divorced person in New Zealand, which is exactly what it is doing.
Parliament is saying that when you are divorced it will change your will for you and if you do
not like that, you will have to write another one. I have a fundamental objection to that,
because the general legal principle that you can write your own will and leave your money to
whoever you like without Parliament telling you what to do is a good one. That right has
been limited, because Parliament has said that a family must be protected under the Family
Protection Act. However, I do not see why a divorced person should have to have his will
rewritten for him. If he is so lazy that he cannot rewrite his will, so be it.
However, in some cases I have dealt with, when I have asked a person about to be
divorced whether he wants to rewrite his will, he has usually said he will wait until he has
remarried. If I had told that person that he must rewrite a will, he would not have left
anything to his former wife. I think many people feel an obligation to their former partners,
and if they want to leave their money to them that is probably the best thing to do.
Mr McLay: They can do that.
Mr PREBBLE: No, they cannot. What I want to point out is that Parliament has now
said that, when divorced, a person cannot leave his or her money to a former partner without
rewriting the will. Parliament is giving some sort of social welfare to divorced people, which I
think is unnecessary.
My other objection, which I raised with the Statutes Revision Committee, on which I
sat, is that I believe that far too much legislation of this sort is being passed, and that quantity
is being mistaken for quality. Last year, 219 Bills were on the Order Paper, some of which
were as long as a book. In 1976, Parliament sat for 5932 hours.
Mr Schultz: What about the year before?
Mr PREBBLE: If we did nothing else, we were passing a Bill every 2.7 hours. This year,
we have a similar rate. The member asks what about the year before. I am not raising this in
a party political sense, because both parties have been guilty of passing too much legislation,
although I point out that the late Norman Kirk was one of the strongest opponents of the
flood of legislation through the House. We are creating uncertainty. The law at the moment
is certain, it is known. There is only one way one can have one's will revoked in law, and that
is on marriage. That is a common-law principle that goes back a good many years. We have
now established divorce as a second way in which a will can become invalid after it has been
written. I do not think there is any evidence in favour of the reform, and it was interesting to
note that no one came to the select committee to give evidence. The Law Society did not
bother, and said it had nothing to say. Trustee associations involved in wills did not see any
need to change the laws. We could say that they were saying they agreed with the reform,
but we could also take it that they did not think it a matter of any great substance. Parliament
should look at all legislation and ask the basic question: is it necessary; do we have to change
the law? If the answer is no, and it is not absolutely necessary, we should not change it,
because the certainty of the law is worth striving for and worth holding.
I have made this speech in the House before, and I shall make it again, because we are
flooding the House with unnecessary legislation. As a result of this Bill a number of former
wives will find themselves in a difficult position, when they may have shared the life of their
husbands for 30 or 40 years before their divorce. If he did not want to cut her out of his will,
and she did not want to cut him out of hers, why should we? For that reason, I am opposed to
the Bill. I will not vote against it, because I would then be offending against the whole
principle that we are wasting our time.
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): The member for Auckland Central claimed that there were
219 Bills on the Order Paper last year. He was completely wrong. There were 219 numbers
in the Bill book, but that was all-not 219 Bills, but 219 numbers in the Bill book. That is an
indication of how detailed his research was into this particular issue. I think all I need to say
to the House on this occasion is that when the member for Auckland Central suggests that
this Bill will be the only legislation in which Parliament interferes with people's wills, he
completely ignores the principle-although he mentioned the Acts briefly in passing-that a
will is revoked automatically on a person's marriage. I refer him also to the provisions of the
Family Protection Act 1955 and the Law Reform (Testamentary Promises) Act 1949. Both
interfere with wills in certain circumstances, and that principle is maintained in this Bill, but
only in the most limited of limited circumstances.
Motion agreed to.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Decentralisation of Government Departments
1. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of State Services: Are any investiga-
tions or plans under way at present to decentralise Government departmental work from
Wellington?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services): The policy on the decentralisation of
Government departmental work is clearly set out in the manifesto. Permanent heads are
consequently required to continually review their departments' functions and activities with
the aim of bringing administration closer to the general public through increased delegation
and decentralisation. Representations have also been received from various regional groups
suggesting dispersal possibilities, and these are all considered by the departments concerned.
At present a number of cost effectiveness investigations are being undertaken in depart-
ments in relation to the dispersal of specific activities from Wellington to smaller centres.
One such investigation includes stage II of the Government Printing Office move to
Masterton.
Mr Marshall: What other moves are being canvassed at present?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I have here a list of possibilities being investigated, but I do not
want to be held to it. In the Department of Lands and Survey, the map depository could
possibly go to Masterton and the cartographic branch to Palmerston North. The transfer of
the district office from Wellington to Palmerston North does not look likely, but is still being
studied. The location of the citizenship branch of the Department of Internal Affairs is being
investigated, and the Ministry of Defence is looking at the possibility of relocating Home
Command in Wellington. There is also a potential change in the motor vehicle registration
section, currently in Palmerston North, being linked into the Wanganui computer.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Native Timber Exports
2. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Forests: What limitations are
there on the export of native timber?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): On 3 July 1967 Cabinet approved of the
removal of prohibition on the export of native timbers, with the exception of kauri. Exports
are approved only under a permit system if sawmills are accumulating stocks—in excess of
local demand-and are not cutting above their normal capacity or working over 40 hours a
week or in any other way increasing their output to supply any export orders. Major
shipments are approved only after consultation with the Department of Trade and Industry.
This Cabinet approval is reviewed periodically on the basis of recommendations by the
Indigenous Forest Timber Advisory Committee.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Oil and Natural Gas Prospecting
3. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Energy Resources: What has
been the success rate in prospecting for either oil or natural gas in the on-shore investigations
in New Zealand over the past 15 years?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): Since 1962 over 60 on-shore
exploration wells have been drilled in New Zealand, and no commercial discoveries have
been made. The Kapuni field was discovered in 1959.
Hon. W. W. Freer: In view of that background, why does the Government, which


## p. 3087 (#725) ###########################################

20 September
3087
Oral Answers to Questions
criticised a Labour Government for having a partial participation in exploration, now want
to accept full economic responsibility for exploration?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I refer only to on-shore exploration. The honourable member will
know that the previous arrangement for Government and private sector participation in off-
shore exploration continues. Licences for on-shore exploration in six areas were taken out
on the day after this year's Budget. The Government is drilling and carrying out seismic
surveys to prove to its satisfaction whether or not these areas have any prospects. The
private sector had been unwilling to continue drilling in these areas, and the Government
considered it necessary to obtain an answer as quickly as possible to whether or not gas or oil
was there so that energy policies could be developed in the light of that knowledge.
Hon. W. W. Freer: As all records of private drilling in these areas are already available
to the Government, why is it necessary to spend a large amount of taxpayers' money in areas
already drilled?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The areas in question have not been thoroughly proven. I remind the
honourable member that the province of Alberta in Canada, which is one of the great oil and
gas areas of the Northern Hemisphere, had this very interesting feature in its history. I read
about this recently.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Before or after the Budget?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: Before the Budget. At a little place called Leduc, not far from
Edmonton, 133 dry holes were drilled. The one hundred and thirty-fourth drilling opened up
a new oil empire.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Why are private interests no longer taking out on-shore licences?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: One reason given by some oil companies was that they felt that the
terms the Government was proposing were too severe, but I think a much more likely
explanation is that the chances of a major find are very small indeed, and the oil companies
are much more concerned with the prospect of a major find of international value which
might occur off shore. The chances of a find of that scale on shore are very small indeed.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
King Country Land Use Study
4. Mr LUXTON (Piako) asked the Minister of Lands: Why has the King Country land
use study extended further than the area originally considered by New Zealand Forest
Products Ltd as appropriate for its afforestation plans for the King Country, and when will
these surveys be complete?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): The boundaries for the King Country land use
study area were extended to better assist the resolution of conflicts of land use, guide
resource developments, and aid decision making. It was recognised that sufficient land
would not be available for the establishment of a viable afforestation industry in the New
Zealand Forest Products study area without conversion of existing farm land. Therefore, the
study area was extended in order to better illustrate the extent of unused land with potential
for afforestation that exists in the enlarged region. Work on stage 1, incorporating the
company's study areas, has been completed and the report will be printed by early October.
However, the full study will not be completed until March 1978, although the maps for the
whole area are likely to be available in November.
Mr Luxton: What is the total area involved in this survey?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The land originally under study, that proposed for afforestation by
New Zealand Forest Products, was 108 000 hectares. Sheet 1 was included in that area,
which extended to 169 000 hectares. Additional areas included are 101 000 hectares on sheet
2 and 166 000 hectares on sheet 3. Therefore, the total extended study area is 436 000
hectares.
Mr Hunt: The Minister mentioned reports which would be published in October and
some maps in November. Can copies of those be made available to at least some members of
the Opposition?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I shall be quite happy to give that assurance because, if for no other
reason, the Opposition spokesman on lands has a distinct interest in the proposals for the
King Country.

Import Deposit Scheme
6. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Customs: What effect has the
import deposit scheme had since its introduction on the volume of imports?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): The Minister of
Customs replies as follows: Volume statistics are not recorded by the Department of
Statistics for all of the items at present covered by the import deposit scheme. In those items
where volumes are recorded it is revealed that the volumes imported decreased by an
average of 30 percent during the period February 1976 to January 1977, being the first year
of operation of the import deposit scheme, when compared to the previous 12-month period.
A comparison of the latest available statistics, covering the 12 months ended 30 June 1977,
indicates that imports have been reduced by volume to a level 25 percent below that
pertaining before the introduction of the import deposit scheme.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Is it not correct that the reduction in volume reflects the inflationary
trend in prices overseas since licences have been held to a 100-percent basis over the last 2
years?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The reduction in volume of any imports has a great
relationship to the costs of imports overseas, which have increased quite spectacularly.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Can the Minister then confirm that it is not correct to claim that the
reduction has been the direct result of the import deposit scheme?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I believe that where the volumes are connected to
these quite impressive figures the scheme has had a very definite effect in relation to the
curtailment—
Hon. W. W. Freer: The Minister has just denied that.
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I am not saying that is the entire reason. I am saying
it has had a distinct effect, because most products which have not been subject to the import
deposit scheme show increases both in volume and value.

Police Patrol Base, Avondale
8. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Police: Is the Avondale police patrol
base manned on a 24-hour basis, and if not, in view of the increasing population in this area,
when will it be so manned?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Police. The Avondale patrol base is not manned on a 24-hour basis. At present the base has
a staff of seven constables under the control of a sergeant. These members carry out
inquiries, foot patrols, hotel visits, and similar duties on a rostered basis between the hours
of 7 a.m. to 11 p.m: 7 days a week, as well as manning the public office of the base during
normal business hours, including late shopping night. In addition, the full resources of the
Auckland Central Police Station are available. Twenty-four-hour crime and incident patrols
are deployed in the areas of Avondale and Mt. Albert to ensure a rapid response to
complaints, and also provide an additional preventive service. When the base is unmanned
personal callers may receive immediate assistance by medium of a telephone provided in the
foyer of the base, which connects the caller direct to the central operations room. It is
considered that the service provided to this suburban area is of the highest possible standard,
and indeed is more than adequate to meet present demands. Any extension of the service
provided at the patrol base cannot be justified at this time, but the matter will, in accordance
with departmental policy, be kept under constant review.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Is it not a fact that a recent survey showed a need for more
police than the Government has made available, and under those circumstances would it not
be an advantage to have the Avondale patrol base open for 24 hours?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: The Government has recently authorised an increase in the
number of police, but the rest of the member's question should be put down with notice to
enable a proper answer to be given.
Mr Hunt: In view of the Minister's reply that the full resources of the Auckland Central
Police Station are available when the Avondale patrol base is closed, does the Minister
realise that the Auckland station is more than 15 minutes away by the fastest possible means,
and that with increasing crime and a very much increased population in the last few years this
now means that a town the size of Blenheim is not being serviced on a 24-hour basis?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: The member's question assumes that there are no crime and
incident patrols in the Avondale and Mt. Albert areas. I have already said that 24-hour crime
and incident patrols are deployed to ensure a rapid response to complaints. It would not
normally be necessary for a car to come from the Auckland Central Police Station.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Accepting the Minister's statement that a phone is available for
emergencies when the base is closed, what happens to telephone calls to the base when it is
not staffed? Are they automatically transferred to the Auckland Central Police Station, or
can that telephone not be manned for 24 hours?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: That is a very important question to which I do not have an
answer. I suggest that the member gives notice to the Minister of Police to get the answer.

Livestock Improvement Schemes, Waihora
9. Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North) asked the Minister of Lands: What increase in

Rotorua blocks for the past 4 years. In this period the lambing for this district has increased
by 12 percent. It is considered that most of this increase is attributable to breeding, and both
the Department of Lands and Survey and the Ministry of Agriculture are satisfied with the
results achieved. Comparisons between Waihora and commercial rams have revealed an
advantage in favour of the former of up to 14 percent in lambs docked. It is also a fact that

Immigration-Traditional-source Countries
12. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt), on behalf of Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central), asked the
Minister of Immigration: Is it correct that certain countries are designated as traditional-


## p. 3091 (#729) ###########################################

20 September
3091
Oral Answers to Questions
source countries for immigration purposes?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): Yes, it is correct that certain countries are
designated traditional-source countries for immigration purposes. They are countries from
which most of our skilled migrants have come, and where the vocational training systems and
work methods are compatible with our own. Migrants from such countries are well fitted by
training and experience to adapt to life and work in New Zealand. In addition, the
traditional migrant source countries are industrialised rather than developing countries
which have need of skilled people. No countries have been added to the list of traditional-
source countries in recent years.
Mr T. J. Young: Can the Minister name the countries that fit into the category?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Yes, I can. Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Finland,
France, the Federal Republic of Germany, Iceland, the Republic of Ireland, Italy, Luxem-
bourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Kingdom of Great
Britain and Northern Ireland, and the United States of America.
Mr Lambert: Can the Minister confirm that the policy on traditional-source countries
has remained a standard immigration policy under both the Government and the previous
Labour Government?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Yes, but I am not quite sure for how long. The list of traditional-
source countries has not been changed for many years.
Mr Lange: In the light of the Minister's answer that Iceland is a traditional migrant
source, would he not agree that as far as the development of New Zealand is concerned over
the years more people have come from India than from Iceland, and is it not time to review
that somewhat hoary tradition?
Hon. T. F. GILL: It is my belief that it is many years since New Zealand has had an
immigrant from Iceland. The United Nations agreement about taking skilled people from
India makes it impossible to call India a traditional-source country. A country cannot
become a traditional-source country by the stroke of a pen.

East Coast Forests-Roading
16. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Forests: What proposals has
the Government to upgrade the roads servicing the Ruatoria, Mangatu, Wharerata, and
Putunama forests?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): Local bodies can and should apply for
National Roads Board subsidy moneys as necessary. Where the Forest Service is one of the
main users of the roads in question I shall sympathetically consider recommending a
contribution to a proportion of the local share of the cost of upgrading it, and each case will
be considered on its merits. At the same time, it should be borne in mind that the Forest
Service is already contributing to local body funds in the form of grants in lieu of rates. This
has been the policy of successive Governments. The position is analogous to a private
landowner paying part of the local share of the cost of improved access to his land.
Hon. W. W. Freer: In view of the statement that local bodies can and should apply for
such grants, can the Minister say which local bodies have applied, the extent of their
applications, and the extent of the approvals?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: Without notice I cannot give the answers to those questions.
Mr Bell: Between 1972 and 1975 how much did the Government provide for the
upgrading of roads servicing the forests mentioned in the original question?
Hon. W. W. Freer: Strangely enough I have those figures!
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: No, and again I cannot give a satisfactory answer. An inter-
departmental committee is at present considering the sharing of the cost of upgrading work
among the National Roads Board, the Government, and the local authorities.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Could the Minister satisfy the curiosity of the member for Gisborne
and me by making available the details I requested in an earlier supplementary question?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I should be only too happy to provide any details that are available.
I know that the need to upgrade the roads, and the question of where the funds are to come
from have been concerning East Coast local authorities, particularly the East Coast Planning
Council.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
