QUESTION FOR WRITTEN ANSWER
Mr HUNT (New Lynn): A point of order, Mr Speaker. On page 957 of today's Order
Paper there is a question for written answer in the name of the member for
Wanganui-notice given 9 September; reply due 16 September. One can be reasonable if
there is a gap of one day, but it is now four days later, even though it is only one sitting day
later. I wonder if this is keeping to the spirit of the report of the last Standing Orders
Committee.
Mr LUXTON (Piako): There is a requirement that the member asking the question have
the answer, but there is no requirement-from my interpretation of the Standing Orders-
that it must be printed on that day.
Mr ACTING DEPUTY SPEAKER: Has the member for Wanganui received a copy of
the reply?
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui): I have not opened all my mail today, but as far as I know
the reply has not yet come to my office.
Mr HUNT (New Lynn): Many members are under the misapprehension that a written
question takes 1 week to answer. In 1974 the Standing Orders were changed, and Standing
Order 85 states. "The written reply shall be furnished not later than the third sitting day
following the first appearance of the notice of question on the Order Paper." If notice was
given on 9 September, that would mean that this question has appeared on the Order Paper
for longer than 3 days. It might be an idea to tidy up this procedure.
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): Standing Order 85 states that the written
reply shall be furnished not later than the third sitting day. We generally get into a jam when
questions are filed on Tuesday or Wednesday, and there is a spillover. There is Thursday and
Friday, and then the next sitting day is Tuesday. That may not be the case here.
Mr Hunt: Five sitting days.
Hon. J. B. GORDON: There is a spillover, and the weekend intervenes. Maybe that is
what happened. I have inquired whether the matter is in hand. Apparently it is under way at
present, and the reply should have been delivered.
Mr ACTING DEPUTY SPEAKER: I see no difficulty in having the matter rectified. If
the member has not received the written answer, I am sure the Minister will supply it to him.
The obligation in Standing Order 85 refers to the furnishing of the written reply to the
member. There is no obligation to print the reply in Hansard by the time specified in the
Standing Order.

A working party had been established recently to investigate the position of supervising
head teachers in kindergartens, and he expected its report soon. In-service training would be
considered at a conference early in November. He had discussed with councils the important
question of the maximum use of education buildings and teachers colleges.
It was essential to maintain a balance in the numbers of overseas students coming to
New Zealand, and it so happened that there had been a high proportion of Malaysians. The
proportion from one country should not exceed 25 percent. That had meant a reduction in
the number of Malaysians, but no attempt had been made to reduce the total. Prospective
students from other countries would be selected in the usual way by the committee set up for
this purpose. It was essentially a matter of foreign relations, and not entirely education.
For many years land in Clermont Terrace had been zoned for halls of residence for
Victoria University, and land was being purchased as it became available. Not enough land
was yet available on which to build the projected residential block.
Most tertiary bursaries were $13 abated bursaries, and the extra $2 was a 16 percent
increase. In 1975, bursaries paid to university students had totalled $12.5 million, compared
with $23.5 million during the current year-an 87 percent increase in 2 years. Total
university grants had risen from $63 million to $87 million-an increase of 37 percent.
Although the site for the new Onerahi school had been retained, he doubted whether
the school would be built until the projected rolls confirmed a need for it. A site had been
acquired for the Weymouth school, and negotiations were in train for a boundary adjust-
ment. It was hoped that the school would open in 1981-82. Most of the land needed for the
Papakura No.3 school had been acquired, and negotiations were under way for the rest.
Land was also held in Settlement Road for the Papakura intermediate school, but on present
projections it seemed unlikely that that school would be needed before 1983. Previously, it
had been stated that the Roscommon Road School-when opened in 1977-would have a
roll of 700, and that, if the Sykes Road School was not built in 1977, the Roscommon Road
School roll would be nearly 1300 by 1978. However, the Roscommon Road School had
opened with a much smaller roll than the projected 700, which showed the difficulties of
projecting too far ahead. Tenders were now being accepted for the Sykes Road School,
which should be opened in late 1978 or early 1979.

The school year and the Government's financial year were different; schools were
supplied with grants at the old rate until the end of March, and for the remainder of the year
they were supplied at the new rate, which transferred into the beginning of the following
year. Every change in the rate was related to the Government's financial year, and the
provisions made applied to a full financial year from 1 April. The only exception was for
heating, lighting, and water charges, which were made fully inflation-proof. Secondary
schools that had not used the grant of $3 a head for heating, lighting, and water were
concerned that the amount not used would be taken off the general grant, which was
established by formula. That was not satisfactory for schools that had conserved energy.
Schools would not be penalised for any savings they could make on the allowable amount,
and this abatement has now been completely removed.
Rather than adopting a policy of dramatic and spectacular expenditure on education,
the Government had adopted a policy of development and improvement. The Budget's
provisions spanned the education field. Pre-school education was the foundation of the
education programme, which lasted throughout a person's life. The Budget contained a
number of small but significant improvements that would enable another 8000 pre-school
children to receive early childhood education in some form. That was a significant step
towards the Government's declared policy of enabling all children under the age of 5 to have
access to some form of pre-school education by 1980. There had been an increase in the
types of courses taught in continuing education programmes in technical institutes and senior
technical divisions of secondary schools. The Government had established a policy for
community colleges, and their development in the future would be a sound basis for
continuing education.

Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) said that 1433 State rental houses were
under construction. Of those, 910 were part of this year's programme, and the remainder
contracts that had been let in the previous financial year. The formula for calculating State
house rentals-introduced by the previous Labour Government-was one-sixth of a person's
income up to $100, 30c in the dollar thereafter, and 40c at higher incomes. The objective was
that every State house tenant on a similar income should pay the same rental. The policy had
not been changed, except that the annual increase had been greater. The Housing Corpora-
tion's report stated that 559 single persons, 1472 solo parents, 3464 married couples with
children, and 238 others had been granted State house tenancies in 1976, a total of 5733.
That was the highest number of tenancies since at least 1963. Loans to single women,
cancelled in July 1975 by the Labour Government, would be reinstated on 1 October 1977.
The home guidance bureau had been set up this year in Auckland on an experimental
basis, and an undertaking given that after it had been in operation for a few months a survey
would be conducted to see whether its continuance was justified. Although no official survey
had yet been carried out, it appeared that the bureau had been an outstanding success in
Auckland. Shortly he proposed to ask the Housing Corporation to investigate the work of
the bureau. The home ownership savings scheme had been initiated by the Labour
Government, but it had been improved by the National Government and was proving to be
extremely popular. Large numbers of depositors in the Post Office Savings Bank and the
trustee savings banks had transferred to the new scheme because of its improved benefits.
The Opposition appeared to judge the success of a housing policy by the number of houses
built. Labour members did not seem to realise that housing policy and housing construction
policy were not the same thing. The Government was responsible for the effective utilisation
of the country's 1 000 000 houses, and that was more important than simply building 30 000
new houses.

SELECT COMMITTEE PROCEDURE
Mr HUNT (New Lynn): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I raise this matter at the first
possible opportunity under Standing Order 360, and I seek your guidance on it. I do not
expect you to rule immediately because a rather complicated point is involved, but I think it
is important both for the standing of this Parliament and for the select committee system.
Standing Order 360 states, "Members of the House may attend the proceedings of a select
committee, but shall have no part therein . . .". It is those six words at the end that I want to
consider today.
This morning I was a member of the Social Services Committee, which heard a petition,
the subject of which I do not intend to discuss-nor could I, under the Standing Orders;
indeed, I will not be referring to any of the deliberations concerning the petition. I
remember that last week you yourself took up this point in reference to the proceedings or
otherwise of a select committee, and said that the point being raised was one of order in the
select committee.
This morning, when the select committee was hearing a petition, the member for
Waitemata was present. As you know, he is entitled to be present at the proceedings of a
select committee, but his conduct on this occasion as a member attending a select committee,
not being a member of that committee, raised some serious doubts. First, he attempted to
interrupt the proceedings of the select committee about three or four times. I took no
objection to this, because I thought the member might have made a chance remark, or even
a second or third chance remark. However, the member then proceeded to hand a note to
one of the witnesses, who is a distinguished mayor in west Auckland. The member then
handed a note—it might have been the same note-to one of the Government members of
the committee. At that point I raised the matter in the committee. The chairman of the
committee quite properly upheld the point of order and asked the member concerned to
desist.
We then had a break for a cup of tea, and I thought the member might have got the
message, but at 11.46 a.m. he once again interrupted the proceedings of the committee, this
time disagreeing with the chairman. This interruption concerned a matter on which there
were obvious differences of opinion between the chairman of the committee and the member
for Waitemata. Once again I raised a point of order, and the chairman properly asked the
member to be silent. At 12.15 p.m. there was the final issue, which I thought was a grave
offence, as the member for Waitemata attempted to influence a member of the committee
itself by passing a copy of the Standing Orders and making a quite loud comment, which we
could all hear, before finally deciding to leave.
There are rules that all members of the House have to obey. The first is that any
member may attend the proceedings of a select committee. Only once in 11 years have I
attended the proceedings of a select committee of which I was not a member. The key words
of the Standing Order 360 are "but shall have no part therein". I recall that on a number of
occasions members have had to be reminded of this. On this occasion, there were two or

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Immigration-Traditional-source Countries
1. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Immigration: What is the
effect of a country being designated as a traditional-source country for immigration
purposes?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): As the House will be aware, certain
occupations have been determined to be in sufficient continuing demand in New Zealand to
warrant recruitment from overseas. Nationals of traditional migrant countries may be
recruited in the full range of 243 occupations on the occupational priority list, while the list
that applies to nationals of non-traditional migration-source countries is very much smaller,
with only 4 occupations. One of the main reasons for this distinction is that New Zealand
agreed at the World Employment Conference not to recruit skills from developing countries,
which themselves have need of them.
Mr Prebble: Is the Minister suggesting that people in all 243 occupations can come from
developed countries, or are there some other criteria; and are developed countries not
regarded as traditional-source countries?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I did not make any suggestions. I gave a proper answer to the
question. Having answered the question I will not interpret any suggestion that might arise in
the member's mind.
Mr Lange: Does the designation of a country as a traditional-source country for
immigration purposes allow the Minister to let someone into New Zealand who, although he
is a citizen of that country, is of different ethnic or racial stock? Is it correct that, although
Iceland is now a traditional-source country for immigration purposes, an Indian of Icelandic
nationality would not be allowed into New Zealand?
Hon. T. F. GILL: No, it is quite incorrect. The Minister is not bound by this list. This is
a matter of policy and procedure. Iceland is a traditional-source country, which means that
New Zealand accepts that it is a developed country and that it would not be harmful to its
economy if we recruited skilled people from there. That is really all it means. We follow that
procedure, but it is not binding on anybody.
Mr Fenton: Will the Minister indicate whether to date he has received any applications
from Indians in Iceland?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I am not sure if the member is speaking about North American
Indians. Some Icelandic people may well qualify. The member would have to state which
type of Indian he was talking about before I could give a proper answer.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Does the Minister's reply to the member for Mangere indicate that
everyone but the Minister is expected to take notice of the traditional sources of migrants,
but only the Minister controls the actual migrants?
Hon. T. F. GILL: No. One would need to have a fertile imagination to construe in that
way what I have said. The member for Mangere implied that I was talking about a legal
situation. The point I was trying to make was that this is a procedural matter. Officers in
Overseas countries are briefed to recruit in those countries for certain skills. There is nothing
in the Immigration Act or the law which constricts us in any way.
Mr Falloon: Can the Minister confirm that the Government's immigration policy is

Matches
Research into Native Timber Usage
4. Mr FENTON (Hastings), on behalf of Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North), asked the
Minister of Forests: In view of the interest by Bryant and May N.Z. Ltd. in manufacturing
matches from indigenous timber, can he indicate what research has been done into the
species and the volume of wood required?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): Bryant and May N.Z. Ltd. became interested
in the possibility of using indigenous timbers-namely, beeches-for matches early in 1975.
Trial splints of red, silver, mountain, and hard beeches were produced in an associated
company's plant in Australia. Good results were obtained except with hard beech, which
presented some problems in absorbing paraffin wax. The matches produced were stronger
than the imported Canadian aspen, which is currently used. Timber requirements for New
Zealand consumption would be 4000 m³ annually. As a result of its research the company is
interested in obtaining beech from the West Coast. At present a major problem in supply is
the lack of outlets for lower grade logs arising during the production of the veneer grade
match splint logs. The disposal of lower grade beech logs is currently under consideration.
Mr Blanchfield: Can the Minister confirm that for matches second growth beech is
preferable to the maiden beech grown in Reefton, and can he also state whether splints from
veneers will be made in Reefton or in the North Island?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: This offers a very interesting opportunity for the management of
beech. The second growth or the younger beech trees would provide a better splint. The
beech forest is an ageing forest and the older logs provide a certain amount of waste, which is
a problem at present. As far as I know, the proposal includes the production of splints at
Reefton, but I would need confirmation about that.
Mr Bell: Does the Minister know the cost in overseas funds of the imported material
used for producing matches?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I am not sure, but a figure that comes to mind is $500,000 a year.
Mr Wetere: What other alternative uses has the Minister or his department got in mind
for beech?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: As a result of the recommendations of the Jaakko Poyry report,
the use of beech in particle board is being investigated by an inter-departmental committee.
Also, at the seminar held on the West Coast on the future of forestry, proposals were put
forward to look at beech as the raw material for ethynol. Both proposals will be considered,
but the first is the one being examined at present, because the particle board plant was
recommended by the overseas consultants.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Forest Products, Taupo
5. Mr LANGE (Mangere) asked the Minister of Forests: What plans has he for the
development of forestry and forest products usage in the Taupo basin, particularly from the
area east of the lake, and does he propose to give the local authority in the area any
information about such use and how the products will be transported from the district?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): The exotic forests of the Taupo basin are
mainly immature at this stage. Not until the late 1980s or the 1990s will their potential for
major industrial development be realised. Until then the limited quantity of forest produce is
most likely to continue to be processed in existing installations at Taupo or outside the basin
itself. The centres of processing for the greatly expanded quantities of wood that will come
on stream as the forests mature is speculative at present. The forests of the Taupo basin are
well placed to deliver saw logs to mills throughout the central North Island and pulpwood to
the industry in the Bay of Plenty, Hawke's Bay, and the King Country. Planning for the
State and Maori lease forests is based on achieving high proportions of quality saw logs and
veneer logs through intensive silviculture with pulpwood simply as an arising. Private forests
might be grown as pulpwood crops, particularly those associated with the proposed King
Country development. As the timing and nature of likely major increases in production
become more definite, discussions will continue with local authorities. However, until
specific proposals are received in response to invitations it is not possible to define the
processing or export centre, and hence the direction in which various qualities and quantities
of wood will be transported.
Mr Lange: Is it to be construed from the Minister's answer that there are about 60 000
hectares of forest in that area for which no end purpose is known? Does the Minister agree
that the local authority has a duty to plan 20 years in advance of its district scheme, and has
he given the local authorities any information at all to enable them to make their plans?

Hon. V. S. YOUNG: It is not correct that there are 60 000 hectares of forest in that area

Forest Products-Processing of Exports
10. Mr BRILL (Kapiti), on behalf of Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei), asked the Minister of
Forests: When do the North Auckland, East Coast, Nelson-Marlborough, and Otago-
Southland regions become net exporters of forest products, and what plans are there to
prepare for the appropriate degree of processing those products within the regions?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): For saw logs and sawn timber, Nelson-
Marlborough and Otago-Southland are already net exporting regions. Exotic forests now
planted in Northland and the East Coast could allow these regions to become net exporters
in the near future. Attention is given in indicative planning to the type of products each
region may be capable of exporting-in Northland, logs, sawn timber, and panel products;
the East Coast, saw logs, sawn timber, and panel products; Nelson-Marlborough can expand
production to include the export of pulp in the 1980s; and Otago-Southland could have small
exports of pulp in the late 1980s, and a large chemical pulp and paper industry after the turn
of the century.
Mr Rogers: What does the Minister mean by "the near future"? Could he be more
specific about when Northland could expand its exports of logs, sawn timber, and panel
products?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I cannot be more specific because a great deal depends on the
internal and overseas demand for panel products. At the same time we would have to look at
the processing facilities available within a region. Some of the regional forests might have to
concentrate on the production of a high quality saw log to get the best return from its
products. This obviously means that sawn timber will become a valuable component in the
processing of those regional forests.
Hon. W. A. Fraser: Can the Minister be a little more encouraging than saying that there
is a possibility of a substantial pulp industry for Otago some time after the turn of the
century?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: Not at this stage. One of the matters that will have to be taken into
consideration, especially during the next 10 years, is the degree to which saw logs in the
Otago-Southland region will be required to meet a demand in Canterbury, where in the past
there has been an unhappy history with the growing of forests. The two obvious areas for a
high degree of processing are, first, Nelson-Marlborough, and second, Otago-Southland.
Mr Wetere: I think I heard the Minister correctly when he said there was to be a pulp
mill in Otago-Southland. Could he say when this will be built, and where?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I cannot say where, because, as has been the procedure in the past,
the Government would have to invite proposals. However, the Otago-Southland area could
have small exports of pulp in the late 1980s. During the mid to late 1980s, in Otago-
Southland there will be surplus wood available of the type to give enough raw material for
the pulp industry.

Works and Development, Masterton, has carried out an inspection and reports that the

flood damage to roading, although quite serious, is not as severe as that experienced in the

FINANCE (INFLATION-ADJUSTED BONDS) BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): I move, That_the_Finance
(Inflation-Adjusted Bonds) Bill be now read a third time. This very good Bill is known as the
Luxton Bill. Some members might have missed that during the second reading, but I think
the name was mentioned. During the Committee stage the Opposition expressed concern
about the placing of moneys in the bonds. They will of course be treated like other
Government securities, and be part of the total funds available to the Government. They will
not be labelled in any particular way-which seemed to be a matter of concern.
The Opposition also expressed concern that demand might get out of hand, but I
reiterate that there are very tight controls on holdings of the bonds. Investments will be
limited to $1,000 per annum, and a maximum of $5,000 in any one holding, quite apart from
the fact that they are tied for 5 years. There was some concern too about the opportunities
for big savers. I should be very surprised if major savers were overinterested in the bonds,
whereas in terms of the minimum contribution of $100-and thereafter multiples of $50-I
believe there will be very considerable interest, as the Prime Minister suggested, by the small
man.
The Government believes that the bonds will be popular with the small saver and with
the older saver nearing retirement. We emphasised in the Committee stage that this was a
policy issue providing a new form of bond; similar to other forms of security, but with special
built-in inflation-proofing. I commend the Bill to the House.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): It was interesting to hear the
Acting Minister's brief apology for the Bill. His claim that the Bill is known as the Luxton
Bill would be contested immediately from this side, because I do not think the originator
really recognised it. Certainly he admitted indirect paternity, but I do not think he claimed
that the Bill before the House embodied his basic ideas. That was discussed at some length in
the Committee stage. In fact, the Opposition moved two amendments that would have
brought the Bill closer to the original purpose of the member for Piako.
One amendment would have reduced the amount of the initial deposit to $10, and
subsequent investments to $10. That was precisely in line with what had been moved by the
member for Piako in two Bills he introduced to the House. But that was not acceptable to
the Government, which had all sorts of excuses, the basic one being the difficulty in paying
the interest. It had nothing to do with the opportunity of savers to put money into the
scheme. The Prime Minister said, "You could not go on paying 20c a year at 2 percent
interest on a $10 bond." That seemed to be his major reason for saying that small savers
should not have the opportunity.
The other change that we proposed-and this was even more in line with what the
member for Piako had intended-was that in clause 2(1) the word "shall" should replace the
word "may". That would get back to the original idea that these were inflation-proof bonds,
not just inflation-adjusted bonds. Of course, the Prime Minister turned it round, saying,
"Oh well, if inflation is less than 5 percent, those poor people would not be able to get 7
percent interest on their bonds, and that is why we must have the word 'may'." We were
prepared to bet him that inflation would be a lot more than 5 percent and that therefore the


## p. 3123 (#761) ###########################################

21 September
3123
Finance (Inflation-Adjusted Bonds) Bill
word "shall" should be put in. However, because he had the resources of his 54 members
behind him, it was clear that the amendments had no chance of being accepted, and they
were simply defeated on the voices. We attempted to make those changes to improve an
otherwise pointless Bill. We voted against the Bill on the second reading, and on the short
title in the Committee stage, and when considering the second clause-when it was obvious
that the Bill would be passed-we attempted to improve it by moving amendments in line
with the views of the member for Piako, as shown in the measure he introduced earlier; but
the member for Piako did not raise his voice on either of the amendments put forward.
Only one other significant point needs to be made. We discussed with Government
members how the money to cover the inflation adjustment was to be obtained. We pointed
out at some length that, in the light of present inflation, there is a virtual certainty that in the
5-year term of the bonds the actual repayments will almost double the original investment. I
think the figure quoted for a 15 percent rate of inflation on an item of $100 was $204 after 5
years. If inflation is at the rate of only 13 percent each year, the $100 will become $195 and
some cents. Clearly a substantial sum of money will have to be found in addition to the 2
percent specifically provided for as the interest rate, which is taxable.
The Government initially claimed that the money would be provided by the natural
growth of the economy, but step by step-by a difficult process of extraction-we gained
from the Minister of Finance an admission that the statement he made after presenting the
Budget was that there would be no growth and that therefore the adjustment could not come
out of natural growth; it had to come out of money changes in terms of people's incomes.
Whereas last year there was a little adjustment for some farmers, particularly wool farmers,
the immediate prospects are for no real growth in the economy, and therefore the money will
have to be extracted from the people, who get only cash adjustments, money-term
adjustments, but not real adjustments or any increase in their living standards. That was a
most significant admission, and it was also significant that the Prime Minister made it when
he was speaking in Committee-as he does so often-when his words are not recorded in
Hansard. That is why we want to make sure that they are recorded now.
We also want to make sure that we record the step-by-step process by which we
obtained that admission. There was no cheerful approach to the problem; but, yes, it is a
fact, and it is what will happen. Each grudging admission had to be drawn from the Prime
Minister. It was a little like getting teeth out of a hen. He was not prepared to admit anything
until he was forced to do so, but in the end he admitted responsibility for his own words,
spoken after presenting the Budget. Of course, he did not make any such statement in a
debate in the House, and it is not recorded in Hansard, but it is recorded in a television
programme, and I am sure it is indelibly imprinted on the minds of many people.
The Prime Minister said that the Budget sacrificed growth to combat inflation. The
whole case put up by the Opposition was that the Bill goes along with inflation, and that a
few privileged people will have their nest-eggs protected while the majority will have to
pay—and pay quite substantially-for that privilege. When the Minister of Finance eventu-
ally admitted that there was no prospect of growth in the immediate future it became clear
that the victims of inflation will pay at least the present rates of tax on their money-inflated
incomes to compensate those who are lucky enough to conform with the terms of the Bill—
that is, they can invest money for 5 years, and they can invest initially in amounts of $100 and
subsequently in amounts of $50. As I indicated, the two amendments moved by the
Opposition were rejected on the voices, and therefore we submit that the Bill is not in the
interests of the ordinary citizen. It does not carry out the intentions of the member for Piako,
but that member did not see fit even to raise his voice when there was a chance of saving part
of his original Bill.
Bill read a third time.
